INTRODUCTION
Karnataka’s development trajectory reflects a calibrated blend of economic dynamism, social commitment, 
and environmental responsibility. Emerging as one of India’s foremost growth engines, the State has leveraged 
progressive policy frameworks, technological innovation, and inclusive governance to build a robust and 
diversified economy. Its prominence in information technology, biotechnology, and high-technology industries 
has positioned it as a premier investment destination, with exports accounting for a substantial share of Gross 
State Domestic Product.
Karnataka’s growth story extends beyond industrial achievement. Agriculture continues to anchor rural 
livelihoods, supported by expanded irrigation, technological integration, and farmer-centric initiatives 
to enhance productivity and resilience. At the same time, the state’s rich ecological heritage, reflected in 
its substantial forest and tree cover and the biodiversity of the Western Ghats, demonstrates a deep and 
continuing commitment to sustainability and conservation.
Infrastructure development has been transformative, particularly in renewable energy and urban mobility, 
reflecting a people-oriented model of progress. Social initiatives, including expanded access to mobility and 
digital governance reforms, have strengthened inclusion and institutional transparency.
Karnataka’s sustained progress in health, education, and the Sustainable Development Goals affirms that its 
vision of development extends beyond mere output expansion to the enhancement of human well-being. 
The State’s trajectory reflects a deliberate and balanced effort to align economic competitiveness with social 
equity, ensuring that growth is both inclusive and environmentally responsible.
1. STATE INCOME AND PRICES 
 Y The State’s GSDP increased from Rs.29.06 lakh crore in 2024-25 to Rs.32.81 lakh crore in 2025-26, 
registering a growth of 12.9 per cent at current prices. At constant prices, it increased from Rs.15.94 lakh 
crore to Rs.17.23 lakh crore, reflecting a growth rate of 8.1 per cent.
 Y During 2025-26, the State recorded a growth rate of 8.1 per cent at constant prices, which is higher than 
the national growth rate of 7.4 per cent.
 Y The State’s share in India’s GDP increased to 9.19 per cent in 2025-26 from 8.79 per cent in 2024-25.
 Y The per capita income of the State stood at Rs.4,33,326 in 2025-26, which is about 97 per cent higher 
than the All-India per capita income of Rs.2,19,575.
 Y Per capita income increased from Rs. 3,86,156 in 2024-25 to Rs.4,33,326 in 2025-26, showing a growth 
of 12.2 per cent at current prices. At constant prices, it increased from Rs.2,08,397 to Rs.2,23, 866 
registering a growth of 7.4 per cent.
 Y The agriculture sector is expected to grow by 9.1 per cent at constant prices in 2025-26, compared to 7.0 
per cent in 2024-25, indicating a recovery.
 Y The industry sector is projected to grow by 6.7 per cent in 2025-26 at constant prices, compared to 4.1 
per cent in 2024-25. Manufacturing growth of 7.2 per cent has contributed significantly to industrial 
expansion.

 Y The Services sector is expected to grow by 8.1 per cent at constant prices in 2025-26, from 8.4 per cent 
in 2024-25. Growth in IT-related services increased from 10.20 per cent to 10.50 per cent. Hotel and 
Restaurants (13.90 per cent) Public Administration (8.6 per cent) and Other Services (7.9 per cent) are 
also key contributors.
 Y Services account for 69.8 per cent of GSVA, followed by Industries at 19.4 per cent and Agriculture at 
10.8 percent.
 Y Bangalore Urban district contributed Rs.11,73,574 crore, accounting for 40.4 per cent of the State GDP 
for the year 2024-25. It is followed by Dakshina Kannada district (5.3 per cent) and Belagavi district (3.9 
per cent).
 Y The Kalaburgi division recorded the lowest per capita income at Rs.1,89,938, followed by the Belagavi 
division (Rs.2,26,213) and the Mysore division (Rs.4,06,257).
 Y Bangalore Urban district recorded the highest per capita income at Rs.8,55,960. It is followed by Dakshina 
Kannada district (Rs.6,26,279), Udupi district (Rs.6,00,683), Chikkamagaluru district (Rs.4,94,787) and 
Shivamogga district (Rs.3,89,743). These districts reported per capita incomes above the State average 
of Rs.3,86,156 in 2024-25.
 Y The inflation rate based on the All-India Wholesale Price Index (WPI) is increased to 1.82 per cent during 
the April to December period of 2025-26, compared with an increase of 1.64 per cent during the same 
period in the previous year.
 Y Based on the All-India Consumer Price Index (CPI), the inflation rate is increased to 3.28 per cent in April 
to December of 2025–26, compared with 3.08 per cent in the corresponding period of the previous year.
2. FISCAL DEVELOPMENT AND STATE FINANCES
Karnataka’s fiscal management framework reflects a sustained commitment to stability, transparency and 
long-term financial sustainability. As the first State to enact the Fiscal Responsibility Act in 2002, Karnataka 
has institutionalised prudent debt management and responsible budgeting practices. Supported by steady 
growth in tax and non-tax revenues and sound policy framework, the State has strengthened its financial and 
economic resilience. When combined with careful expenditure management, it has created the fiscal space 
needed to sustain investments in infrastructure, social services and human development, thereby supporting 
balanced and inclusive progress.
 Y The State has consistently maintained fiscal discipline by keeping the fiscal deficit within 3 percent of 
GSDP , recording 2.90 percent in 2024–25 (RE) and targeting 2.95 percent in 2025–26 (BE) in compliance 
with the Karnataka Fiscal Responsibility Act, 2002, reflecting a sustained commitment to responsible 
fiscal management.
 Y In 2025–26 (BE), the State’s total receipts is expected to increase by 13.94 percent, rising from 
Rs.358656.74 crore in 2024–25 (RE) to Rs.408646.56 crore. Revenue receipts expected to grow by 13.45 
percent from Rs.257800.73 crore to Rs.292476.54 crore, while capital receipts expected to grow by15.18 
percent from Rs.100856.01 crore to Rs.116170.02 crore.
 Y The State’s own tax revenue estimated a growth by15.37 percent, increasing from Rs.180368.00 crore in 
2024–25 (RE) to Rs.208100.00 crore in 2025–26 (BE), while non-tax revenue anticipated to grow by 13.79 
percent from Rs.14500.00 crore to Rs.16500.00 crore, indicating strengthened revenue mobilisation 
efforts.
 Y Revenue expenditure in 2023-24 at Rs.242614.43 crore is anticipated to increase to Rs.283927.76 
crore in 2024–25 (RE) and further to Rs.311738.73 crore in 2025–26 (BE), reflecting rising spending 
commitments, particularly towards welfare programmes and obligatory payments. During the same

3. INVESTMENT AND EXPORTS
 Y Karnataka has emerged as one of India’s most competitive investment destinations, supported by 
sustained policy reforms, efficient governance, and a strong institutional framework. The State promotes 
private sector participation, innovation and industrial diversification to strengthen its economic base. 
Its focus on high-growth sectors such as information technology, biotechnology, electronics, renewable 
energy, and advanced manufacturing has enhanced global integration. Nearly 40 per cent of GSDP is 
linked to export-oriented activities, reflecting a strong outward orientation. Continuous improvements in 
infrastructure, skill development and regulatory simplification have further strengthened the investment 
climate, leading to steady growth in industrial output, employment exports and reinforcing Karnataka’s 
position as a leading investment hub.
 Y The Karnataka Data Centre Policy 2022–27 aims to establish the State as a major hub for next-generation 
data centres by providing attractive incentives. The State has surpassed its initial target of 200 MW by 
achieving 245.5 MW capacity, with eight companies registered under KITS in Bengaluru. The inauguration 
of NTT’s 100 MW data centre is expected shortly, while NTT, STT and Nxtra have planned further expansions 
by mid–end 2027. Major operators include Tata Communications, Reliance, Sify, CtrlS, DataSamudra, 
NxtGen, CapitaLand and ESDS.
 Y The Nipuna Karnataka Scheme, launched on 24 September 2024 with an outlay of Rs.100 crore, aims to 
enhance youth employability by bridging skill gaps through upskilling, reskilling and vocational training in 
emerging sectors such as information technology, biotechnology, artificial intelligence, data science and 
cybersecurity. The scheme supports the development of a future-ready workforce aligned with industry 
requirements and technological advancements.
 Y Karnataka has introduced India’s first Global Capability Centres (GCC) Policy 2024–29 to position the 
State as a global hub for knowledge services. The policy aims to attract 500 new GCCs, generate 3.5 lakh 
jobs and contribute USD 50 billion to the State economy by 2029.
 Y The Karnataka Industrial Policy 2025–30 focuses on developing Karnataka as a competitive, inclusive and 
sustainable industrial hub, with a targeted investment of Rs.7.5 lakh crore and employment generation 
of 20 lakh jobs by 2030.
 Y Karnataka continues to attract major investments in the large and medium industries sector, supported by 
policy initiatives such as the Clean Mobility Policy 2025–30, which targets Rs.50,000 crore of investment 
and one lakh jobs.
 Y Karnataka’s overall exports have increased by 13.78 per cent during 2025–26 compared to 2024–25.
 Y Exports of agricultural commodities rose from USD 2,043.70 million in 2023–24 to USD 2,457.42 million 
in 2024–25, registering an increase of nearly 20 per cent. The growth in exports reflects the improved 
competitiveness, diversification and global integration of the State’s production base.

4. RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
Karnataka is deepening its commitment to inclusive rural transformation through empowered Panchayat 
Raj Institutions and robust decentralised governance. With nearly 61 per cent of its population residing 
in rural areas, the State places villages at the centre of its development strategy. Its three-tier Panchayat 
system, 5,946 Gram Panchayats, 239 Taluk Panchayats, and 31 Zilla Panchayats, anchors grassroots planning 
and accountability. The 2025–26 Budget strengthens this framework through enhanced allocations, digital 
reforms, infrastructure expansion, and livelihood initiatives, fostering resilient, participatory, and sustainable 
rural growth.
 Y A total of 5,888 Gram Panchayat libraries have been upgraded into digital “Arivu Kendra” with 8-hour 
operations benefiting 50.92 lakh children. The Dharshiniprogramme is launched to provide assistive 
devices to specially challenged.
 Y For the first time, online counselling-based transfers were conducted for 1,574 Panchayat Development 
Officers, 894 Secretaries, and 402 Second Division Account Assistants. Officials serving over five years in 
one GramPanchayat were mandatorily transferred, improving transparency and administrative efficiency.
 Y  Be tween 2000–01 and December 2025, 47,60,879 houses were constructed under schemes including 
Rural Ashraya/BasavaVasathi, Rural Ambedkar, DevrajUrs Housing, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Nivas, IAY/PMAY 
(G), and PM-Janman. Additionally, 1,40,749 house sites have been distributed.
 Y Solid Waste Management units are functional in 5,213 Gram Panchayats, and 10,950 villages have 
achieved ODF Plus Model status under SBM-G. Renewable energy and waste management initiatives 
were showcased at Mysuru Dasara and World Environment Day exhibitions.
 Y  Under Jal Jeevan Mission, rural tap connections increased from 24.51 lakh to 63.12 lakh, achieving 86.51% 
coverage, with 6,768 villages attaining 100% Functional Household Tap Connections. Up to December 
2025, 2.39 lakh FHTCs were provided at a cost of Rs.446.15 crore.
 Y  Mor e than 28,000 Village Water and Sanitation Committees have been formed, with over 1.5 lakh women 
leading local water management, strengthening community participation and women’s empowerment.
 Y  During 2025–26, 14,694 litres of biodiesel were produced and utilised, promoting renewable energy 
adoption.
 Y  Under PMGSY (2025–26), Rs.156.60 crore was allocated, with Rs.22.85 crore spent for 22.834 km of 
road works. For maintenance, Rs.59.08 crore was earmarked and Rs.19.77 crore utilised to maintain  
3,270.49 km.
 Y  The Kalyan Path Scheme plans 1,150 km of roads in 38 constituencies of Kalyana Karnataka at Rs.1,000 
crore. As of December 2025, 63 packages (286 works) covering 1,124.91 km were taken up; 168.37 km 
completed with Rs.208.56 crore expenditure.
 Y Under MGNREGA, against an allocation of Rs.5,800.0 crore, Rs.3,404.13 crore was released and 
Rs.2,918.97 crore utilised up to December 2025, generating 680.35 lakh person-days. Employment was 
provided to 21.5 lakh households; 8.93 lakh works were undertaken (2.94 lakh completed; 5.99 lakh 
ongoing).
 Y Android PoS machines were distributed to all 5,946 Gram Panchayats, enabling property tax collection 
of Rs.1,313 crore. The Panchamitra WhatsApp Chatbot has served 1,70,659 users and registered 7,136 
grievances, enhancing digital access and transparency.

5. URBAN DEVELOPMENT
Urban development remains an important pillar of Karnataka’s growth strategy, shaping cities as engines 
of economic dynamism and social inclusion, through investments in infrastructure, water security, mobility, 
and inclusive housing. With rapid urbanisation reshaping economic and demographic patterns, the State 
is strengthening Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) to deliver sustainable, resilient, and citizen-centric services. 
The Government strategy integrates fiscal investment, environmental stewardship, and technology-driven 
governance to enhance liveability and competitiveness. Together, these initiatives position Karnataka’s cities 
as resilient, inclusive, and future-ready spaces that support balanced regional development and improved 
quality of life.
 Y In 2025–26, Rs.18,249.71 crore was allocated for Urban Development, of which Rs.12,183.58 crore has 
been utilised by December 2025, indicating steady progress in strengthening urban infrastructure and 
service delivery across the State.
 Y The 24x7 “Drink from Tap” project in Alnavar, implemented at Rs.71.90 crore using Kali River water, 
became Karnataka’s first fully metered small-town model and received a Special Mention at Urban 
Learnathon 2023 by NIUA, MoHUA, GoI.
 Y Under the Jalashuddhi Mission for water management, KUIDFC, as nodal agency under SBM(U)-2.0 and 
the NGT Environment Compensation Fund, oversees grants totalling Rs.3,277.28 crore. This includes 
FSTPs in 110 towns (Rs.400.24 crore; 9 completed and 101 ongoing), sewerage system upgrades in 55 
towns (Rs.1,518 crore; works in progress, tender, or DPR stage), and STP construction/upgradation in 268 
towns (Rs.1,359.04 crore; implementation underway).
 Y Under AMRUT 2.0, 616 projects have been approved at a total cost of Rs.10,258.46 crore (including 
O&M), with Rs.3,407.58 crore released and Rs.3,227.17 crore incurred since inception.
 Y  Through AMRUT Mitra, 740 proposals worth Rs.56.29 crore were approved to engage women self-help 
groups in maintaining parks and water infrastructure, and 150 SHGs have received capacity-building 
support.
 Y  The Bengaluru Sub-Urban Rail Project, implemented by K-RIDE at a revised cost of Rs.23,103 crore, 
will cover 148.17 km across four corridors—Bengaluru–Devanahalli (41.40 km), Byappanahalli–
Chikkabanavara (25.01 km), Kengeri–Cantonment (35.52 km), and Heelalige–Rajanukunte (46.24 km). 
Scheduled for completion in six years, the project aims to serve 8.9 lakh daily commuters and promote 
transit-oriented development.
 Y  Beng aluru Metro expansion continues with Phase-2 (75.06 km; 61 stations), of which 53.80 km is 
operational, and Reach-6 sections are scheduled for completion in May and December 2026. Phase-2A 
and 2B (58.19 km; 29 stations) connecting Central Silk Board to the airport are targeted for completion 
between December 2026 and December 2027. Phase-3 (44.65 km; 31 stations), including a double-
decker corridor, is underway, and Phase-3A (36.59 km, Sarjapura–Hebbal) has received DPR approval 
from GoK and has been submitted to GoI.
 Y  T o ease traffic congestion, the Outer Ring Road concept has been strengthened, while the Peripheral 
Ring Road project, estimated at Rs.27,000 crore (Rs.21,000 crore for land acquisition and Rs.6,000 crore 
for construction through a HUDCO loan), is planned to connect five major national highways and the 
international airport. Phase-2 (52.38 km; 6-lane, 100-metre width) is under DPR preparation for 41.61 
km, with 10.77 km already integrated into the Nadaprabhu Kempegowda Layout project.
 Y At Hebbal Junction, the widened flyover towards Bengaluru, the K.R. Puram–Baptist Hospital approach, 
and two carriageways from Esteem Mall to Baptist Hospital have been completed and opened to traffic, 
while a new flyover from K.R. Puram to Kempegowda Airport is planned.

6. AGRICULTURE AND FOOD MANAGEMENT
Karnataka has achieved notable progress in agriculture and allied sectors through sustained public investment, 
technological integration, and institutional strengthening. The State’s emphasis on productivity enhancement, 
water-use efficiency, risk mitigation, and market linkage has reinforced farm resilience and rural incomes. 
Focused interventions in horticulture, animal husbandry, fisheries, and food management have improved 
livelihood security and food accessibility. These measures reflect Karnataka’s commitment to sustainable, 
inclusive, and growth-oriented agricultural development.
Karnataka’s Agricultural Progress and Key Developments
 Y  K arnataka received adequate rainfall during the monsoon season of 2025. As per the Second Advance 
Estimates of area and production for Kharif and Rabi seasons for 2025-26, the area of major agricultural 
crops is 107.1 lakh hectares of which the area under food grains is 78.6 lakh hectares. The estimated food 
production is 136.22 lakh tons.
 Y During Kharif, Rabi/Summer 2025–26 (up to 31.12.2025), 6.49 lakh quintals of quality seeds were 
distributed with a Rs.171.74 crore subsidy, benefiting 12.62 lakh farmers.
 Y  F ertilizer availability remained stable, and by the end of December 2025 for Kharif and Rabi, the State 
has received 38.73 lakh tons of different grades of fertilizers as against the allocation of 44.98 lakh tons 
by the Government of India.
 Y  The department has extensively supported providing subsidy to farmers under various farm mechanization 
schemes.An amount of Rs.38809.18 lakhs was allocated for mechanization and an expenditure of 
Rs.29819.52 lakhs has been incurred by December 2025 out of the releases of Rs.33353.95lakhs. The 
scheme has supported 1,30,454 farmers across the State.
 Y  Under the Micro-Irrigation programme in 2025–26, Rs. 44,092.86 lakh has been allocated, Rs. 38,304.59 
lakh released, and Rs. 27,059.81 lakh spent up to December 2025, bringing 1,00,956 hectares under 
micro-irrigation coverage and strengthening water-use efficiency.
 Y For Krishi Bhagya, Rs. 100.00 crore has been allocated to implement 5,063 packages all over the State, and 
under Krishi Bhagya (State Disaster Mitigation Fund -SDMF), another Rs.100.00 crore has been allocated 
targeting 5,482 packages in 223 taluks; during 2025–26, Rs.175.00 crore has been released and Rs.58.07 
crore spent, resulting in the construction of 4,529 farm ponds up to December 2025.
 Y Under Karnataka Raitha Suraksha Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana, the total number of farmers enrolled 
up to the end of December 2025 is 25,76,388 and premium paid by farmers is Rs.22324.79 lakhs covering 
22.64 lakh hectares and total number of beneficiary farmers is 578985.
 Y Thrust has given for organic farming activities in the State with an objective of converting Joida taluk of 
Uttar Kannada as first completely organic taluk over next three years, Establishment of Organic and Millet 
Hub, implementing National Mission on Natural farming, Raithasiri, Integrated Farming System.
 Y For the first of its kind the Department has pioneered in establishing Directorate of Secondary Agriculture 
with the mission of doubling the farmer income by promoting support for post-harvest and processing 
activities. The schemes implemented, will extend 50% subsidy to all categories of farmers for setting up 
of units related to secondary agricultural industry.

 Y The Mission of Watershed department is to develop, promote and implement a decentralized, cost 
effective, productive, transparent and sustainable watershed development treatment package through 
participatory approach. The geographical area of the State is 190.50 lakh ha., of which 129.70 lakh ha. 
is available for watershed interventions. Up to the end of March 2025, an area of 74.94 lakh ha has 
been developed with watershed interventions (treated) thereby strengthening climate resilience and 
improving water security in vulnerable regions
 Y Under the Watershed Development Component of Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana–2. and the 
REWARD project, 34,855 hectares of watershed area have been treated, with 2,964 hectares of forestry 
and 2,411 hectares developed under dryland horticulture. 
 Y Under the Central Sector Scheme for the Formation and Promotion of 10,000 FPOs, the Department of 
Watershed Development has received an award atthenation allevel formobilizing a highest number of 
share holders and for releasing the highest amount of equity grants.  
 Y Agriculture Marketing forms the cornerstone of economic development by creating efficient pathways 
between producers and consumers. The State has 170 Agricultural Produce Market Committees (APMC’s) 
out of which 167 APMCs have been linked to Unified Market Platform of Rashtriya e-Market Services and 
the Kalaburagi & Chincholi APMCs have been linked to the e-NAM platform of the GoI. 
 Y  As on December 2025. The Unified Market Platform has transacted 12.67 Crore MTs of agricultural 
commodities worth Rs.4,39,852.54 Crore.
 Y During 2025-26, under support price scheme, approximately 88,252 lakh quintals of Green gram, Urad 
dal, Sunflower, Soyabean, Ground nut, Maize and Cotton commodities have been procured from 1,55,793 
registered farmers, at an estimated cost of Rs. 1,239 crore.Procurement operation is under progress.
Horticulture
 Y Under PMRKVY , 2025–26(up to December), Rs.545.66 crore was allocated, covering 30,653.66 hectares 
under micro-irrigation and benefiting 35,021 farmers through subsidies of Rs.246.66 crore. This large-
scale expansion of drip and sprinkler systems has improved water-use efficiency and reduced dependence 
on rainfall. It has enhanced crop productivity and resilience against climatic variability. The programme 
has also promoted long-term sustainability of horticultural farming systems.
 Y Under the Apiculture Development Programme, 859 beneficiaries were trained, 7,245 honey boxes 
distributed, 17 Madhuvanas established, and 48 honey extractors supported. These initiatives have 
strengthened scientific beekeeping and pollination services. They have created supplementary income 
opportunities for rural households. Enhanced honey production has also improved value addition and 
marketing prospects.
 Y During 2025–26, 26.95 lakh grafts and seedlings were produced against a target of 70.80 lakh, with 43.60 
lakh available for sale. This has ensured the availability of quality planting material to farmers. It has 
facilitated orchard expansion and crop diversification. Improved access to seedlings has strengthened 
long-term horticultural productivity.
 Y Distribution of 215 tonnes and 31,070 litres of bio-inputs at affordable rates has promoted eco-friendly 
cultivation practices. This initiative has reduced excessive dependence on chemical fertilisers and 
pesticides. It has contributed to soil fertility improvement and environmental sustainability. Farmers 
have benefited from reduced input costs and enhanced crop quality.
 Y Currently, 9,254 farmers cultivate oil palm on 13,223 hectares, with 4,442 hectares under yielding 
area. Additionally, 13,651 hectares were brought under diverse horticultural crops in 2025–26. These 
measures have strengthened crop diversification and regional specialisation. They have enhanced income 
opportunities and reduced production risks.

 Y  An area of 30,653 hectares is irrigated through drip systems, and 177 water storage structures were 
constructed in the current year. These investments have strengthened water conservation and irrigation 
infrastructure. They have supported year-round cultivation and stabilised yields. Improved water

 Y Hi-tech horticulture practices such as precision farming, protected cultivation, and mechanization were

 Y Under the Weather-Based Crop Insurance Scheme, 9.81 lakh farmers were registered, and Rs.1,158.31

investment in horticulture.
Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Services
 Y As per the 20th Livestock Census, Karnataka has 3.03 crore livestock and 5.95 crore poultry, contributing 
5.41% and 6.98% nationally. This reflects the sector’s strong resource base. It supports large-scale rural 
employment. Livestock remains central to livelihood diversification.
 Y Animal Husbandry contributes 3.64% to GSDP , ranking Karnataka 8th nationally in milk production. This 
indicates steady sectoral growth and economic relevance. The sector complements agricultural income. 
It reduces vulnerability to crop failures.
 Y  Milk production reached 13.89 million metric tonnes in 2024–25, supported by cooperative networks. 
This reflects strong institutional capacity and farmer participation. Dairy farming provides regular income. 
It strengthens nutritional security.
 Y  Nandin i Semen Station processes 40 lakh doses annually, and 40 lakh AIs resulted in 10 lakh calf births. 
This reflects successful genetic improvement programmes. It has upgraded herd quality. Long-term milk 
yield potential has increased.
 Y  Under Amrutha Swabhimani Kurigahi Yojane, 1,569 beneficiaries were identified by December 2025. The 
scheme supports sheep and wool producers. It promotes asset creation and income diversification. It 
strengthens community-based livestock systems.
 Y  P oultry and piggery sectors were strengthened through the distribution of chicks, eggs, and 3,954 
piglets. During 2025-26 (up to December 2025) in poultry rearing 56.94 lakhs eggs and 4.84 chicks were 
produced. These activities support small-scale entrepreneurship. They enhance nutritional supply. They 
generate quick-return income.
 Y Under fodder development, 14,150 fodder seed mini-kits have been procured and produced 70,750 
tonnes of green fodder. This has reduced feed shortages and production costs. It has stabilised milk 
yields. Nutritional management has improved.
 Y  KMF achieved average daily milk procurement of 1 crore litres in June 2025. Peak procurement reached 
106.54 lakh litres. This reflects strong cooperative performance. It ensures stable market access for 
farmers.
 Y  Nandin i improved its ranking from 43rd (2024) to 38th (2025) in Brand Finance. This indicates enhanced 
brand value. Market credibility has increased. Competitive positioning has strengthened.
 Y  Ex tensive vaccination under ASCAD and Brucellosis programmes improved disease control. Over 3.61 
crore animals were covered under various schemes. Preventive healthcare reduced economic losses. 
Biosecurity standards improved.

 Y KMF has 27.19 lakh members and disburses Rs.35.36 crore daily through DBT. This ensures financial

Fisheries
 Y About 9.84 lakh fishermen are engaged in marine and inland fisheries, including 3.31 lakh in the marine 
and 6.53 lakh in the inland sectors. This reflects the sector’s livelihood importance. It supports coastal 
and rural economies. Employment generation is significant.
 Y Fish production reached 9.63 lakh MT in 2024–25, contributing 0.48% to GSDP . This indicates steady 
sectoral growth. Improved practices enhanced productivity. Economic contribution has expanded.
 Y  B y December 2025, 62 Fish Farmers Producer Organizations (FFPOs) were registered and 12,122 Kisan 
Credit Cards (KCCs) distributed. These measures strengthened institutional support. Credit access 
improved. Collective entrepreneurship was promoted.
 Y Inland fisheries operate through 16 seed centres producing over 7,843 lakh fry fishes (2024–25). In 
2025–26, 6,311 lakh fry fishes were produced by December. Seed availability improved survival rates. 
Productivity was enhanced.
 Y  Fish production increased from 5.81 lakh MT (2015–16) to 9.63 lakh MT (2024–25), with 8.31% annual 
growth. This reflects technological adoption. Resource management improved. Sectoral resilience 
strengthened.
 Y  Under PMMSY , Rs.19.37 crore supported 245 beneficiaries and 150 e-Autos under Matsya Vahini. This 
strengthened marketing linkage. Last-mile connectivity improved. Value chains were reinforced.
 Y  R elief of Rs.7.05 crore and Rs.5.13 crore under welfare schemes supported distressed fishermen. Social 
security coverage improved. Income risks were reduced. Livelihood stability strengthened.
Food Management and Public Distribution
 Y A total of 1.25 crore ration cards covering 4.42 crore members were active by December 2025. This 
reflects extensive food security coverage. Vulnerable groups are protected. Welfare outreach is strong.

7. NATURAL RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND ENVIRONMENT 
Forest
Forests are a key part of Karnataka’s natural wealth, with nearly 60% of the Western Ghats located in the State. 
Karnataka remains a national leader in wildlife conservation and biodiversity management, with measurable 
improvement in forest cover and strong institutional frameworks. However, sustained policy attention is 
required to improve forest quality, manage conflict pressures, and ensure long-term ecological sustainability 
aligned with climate and development goals.
 Y Karnataka has a recorded forest area of 40,678 sq. km (21.21%), and as per ISFR 2023, the total forest and 
tree cover stands at 24.52% of the State’s geographical area.
 Y The Protected Area network spans 11,399 sq. km, comprising 5 National Parks, 37 Wildlife Sanctuaries 
including 5 Tiger Reserves, 19 Conservation Reserves, and 1 Community Reserve.
 Y To strengthen grassroots biodiversity governance, 6,554 Biodiversity Management Committees have 
been constituted at the Gram Panchayat level.
 Y The State has a total forest area of 40,67,823 hectares, of which 30,27,799.33 hectares have been mutated 
in revenue records, achieving 74 percent progress. Mutation of the remaining 10,40,024 hectares is 
under various stages of completion.
 Y Recognising the challenges of human–wildlife conflict, the Government has strengthened monitoring 
mechanisms and enhanced ex-gratia compensation to Rs. 20 lakh in cases of loss of human life during 
2025-26, ensuring support to affected families.
 Y To mitigate human–wildlife conflict, 428 km of railway barricades, 1,360.87 km of solar fencing, and 
1,775.41 km of elephant-proof trenches have been created. Institutional initiatives include the declaration 
of Hesarghatta Grassland as a Conservation Reserve and the formation of the Bandipur Elephant Task 
Force.
 Y The State ranks first in elephant population (6,395) and second in tiger population (563) in the country, 
reaffirming its leadership in wildlife conservation.
 Y In 2025, a Marine Wildlife Sanctuary at Apsarakonda–Mugali was notified, expanding biodiversity 
protection to coastal and marine ecosystems.
 Y During 2025–26, 2.87 crore saplings were planted over 62,526 hectares, and 0.57 crore saplings 
distributed under agroforestry programmes.
 Y Urban green cover has been strengthened under the Tree Park Scheme, and 87.91 tonnes of quality 
seeds were distributed for regeneration.
 Y Information and Communication Technology (ICT) - enabled governance mechanisms are being expanded 
to enhance transparency, monitoring, and accountability in forest administration.
Water Resources
 Y In the 2025–26 Budget, Rs.18,826.93 crore has been allocated to the Water Resources Department for 
Major and Medium Irrigation projects. By December 2025, Rs.8,980.00 crore (47.70%) has been spent, 
creating an irrigation potential of about 23,960 hectares (59,181 acres), reflecting steady progress in 
expanding water access for agriculture.
 Y  Under the Yettinahole Drinking Water Project, Stage-I lift works have been commissioned and water 
conveyance has commenced successfully. Stage-II gravity canal and feeder pipeline works are progressing 
in phases to ensure reliable drinking water supply and groundwater recharge in drought-prone districts.

Environmental Management 
 Y KSNDMC has established a network of GPRS enabled and solar-powered 6,605 Telemetric Rain Gauges 
(TRG) at all the Gramapanchayaths at every 25 sq. km and 843 Telemetric Weather Stations (TWS) at

Humidity (%), Wind Speed (m/s), Wind Direction (Degrees), Rainfall amount (mm) and intensity (mm/hr) 
data is being collected at every 15 minutes through these weather monitoring stations. The density of 
weather monitoring stations network is the highest and first of its kind in the country.

impact of floods, for providing flood forecast, alerts and early warnings. 
 Y An efficient forecast system with a well-established network of 100 Telemetric Rain gauge Sensors and

8. INDUSTRY 
Karnataka continues to play a leading role in India’s industrial and services-led growth, supported by strong 
institutional frameworks, technology-driven enterprises and proactive investment promotion. The State’s 
industrial ecosystem reflects a balanced combination of high-technology, knowledge-intensive and traditional 
manufacturing activities. Focused policy interventions, infrastructure expansion and ease-of-doing-business 
reforms have strengthened industrial competitiveness, employment generation and export performance. At 
the same time, sustained investments in tourism infrastructure and destination development have enhanced 
Karnataka’s position as a major domestic and international tourism hub.
 Y  The industrial sector GSDP increased from Rs.5,25,907 crore in 2024–25 with 8.1% growth to 
Rs.5,80,144 crore in 2025–26 with 10.3% growth, contributing 19.36% to State GDP , including 11.33% 
from manufacturing. This sustained expansion reflects improvements in productivity and technological 
adoption. It has been driven by export-oriented and capital-intensive industries. Consequently, the sector 
continues to serve as a major pillar of economic growth and employment.
 Y  The Government of Karnataka has unveiled the Karnataka Startup Policy 2025-30 with an approximate 
outlay of Rs.518.27 crore. The policy aims to foster 25,000 new start-ups, with a strategic focus on 
emerging domains such as Artificial Intelligence, blockchain, quantum computing and other deep-tech 
sectors. A distinctive feature of the policy is its emphasis on spatial decentralization, with a target of 
nurturing 10,000 start-ups outside Bengaluru.
 Y The Karnataka Industrial Policy 2025–30 focuses on developing Karnataka as a competitive, inclusive and 
sustainable industrial hub, with a targeted investment of Rs.7.5 lakh crore and employment generation 
of 20 lakh jobs by 2030.
 Y  The “Invest Karnataka 2025 – Global Investors Meet” generated investment proposals worth Rs.4,16,848

9. SKILL, ENTREPRENEURSHIP AND LABOUR & EMPLOYMENT
Karnataka is advancing a comprehensive human capital strategy centred on skill development, entrepreneurship, 
employment generation and labour welfare. Leveraging its strong youth demographic, the State is aligning 
vocational training with industry demand while strengthening social security and livelihood systems. Through 
mission-driven institutions, industry partnerships and targeted welfare initiatives, Karnataka is enhancing 
employability across rural and urban sectors. This integrated approach positions the State to harness its 
demographic dividend and sustain inclusive, innovation-led economic growth.
Harnessing Karnataka’s Demographic Dividend for Sustainable Growth
 Y Karnataka is strategically leveraging its demographic dividend, recognising that its strong youth population 
offers a decisive advantage over the next 25 years. By aligning skill development with sectoral needs 
across agriculture, industryand services, the State aims to build a productive, industry-ready workforce 
capable of sustaining long-term economic growth.
 Y  B y 2030, nearly 1.88 crore young individuals—including informal workers, school dropouts, secondary 
graduatesand homemakers—will require vocational training. To meet this demand, the State has 
operationalized a Skill Mission Unit at the State level and District Skill Development Offices, while over 
13 lakh individuals have registered on koushalkar.com.
Bridging the Gap Between Skilling and Employment
 Y  Under the Yuvanidhi scheme, 3,93,358 candidates have registered and 3,08,267 beneficiaries have 
received financial support. Through Yuvanidhi Plus, 1,615 candidates have completed skill training 
underKarnataka Skill Development Corporation(KSDC) initiatives and training for 1,100 candidates is 
currently underway to enhance employability.
 Y  The TATA Udyoga Project has upgraded 150 Government ITIs in partnership with Tata Technologies and 
20 consortium partners. These institutes offer 6 long-term and 23 short-term Industry 4.0 courses with 
annual capacity of 1.20 lakh trainees; 22,237 candidates have been trained and 3,488 placed.
 Y  In India Skill Competition 2024, Karnataka secured 48 medals from 62 participants, ranking second 
nationally. At the World Skill Competition 2024 in Lyon, France, 9 participants from the State represented 
India and won 4 Medallions of Excellence.
 Y  Emplo yment facilitation efforts have led to issuance of over 4.14 lakh offer letters through 414 Mega Job 
Fairs conducted across Karnataka, strengthening the linkage between job seekers and employers.
 Y  En trepreneurship development through CEDOK has trained 28,851 candidates, with 5,049 becoming self-

supporting livelihood generation.

10. ECONOMIC INFRASTRUCTURE
Power
 Y Karnataka has achieved substantial progress in strengthening its economic infrastructure, with particular 
emphasis on ensuring energy security, operational efficiency and sustainability. The State has moved 
towards near self-sufficiency in power generation through systematic capacity expansion, promotion of 
renewable energy and modernisation of transmission and distribution networks. Policy initiatives such as 
feeder solarisation, smart metering and grid automation have enhanced service reliability and financial 
viability. Simultaneously, investments in storage systems, green energy corridors and long-term resource 
planning are reinforcing Karnataka’s preparedness for future energy demand and low-carbon growth.
 Y  Under the Gruha Jyothi Yojana, since inception a total subsidy of Rs.22,040 crore was disbursed up to 
December 2025, ensuring free electricity of up to 200 units per month for 1.65 crore households. This 
measure has significantly reduced household energy expenditure. It has strengthened social equity and 
energy access. At the same time, targeted subsidy delivery has improved welfare effectiveness.

 Y  As of December 2025, the State’s total installed generation capacity stood at 37,072.95 MW, comprising 
13,759.78 MW from the public sector (including CGS allocation) and 23,313.17 MW from the private 
sector. Renewable sources contributed over 53.32% of installed capacity, excluding IPP thermal and  
mini-hydro. This reflects Karnataka’s strong transition towards clean energy. The diversified capacity mix 
has enhanced system resilience.
 Y  Con tinuous investments in transmission expansion and network upgradation have reduced technical 
losses and improved operational efficiency. Inspections to curb power theft increased fivefold between 
2021–22 and 2024–25, strengthening regulatory compliance. Consequently, T&D losses declined from 
16.34% in 2021–22 to 12.57% in 2024–25. AT&C losses also fell significantly from 16.99% in 2020–21 to 
10.89% in 2024–25.
 Y  In 2024–25, consumers in the Low-Tension (LT) category accounted for 75.75% of electricity consumption 
and contributed 71.37% of ESCOM revenue, reflecting the dominance of household and small commercial 
users. In contrast, High-Tension industrial and commercial consumers used 24.25% of power but generated 
28.63% of revenue. This consumption-revenue structure highlights cross-subsidisation patterns. It also 
underlines the importance of industrial demand for financial stability.
 Y  Implemen tation of the Karnataka Renewable Energy Policy 2022–27, led by KREDL, has accelerated 
private investment in renewable sources. Capacity additions reached 1,209.19 MW in 2024–25 and 
1,762.64 MW in 2025–26 (up to December 2025). This growth has reduced dependence on coal and 
strengthened environmental sustainability.
 Y  K arnataka has received multiple national recognitions for excellence in renewable energy development. 
At Global Wind Day 2025, the State secured first prize for the highest installed wind capacity in 2024–25. 
Pavagada Solar Park won four awards at RE-Invest 2024 and Karnataka was recognised as the second-
largest solar park host nationally. Additional awards at Windergy India 2025 further reinforced its 
leadership in clean energy.
 Y During 2025–26, the State recorded a peak demand of 18,395 MW and a highest daily consumption of 
356.88 MU, reflecting rising energy requirements. Strategic power procurement, surplus energy trading 
during the monsoon and inter-state banking arrangements ensured supply stability. These measures 
strengthened short-term energy security. They also optimised resource utilisation.
 Y Agricultural power supply was enhanced through solar pump installations, feeder solarisation under PM-
KUSUM, rooftop solar promotion and expansion of HVDS beyond pilot areas. These initiatives reduce 
transmission losses and improve supply quality. They lower dependence on conventional power. Farm 
productivity and energy efficiency are thereby strengthened.

 Y Under State Highway Development Plan (SHDP-V) (Stage-1), Rs.4,000 crore has been allocated for the 
development of state highways and major district roads with high vehicular density. As of December 
2025, Rs.527.11 crore has been spent for 820 km, with 43 of 218 packages completed and the remaining 
works in progress at various stages.
 Y To improve connectivity, 237 bridges are being constructed on a turnkey basis. By December 2025, 197 
bridges have been completed, with Rs.1,838.79 crore expended, while the remaining bridges are under 
execution.
 Y Under Karnataka State Highway Development Project (KSHIP-III) (2017–2024), supported by a $346

Transport Sector Reforms and Sustainable Mobility
 Y The launch of the ‘Shakti – Free Travel for Women’ scheme on 11 June 2023 marked a transformative step 
in inclusive mobility and women’s empowerment. During 2025-26 upto December 2025, 208.11 crore 
passengers had benefited across KSRTC, BMTC, NWKRTC, and KKRTC, with a government expenditure of 
Rs.3,975.70 crore. Women’s daily ridership rose from 40% (37.49 lakh) in 2022–23 to 62% (75.68 lakh) by 
December 2025, reflecting expanded access to employment, education, and public spaces.
 Y For 2025–26, the Transport Department (including State Transport Undertakings) set a revenue target of 
Rs.15,000 crore. During the year 2025-26 upto December 2025, Rs.9,355.55 crore had been collected, 
achieving 89.42% of the cumulative target of Rs.10,463 crore. This performance indicates strong fiscal 
mobilization alongside expanding public service commitments.
 Y Aligned with the “Green Global World” vision, the state is actively promoting electric, battery-operated, 
LPG, CNG, and other low- or zero-emission vehicles to curb air pollution. Green Tax collections are 
channeled into awareness initiatives through theatre, LED vehicles, radio jingles, hoardings, and bus 
shelters via the Department of Information and Public Relations. Rs.17.95 crore was collected in 2024–25 
and Rs.15.13 crore up to December 2025 in 2025–26, strengthening environmental governance.
 Y The Shakti scheme has also produced measurable socio-economic outcomes, with women’s employment 
rising by 23% in Bengaluru and 21% in Hubballi-Dharwad. Beneficiaries report monthly savings of 30%–
50% due to free bus travel, enhancing household financial stability. The programme thus extends beyond 
mobility to broader economic participation.
 Y  Within BMTC alone, 202.10 crore women passengers benefited under the Shakti scheme between 11 
June 2023 and 31 December 2025, with a daily average of 21.62 lakh passengers. On 14 July 2025, 
Karnataka reached a milestone of 500 crore women passengers across the four RTCs, establishing a 
national benchmark in gender-responsive public transport.
 Y Looking ahead to 2026–27, KSRTC plans to induct 1,500 new buses while implementing a Vehicle Tracking 
and Monitoring System (VTMS) with AIS-140 compliant tracking and panic buttons under the “Central 
Assistance for Strengthening Public Transport” scheme. Surveillance cameras are proposed in 1,000 
buses—two per bus, one for passenger monitoring and another for road-facing surveillance—enhancing 
operational safety and transparency.
 Y In a pioneering welfare measure among India’s road transport corporations, KSRTC introduced a Rs.1 
crore accident insurance scheme covering both on- and off-duty incidents, with Rs.20 lakh compensation 
to dependents in case of employee death. The corporation also launched “KSRTC-Arogya,” a cashless 
medical treatment scheme for employees and their dependents. These initiatives reinforce institutional 
commitment to workforce security.
 Y BMTC has diversified services through the “Divya Darshana” one-day package tours to major and historic 
temples in Bengaluru. Presently, 11 routes operate, with around 1,200 tourists availing services every 
weekend. This initiative integrates urban transport with religious and cultural tourism.

Integrated Urban, Rail and Maritime Infrastructure Development
 Y  The State has approved the construction of a 2+2 lane access flyover connecting the Bengaluru Signature

 Y Under Railway Doubling Projects implemented through K-RIDE on a 50:50 cost-sharing basis, the

with commissioning expected by February 2027, while the Yeshwantpur–Channasandra line, revised to 
Rs.683.57 crore, has achieved 45% financial and 52% physical progress, targeted for March 2027. These 
projects enhance rail capacity and regional integration.
 Y Karnataka’s minor ports continue to contribute to trade and revenue generation. During 2024–25, 
6.07 lakh metric tonnes (MT) of cargo were handled, generating Rs.23.80 crore, while 4.54 lakh MT 
handled between April and December 2025 yielded Rs.11.35 crore. The figures underscore the sustained 
economic relevance of decentralised port infrastructure.
 Y To address coastal erosion, 2,285 metres of protection walls were constructed across three coastal 
districts in 2024–25 at a cost of Rs.28.57 crore. For 2025–26, Rs.15 crore has been allocated, with 600 
metres of seawalls completed up to December 2025 at an expenditure of Rs.7.50 crore. These measures 
safeguard coastal communities and infrastructure against environmental vulnerabilities.

Strengthening Financial Inclusion and Cooperative Infrastructure
 Y Karnataka’s banking outreach has strengthened steadily, with total branches rising from 12,001 in 
March 2023 to 12,659 by September 2025, reflecting expansion across rural, semi-urban and urban 
areas. In contrast, the ATM network declined from 16,978 to 15,398 during the same period, largely 
due to a reduction in urban ATMs. The trend /indicates a shift toward branch-based and digital banking 
penetration.
 Y The cooperative banking structure remains robust under the State Cooperative Apex Bank, with all banks 
meeting the 9% CRAR norm except Bidar DCCB (2.32%). NABARD plans inspections of 2O DCCBs in 2025-
26 to strengthen oversight.Following the merger of KVGB and KGB, the unified Karnataka Grameena Bank 
headquartered in Ballari reports assets of Rs.68,703.09 Crore, accumulated losses of Rs.255.57 Crore &a 
CRAR of 8.26% as of 1st May,2025, while full CBS implementation enables RuPay, RTGS/NEFT, DBT and 
SMS alerts for KCC accounts.
 Y Through the GRAMA One model, 4701 PACS function as Common Service Centres delivering nearly 300 
central and state e-services, including money transfer, ticket booking and Aadhaar services. Additionally, 
167 PACS operate as Organic Societies, 232 as Export Societies, 650 under the National BheejSahakari

 Y Skill Development remains a priority with NABARD,investing Rs. 339.06 lakh over the past six years to

installation, health care, computer-based skills, farm machinery repair, banking & financial services, 
insurance, panchakarma therapy andyoga. Approximately 80% of trainees have secured employment or 
initiated self employment, strengthening rural livelihoods.

benefit 3636 habitations and approximately 71.87 lakh people through household-level water access. As 
of 26 December 2025, Rs.2619.19 Crore has been released for implementation.
 Y Under RIDF tranches I to XXXI, 44,612 projects have been sanctioned amounting to Rs. 24,563.73 crore with 
Rs. 19,800.70 crore disbursed as of December 24, 2025. Sectors allocation prioritizesAgriculture(43%), 
Rural Connectivity(30%)andSocial Sector (27%). In 2024-25, 299 projects received Rs.2242.11 Crore,

 Y RIDF interventions have expandedirrigation potential to 5.64 lakh hectares and strengthened 45,972 km

11. HUMAN DEVELOPMENT
Karnataka has maintained a leading position in human development through sustained investments in 
education, health, and social welfare, consistently performing above the national average. The State has 
continuously strengthened healthcare systems, SC/ST welfare, backward classes and minority development, 
women and child protection, disability and senior citizen empowerment, and gender equity through targeted 
investments, digital platforms, and inclusive welfare programmes.
As one of the first States to publish a Human Development Report, Karnataka has demonstrated a long-standing 
commitment to evidence-based policymaking. Targeted interventions for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, 
and other backward classes remain central to its strategy for advancing social equity, strengthening human 
capital, and promoting inclusive and balanced growth across districts and communities.
Health and Family Welfare 
 Y  Ma ternal Mortality Ratio declined from 97 (2015–17) to 68 (2021–23), and Infant Mortality Rate reduced 
from 28 (2015) to 14 (2023). As per the Sample Registration System(SRS 2023), Under 5 Mortality Rate 
stands at 17, the Infant Mortality Rate at 14, and the Neonatal Mortality Rate at 11 per 1,000 live births. 
These improvements indicate effective maternal and neonatal interventions, though continued emphasis 
is required to achieve single-digit child mortality indicators.
 Y  In 2025–26, a total of 31,920 private medical establishments are registered under the Karnataka Private 
Medical Establishments Act. Of these, 9,214 (29%) are located in Bengaluru district, followed by Dakshina 
Kannada with 2,341 (7%) and Dharwad with 1,229 (4%). This concentration highlights the need to expand 
private healthcare services in underserved regions to ensure balanced access across the State.
 Y  Budg et allocation for 2024–25 was Rs.11,545.28 crore, of which Rs.10,909.48 crore (including OB) 
was released and Rs.10,237.68 crore expended. For 2025–26, against Rs.11,991.17 crore allocation, 
Rs.8,239.32 crore (including OB) was released and Rs.7,294.88 crore spent up to December 2025. The 
high expenditure ratio reflects sustained fiscal commitment to health sector strengthening.
 Y  Under Ayushman Arogya Kendras, 9,058 Health & Wellness Centres have been upgraded as of December 
2025, including 6,532 Rural Sub Centres, 2,161 Rural PHCs, and 365 Urban PHCs. This transformation 
enhances preventive, promotive, and comprehensive primary healthcare services at the grassroots level.
 Y  The Routine Immunisation Programme targets 10.02 lakh children annually and 10.88 lakh pregnant 
women. During 2025–26 (up to December), 7.56 lakh children were immunised against a target of 7.51 
lakh, achieving 101% coverage. This performance demonstrates strong outreach and immunisation 
system efficiency.
 Y  Under the third phase of Ashakirana, 393 Vision Centres have been established across District Hospitals, 
Medical Colleges, Taluka Hospitals and Community Health Centers. Free eye check-ups and spectacles 
were provided to 2,91,400 beneficiaries, and 3,75,958 cataract surgeries were conducted (52,620 
in Government facilities and 3,23,338 in private hospitals) up to December 2025. The hub-and-spoke 
referral system enhances accessible and sustainable eye care services.
 Y  Gruha Arogya Yojane screened 62,37,026 persons for hypertension and diabetes (August to December 
2025), identifying 3,65,193 hypertension and 2,63,970 diabetes cases. Additionally, 54,72,223 individuals 
were screened for oral, breast, and cervical cancers, detecting 473 oral, 353 breast, and 364 cervical 
cancer cases. Early detection and protocol-based treatment strengthen NCD control strategies.
 Y  The ST-Elevated Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) programme operates in 31 districts through a Hub-and-
Spoke model. From March 2023 to December 2025, 10,75,535 ECGs were conducted, 16,161 acute heart 
attack cases were identified, and 9,202 were successfully treated. Under the Puneeth Rajkumar Hrudaya

Karnataka 6th at the national level in telemedicine services. These digital health initiatives have

 Y AYUSH services operate through 726 government dispensaries and 168 government hospitals with 2,766

Education 
 Y  Rapid advances in knowledge and rising aspirations have made education central to both individual 
empowerment and national development. Recognized as a fundamental right and a public good with 
strong positive externalities, education in Karnataka is supported through sustained public investment 
and reform. As a knowledge-driven economy, the State continues to prioritize access, equity, and quality 
enhancement across all levels of education.
 Y  K arnataka has developed a strong and extensive school education network. In 2025–26, totally 70392 
schools in the State of which 21,864 Lower Primary, 29,519 Upper Primary, and 19,009 Secondary 
schools. Government management accounts for 89.35% of Lower Primary and 72.93% of Upper Primary 
schools, demonstrating strong public provisioning at foundational levels. In secondary education, 26.52% 
of high schools are managed by the department of Education, with private institutions playing a larger 
role, particularly in urban areas, while government schools remain predominantly rural-based.
 Y  Studen t enrolment in 2025–26 reached 50.52 lakh at the Primary level (Classes I–V) and 31.45 lakh at 
the Upper Primary level (Classes VI–VIII), with 84.04% of students studying in rural government schools.

Human and Gender Development
 Y Karnataka’s Human Development Index (HDI) has improved significantly from 0.432 in 1999 to 0.644 in 
2022, reflecting sustained progress in health, education, and income indicators. The state has consistently 
ranked between 10th and 11th among Indian states, indicating steady but competitive advancement 
within the national context.
 Y  A t the district level, disparities remain evident. Bengaluru Urban (0.738) leads in HDI, followed by Dakshina 
Kannada (0.687), Chikkamagaluru (0.668), and Udupi (0.665), whereas Yadgir (0.538), Kalaburagi (0.539), 
and Raichur (0.562) record the lowest values. These variations highlight uneven regional development 
patterns across Karnataka.
 Y Taluk-level analysis further underscores intra-district inequality: Mangalore Taluk (0.786) in Dakshina 
Kannada records the highest HDI, while Yadgir Taluk (0.325) in Yadgir District registers the lowest. Notably, 
76 taluks fall below the state average of 0.573, signalling the need for targeted localised interventions.
 Y  T o strengthen evidence-based planning, the preparation of the “District Human Development 
Report–2025” is currently underway across all 31 districts. The report is expected to guide decentralised 
policy design and focused developmental strategies.

13. SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT GOALS: KARNATAKA’S INTEGRATED APPROACH TOWARDS 
SDG 2030
 Y The United Nations’ 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development outlines 17 Sustainable Development 
Goals (SDGs), 169 targets, and 232 indicators, expanding the earlier Millennium Development Goals 
to address climate change, inequality, innovation, sustainable consumption, peace and justice. The 
framework is universal, inclusive, and indivisible, integrating economic, social and environmental 
dimensions of development. Its design enables adaptation to local contexts while maintaining global 
coherence
 Y At the national level, initiatives such as the Aspirational District Programme and Aspirational Block 
Programme have advanced SDG localization. Karnataka, however, had already initiated corrective 
measures for regional disparities through the Special Development Plan, positioning itself as an early 
mover in balanced development. This alignment reflects the state’s proactive commitment to equitable 
growth.
 Y With only four years remaining until 2030, global assessments indicate that merely 17% of SDG targets 
are currently on track, there is an urgency for coordinated and sustained efforts by governments, private 
sector actors, and civil society. 
 Y Karnataka has prepared SDG vision 2030 document by forming Goal Committees, Monitoring Committees 
and a Steering Committee to plan and monitor progress of SDGs. The committees have identified around 
670 indicators, developed baseline data and recommended strategies for achieving SDGs by 2030.
 Y According to NITI Aayog’s SDG India Index reports version 3 (2020-21) and version 4 (2023-24), Karnataka 
improved its score from 72 in 2020–21 to 75 in 2023–24, ranking 5th among major states. The state has

33

shown strong progress in 11 goals, including poverty reduction, health, clean water, economic growth, 
climate action, reduced inequalities, sustainable cities, responsible consumption, life below water, life on

 Y The Voluntary National Review (2020) provisionally estimated that India would require an additional 
annual expenditure of 6.2% of GDP by 2030 to meet SDG commitments. This highlights the scale of

accountability and evidence-based policy actions for achieving SDGs.
 Y Karnataka is aligning GSDP sectors with Sustainable Development Goals, while promoting SDG

1.1 INTRODUCTION
1.1.1 Karnataka is a State characterised by rich cultural and linguistic diversity; its economic and social 
conditions broadly reflect those prevailing at the national level. Situated in the southern part of India, the 
State is bordered by Maharashtra and Goa to the north, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana to the east, Tamil 
Nadu and Kerala to the south and the Arabian Sea along its western coast.
1.1.2 The State covers a geographical area of 1,91,791 square kilometres, accounting for 5.83 per cent of 
the country’s total area. As per the 2011 Census, Karnataka’s population stood at 6,10,95,297, constituting 
5.05 per cent of India’s total population. In terms of population size, Karnataka ranks ninth among India’s 
States and union territories. Urbanisation in the State has progressed steadily, with the share of the urban 
population increasing by 4.68 percentage points during the period 2001–2011. As per 2011 census, 61.33 per 
cent of the population resides in rural areas, while 38.67 per cent lives in urban centres. The proportion of 
urban population in Karnataka is higher than the national average.
1.1.3 Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) or State income is one of the primary indicators used to assess 
the economic condition and progress of the State. The growth rates of the Gross State Domestic Product 
(GSDP) and Per Capita Income reflect the direction, pace, and stability of economic activities within the State. 
The overall economic growth of the State is determined by the performance of the Agriculture, Industry and 
Services sectors.
1.1.4 Changes in the price level constitute another important indicator for understanding the state of the 
economy. The movement of the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) and Consumer Price Index (CPI) indicates the 
level of price stability or inflation prevailing in the economy. Controlling inflation is essential for protecting 
purchasing power and ensuring balanced economic development.
1.1.5 This chapter presents an analysis of sector-wise growth in GSDP , trends in per capita income, movements 
in price indices and the prevailing inflationary conditions. In addition, district-wise GDP estimates and inter-
district disparities are examined to provide a comprehensive picture of the State’s economic progress.
1.2 GROSS STATE DOMESTIC PRODUCT
1.2.1 Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) is a key indicator used to assess the economic growth of a State, 
as it provides a comprehensive view of the overall economic activity. GSDP serves as an essential tool for 
policymakers, administrators and planners in formulating, implementing and evaluating development plans 
aimed at achieving balanced economic growth. An analysis of GSDP at both aggregate and sectoral levels 
offers valuable insights into the structure, patterns and sources of economic growth.
1.2.2 State Domestic Product is defined as the aggregate monetary value of all goods and services produced 
within the geographical boundaries of a state during a specified period, generally a financial year, without 
any duplication.
1.3 GROSS STATE DOMESTIC PRODUCT: OVERVIEW FOR 2025–26
1.3.1 The Advance Estimates of Karnataka’s Gross State Domestic Product for the year 2025–26 indicate that 
the GSDP is estimated at Rs.32,81,065 crore at current prices, registering a growth rate of 12.9 per cent. At

1.5 COMPARISON BETWEEN ADVANCE ESTIMATES FOR 2025–26 AND FIRST REVISED 
ESTIMATES FOR 2024–25
1.5.1 At constant (2011–12) prices, Karnataka’s Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) is expected to grow by 
8.10 per cent in 2025–26.
1.5.2 The agriculture sector is estimated to grow by 9.1 per cent in 2025–26, compared to 7.0 per cent in 
2024–25. Good monsoon during this year and anticipated growth of meat production are the main reasons 
for this achievement.  
1.5.3 The industry sector, which includes mining and quarrying, manufacturing, construction and electricity, 
gas and water supply, is expected to grow by 6.7 per cent in 2025–26, compared to 4.1 per cent growth 
in 2024–25. Manufacturing (7.20 per cent) and Electricity (7.50 per cent) are the main factors supporting 
industrial growth in 2025-26.
1.5.4 The services sector is expected to grow by 8.1 per cent in 2025–26, compared to 8.4 per cent in 2024–
25. The growth in service sector is mainly due to the expansion of IT-related services, which are projected 
at 10.50 per cent in 2025-26 over 10.20 per cent in 2024–25. Hotel and Restaurants (13.90 per cent) Public 
Administration (8.6 per cent) and Other Services (7.9 per cent) are the major contributors to services sector 
growth.
1.5.5 At the national level, as per the First Advance Estimates, India’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) at 
constant (2011–12) prices is expected to grow by 7.4 per cent in 2025–26. The agriculture, industry and 
services sectors at the all-India level are projected to grow by 3.1 per cent, 6.2 per cent and 9.1 per cent, 
respectively.

1.6 NET STATE DOMESTIC PRODUCT
1.6.1 Net State Domestic Product (NSDP) is obtained by deducting Consumption of Fixed Capital (depreciation) 
from the Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP).
1.6.2 For the year 2025–26, at current prices, the Net State Value Added (NSVA) of the agriculture, industry 
and services sectors is expected to grow by 10.5 per cent, 10.3 per cent and 14.1 per cent, respectively. 
As a result, NSDP at current prices is estimated at Rs.29,80,634 crore, recording a growth of 12.9 per cent, 
compared to 12.1 per cent in 2024–25.
1.6.3 At constant (2011–12) prices, NSDP is estimated at Rs.15,39,862 crore, reflecting a growth of 8.1 per 
cent (Table 1.4) for 2025-26. At constant prices, the NSVA of agriculture, industry and services sectors is 
projected to grow by 9.1 per cent, 6.7 per cent and 8.0 per cent, respectively.

1.7 SECTORAL COMPOSITION OF GROSS STATE DOMESTIC PRODUCT
1.7.1 Between 2024–25 and 2025–26, the share of agriculture and industry in Karnataka’s Gross State 
Domestic Product (GSDP) declined marginally. The contribution of agriculture decreased from 11.02 per cent 
to 10.77 per cent, while that of industry declined from 19.82 per cent to 19.36 per cent.
1.7.2 The services sector, which is the largest contributor to GSDP , recorded a slight increase in its share, 
rising from 69.16 per cent in 2024–25 to 69.87 per cent in 2025–26. Within the services sector, Real Estate, 
Professional Services and Ownership of Dwellings accounted for the highest share at 41.28 per cent in 
2025–26. This was followed by Computer-related Services and Research & Development (31.85 per cent), 
Manufacturing (11.33 per cent), Trade and Repair Services (8.93 per cent), Other Services (6.31 per cent) and 
Crops (5.99 per cent).

1.8 PER CAPITA INCOME
1.8.1 Per capita income is calculated by dividing the Net State Domestic Product (NSDP) at current prices by 
the projected mid-year population (as on 1st October).
1.8.2 For 2025–26, Karnataka’s per capita income is estimated at Rs.4,33,326 at current prices, registering a 
growth of 12.2 per cent over Rs.3,86,156 in 2024–25. Karnataka’s per capita income is 97 per cent higher than 
the all-India average of Rs.2,19,575.
1.8.3 Figure 1.3 presents a comparison of per capita income of Karnataka and all-India from 2020-21 to  
2025–26. The data indicate a sharp increase in per capita income after 2020–21, reflecting the gradual 
recovery of the State’s economy following the economic slowdown caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

1.11 DISTRICT INCOME
1.11.1 The estimates of District Domestic Product are prepared on a provisional basis. Data required for 
estimation od District Domestic Product are directly available only for the primary sector. For the secondary 
and tertiary sectors, State-level estimates are apportioned to districts using suitable indicators and workforce 
distribution under each sector, as reported in the Sixth Economic Census.
1.11.2 The Directorate of Economics and Statistics publishes annual reference documents such as Karnataka 
at a Glance and District at a Glance. These publications provide around 2,340 indicators, including static data 
from the Population Census, Agricultural Census and Livestock Census, as well as dynamic data relating to 
various development programmes. They also contain socio-economic and geographical information at the 
district and taluk levels.
1.11.3 These publications serve as the primary data source for computing District Domestic Product estimates 
and also include maps of districts and taluks. The estimates of Gross District Domestic Product and per capita 
income for 2024–25 are presented in Appendix 1.6, while district-wise sectoral contributions for all 31 
districts are given in Table 1.8.

1.11.4 An analysis of Table 1.8 indicates that districts with stronger performance in the services and industrial 
sectors record higher overall growth in District Domestic Product (DDP). In contrast, districts positioned at the 
lower end of the DDP ranking are relatively stronger in the agriculture sector but perform poorly overall due 
to the limited presence of industrial and services establishments.
1.11.5 Further, with the inclusion of new data components such as the private corporate sector and the 
availability of additional data sources in the computation of State GSDP , the process of identifying appropriate 
physical indicators for allocating sector-wise estimates to districts is currently underway. Owing to data 
constraints, sector-wise analysis of district estimates across different time periods may not yield meaningful 
conclusions, as these estimates are yet to stabilise.

of industries and services in these regions, particularly through measures that encourage private investment.

1.12 PRICES
1.12.1 Prices play a vital role in the process of economic planning. They act as a mechanism for allocating 
goods and services among consumers. Any change in prices affects every section of society, irrespective 
of their standard of living. Prices influence decisions about what goods should be produced and in what 
quantities. They also serve as indicators of the demand and supply of goods & services in the economy.
1.13 INFLATION
1.13.1 Inflation at the wholesale and retail levels is measured through two main indices: the Wholesale Price 
Index (WPI) and the Consumer Price Index (CPI). Inflation refers to a sustained increase in the general price 
level of goods and services over time. It represents a continuous rise in prices, which reduces the purchasing 
power of money, meaning a unit of currency buys fewer goods and services than it did in the past. Thus, 
inflation reflects the declining value of a nation’s currency.
1.13.2 In India, inflation is commonly measured using two indices: the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) and the 
Consumer Price Index (CPI). As the names suggest, the WPI tracks prices at the wholesale level, while the 
CPI measures prices at the consumer level. Apart from this basic difference, the composition and number of 
items in their respective baskets vary, as do the weights assigned to them. Food items carry a higher weight in 
the CPI than in the WPI, making the CPI more sensitive to changes in food prices. On the other hand, the fuel 
group has a significantly higher weight in the WPI compared to the CPI.
During the first nine months of 2025–26 (April–December), the All-India Wholesale Price Index (WPI) 
inflation rate increased to 1.82 per cent, compared with an increase of 1.64 per cent during the same period 
in the previous year.
Similarly, based on the All-India Consumer Price Index (CPI), the inflation rate is increased to 3.28 per cent 
in April–December 2025–26, compared with 3.08 per cent in the corresponding period of the previous year.
1.14 ALL INDIA WHOLESALE PRICE INDEX
1.14.1 The Wholesale Price Index (WPI) measures the average change in prices of commodities traded in bulk 
at the early stage of transactions. The WPI basket comprises three major groups: Primary Articles, Fuel and 
Power and Manufactured Products.
1.14.2 The WPI is released by the Office of the Economic Adviser (OEA) under the Department for Promotion 
of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry. The base year for the current 
series is 2011–12 (=100). The 2011–12 series consists of a total of 697 items, including 117 items under 
Primary Articles, 16 items under Fuel and Power and 564 items under Manufactured Products. The WPI 
basket does not include services.
1.14.3 The WPI is used to measure inflation at the wholesale transaction level and is also utilized by the 
Central Statistical Office (CSO) for estimating Gross Domestic Product (GDP). This index is released monthly 
at the national level.

1.16 CONSUMER PRICE INDEX
1.16.1 The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the change in retail prices of goods and services consumed 
by a specified population group in a particular area, with reference to a base year.  At present, the CPIs 
compiled in India include:
 Y  CPI f or Industrial Workers (CPI-Industrial Workers)
 Y  CPI f or Agricultural Labourers (CPI-Agricultural Labour)
 Y  CPI f or Rural Labourers (CPI-Rural Labour)
 Y  CPI f or Rural and Urban (CPI-Rural & Urban)
1.16.2 The first three indices are compiled and released by the Labour Bureau, Chandigarh, while the CPI 
(Rural & Urban) is compiled and released by the Central Statistical Office (CSO), New Delhi. In Karnataka, the 
Directorate of Economics & Statistics compiles and releases only the CPI-IW for nine centres as part of the 
state series every month.
1.16.3 The Consumer Price Index is widely regarded as a barometer of inflation and an important tool for 
monitoring price stability. It is also used for determining Dearness Allowance (DA) for government employees 
and for revising wages under labour–employer agreements.
1.17 CONSUMER PRICE INDEX FOR INDUSTRIAL WORKERS
1.17.1 The target group of the Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW) includes workers 
employed in factories, mines, plantations, motor transport, docks, railways and electricity establishments. 
This index is primarily used to determine the Dearness Allowance (DA) for employees in both the public and 
private sectors.
1.17.2 At the national level, the base year of the CPI-IW (Central Series) was revised from 2001=100 to 
2016=100 with effect from September 2020. Under the 2016 series, the CPI-IW is compiled for 88 selected 
industrially developed centres across the country. Out of these, seven centres are located in Karnataka, 
namely Bengaluru, Belagavi, Hubballi-Dharwad, Madikeri, Mysuru, Davanagere and Chikmagaluru.

1.20 PRICE SITUATION IN RURAL AND URBAN KARNATAKA
1.20.1 The Directorate of Economics & Statistics, Government of Karnataka, collects retail prices of a basket 
of essential commodities from selected rural and urban centres to assess the price situation in the State. 
Rural retail prices are collected monthly, while urban retail prices are collected weekly for the compilation of 
the Rural Retail Price Index (RRPI) and the Urban Retail Price Index (URPI). With effect from February 2022, 
the base year for both indices has been revised from 1970 = 100 to 2018 = 100. These indices are based on 
an unweighted average method and are intended to reflect broad price trends in rural and urban areas to 
support policy decisions.

(a) Price Situation in Urban Areas
1.20.2 Retail prices of 26 important commodities are collected weekly from 31 urban centres across the State 
for the compilation of the URPI. During 2025–26, the URPI increased from 163.52 in April 2025 to 166.40 in 
December 2025, registering a rise of 1.76 per cent. The increase in the index was mainly due to a rise in the 
prices of Coconut (27.42 per cent), Coconut Oil (17.95 per cent) and Eggs (12.79 per cent). However, during 
2025–26 (up to December 2025), the average URPI stood at 164.59, which showed a marginal decrease of 
0.08 per cent compared to the corresponding period of the previous year (164.72).
(b) Price Situation in Rural Areas 
1.20.3 For the compilation of the RRPI, retail prices of 32 essential commodities are collected monthly from 
452 villages across the State. During 2025–26, the index increased marginally from 145.42 in April 2025 to 
145.56 in December 2025, showing a rise of 0.10 per cent. This increase was mainly due to a sharp rise in the 
price of Tomato (66.37 per cent), while the price of Coconut also increased by 22.94 per cent. Up to December 
2025, the average RRPI was 145.12, indicating a decrease of 1.27 per cent compared to the corresponding 
period of the previous year (146.99).

1.21 WAY FORWARD
1.21.1 The Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) is expected to achieve 8.1 per cent growth during 2025-26 
as comparedto 7.3 per cent during 2024-25.
 Y  The Government has constituted an advisory committee on GSDP to review the methodology, quality, 
Consistency of input data used for the estimation of GSDP and also recommend suitable measures for 
timely flow of data and data sources.
 Y Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, Government of India is proposing to revise the 
base year of Gross Domestic Product and Index of Industrial Products from 2011-12 to 2022-23. With 
the guidance of MoSPI, Directorate of Economics and Statistics will also revise the base year to 2022-23. 
 Y To increase the GSDP of the state, The Government of Karnataka unveiled the new IT Policy 2025–30, 
reinforcing the state’s leadership in deep-tech and Artificial Intelligence while accelerating the growth 
of emerging clusters across the Beyond Bengaluru region. Anchored on four strategic pillars—Smart & 
Green Infrastructure, Future-Ready Talent, Business-Ready Support and Market Acceleration
 Y To increase the service sector contribution, the Government of Karnataka has introduced India’s first 
Global Capability Centers (GCC) Policy 2024–29, designed to position the state as a global hub for GCCs. 
The policy sets an ambitious vision to attract 500 new GCCs, create 3.5 lakh jobs and contribute USD 50 
billion to Karnataka’s economy by 2029.
 Y Karnataka Acceleration Network is India’s first-of-its-kind state-wide initiative dedicated to accelerating 
growth-stage startups. It connects Bengaluru-based accelerators with regional incubators in cities such as 
Mysuru, Mangaluru, Hubballi-Dharwad and Belagavi. The program supports startups through structured 
mentorship, fundraising assistance, customer access, IP services and go-to-market strategies.
