2.1 INTRODUCTION
The Budget for 2025–26 reflects Karnataka’s balanced approach to development, combining the pursuit of 
higher economic growth with a strong commitment to fiscal discipline and macroeconomic stability. This 
growth momentum has been supported by prudent financial management, prioritisation of productive 
expenditure, and sustained efforts to strengthen revenue mobilisation.
Although containing the fiscal deficit remains a persistent challenge in a developing economy, the State 
has demonstrated a consistent commitment to fiscal prudence. The fiscal deficit for 2024–25 (RE) has been 
estimated to contain at 2.90 percent of GSDP , and for 2025–26 (BE), it has been targeted at 2.95 percent. 
These levels remain comfortably within the statutory ceiling of 3 percent stipulated under the Karnataka 
Fiscal Responsibility Act, 2002, underscoring the State’s commitment to prudent and responsible fiscal 
management.
2.2 FISCAL CONSOLIDATION
Fiscal consolidation, which reflects both the extent of fiscal discipline and the quality of public expenditure, 
has remained a central pillar of Karnataka’s fiscal strategy. Since the enactment of the Karnataka Fiscal 
Responsibility Act (KFRA), 2002, the State has consistently pursued prudent financial management and placed 
fiscal sustainability at the core of its policy framework. Over the years, Karnataka has largely succeeded in 
maintaining its fiscal deficit below 3 percent of GSDP , preserving revenue surpluses and containing public 
debt within 25 percent of GSDP . This disciplined approach has strengthened the State’s credit profile, reduced 
borrowing costs and reinforced overall macroeconomic stability.
The few deviations from prescribed fiscal targets reflect responsiveness to extraordinary economic 
circumstances rather than fiscal laxity. In 2009–10, the fiscal deficit rose to 3.24 percent in response to the 
global financial crisis. Similarly, during the COVID-19 pandemic, the deficit increased to 3.72 percent in 2020–
21 and 3.84 percent in 2021–22, as higher public spending became essential to support health systems, 
livelihoods and protect vulnerable sections during periods of severe stress.
Although the Fifteenth Finance Commission permitted States to raise fiscal deficits to 4 percent of GSDP , 
Karnataka has chosen to budget a lower deficit of 2.95 percent for 2025–26 (BE). This voluntary adherence to 
tighter limits reflects the State’s long-term commitment to fiscal sustainability.
On the revenue account, a modest deficit of 0.6 percent of GSDP is anticipated in 2025–26. This represents 
a limited shift from earlier surpluses, primarily arising from the discontinuation of GST compensation from 
2023–24 and a reduction in devolution under the Fifteenth Finance Commission Grants. Fiscal and revenue 
deficits for the period 2018-19 to 2025-26 (BE) are presented in Figure 2.1.

2.3 KARNATAKA VIS-À-VIS OTHER SOUTHERN STATES
When the fiscal situation of Karnataka is compared with other southern states, which is largely comparable 
in terms of strength, structure, inter-connectedness as well as proximity of the economies, it is clear that 
Karnataka has performed better in managing its fiscal position. This is reflected in Table 2.1, Figure 2.2 and 
some other tables discussed in subsequent sections. With regards to capital outlay (Rs.68172.20 crore), 
outstanding debt as % GSDP (24.91%) and fiscal deficit as % GSDP (2.90%), the State stands first among 
all southern states. Similarly, with regards to revenue deficit (Rs.19262.00 crore) and interest payment to 
revenue receipts (15.59%), the State stands second after Telangana.

2.4 STATE FINANCES
Karnataka has been in the forefront in terms of adhering to the fiscal consolidation efforts as mandated by 
the FRA 2002. To achieve this, similar to the Centre’s Expenditure Management Commission, the state had its 
own Expenditure Reforms Commission. Based on the Commission’s recommendations, by and large, the state 
has been protecting the targets on the capital outlays even when there are some distresses on the revenue 
side. In other words, the state has been trying not to resort to compression of capital outlays even when 
there are revenue shortages compared to budgeted numbers. In addition to expenditure reforms, the state 
has also undertaken tax reforms and revamped the tax administration, which seems to have yielded results in 
terms of higher revenue receipts. This may be noted in Table 2.2. The revenue receipts have been increasing 
every year with a focus on strengthening tax administration and improving GST collection efficiency. Nontax 
revenues will also be optimized through better asset utilization and streamlining of user charges. Similarly, the 
revenue expenditure have also been increasing every year, the rise in revenue expenditure is on account of 
implementing various subsidies and financial assistance schemes in order to ensure equity and social justice.
However, the State has maintained revenue surplus for several years and has an insignificant revenue deficit 
in recent years. The capital receipts have increased from Rs.84843.03 crore in 2020-21 to Rs.116170.02 crore 
in 2025-26 (an increase of 36.92%). The capital expenditure has increased from Rs.59091.02 crore in 2020-21 
to Rs.97810.51 crore in 2025-26 (an increase of about 65.52%). Receipts and expenditure of both revenue 
and capital as a percent of GSDP augurs well for the state in order to double the state’s income in coming 
years.

2.4.1 Revenue Receipts and its Composition:
As may be noted in Table 2.3, the major component of the State’s revenue receipts is the own tax collections. 
The annual average share of the state’s own tax in GSDP in the last six years(2020-26) is about 6.90 percent. 
However, serious cause for concern is the declining share of central taxes, which has been declining from 1.93 
percent in 2021-22 to 1.69 percent in 2025-26(BE). The trend is expected to be similar when we look at the 
grants from the centre which has declined from 1.22 percent to as low as 0.52 percent for the same reference 
period. The other source of revenue receipts, i.e., non-tax revenue, has been sticky at around 0.5 percent. 
This shows that Government faces constraints in mobilizing additional non-tax revenues.

2.4.2. On Finance Commission Grants
One of the important and serious challenges for the state of Karnataka during the 15th Finance Commission 
period is the decline in the share of state in the divisible of pool of central taxes. It may be noted from Table 
2.4, the overall share of the Finance Commission grants for Karnataka is about 3.7 percent which is reduction 
of over one percentage point compared to 14th Finance Commission, which was at 4.71 percent, which is 
going to pose a sever challenge for the state to cope up in the coming years.

2.5 BUDGETARY DEVELOPMENTS IN 2025-26
2.5.1. Main Trends 
Revenue receipts largely follow the extent of economic activities. With the recovery in most of the economic 
activities from 2021-22, the state is in a position to improve its revenue collection capacity. This may be noted 
from Table 2.5, the growth rate of revenue receipts is 13.45 percent in 2025-26, the growth rate of capital 
receipts for the same reference year is 15.18 percent and the overall receipts are expected to increase by 
13.94 percent.  In terms of shares, the share of revenue and capital receipts in total receipts is 71.57 and 
28.43 percent respectively.
In case of expenditures, Revenue expenditure is expected to increase by 9.80 percent in 2025-26, capital 
expenditure is expected to increase by 19.37 percent and the overall expenditure is expected to increase by 
11.94 percent for the same reference period.

2.5.2 Receipts
2.5.2.1 Revenue Receipts
By definition, total revenue receipts include four major components: Own tax revenue, non-tax revenue, 
devolution from the Central Government and Grants-in-Aid & contributions. The large chunk of revenue 
receipts is coming from state’s own tax revenue which is estimated to be 71.15 percent in 2025-26(BE). The tax 
devolution from Government of India constitutes 17.74 percent of revenue receipts. The lowest contributor 
to the revenue receipts is Grants from Centre at 5.47 percent (Table 2.7).
Tax Revenues and Tax effort: The State’s own tax revenues (SOTR), which is identified as a crucial parameter 
to understand the fiscal strength of the State, is expected to increase from Rs. 180368 crore in 2024-25(RE) to 
Rs.208100 crore in 2025-26(BE), an increase of 15.38%, which  reflect the efficiency of the tax administration 
in the state. The year wise State’s own tax revenue from 2019-20 to 2025-26(BE) is given in Figure 2.5.

With respect to the composition of the total revenue receipts, while there are various sources, as shown in 
Table 2.7, the State’s own tax revenue has been performing very well. The total revenue receipts (consisting 
of taxes on income & expenditure, entry tax, taxes on property and capital transactions, VAT, sale of goods, 
commodities & services, State excise, motor vehicle taxes and the State’s share in central taxes) is estimated 
at Rs.292476.54 crore in 2025-26(BE) as against Rs.257800.70 crore in 2024-25(RE). Taxes on property and 
capital transaction (39.15%) and  Goods and Service Tax (GST) is the main source of indirect tax revenue 
(31.50%) in 2025-26 (BE).
The State’s share in central taxes: It is anticipated to increase from Rs.46932.67 crore in 2024-25(RE) to 
Rs.51876.54 crore in 2025-26(BE) with a growth of 10.53 percent.
Non - tax Revenues: The non-tax revenues, which is largely through the usage of social, economic and 
general services as well as a small component of interest and dividends, is expected to increase from                           
Rs.14500.00 crore in 2024-25(RE) to Rs.16500.00 crore in 2025-26(BE). The share of these revenues in the 
total revenues has been at 5.62 percent and 5.64 percent in 2024-25(RE) and 2025-26(BE) respectively. 
This suggest that there are increasing implicit subsidies in the form of un-recovered user charges across 
the services. This could pose serious challenge to the fiscal strength of the state. Any effort to reduce these 
subsidies could be beneficial for increasing social sector expenditure in the state. For a state like Karnataka 
with non-tax revenue being just about one percent of GSDP , it suggests a substantial increase in recovery 
costs, user charges, fees, etc. is essential. Hence, it is necessary to relook at the recommendations of the 
Expenditure Reforms Commission and implement in order to improve this source of revenues.

Capital receipts could come in the form of loans from Central Government, internal debt management 
(excluding ways & means, advances and market loans), recoveries of loans and advances, and miscellaneous 
capital receipts. The state has budgeted an increase in capital receipts from Rs.100856.00 crore in                                   
2024-25(RE) to Rs.116170.00 crore in 2025-26(BE), which is higher by 15.18 percent compared to  
2024-25(RE). Details of the Revenue and Capital Receipts are given in Table 2.7.

2.5.3 Major items in Revenue Expenditures:
As may be noted in Table 2.8, the Budget for 2025-26 had reverted back to pre-pandemic levels in terms 
of expenditures. The subsidies and financial assistance has increased from Rs.77412 crore in 2024-25(RE) 
to 79925 crore in 2025-26 (BE). The rise in revenue expenditure is also on account of implementing various 
subsidy and financial assistance schemes in order to ensure equity and social justice. The interest payment 
as a percent of revenue receipts has increased from 14.21 % in 2024-25 (RE) to 15.59 % in 2025-26 (BE). This 
is the outcome of increase in borrowings of the State to meet its developmental obligations of the State in 
the context of declining central transfers to State. This compel the Govt to cutdown productive expenditure 
affecting medium term growth perspective and the capital expenditure as % GSDP would become around 3%. 
This calls for  fiscal reforms with emphasis on improving quality of expenditure.

2.5.3.1 Functional Categories of Expenditure
In terms of various types of expenditures by the government, they are divided into three functional categories 
namely, General, Social and Economic and this forms the basis for allocating resources as per the broad 
objectives of the governments. The composition of the functional categories of expenditure reveal that the 
government focuses on social services covering the sectors such as education, health, housing, water supply 
etc. For the year 2025-26(BE), Karnataka has budgeted to spend 35.39 percent of the total budget on social 
services, while its spending proposal on economic and general services are 27.81 percent and 28.00 percent 
respectively (Table 2.9).
1.  E conomic Services cover activities or assistance provided to agencies in the fields of production and trade 
such as Agriculture, Industry, Power, Transport, Communication, Storage etc. 
2.  Soc ial Services cover activities associated with provision of basic social services to consumers such as 
Education, Health, Social Security services and provision of services needed for community living such as 
Water Supply & Sanitation. 
3.  Ge neral Services covers services such as Police, General Administration etc., which are indispensable to 
the existence of an organized State and can’t be conceptually allocated to particular group of beneficiaries. 
4.  Public Debt: This has two components, viz., Repayment Internal debt of the State Government and 
repayment of GoI loans & advances.
5.  Loa ns & Advances: Loans and advances for different activities viz., loans for (i) Urban development                 
(ii) Water supply and Sanitation (iii) Food Storage & Warehousing (iv) Agricultural Financial institutions 
etc. 
6.  Assis tance to Local Bodies: Assistance is being given to both rural and urban local bodies in the form of 
untied grants.

2.5.3.2 Expenditure Highlights: 2025-26
The expenditure incurred on activities related to economic development is called developmental expenditure. 
Hence, expenditure incurred on education, health care, scientific research, infrastructure etc., is developmental 
expenditure. Expenditure incurred on general essential services required for normal running of the government 
is called non-developmental expenditure. Expenditure incurred on general administration, police, judiciary 
etc.  is non-developmental expenditure. In this section, disaggregated information on developmental and 
non-developmental expenditures is discussed and the same is presented in Table 2.10 and Table 2.11. 
Between 2024-25(RE) and 2025-26(BE), the overall developmental expenditure appears to have increased 
from Rs.241195.69 crore to Rs.262001.05 crore (8.63% increase). Since the pandemic, with the increased 
pressure on the health care services, the overall expenditure on social services within the developmental 
expenditure has increased from Rs.133462.83 crore in 2024-25(RE) to Rs.147018.56 crore in 2025-26 (BE)
(10.15% increase). Similarly, the expenditure under economic services is expected to increase Rs.107726.36 
crore to Rs.114975.99 crore (6.72 percent increase) for the same reference period.

2.5.4 Review of trends in Receipts and Expenditure during April-November 2025
This section analyses the fiscal situation of the state from April to November of the current financial year. 
The summary of state’s financial performance for the first eight  months of 2025-26 is compared with Budget 
Estimates of 2025-26 and with the corresponding period in the previous year (2024-25) which is summarized 
in Table 2.14. Further, various components of own tax revenue have been compared and the same is presented 
in Table 2.15.
The total revenue receipt of the state during the first eight months of financial year 2025-26 from April 
to November 2025 is Rs.177226.69 crore. The state achieved 60.60 percent of its revenue receipts targets 
for 2025-26 within first eight months which includes the states own tax revenue of Rs.123278.30 crore, 
State’s non-tax revenue of Rs. 12241.79 crore, the devolution from Government of India of Rs 34156.42 
crore and grants-in-aid from Government of India of Rs.7550.19 crore. Component wise, the government 
collected 59.24 percent of own tax revenue during April-November of budget estimates 2025-26. Further, the 
collection of non-tax revenue reached 74.19 percent of the budget estimates 2025-26 for the same reference 
period. There is a growth of total receipts of 8.57 percent during April-November 2025 compared to the 
corresponding period of 2024. The State own tax revenue also rose by 7.47 percent for the same reference 
period, which shows that the economy is on the recovery path.
State’s own tax revenue includes, among others, the four major state taxes viz. commercial taxes, state excise, 
motor vehicle taxes and taxes on stamps and registration. The large proportion of the own tax revenue is 
coming from commercial tax collections. Out of the total own tax revenue of Rs.123278.30 crore collected 
during April–November 2025, Rs.72011.33 crore is from the commercial taxes, which is 60.01 percent of the 
budget estimated and 6.71 percent higher than the achievement made during the corresponding period in 
2024-25. State excise collections for first eight months of 2025-26 is Rs.26213.69 crore which is 65.53 percent 
of the budget estimate 2025–26, and 10.45 percent over the achievement made during the corresponding 
period of 2024-25. Taxes from motor vehicles during April-November 2025 is Rs.8333.32 crores, which is 
55.56 percent of the budget estimates 2025-26 and 7.04 percent higher than the achievement made during 
the corresponding period of 2024-25. The revenue collected under the stamps and registration is Rs 15969.78 
crore in the first eight months of 2025-26, which is 57.03 percent of the budget estimates and an improvement 
of 6.14 percent over the achievement made during the corresponding period in 2024-25.
On the expenditure front, the share of total expenditure spent during first eight months of 2025-26 with 
respect to the budget estimates is 51.17 percent and 5.13 percent higher than the expenditure happened 
during corresponding period of 2024-25. This suggests the smooth fund flow to the needy sectors of the 
economy. The revenue expenditure was spent by 54.76 percent of the budget estimates during April- 
November 2025 and it is 3.48 percent higher to the revenue expenditure during the corresponding period of 
2024. Similarly, April-November 2025 witnessed 35.50 percent of capital expenditure estimates 2025-26 and 
it is 17.82 percent higher to the capital expenditure during the corresponding period of 2024.
The total expenditure (including public debt) spent during the first eight months is 50.82 percent of the 
total budget estimates 2025-26 and it is 4.28 percent higher than the total expenditure made during the 
corresponding period in 2024-25. This seems to have been largely supported by better revenue mobilization. 
The total receipts (including public debt) during April-November 2025 is 44.53 percent of the budget estimates 
2025-26. The experience of the state in the revenue collection and expenditure happened during the first 
eight months of 2025-26 indicates that the fiscal management of the state is satisfactory during 2025-26.

State’s performance in some of the major fiscal indicators comparing with southern states has been analysed 
and given in Table 2.16 and Figure 2.6. From the analysis, it implies that among southern states, Karnataka

transfers to  State.

2.7 RESOURCE AND EXPENDITURE  OF THE BUDGET: 2025-26
2.7.1 Resources of the Budget (2023-24 to 2025-26)
For the year 2025-26, while the budget assumes a nominal GSDP growth of 7.27 percent (as per MTFP 2025-
29) over 2024-25(RE), the increase in the size of the budget is about 11.94 percent for the same reference 
period.The Budget size in the current year is about Rs. 4.09 lakh crore. In terms of resources for the budget, a 
large part of the resources in 2025-26(BE)  is  state own resources at 67.77 %. The borrowings constitute about 
28% of the resources however, these borrowings underscore the State’s commitment to capital investment 
that drive long term economic benefits apart from maintaining fiscal prudence.  With expected increase in 
own revenue in 2025-26, the overall borrowings of the state in 2025-26 could be less than the budgeted level 
of Rs.116000.01 crore. The share of central assistance in the total resources of the budget is very insignificant 
and also  declining every year (Tables 2.17 & 2.18).

2.7.2. Inter-sectoral Outlays of the Budget (2024-25 and 2025-26) 
The expenditure proposals of the state could depend on the needs as well as growth and development 
priorities. For the year 2025-26, as there is recovery in the economic activities, Karnataka has reprioritized 
the economic sectors that could help reviving the growth as well as employment opportunities in the state.  
Some of the crucial departments that the state has focused in this year’s Budget on capital expenditure 
are Water Resources (Rs.17641.68 crore), Rural Development and Panchyathraj (Rs.13446.87 crore), Urban 
Development (Rs.11064.88 crore), PWD (Rs.9243.91 crore) Planning & Statistics (Rs.3685.06 crore) etc., 

PDF_PAGE 103
95
Fiscal Development and State Finances
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
(Table 2.19). All these expenditures help to uplift the growth potential of the state as well as support the 
state’s efforts in achieving the development of the State.
In 2025-26 budget, State Govt. continuing the five Guarantee schemes, namely, 1) Shakti Scheme for Women 
(Transport Department): Allows women domiciled in Karnataka to travel within State free of cost. An amount 
of Rs.5300.00 crore is provided. 2) Under Anna Bhagya Scheme (Food & Civil Supplies Department) in addition 
to 5 KGs of food grains provided by GoI, the State Government is committed to provide an additional 5 KGs of 
Food Grains totaling to 10 KGs of Food Grains to every beneficiaries every month. An amount of Rs.6426.00 
crore is provided. 3) Under Gruha Jyothi (Energy Department), every house hold in Karnataka will be exempted 
to pay electricity bill upto 200 units. An amount of Rs.10100.00 crore is provided. 4) Under Gruha Lakshmi 
Scheme (Women & Child Development Department), all women who are the heads of their households will 
be paid Rs.2000 per month. An amount of Rs.28608.40 crore is provided. 5) Under Yuva Nidhi scheme (Skill 
Development Department), allowance of Rs.3000 per month will be paid to unemployed graduates and 
Rs.1500 per month will be paid to unemployed diploma pass outs. These unemployment allowances will be 
paid maximum two years or till they get job, whichever is early. An amount of Rs.600.00 crore is provided. All 
these guarantees amount to Rs.51034.40 crore which is about 12.46% of the State Budget.

2.7.3 Heads of  Accounts (H/Acs) in the Budget 
State has introduced various schemes to address the needs of the regions, sectors, sections, etc., from time 
to time. However, as most of the schemes lack sunset clauses, they are expected to continue even after 
achieving the scheme’s objectives, thus putting continuous pressure on the state fiscal space. This could 
also have potential to limit the state’s capacity to address some of the emerging challenges that may need 
substantial resources. It may be noted from Table 2.20 that there are about 1876 H/Acs in 2025-26 (BE). 
Within that, about 820 H/Acs have allocations up to 10.00 crore. To improve the public delivery mechanism 
and to ensure resources for other pressing needs of the state, there is an urgent need to rationalize the H/Acs 
and bring down the number of H/Acs substantially. The same has also been recommended by Expenditure 
Reforms Commission of the state, Administrative Reforms Commission and also the successive Central 
Finance Commissions. The State Finance Commission, as and when it is formed, may relook at these H/Acs. 
Department-wise classification of H/Acs is given in Table 2.21.

2.8 HUMAN DEVELOPMENT RATIOS
Analysis of spending on Human Development sectors will be made in terms of four ratios suggested by UNDP . 
They are (i) Public Expenditure Ratio (PER) (ii) Social Allocation Ratio (SAR) (iii) Social Priority Ratio (SPR) and 
(iv) Human Expenditure Ratio (HER). PER refers to total budgetary expenditure as a proportion of GSDP . The 
SAR refers to expenditure under social services (includes Education, Health and Rural Development) as a 
proportion of total budget expenditure. SPR refers to expenditure under human priority areas (Elementary 
Education / Health (excluding Medical Education) / Rural Development / Nutrition) as a proportion of social 
sector expenditure. HER is the product of above three ratios. As per UNDP norms, PER should be around 25 
percent; SAR should be around 40 percent; SPR should be around 50 percent and HER should be round 5 
percent. Human Development ratios computed for 2023-24 to 2025-26 is given in Table 2.24.
Table 2.24 : Human Development Ratios: 2023-24 to 2025-26

2.9. FISCAL CHALLENGES OF THE STATE AND WAY FORWARD
Similar to all India trends: Fiscal situation even in the state of Karnataka also has come under pressure. 
However, with some prudent fiscal management, the state could ensure that the fiscal deficit has not crossed 
3.0 per cent of GSDP . However, following the trends in outstanding liabilities, it appears that the medium-
term fiscal risk is for real. And this could put pressure on the quality of expenditures in the coming years.In 

PDF_PAGE 110
102
Fiscal Development and State Finances
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
addition to this, there are other challenges that the state is expected to address in the coming years. They 
are as follows:
Ensuring quality of expenditure: As the State that had experienced surplus on revenue account, has started 
running revenue deficit of about 1 percent of GSDP for some time. While this is against the FRA, the state 
needs to undertake hard decision with regard torationalizing of some of the revenue expenditures. This 
could have implications on the outstanding liabilities in the medium term. Further, as RBI Monetary Policy 
Report in April 2019 suggest, the size of states’ revenue expenditure multiplier is 0.82 compared to its capital 
expenditure multiplier of 2, it would be prudent for the state to adopt the expenditure switching mechanism 
to improve the potential GSDP of the state.
Improving efficiency of public expenditures: With the hard budget constraints, one way to address this 
issue is to ensure maximum outcomes of the public expenditures. For this, the state needs to focus on the 
enhancing public expenditure efficiency. 
Ensuring flow of resources for SDGs: SDG needs are going to put pressure on the government finances. It is 
very opt time to think about sources of SDG financing, its impact on  the fiscal conditions, as well as its impact 
on the other macroeconomic conditions. In a way, the time is very conducive to work on SDG-consistent 
macro frameworks that take a little longish perspective up to 2030. Without such exercise, the realization of 
such homogeneous target could be very limited.
Rationalization of various Heads of Accounts(H/Acs): As discussed earlier, Karnataka currently has about 
1876 heads of accounts. While allocating resources could be one issue, management of such a large number 
of H/Acs could limit the administration capabilities and reduce the efficiency of those expenditures sharply. 
The Central Government has taken an exercise to bring down the Centrally Sponsored Schemes substantially. 
As was done by the Centre, rationalization of these H/Acs and bringing down to manageable level may be an 
utmost priority.
Rationalization of subsidies: Subsidies in Karnataka are higher than any comparable states and within that 
non-merit component appear to be larger. Quick rationalization of non-merit subsidies is one clear way for 
freeing more resources for achieving growth and development objectives.
Ways to improve revenue sources: With the decline in the share of state in the central government devolution 
and with GST in place, the pressure on state’s own tax revenue has increased manifolds. Further, with the 
stoppage of GST compensation to states and with decline in the grants-in-aid, the state is in dire need to look 
for alternative sources of revenues. One way that the state could do is to improve the tax administration 
through use of IT services to improve the buoyancy.
Nontax Revenue: The State has taken several measures to increase the revenue generation from nontax 
sources. They are:
(i) The allocation of new mines through a transparent online auction mechanism has resulted in substantially 
higher premium on royalty.
(ii)  Con certed efforts to resolve issues related to forest clearances for new mining blocks is expected to aid 
higher resource mobilization.
(iii)  Strict er enforcement,including periodic tariff updates for utilities, transport and urban services, digital 
tracking,automated billing and tighter compliance is expected to reduce leakeges, improve transparency 
and payment efficiency.

PDF_PAGE 111
103
Fiscal Development and State Finances
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
Regional Imbalance: State has suffered with major setback in resource sharing as per 15th Finance Commission 
recommendations. The devolution has cutdown from 4.74% to 3.64%. This is because of high income per-
capita. Largely, it comes from Bangalore and southern Districts of the State. But the state also have severe 
regional imbalances. The socio-economic indicators or Human development indicators are far less than 
backward states in the Country. State Government is providing funds to the tune of Rs.3000 crore per year for 
seven districts of the backward region of the State. GoI should supplement the efforts by providing matching 
contribution for the development of this region.
Centrally Sponsored Schemes: (i) There should be clear indication of allocation to each State under various 
CSS Schemes in the Union Budget Volumes, so that the States can prepare their budget on a realistic basis. (ii) 
In several CSS Schemes, there is a significant gap between approved annual action plan and actual release. 
This leads to State Government to bear the unreleased portion of GoI. Hence, the entire funds as approved in 
the annual action plan should be released by GoI. (iii) Release of funds under CSS Schemes should be changed 
from reimbursement mode to advance release mode.
State’s fiscal policy and debt management strategy: This is firmly rooted in the fiscal discipline indicators 
outlined in Karnataka Fiscal Responsibility Act. This approach judiciously balances welfare commitments  with 
infrastructure development, ensuring the fiscal space is preserved for priority investments.

3.1 INTRODUCTION
Encouraging private investment has been a top priority for the Karnataka government, resulting in a 
substantial influx of investments in recent years. The state has implemented a well-defined policy framework 
and established dedicated institutions to streamline approval processes. Offering a diverse range of fiscal and 
financial incentives, Karnataka is committed to supporting investors while developing essential infrastructure 
like technical institutions, laboratories and research centres. Notably, the state has witnessed significant 
investments in information technology and biotechnology, contributing substantially to the country’s exports. 
Approximately 40% of the Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) is attributed to exports, with electronic, 
computer software and biotechnology playing a crucial role. To further accelerate economic growth, Karnataka 
aims to maintain its focus on promoting private investment, fostering a business-friendly environment and 
enhancing industrial competitiveness.
3.2 INVESTMENT IN KARNATAKA
Karnataka stands as a trailblazer in introducing pioneering reform initiatives within India, showcasing a proactive 
approach to attracting private investment. The state consistently formulates lucrative policies to incentivize 
both domestic and foreign investments, creating a favourable investment climate. Notably, Karnataka has 
successfully attracted significant private investments, particularly in Information and Communication 
Technology (ICT), Electronics Semiconductor Design & Manufacturing and Biotechnology (BT) sectors.
The Karnataka Innovation and Technology Society (KITS), operates under the Department of IT, BT, and S&T, 
with a specific focus on promoting and facilitating investments in the state. The state’s rich and diverse 
resource base has positioned it as a reputable global investment destination. Karnataka took the lead by 
enacting the Industrial Facilitation Act, streamlining processes for investors.
Karnataka boasts a single-window system, serving as a comprehensive hub for investors seeking opportunities 
in the state. Specific advantages for investors in Karnataka include a conducive law and order situation, the 
availability of highly skilled manpower, a position among the top 5 industrially developed states in India, 
excellent logistical support and connectivity for investors and access to one of the largest and rapidly expanding 
markets in the country. These factors collectively contribute to Karnataka’s standing as an attractive and 
investor-friendly destination.
Karnataka’s investor-friendly and responsive administration has worked towards easing administrative 
procedures and implementing policy measures for faster and smoother industrial growth. Some of the 
significant measures are as follows:
 Y An investor-friendly responsive administration. 
 Y The State-level single window clearance committee and the State high level clearance committee facilitate 
clearance of proposals in a speedy manner.
 Y Sector-specific industrial zones and SEZs that match the natural resources and capabilities of a region 
with the industry requirements.
 Y Creation of World-class, ready-to-use infrastructure through investments in power, roads, water, 
warehouse and logistic facilities, connectivity through rails and ports etc.
3 INVESTMENT AND EXPORTS

 Y The State Government’s packages of incentives and concession for new industrial investments announced 
from time to time.
 Y Special focus on skill development to enhance generation of technical manpower.
 Y Excellent telecommunication network and optical fibre connectivity throughout the State.
3.3 SCHEMES AND POLICY SUPPORT
3.3.1 Karnataka IT Policy 2025-30
The Government of Karnataka unveiled the new IT Policy 2025–30 at the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2025, 
reinforcing the state’s leadership in deep-tech and Artificial Intelligence while accelerating the growth of 
emerging clusters across the Beyond Bengaluru region. Anchored on four strategic pillars—Smart & Green 
Infrastructure, Future-Ready Talent, Business-Ready Support and Market Acceleration—the policy introduces 
key interventions to strengthen R&D, nurture innovation and enable global competitiveness. By fostering 
inclusive regional growth and building robust innovation ecosystems, the policy aims to position Karnataka as 
a premier destination for next-generation technologies and AI-driven transformation.
3.3.2 Karnataka Data Centre Policy 2022-27
The Government of Karnataka has introduced the Data Center Policy 2022–27 with the vision of positioning 
the State as a preferred destination for next-generation data centers and as an integral component of the 
global data center ecosystem. The policy seeks to strengthen Karnataka’s digital infrastructure in alignment 
with its overarching mission to lead the world in the Digital Industrial Revolution and to leverage emerging 
technologies such as big data and high-performance computing.
To achieve this vision, a three-pronged strategy has been adopted. The policy emphasizes the promotion of 
emerging technology clusters, facilitation of ease of doing business for the establishment of data centers and 
the creation of an enabling environment for data management, security, transactions and storage services 
catering to technology-driven industries. A strong focus has been placed on sustainability, with measures 
aimed at ensuring low-carbon operations and the adoption of renewable energy sources for powering data 
centers.
The policy offers a comprehensive framework of incentives and support mechanisms to attract investments 
in the data center industry within the State. It targets the development of more than 200 MW of data center 
capacity and aims to attract investments of approximately INR 10,000 crore during the policy period. Through 
these initiatives, Karnataka seeks to establish itself as a hub for data-driven innovation and global connectivity.
Achievements under Data Center Policy 2022-27
With eight Data Centre companies registered till date under this Policy with KITS in Bengaluru, Karnataka as 
of today has exceeded its own target of 200 MW a year before the policy deadline, reaching at 245.5 MW. 
Karnataka is now also expecting inauguration of NTTs latest 100 MW DC in Bengaluru.NTTs, STT and Nxtra 
are also preparing for expansions, whose DCs are expected to be operational by mid – end 2027.M/s. Tata 
Communications, M/s. Reliance, M/s. Sify,M/s. CtrlS, M/s. DataSamudra, M/s. NxtGen, M/s. CapitaLand, M/s. 
ESDS are few of the other major players in Karnataka.
3.3.3 Karnataka Cybersecurity Policy 2024-29
The Karnataka CyberSecurity Policy 2024 has been formulated to establish a secure and resilient digital 
ecosystem within the State. The policy emphasizes the protection of critical infrastructure, adoption of global 

PDF_PAGE 117
109
Investment and Exports
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
best practices and strengthening of data security measures to ensure trust and reliability in Karnataka’s digital 
economy. It seeks to promote cybersecurity awareness and foster innovation in security technologies through 
strategic initiatives.
To achieve these objectives, the policy encourages collaboration among government, industry and academia 
while extending incentives to cybersecurity start-ups. By creating an enabling environment for R&D and 
deployment of advanced security solutions, Karnataka aims to position itself as a leading hub for cybersecurity 
and safeguard its digital infrastructure against emerging threats.
Achievements under Cybersecurity Policy 2024-29
With around 13 companies already applying for incentives within a year of launch, Karnataka hosts a robust 
policy around cyber security, promoting start-ups in the sector. To add more light to the growth ecosystem, 
KITS has recently co-signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Coinbase. This growth in the sector 
is promising for the industry to invest in the state of Karnataka. 
3.3.4 Karnataka Global Capability Center (GCC) Policy 2024-2029
The Government of Karnataka has introduced India’s first Global Capability Centers (GCC) Policy 2024–29, 
designed to position the state as a global hub for GCCs. The policy sets an ambitious vision to attract 500 new 
GCCs, create 3.5 lakh jobs and contribute USD 50 billion to Karnataka’s economy by 2029.
Beyond job creation, the policy focuses on fostering innovation, strengthening infrastructure and building 
strategic partnerships. It aims to make Karnataka the preferred destination for global technology leaders 
by streamlining regulations, offering incentives for sustainable development and driving skill development 
programs tailored to GCC-specific roles. These measures reaffirm Karnataka’s leadership in technology and 
global collaboration, cementing its reputation as a hub for business excellence and talent.
Key achievements under the GCC Policy
 Y The Government has launched KATALYST – Ease of Doing Business Cell, a dedicated facilitation mechanism 
to assist GCCs in setting up and expanding operations in Karnataka. The cell operates on three guiding 
principles: Empower, Enrich and Engage, ensuring seamless support for businesses.
 Y The Government conducted a high-level U.S. Roadshow from June 16–25, 2025, covering Boston, New 
York and San Francisco. The delegation included senior officials from KITS and KEONICS. The objective 
was to position Karnataka as a global hub for innovation, attract strategic investments in key sectors 
such as semiconductors, biotechnology and digital technologies and build long-term partnerships with 
academia, industry and the startup ecosystem. The delegation engaged with over 50+ companies and 
participated in two international conferences. This initiative generated prospective investments of INR 
5,500 crore with a potential employment generation of 7200+ over the coming years.
3.3.5 Nipuna Karnataka (Skill Locally Work Globally)
The Government of Karnataka launched the Nipuna Karnataka Scheme on 24th September 2024, with an 
outlay of Rs.100 crore to enhance youth employability by bridging the gap between industry requirements 
and existing skill levels. This flagship initiative aims to build a future-ready workforce through upskilling, 
reskilling and vocational training in high-growth sectors such as Information Technology, Biotechnology, 
Artificial Intelligence, Data Science and Cybersecurity.
The scheme is implemented through strong public-private partnerships, bringing together industry leaders, 
academic institutions and training providers to ensure alignment with global standards. A key focus is on

inclusive access, extending opportunities to both urban and rural areas to promote equitable growth across 
the State. Under Nipuna Karnataka, trainees receive industry-recognized certifications and comprehensive 
placement support, ensuring that skill development translates into tangible employment outcomes. By 
addressing the evolving needs of the digital economy and fostering collaboration among stakeholders, the 
scheme positions Karnataka as a national leader in skill development and future-ready talent creation.
Key Achievements
Following CHRO roundtables and inputs from the Skill Advisory Committee, 18 training proposals were 
received and evaluated by expert working groups. These proposals target over 15,000 beneficiaries in high-
demand roles such as AI/ML, Cloud, Full Stack Development, Data Science, Digital Marketing and BFSI. Strong 
industry-academia partnerships and a focus on placement-linked, project-based learning have emerged as 
key strengths, while evaluators flagged gaps in cost-effectiveness and placement clarity.
The next phase will focus on onboarding partners, integrating skilling with real-time placements and activating 
cluster-specific talent pipelines. Digital assessments, live dashboards (in collaboration with vendors like 
Unstop) and institutional adoption across clusters are in progress, with rollout readiness planned for Q4 2025.
3.3.6 Karnataka Acceleration Network (KAN)
Karnataka Acceleration Network is India’s first-of-its-kind state-wide initiative dedicated to accelerating 
growth-stage startups. It connects Bengaluru-based accelerators with regional incubators in cities such as 
Mysuru, Mangaluru, Hubballi-Dharwad and Belagavi. The program supports startups through structured 
mentorship, fundraising assistance, customer access, IP services and go-to-market strategies. The first cohort 
under KAN has been successfully completed. With six regional partners, KAN aims to support 360 growth-
stage startups over three years, covering sectors such as technology, healthcare, industrial tech, agritech, 
mobility and finance.
3.3.7 Quantum Roadmap
The Government of Karnataka unveiled the Karnataka Quantum Roadmap during the Quantum India 
Summit in Bengaluru, reaffirming the state’s ambition to become a global leader in quantum technologies. 
The roadmap adopts a strategic, phased approach to position Karnataka across the entire quantum value 
chain, with a vision to contribute USD 20 billion to the state’s economy by 2035. Built on five pillars—Talent 
Development, R&D Excellence, Infrastructure Creation, Industry Enablement and Global Partnerships—it 
leverages Karnataka’s strengths in deep tech, academia and startups through initiatives such as IISc’s Quantum 
Research Park, Q-Daksha and Q-Karyashala. Key actions include launching the Karnataka Quantum Mission 
and Quantum Policy, establishing a Quantum Hardware Park and an international advisory board, creating 
Quantum Innovation Zones and developing indigenous hardware, skilling programs and pilot use cases. With 
phased goals spanning infrastructure development to full-scale commercialization and export, the roadmap 
aims to create over 10,000 jobs, nurture 100+ quantum startups, file 150+ patents and position Karnataka at 
the forefront of global quantum R&D and innovation.

3.5  BIOTECHNOLOGY
Karnataka’s Bio Economy represents India’s most mature and innovation-driven biotechnology ecosystem. 
The biotechnology sector has recently matured from foundational research to a vibrant, production-oriented 
industry, driven by cutting-edge R&D and entrepreneurial initiatives. At the policy level, Karnataka continues 
to stand apart as the only State with a dedicated Department of Biotechnology since 2001. The Biotech Policy 
2024-2029 serves as the new roadmap, outlining sustainable growth, innovation and regulatory strategies.
3.5.1 Karnataka Biotechnology Policy 2024-2029
The Karnataka Biotechnology Policy 2024-2029 sets a forward-looking vision to position Karnataka as a global 
leader in biotechnology, focusing on sustainable and inclusive growth. Building upon its existing ecosystem, 

PDF_PAGE 128
120
Investment and Exports
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
the policy aims to leverage the state’s rich talent pool, advanced infrastructure and favourable government 
support to accelerate growth in key biotech areas. 
The objectives are as detailed below:
1. Str engthen the biotech ecosystem through collaboration between academia, industry and government 
to foster innovation, entrepreneurship and global partnerships.
2. Sup port bio-manufacturing, aligning with health, climate and energy goals to establish Karnataka as a 
global bio-manufacturing hub.
3. Str eamline regulations to promote ease of doing business and attract investments, especially in emerging 
biotech areas such as synthetic biology, AI/ML and medical technologies.
4. Ski lling and workforce development through initiatives like the Biotechnology Skill Enhancement 
Programme (BiSEP), with a target of creating 30,000 high-quality jobs by 2029.
5. Pr omote R&D and commercialization by supporting emerging areas like cell and gene therapies, 
antimicrobial resistance, marine biotechnology and multi-omics.
6. F oster a robust startup ecosystem through funding, incubation and mentorship for early- and mid-stage 
biotech ventures.
The Key Initiatives of the policy are Fiscal incentives, Sectoral Focus, Biomanufacturing hubs and Innovation 
Clusters.
The integration of policy design and innovation delivery in Karnataka is visible across several initiatives that 
contribute to the growth and diversification of the bio-based economy. These include: 
 Y The evolution of the Karnataka Biotechnology Policy, now oriented towards next-generation domains like 
synthetic biology, gene therapy, Bioinformatics, bioengineering and circular bioeconomy applications.
 Y The creation of dedicated innovation infrastructure, such as biotechnology parks, Centres of Excellence 
and incubation networks that connect startups with academic and industrial ecosystems. 
 Y The deepening of funding mechanisms, enabling startups and researchers to move from proof-of-concept 
to commercial scale.

infrastructure to Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities.

healthcare, agri-tech, aerospace, defence, food-tech and other emerging domains. The initiative emphasizes 
strong academic–industry linkages and provides start-ups with access to advanced infrastructure, mentorship, 
intellectual property support and funding opportunities.

3.5.7  Institute For Bioinformatics And Applied Biotechnology (IBAB), Bengaluru
IBAB is a non-profit autonomous institute set up by the Department of Electronics, IT, BT and S&T, Government 
of Karnataka to undertake research and development in advanced areas of Biotechnology including 
Bioinformatics, Cancer Biology, Synthetic Biology, Structural Biology etc., also to produce skilled manpower in 
these areas for the benefit of growing Biotechnology industry in the state.
IBAB offer PG Diploma, M.Sc. and Doctoral programs in the areas of Bioinformatics and applied Biotechnology. 
An amount of Rs. 916 lakhs annual grant was sanctioned and released for FY 2025-26 towards maintenance 
and academic activities. With the support from the GoK, two flagship projects on Synthetic Biology (Rs. 985 
Lakhs) and Bio-IT (Rs. 946.02 Lakhs) were undertaken.
Sponsored projects worth Rs. 14.45 crore and Industry projects worth Rs. 4.54 crore are currently being 
carried out by various faculty members of the Institute. The major Institutional grants received by the Institute 
from national funding agencies and in operation during this period include DST-FIST (Fund for Improvement 
of Science and Technology infrastructure in Universities and Higher Educational Institutions), DBT-CCB (Centre 
for Disease Genomics, Bioinformatics and Big Data Analysis in Biology and Healthcare), DBT-NNP (National 
Network Project) and DBT-BUILDER (Boost to University Inter disciplinary Life Science Departments for 
Education and Research).
3.5.8 Centre of Excellence In Aqua-Marine Innovation (CoE in AMI), Mangaluru
The Department of Electronics, IT, BT and S&T has set up the Centre of Excellence in Aqua-Marine Innovation in 
Mangaluru with a budget of Rs. 741.98 lakhs for three years to boost Aqua marine biotech research, aiming to 
enhance production and create new Aqua marine bioactive products, with a focus on seaweed bioprospecting. 
An Aqua Marine Biotech Cluster, including several institutions and industries, is being established to provide 
training in Aqua marine agriculture, seaweed farming and genetic improvement programs.
3.5.9 Bengaluru Lifesciences Park (Industry Zone), Bengaluru
Bengaluru Lifesciences Park is being developed in 52 acres 27 guntas of land in PPP mode is an integrated 
Industry zone with total built-up area of about 60 lakhs sq. ft when fully developed to have best-in-class 
laboratory infrastructure to support a host of R&D activities to have 60% of the area reserved for biotech/
life sciences companies. It is estimated that the industry zone with 150+ biotech/life sciences companies and 
over 50000+ employees will be the growth engine of the biotech sector in the State.

3.6  KARNATAKA STRAT-UP POLICY 2022-27
Karnataka has emerged as one of India’s most dynamic hubs for innovation and entrepreneurship, driven by 
a strong policy framework, robust infrastructure and a thriving talent pool. The Government of Karnataka has 
consistently prioritized the growth of the startup ecosystem by introducing targeted programs and initiatives 
that nurture early-stage ventures, support research and development, facilitate funding, global market access 
and much more. These efforts have not only strengthened the state’s position as a leader in technology-
driven entrepreneurship but have also contributed significantly to investment inflows and inclusive economic 
growth. The details below present all the programs and initiatives undertaken, along with their objectives, 
impact and future vision, outlined one by one.
3.6.1 Entrepreneurship development initiatives
Entrepreneurship development initiatives by the Department have been designed to foster innovation, build 
capacity and create a supportive environment for aspiring entrepreneurs across diverse sectors. Through 
targeted programs such as the following, the state has enabled startups to elevate from ideation stage with 
greater ease. These initiatives not only strengthen the entrepreneurial ecosystem but also contribute to 
positioning of Karnataka as a leading hub for technology-driven enterprises.
3.6.2  WEscalate
One of the major priority areas for the Department of Electronics, IT and Biotechnology, Government of 
Karnataka is promoting the women entrepreneurship in the state. In this regard, the Department launched 
the WEscalate program with the following board objectives.
 Y To nurture and grow early-stage women entrepreneurs.
 Y To accelerate the growth stage women entrepreneurs to scale up their ventures. 
 Y To make startup ecosystem in Karnataka more inclusive.
With WEscalate, to ensure the continuity of incubation program and handhold startups to be investment 
ready, a dual program with Incubation and acceleration has been implemented. Under this program, upon 

PDF_PAGE 134
126
Investment and Exports
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
successful completion of Incubation program, the Incubator/Accelerator will be eligible for funding under 
acceleration program. In the acceleration phase preference is given to incubates who have graduated in 
incubation program. To be eligible for acceleration grant, a minimum of 30% incubates from incubation 
program should be able to transition into acceleration phase. The Department intends to implement 2 cohorts 
every year with the support from Incubators/Accelerators. Each cohort will be sector specific. Incubators and 
Accelerators will be mapped and selected basis on their capability to execute region specific Incubation/
Acceleration programmer  Impact and update.
The call for applications for WEscalate 2025–26 was announced in February 2025, following which two 
organizations were selected- IKP EDEN (IKP Knowledge Park Engineering Design and Entrepreneurship 
Network) and the Centre for Cellular and Molecular Platforms (C-CAMP). As part of the funding support, 
Rs. 20 lakhs were disbursed to IKP EDEN and C-CAMP for conducting the incubation program, while the 
acceleration tranche is yet to be released.
3.6.3 Rajiv Gandhi Entrepreneurship Programme
The Rajiv Gandhi Entrepreneurship Program (RGEP) is an early-stage entrepreneurship support program of 
the Government of Karnataka, designed with the following clearly defined objectives.
 Y To identify and nurture early sustainable and scalable entrepreneurial ventures.
 Y To enable talented graduates and innovators to transition from job-seeking to job-creating roles.
 Y Early stage structured funding that lets innovators focus on developing ideas without commercial 
pressure.
 Y To facilitate the development of prototypes, Minimum Viable Products (MVPs) or Proofs of Concept 
(PoCs) with clear commercial and societal relevance.
 Y To ensure continuous mentoring, monitoring and ecosystem support through milestone-based guidance 
from programme partners.
 Y Supporting technology-driven economic growth and job creation in Karnataka by assisting early-stage 
innovation ventures.
Impact and update
Thirty Innovators have been selected under RGEP 2024-25 and the mandate of Government Order for 2024-
25 has been fulfilled. During 2025–26, two Calls for Applications were undertaken, under which 30 innovators 
were selected for support under the programme.
RGEP has contributed to strengthening the early-stage innovation and startup ecosystem in the State by 
providing financial sustenance and structured mentorship during the ideation phase for 60 innovators who 
have been selected under the Program across FYs 2024-25 and 2025-26.
A key outcome of the Rajiv Gandhi Entrepreneurship Program (RGEP) is the creation of a structured innovation 
pipeline within the Department’s startup support ecosystem. RGEP innovators have subsequently progressed 
to and secured support under flagship Department-led initiatives such as ELEVATE, Grassroot Innovation and 
other sector-specific programs. This progression demonstrates that RGEP is effectively fulfilling its intended 
role as a feeder and validation layer, enabling early-stage ideas to mature into investable, scalable ventures 
that are competitive within more advanced funding and acceleration programs of the Department.

3.6.4 Grassroot Innovation
The Grassroot Innovation Programme is an initiative by the Department of Electronics, IT, BT and Science & 
Technology, Government of Karnataka. It aims to identify, promote and support grassroots-level innovations. 
The focus is on enhancing these innovations for broader applications and reducing the hardships faced by 
rural households. Assistance is offered to grassroots innovators such as farmers, artisans, laborers, technicians 
and others to refine their technologies and bring their solutions to the market.
3.6.5 ELEVATE
The Department’s flagship Grant-in-Aid scheme ELEVATE is a testament to the Government of Karnataka’s 
commitment to nurturing the startup ecosystem within the state and driving innovation across sectors. A 
one-time grant of up to INR 50 Lakhs is given to encourage startups who may need early-stage funding to 
develop a prototype, market development and scale-up. The aim of the initiative is to provide a comprehensive 
entrepreneurship platform for startups along with giving access to mentors, networking opportunities, funds, 
idea validation, incubation facilities, among others. The Department has set a benchmark of selection of 
innovative startups under ELEVATE within a period of 100 days from the date of announcement of applications 
to the final selection. The main objective of the programme is to promote innovation-driven entrepreneurship 
by providing early-stage financial support to technology-based startups for product development, proof of 
concept and market validation.
 Y To strengthen the startup ecosystem of Karnataka by enabling startups to scale through structured 
mentorship, incubation support and industry linkages.
 Y To facilitate access to seed funding for promising startups to accelerate commercialization and improve 
their readiness for further investments.
 Y To encourage inclusive entrepreneurship by supporting startups led by women, founders from 
underserved communities and entrepreneurs from Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities.
 Y To foster statewide startup development by promoting innovation beyond Bengaluru and ensuring 
balanced regional growth across Karnataka.
 Y To align startup growth with the Karnataka Startup Policy and enable startups to leverage policy incentives, 
Centre of Excellence and ecosystem partners.
 Y  T o position Karnataka as a global innovation hub by nurturing scalable, high-impact startups contributing 
to employment generation and economic development.

3.6.6 Centres of Excellence (CoEs)
CoE Fin-Tech
As per the budget announcement in 2024-25, the Department of Electronics, IT and Bt, Government of 
Karnataka has initiated the establishment of a Centre of Excellence (CoE) for FinTech under the aegis of the 
Karnataka Innovation and Technology Society (KITS), Department of Electronics, IT and Bt, GoK. Through a 
strategic partnership with NSRCEL, at IIM Bangalore, this CoE is envisioned to foster innovation, develop a 
robust Fin-Tech ecosystem and position Karnataka as a global Fin-Tech leader. The CoE has been sanctioned 
with INR 13.24 Crores earmarked over a period of five years. KITS and NSRCEL will collaborate to operationalize 
this initiative, focusing on incubation, mentoring, skill development and facilitating regulatory sandboxes to 
enable FinTech innovation. The objective of the programme is to incubate, mentor, regulate and skill FinTech 
startups and professionals for sustainable innovation and growth. 
Objectives
 Y Provide structured incubation programs to early and growth-stage FinTech startups, enabling them to 
achieve scalability and sustainability.
 Y Offer tailored mentoring services by domain experts to address specific challenges faced by startups.
 Y Operationalize a regulatory sandbox to allow startups to test and validate innovative solutions in a 
controlled environment in collaboration with regulators, infrastructure providers and industry leaders.
 Y Develop a pipeline of skilled professionals through high-quality certification programs:
i. Fin-T ech Foundation Certificate Program (basic concepts of FinTech, blockchain, digital payments 
and statistics).
ii. Fin-T ech Advanced Certificate Program (Insurtech, regtech, AI in FinTech, financial modeling and 
trends)
Status of Implementation
The establishment of the Centre of Excellence (CoE) has been approved through a Government Order, with 
NSRCEL, IIM Bangalore, designated as the Implementing Partner. The Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) has 
been duly executed. A press meet was conducted on 11th August 2025 to announce the launch of the IIMBx 
Fintech Certification Program, which was formally launched on 24th October 2025 with an inaugural cohort 
of over 500+ learners.The Centre of Excellence (CoE) Fin-Tech is a landmark initiative aimed at accelerating

3.6.7 CoE IoT powered by NASSCOM
The K-Tech Center of Excellence for IoT, at Bangalore, is a Digital India Initiative to jump start the IoT ecosystem 
in India taking advantage of India’s IT strengths and help country attain a leadership role in the convergent 
area of hardware and software. The main objective of the K-Tech CoE IoT is to help Indian IoT Startups leverage 
cutting edge technologies to build market ready product. The CoE, since its establishment in the year 2015 
has impacted over 1400+ Startups and the employees generated is 3500+ with more than 30+ IPs created and 
INR 1370 crore funds raised by the Startups associated with CoE – IoT.
3.6.8 K-Tech Innovation Hub by powered by NASSCOM Startups
The Government of Karnataka in line with its IT policy has set up a K-Tech Innovation Hub by NASSCOM, 
which is located in K-Wings, HSR Layout, Bengaluru with an objective to provide state of the art incubation & 
support for startups working on all kind of IT based applications, platforms or products and shared services 
in area such as marketing, finance and human resources which will help startups focus on their innovations.
During 2026, the innovation hub will start its Deep tech programme which will focus on strengthening the 
deep-tech ecosystem of Karnataka by supporting startups working in advanced areas such as AI, robotics, 
biotechnology, semiconductors, clean energy and aerospace. The programs will provide structured incubation 
and acceleration, mentorship, access to funding and advanced infrastructure such as prototyping facilities, 
while fostering strong industry–academia collaboration and partnerships with corporates, investors and 
government agencies.
3.6.9 CoE AVGC

interventions to upskill graduates, enhancing their production readiness and employability.

innovation and entrepreneurship. Investor Connect, the premier platform for early-stage funding, facilitated 
140 startup pitches over three days, fostering a vibrant atmosphere of dialogue and collaboration while 
enabling investors to discover ventures aligned with emerging technologies, market trends and representing 
diverse sectors such as Artificial Intelligence, MedTech, EdTech, SaaS, Cybersecurity, FinTech, Cleantech, 
Agritech and more. The Mentor–Mentee Sessions provided a powerful forum for 107 knowledge-sharing 
interactions, where industry leaders, investors and subject-matter experts offered practical insights and 
constructive guidance to aspiring entrepreneurs.
At the landmark Product Launch event, 50 cutting-edge and innovative products spanning diverse sectors 
such as Artificial Intelligence, Food Processing, Agritech, MedTech and more were unveiled, showcasing the 
creativity and entrepreneurial spirit of the ecosystem. The occasion was graced by the Hon’ble Minister for 
Information Technology and Biotechnology, whose presence underscored the government’s commitment to 
fostering innovation, supporting startups and accelerating technological advancement.
3.6.14 Bengaluru GAFX 2025 (Games, Animation, Visual Effects)
Bengaluru GAFX 2025 which took place between February 27th to March 1st 2025, emerged as one of India’s 
largest and most impactful AVGC-XR (Animation, VFX, Gaming, Comics & XR) conferences, supported by the 
Government of Karnataka.
Outcome: The event has achieved strong industry impact with massive participation, global presence, 
high value business outcomes, talent engagement and wide digital research by implementing Karnataka’s 
leadership in the AVGS and gaming ecosystem.  
Progress: The event has showed strong progress through high participation, global industry engagement, 
successful business outcomes, talent development and significant media research strengthening Karnatakaʼs 
AVGC ecosystem.
3.6.15 Global Linkages and Market Access
The Department of Electronics, IT, Biotechnology and Science & Technology has consistently advanced 
Karnataka’s vision of building a globally competitive and inclusive startup ecosystem. In 2025–26, landmark 
initiatives such as the Global Innovation Alliance Connect (GIA), Preferential Market Access (PMA) and the 
Propel Platform have been instrumental in empowering startups to access international markets, integrate 
into public procurement systems and accelerate growth through structured industry collaborations. These 
programs collectively strengthen Karnataka’s position as a hub for innovation-driven entrepreneurship 
by providing startups with global exposure, market validation and pathways to scale, while ensuring that 
government departments and industries benefit from cutting-edge technologies and solutions.

Global Innovation Alliance Connect (GIA)
The Objective of this programme is to explore technology and startup in GIA partner countries and also 
in Karnataka, connecting with the relevant stakeholders by understanding the regulations and other due 
diligence processes in GIA partner countries to help setup operations.
Achievements
 Y The Market Access Programs conducted across FY 2023–24 and 2024–25 connected Karnataka startups 
with global ecosystems through delegations to the UAE, Singapore, Belgium, Australia, Germany and 
Japan. 
 Y Across these missions, startups working in sectors such as Deep Tech, FinTech, Health Tech, Travel 
Tech, Cleantech, Biotech and other emerging technologies engaged with innovation hubs and industry 
partners. Programs were held in major global cities including Dubai, Sharjah, Abu Dhabi, Singapore, 
Brussels, Sydney, New Castle, Parramatta, Frankfurt, Cologne, Düsseldorf and Tokyo. 
 Y In total, 50 startups participated across these six international cohorts, gaining exposure to international 
markets, potential partnerships and investment opportunities.
Impact
The programme enables startups to access international innovation ecosystems in a structured way by 
reducing the financial barriers typically associated with global market exploration.
Key benefits include
 Y Facilitated international exposure: Startups gain curated access to global innovation hubs, including 
interactions with relevant industry stakeholders, ecosystem partners and institutional entities, enabling 
informed assessment of international market opportunities.
 Y Ecosystem and market understanding: The program enables startups to gain first-hand insights into 
regulatory environments, business practices and ecosystem dynamics of partner countries, supporting 
more informed internationalization decisions.
 Y Cost support through reimbursement: To ease the financial burden of participation, the program 
provides partial reimbursement of select travel-related expenses, subject to prescribed guidelines. This 
support is intended to encourage participation by reducing upfront costs associated with international 
engagement.
 Y Risk mitigation for early market exploration: By combining structured facilitation with financial 
support, GIA-MAP allows startups to explore global markets in a measured manner, without committing 
disproportionate resources at an early stage.
 Y Long-term collaboration opportunities: Beyond immediate exposure, the program helps startups 
establish initial international linkages that may be leveraged for future partnerships, pilots or expansion 
initiatives.

Karnataka Innovation Authority (KIA)
Objectives
The primary objective of the Karnataka Innovation Authority is to foster and regulate innovation in the 
state through a statutory framework. Its specific goals is to position Karnatakaas a prime destination for 
innovation and entrepreneurship, allowing businesses to conduct live testing of innovative products and 
services, by providing a safe and clear legal pathway for businesses to undertake product innovation, ensuring 
protection of citizens, consumers and workers from the potential harmful effects and risks associated with 
new technologieswhile innovation is encouraged, by allowing wide range of technological innovations to be 
tested.   
Impact
The establishment of the KIA and the implementation of the Regulatory Sandbox are designed to have the 
following impacts on various stakeholders:
For the Government and Regulators
 Y It enables regulators to make faster and better-informed decisions regarding emerging technologies. By 
observing innovations in a sandbox, the government can understand their implications before framing 
permanent laws.
 Y It helps in identifying and addressing regulatory barriers that hinder innovation. Successful experiments 
can lead to amendments in state laws, ensuring the legal framework keeps pace with technological 
advancements.
 Y By lowering entry barriers for innovative solutions, the Authority fosters a more competitive market 
environment.
For Businesses and Startups
 Y It provides a “safe space” for businesses to test the viability of their products without the fear of regulatory 
punitive action during the testing phase.
 Y Innovations that are successfully tested and deemed “safe” and “workable” are granted a clear path to 
enter the market.

PDF_PAGE 142
134
Investment and Exports
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
 Y If a product is successfully tested in the sandbox, businesses do not need to apply afresh for permissions 
to operate in the wider market, provided the legal framework is amended to accommodate them.
For Citizens and Consumers
 Y The framework includes rigorous risk mitigation strategies to ensure that innovations do not harm 
consumers. The sandbox acts as a filter to stop unsafe products from reaching the wider market.
 Y Citizens gain earlier access to beneficial technological solutions that might otherwise be delayed by 
outdated regulations.
3.7  VISVESVARAYA TRADE PROMOTION CENTRE
3.7.1 Exports of Karnataka
Karnataka maintains a distinguished legacy in overseas trade. Historically, the State has been a primary 
exporter of coffee, spices, silk, cashew nuts and handicrafts. However, in the current decade, it has evolved 
into a global powerhouse for Knowledge and Technology.
Karnataka has carved out a niche for itself in the global marketplace as India’s premier knowledge and 
technology capital and a Global Innovation Hub. The State has made rapid and spectacular strides in the 
new economy. Information technology, biotechnology and a dense ecosystem of research and development 
institutions (like ISRO and DRDO) have significantly enhanced Karnataka’s achievements at national and 
global levels. As of 2025, Karnataka accounts for over 40% of India’s total computer software and services 
exports and is the undisputed leader nationally. The State of Karnataka also contributes to the country’s 
aerospace-related exports. The state is also a leader in exports of traditional commodities like coffee, spices 
and engineering goods from the Southern Region.
3.7.2 Export performance of Karnataka
As of 2025, Karnataka continues its dominance as India’s leading export powerhouse, ranking 1st in Services 
exports with a 41% national share and 4th in Merchandise exports. The State remains the national leader 
in overall combined exports. The Visvesvaraya Trade Promotion Centre (VTPC), under the Department of 
Industries and Commerce, serves as the Nodal Agency, facilitating global trade and promoting Karnataka’s 
record 49 Geographical Indication (GI) products. Export performance analysis is conducted using data from 
Directorate General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics (DGCIS), Kolkata.
Karnataka’s overall exports have increased by 13.78% during 2025-26 as compared to the year 2024-25. 
Karnataka’s exports in terms of value in 2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26 (April to September 2025) 
are shown in Table 3.3.
Karnataka’s exports amounted to about Rs.16,02,865.29 Crores in 2024-25 which constituted about 22.96% 
of the Country’s exports in the year. The share of Merchandise exports in the National exports constitutes 
around 6.96% and Software/ Service exports around 41 % for the year 2024-25. Exports of electronics and 
computer software and other service sector constitute the largest share in the State’s exports. The other 
commodities which registered good increase in share of Karnataka’s exports in 2024-25 as compared to 2023-
24 are Coffee, Engineering Goods, Spices, Chemical and Allied Products, Plastic Goods, Aerospace and Optical 
and Medical Instrument. Decline in exports in 2024-25 comparison to 2023-24 were witnessed in the case 
of Petroleum, Agriculture and Processed Food Products, Iron Ore and Minerals, Gems & Jewellery, Semi-
Conductor, Wool and Woolen Products. All other sectors recorded increase in State export performance.

3.7.5 Policy support for exports
While foreign trade remains under the Central List of the Indian Constitution, Karnataka’s role is vital in 
creating a competitive local ecosystem. Under the Karnataka Industrial Policy 2025-30, the State has launched 
a transformational roadmap to attract investments.
For MSMEs, the policy offers a capital subsidy and turnover-based PLI to enhance global competitiveness. 
Further support includes stamp duty exemptions, land conversion fee reimbursements and specific grants for 
international quality certifications. By prioritizing Beyond Bengaluru industrial clusters and providing extra 
booster incentives for women-led enterprises, Karnataka ensures that its MSMEs are not only export-ready 
but are also integral to the state’s vision of a $1 trillion economy.

3.8  KARNATAKA UDYOGA MITRA
Ease of Doing Business initiatives in Karnataka
Under Ease of Doing Business, Karnataka has achieved the following:
 Y Karnataka has been recognized as a “Top Achiever” under the EoDB-Business Reform Action Plan 2024, 
having secured this position by successfully implementing 434 reform recommendations for businesses 
3 times consecutively.
 Y Karnataka has strengthened its governance framework by ensuring the time-bound delivery of public 
services, thereby enhancing transparency, accountability and citizen trust. Through the SAKALA 
initiative, the state guarantees timely delivery of 1,300+ services, supported by clearly defined timelines, 
real-time tracking and automatic escalation mechanisms. This has significantly reduced delays, improved 
administrative efficiency and ensured that citizens receive services within the stipulated timeframes.
 Y Karnataka has adopted LGD codes across all departments, along with PAN as unique business identifier, 
to create a common and standardized data system. This ensures accurate, consistent and seamless data 
sharing between departments, improving coordination and efficiency. It also strengthens monitoring and 
feedback systems by using uniform identifiers for all administrative units. In the future, linking LGD codes 
with GIS mapping will support better planning, targeted development and data-driven decision-making.
 Y Karnataka Decriminalization Bill 2025 - Karnataka is 1st State to decriminalize highest number of clauses 
282 clauses under 12 Acts under single enactment. 
 Y MRCB-Decriminalization - A consolidated inventory of 606 identified Compliances and imprisonment/
Fine Clauses across 112 Central & State Acts/Rules (30 Central Acts and 36 State Acts, 6 Central Rules and 
40 State Rules) and conducted consultation meetings with Law Commission of Karnataka for UDD related 
Acts for decriminalization.
 Y Under Minimizing Regulatory Compliance Burden (MRCB) Government of Karnataka has undertaken 
initiatives to simplify, rationalize and digitize Government procedures and interfaces. Out of 3,556 
compliances identified, 3,458 (97.24%) burdensome compliances were reduced, including simplification 
of 2,248 business compliances and 824 citizen compliances. 
 Y Business-centric services with processing timelines exceeding 20 working days were identified for 
Government Process Re-engineering, including the rationalization of timelines, required documents and 
the number of steps involved in the existing service procedures.

PDF_PAGE 151
143
Investment and Exports
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
 Y Karnataka has successfully completed Compliance Reduction and Deregulation across 23 priority 
areas related to Land, Building and Construction, Labor, Utilities & Permissions and Overarching areas, 
simplifying regulations and removing outdated & redundant compliances. 
 Y Karnataka has developed the State-of-the-Art Single Window System enabled with Artificial Intelligence 
for auto-scrutiny of DPRs, Power BI based analytical dashboards, Chatbots for query resolution etc. has 
been envisioned to facilitate Ease of Access to information. As on date a total of 114+ Departmental 
Services have been onboarded to Single Window System.
 Y A list of 125 Business Specific Services has been notified under Sakala. 
 Y As part of its Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) reforms, Karnataka has introduced a first-of-its-kind combined

 Y During 2025–26, six meetings of the State Level Single Window Clearance Committee (SLSWCC) were

Way forward of Karnataka Udyoga Mitra
 Y Karnataka would be working on implementation of reforms shared under by DPIIT, GoI.
 ) State Business Action Plan (SBRAP) 2026 includes 74 services that are scheduled to be implemented

This phase will focus on further simplifying rules, removing residual and low-value compliances,

 Y Government Process Re-engineering of business-centric approvals will be focused by analyzing the

Executive Summary
 Y Karnataka continues to be one of India’s leading industrial States with a diversified industrial base covering 
MSMEs, large and medium industries and high-technology sectors such as aerospace, electronics, 
biotechnology, renewable energy, EVs, clean mobility and advanced manufacturing.
 Y Progressive policies, robust infrastructure and an investor-friendly ecosystem have strengthened 
Karnataka’s position as a preferred destination for domestic and global investments.

industrial hub, with a target of Rs.7.5 lakh crore investment and 20 lakh jobs by 2030.
