INTRODUCTION
Rural development is a foundational pillar of Karnataka’s development architecture, encompassing systematic, 
multi-dimensional interventions aimed at enhancing the quality of life and economic well-being of the state’s 
rural population. Despite accelerating urbanisation, nearly 61 per cent of Karnataka’s residents continue to 
reside in rural areas. Although the rural share of the population has gradually declined over time and at 
a pace faster than the national average, the state, like India as a whole, continues to retain the essential 
characteristics of a predominantly rural and agrarian economy. Over the past two decades, economic growth 
has facilitated a structural transformation marked by the progressive movement of labour from agriculture to 
non-agricultural sectors. Yet, the persistence of rural demographic predominance underscores the continued 
relevance of targeted rural development strategies. In this context, a focused and integrated approach to 
rural development remains indispensable for achieving sustained economic growth alongside inclusive and 
equitable human development.
Decentralised planning, aligned with effective implementation of rural development programmes, plays a 
transformative role in strengthening service delivery and deepening grassroots democracy. Karnataka’s 
Panchayat Raj system represents one of the most extensive and institutionally evolved decentralised 
governance frameworks in the country, comprising 5,946 Grama Panchayats at the lower level, 239 
Taluk Panchayats at the intermediate tier, and 31 Zilla Panchayats at the district level. Following the 73rd 
Constitutional Amendment, Karnataka became the first state in India to enact comprehensive enabling 
legislation, the Karnataka Panchayat Raj Act, 1993. This legislative framework conferred constitutional status 
upon Panchayat Raj Institutions (PRIs), formally recognising them as institutions of self-government entrusted 
with the preparation and implementation of development plans that foster economic growth while ensuring 
social justice through equitable distribution of developmental benefits.
4.1 RURAL DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMMES: FOUNDATIONS AND INSTITUTIONAL IMPERATIVES
Rural development programmes in Karnataka are designed to promote dignified and sustainable living 
conditions in rural areas by ensuring access to essential public services through safe drinking water, sanitation, 
street lighting, primary healthcare, elementary education, and reliable transport connectivity. These 
foundational amenities not only improve quality of life but also enhance agricultural productivity, support 
allied rural enterprises, and promote efficient management of natural and financial resources. Accordingly, 
rural development interventions emphasise housing, water supply, sanitation, road infrastructure, and 
employment generation, recognising that infrastructure and livelihoods must advance together to achieve 
sustainable progress.
The effectiveness of these programmes depends significantly on the institutional capacity of Panchayat 
Raj Institutions (PRIs). Despite their constitutional status, Panchayats continue to face constraints such as 
limited financial autonomy, inadequate devolution of authority, insufficient women, youth participation, 
and political interference. Addressing these challenges requires meaningful devolution of funds, functions, 
and functionaries, the “three Fs” central to genuine decentralisation. Greater fiscal empowerment, clearly 
defined responsibilities, and adequate staffing would enable Panchayats to undertake responsive and context-
specific planning. Expanding their role into areas like renewable energy promotion, rural electrification, skill 
development, small-scale industries, and vocational education would further align local governance with 
evolving rural needs.

4.1.1 Strengthening Accountability and Institutional Capacity
Sustained rural development also requires robust accountability mechanisms. Effective utilisation of Finance 
Commission grants, particularly for water supply, sanitation, sewage, and solid waste management, demands 
systematic monitoring and regular statutory audits at the local level. Transparent audit practices can 
strengthen financial discipline and public trust.
Simultaneously, structured capacity-building initiatives are essential to enhance the effectiveness of PRIs. 
Training in the preparation and implementation of Grama Panchayat Development Plans (GPDPs) would 
promote evidence-based and participatory planning. The recruitment of adequate technical and support staff 
at the village level would further improve administrative efficiency. Together, financial devolution, functional 
strengthening, rigorous oversight, and institutional capacity-building form the cornerstone of accountable 
and effective rural governance in Karnataka.

For the financial year 2025–26, the department has been allocated a total budget of Rs.26,735.74 crore to 
implement its various programmes and initiatives. Out of this allocation, Rs.8,894.46 crore has been released 
so far. An amount of Rs.7,910.03 crore has been utilised up to the end of December 2025, including expenditure 
met from the opening balance, reflecting the ongoing implementation of schemes across sectors.

4.3 HOUSING
Housing is a basic and very important need for every citizen. Housing not only provides social security to human 
beings but it also provides status in the society.  Housing has evolved as a prime component over the period 
of time not only in providing shelter but also for providing employment opportunities and in development of 
localities. To meet the growing demand for housing, the State Government has been pro-active in its housing 
policies. Housing for the poor and down-trodden assumes greater importance in the State. Every successive 
Government has given greater attention to the problem of housing scarcity and increased the budgetary 
allocation year after year. 
4.3.1 Rajiv Gandhi Housing Corporation Limited
This Corporation has been established by the State Government on 20.04.2000, to implement all the State 
and Central Government sponsored housing schemes for economically and socially weaker sections of the 
Society both in rural and urban areas. The main objectives of the Company are:
 Y To provide houses to the Socially and Economically Weaker sections of the society. 
 Y Speedy implementation of schemes.
 Y Transparency in implementation.
 Y Smooth flow of funds to ensure that the funds reach the ultimate beneficiaries in time.
 Y To encourage cost effective technology in construction through District Nirmithi Kendras. 
 Y Strengthening of Nirmithi Kendras.
Various housing schemes implemented in rural areas are Rural Ashraya /Basava Vasathi yojane, Devraj Urs

4.4 RURAL INFRASTRUCTURE
4.4.1 Karnataka Rural Infrastructure Development Ltd (KRIDL)
The Karnataka Rural Infrastructure Development Limited (Formerly known as Karnataka Land Army Corporation 
Limited) is having an objective to undertake and carry out all types of rural development work either entrusted 
to it by Government, Government Departments, Local Bodies, Undertakings, Institutions, Individuals etc., or 
on its own, and to provide assistance, advice and services therefore, including capital resource and technical, 
managerial and other services. The objective is to concentrate on labour intensive infrastructure works which 
are vital for development by providing employment opportunities to rural unemployed and under employed 
to improve their economic conditions and to undertake all rural development construction works directly by 
eliminating middlemen i.e., Contractors, to avoid exploitation of the rural poor, thereby passing on the full 
worth of money to the people. 
To attain the main object of the Company, the Company undertakes civil construction of tanks, irrigation 
works, low-cost housing, roads, culverts and buildings etc., in rural areas employing rural youth. The works 
are being executed directly at Government Scheduled Rates without the involvement of contractors. The 
Organization is a designed agency of the State Government for the purpose of departmental execution of 
works. 
4.4.2 Quality Policy
KRIDL is committed for enhancing its success with services and responsiveness that set industry standards 
for not only quality and value, but for efficiency as well. The Company relentlessly strive to be the best in 
every aspect of the Company’s business, fostering a culture of high expectations and accurate delivery-at 
quick turn-around times. Credibility is everything, trust is inherent and responsibility lies with each individual. 
Transparent processes guarantee progression and efficient delivery controls reputation.    
During 2024-25, KRIDL has achieved turnover of Rs. Rs.2872.67 Crores with a net profit of Rs.292.42 crores. 
During the year 2025-26, the agency has achieved a progress of Rs.2193.15 crores (provisional) and  profit is 
Rs. 231.81 crores up to end of December 2025.

4.6  RURAL WATER SUPPLY
The Department of Rural Drinking Water and Sanitation is providing safe and adequate drinking water and 
sanitation facilities to the rural areas. Initially it was aimed to supply 55 LPCD potable water to each person 
every day and aims to provide household connections in all the habitations through the piped water supply 
schemes.
4.6.1 Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM)
The Central Government has an ambitious project, Jal Jeevan Mission, titled ‘Har Ghar Jal’, to provide clean 
water to all households in the country. The Jal Jeevan Mission Project is being implemented with the great 
objective of providing safe drinking water to all households in rural India by 2024 by providing Functional 
Household Tap Connection (FHTC). In addition to maintaining water sources, grey water management, water 
conservation, rain water harvesting and water source replenishment are also part of the project. Effective 
information, education and communication are the highlights of the project, which include a community-
based approach to aquatic life. The Water Life Mission will create a nationwide movement for water and this 
is everyone’s priority. 
Out of a total of 101,30,702 households in rural areas of the State, access to drinking water to the households 
is 24,51,220 before the implementation of the Jal Jeevan Mission and 63,12,480 households have been 
provided with water supply after the implementation of the Jal Jeevan Mission. 86.51 % of households in the 
State have water connection. Each of the 6768 villages in the State has the distinction of being 100% FHTC-
enabled villages with water connections under the Jal Jeevan Mission.
In rural areas, the water system is considered to be the responsibility of the women in addition to maintaining 
the households. Village Water and Sanitation Committees have been set up in more than 28,000 villages 
across the State, with over 1.5 lakh women taking a leadership role in managing their community water 
resources, to make them self-sufficient and empowered.
Women in rural areas may have greater responsibilities with managing water at home. Water quality 
surveillance from the local community of women enlightened citizens are essential for the delivery of service, 
training at least five women in each village to test the quality of potable water using Field Testing Kits (FTK) 
to test the quality of drinking water and to understand the effects of water-based chemical or bacterial 
contamination. Their ability to conduct hygiene checks is being developed. Information from women’s 
inspection is being given priority to take appropriate remedial measures to improve or protect drinking water 
sources and supply systems. Mason, plumber, electrician, motor mechanic and pump operator are being 
trained by the department to ensure long-term sustainability of water supply systems.
For 2025-26, it is targeted to provide 10.00 lakh FHTCs, 2.39 lakh FHTCs are provided by incurring an 
expenditure of Rs. 446.15 crore up to the end of December 2025.
4.7 WATER QUALITY MONITORING AND SURVEILLANCE PROGRAMME (WQM&SP)
Under Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM), water quality monitoring has been given utmost importance, as the water 
quality needs to be monitored on a regular basis to ensure potable water gets supplied to the rural households. 
There are about 2,20,000 rural public drinking water sources established in the State. 
At present, there are 31 District/ division level water quality testing laboratories and 47 Sub-divisional/Taluka 
level water quality testing laboratories in the state. Out of these 28 District/division level laboratories are 
NABL accredited & 46 Sub-divisional/Taluka level are recognized by NABL. These laboratories undertake 
analysis of totally 16 physio-chemical and microbiological parameters for the drinking water sources.

PDF_PAGE 161
153
Rural Development
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
Field water testing kits have been distributed to all the 5946 Gram Panchayaths to test the water during pre- 
and post-monsoon seasons. Training is also imparted to village water and sanitation committee (VWSC) for 
testing water quality using the kits.
4.8 MULTI VILLAGE SCHEME 
Drinking water supply schemes under Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) have been formulated in rural areas with surface 
water as source to tackle water quality problem. Habitations having ground water chemical contamination like 
Arsenic, Fluoride, TDS, Nitrate and Iron, the drinking water, will be supplied from nearest sustainable surface 
source after treatment. A total of 160 MVS schemes are taken up with an estimated cost of Rs. 37,561.36 
Crores, of which 136 MVS schemes are under progress with an estimated cost of Rs. 35,836.79 Crores and 1 
MVS scheme is yet to be awarded, remaining 23 MVS schemes are under administrative approval.
4.9   RURAL SANITATION
4.9.1 Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM)-Gramin
As per the baseline survey conducted during the year 2012, it was reported that there were 70.26 lakh 
households, out of which 24.84 lakhs households had toilets and 45.42 lakh households were without 
toilets. Individual Household Latrines (IHHLs) were constructed for all the households that were reported to 
be without toilets by 19 th November 2018 and Rural Karnataka was declared Open Defecation Free on 19 th 
November 2018 on the eve of World Toilet Day. For the year 2025-26, an amount of Rs.383.04 Crores has 
been allocated in the budget for implementation of SBM-G scheme of which an amount of Rs.140 crores is 
released. Rs.77.78 crores has been spent at the end of Dec-2025.
4.9.2 Objectives of SBM (G) Phase II
The key objective of SBM (G) Phase II is to sustain the ODF status of villages and to improve the levels of 
cleanliness in rural areas through solid and liquid waste management activities, making villages ODF Plus. 
The above objective is to be achieved through continued Behaviour Change Communication and Capacity 
Strengthening at all levels. The biggest challenge of the SBM-G Program is to sustain the Open Defecation 
Free Status. In this regard, to sustain the Open Defecation Free Status, and to work on ODF-Plus activities, 
the Ministry of Jal Shakti, Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation has continued the implementation of 
Swachh Bharat Mission-Gramin (SBM-G) Phase II from 2020-21 to 2025-26. 
As per the guidelines of the programme, the following ODF-S (Sustainability) and ODF-Plus activities are being 
undertaken. 
 Y  Cons truction and usage of Individual Household Latrines (IHHL).
 Y  Cons truction of Community Sanitary Complex (CSC).
 Y  Solid an d Liquid Waste Management (SLWM).
 Y  Ma terial Recovery Facility (MRF).
 Y  Cons truction of Faecal Sludge Management (FSM) Unit.
 Y  Cons truction of GOBARDHAN Unit.
 Y  ODF-S a nd ODF-Plus centric Information, Education and Communication, and Training activities.
The responsibility of implementation of SBM(G) programmes and activities fully vests with the Gram Panchayat 
institutions.

4.12 WAGE EMPLOYMENT PROGRAMMES
4.12.1 Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS)
Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act is being implemented in all the districts with an 
objective to enhance livelihood security in rural areas by providing 100 days of guaranteed wage employment 
in a financial year to every household whose adult members volunteered to do unskilled manual work as per 
demand, resulting in evaluation of productive assets of prescribed quality and durability, Strengthening the 
livelihood resource base of the poor, Pro actively ensuring social inclusion and strengthening of PRIs. Funds 
will be shared between the GoI & GoK in the ratio of 90:10 Labour and material ratio shall be maintained at 
60:40.
For 2025-26, an amount of Rs.3404.13 crores has been released as against the outlay of Rs. 5800.0 crores 
(including wage component), of which Rs.2918.97 crores has been utilized to generate 680.35 lakh mandays 
up to Dec 2025. About 21.5 lakhs households have been provided employment as against the demand of 
45.28 lakh during the current year.  8.93 lakh works have been undertaken of which 2.94 lakh works are 
completed and the remaining 5.99 lakhs works are under progress.

4.14 RESPONSIBILITY MAP 
As part of the 30th anniversary of the Karnataka Gram Swaraj and Panchayat Raj Act, 1993, a responsibility 
map has been scientifically formulated to strengthen the decentralization system and to transfer the functions 
allocated to the Gram Panchayats under the 73rd Amendment to the Constitution.
The Notification has been issued for fixing the responsibility of the programmes/activities among the 
Panchayath Raj Institutions of the following departments namely, Scheduled Tribes Welfare, Health and 
Family Welfare, Backward Classes Welfare, Agriculture, Watershed Development, Sericulture, Minority 
Welfare, Scheduled Castes Welfare, Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Services, Energy and Horticulture.
4.15 VISION PLAN
The 73rd Amendment to the Constitution has transferred 29 functions to Panchayat Raj Institutions and 
Karnataka has made significant progress in strengthening these institutions along with empowering 
the community. The provisions of the Karnataka Gram Swaraj and Panchayat Raj Act have provided a 
good opportunity in this direction. An important provision as per Section 309(B) of this Act relates to the 
preparation of vision plans of Gram Panchayats after the elections. Apart from involving the community 
through Participatory Rural Appraisal (PRA), it should be prepared keeping in mind the state and local goals. 
Karnataka has taken up this initiative.
The State has considered local sustainable development goals in the process of preparing the vision plan and 
the Panchayat Raj institutions, especially the Gram Panchayats are the focal points for these achievements. 
The state has identified the following areas namely, Poverty, livelihood and skill development, Health, 
Education, Women and child development, Environment and natural resources, Socially Secured Panchayats, 
Infrastructure self-sufficient Gram Panchayats and Good governance for preparing the Gram Panchayat Vision 
Plan.
For each of the above areas, indicators have been identified for the purpose of setting targets and the Gram 
Panchayats have collected the relevant data with the support of officials from other development departments.
The following process has been adopted for preparing the plan at the Gram Panchayat level:
Step –1: Formation of Gram Panchayat and Village Planning Committees
Step –2: Secondary Data collection

4.17 e-GOVERNANCE
4.17.1 eSwathu 2.0
The Rural Development and Panchayat Raj (RDPR) Department manages approximately 1.5 crore property 
records (Khatas), which were traditionally maintained in manual registers at the Gram Panchayat level. 
Citizens were previously required to physically visit Gram Panchayat offices to avail Khata-related services. 
To modernize and streamline property administration, the Government of Karnataka has mandated eKhata 
for all property registrations with effect from October 2024. Further, pursuant to the Karnataka Gram Swaraj 
and Panchayat Raj (Amendment) Act, 2025, the Department is shifting from a demand-driven model to a 
campaign-based initiative.
In line with the above statutory amendments, the Department has notified the Karnataka Gram Swaraj and 
Panchayat Raj (Taxes, Rates and Fees of Gram Panchayats) Rules, 2025. Under these Rules, the Department 
shall facilitate the issuance of eKhatas for over 95 lakh digitized properties available on the Panchatantra 2.0 
platform, enabling citizens to obtain their eKhatas completely through online mode, without the need to visit 
the Gram Panchayat office through eSwathu 2.0 Application.

5.1 URBAN DEVELOPMENT
Urban development remains a central pillar of Karnataka’s growth strategy, positioning cities as engines of 
economic dynamism and social inclusion. With rapid urbanisation reshaping demographic and economic 
patterns, the State is strengthening Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) to deliver sustainable, resilient, and citizen-
centric services. The Government’s approach integrates fiscal investment, environmental stewardship, and 
technology-driven governance to enhance liveability, competitiveness, and balanced regional growth.
The Urban Development Department, excluding housing and slum development, is responsible for ensuring 
essential civic amenities, progressive urban planning, infrastructure upgradation, and effective implementation 
of State and Central schemes. With rapid urbanisation and expanding city boundaries, the Department’s 
mandate has widened considerably to address growing infrastructural and governance demands. Its core 
responsibilities include the provision of urban infrastructure, ensuring drinking water supply and sewerage 
systems, preparation of comprehensive and progressive development plans for sustainable city management, 
upgrading and reforming basic infrastructure, extending accommodation and support services to vulnerable 
groups, and implementing State, Central, and other externally supported schemes.
5.2 URBAN DEVELOPMENT: BUDGETARY COMMITMENT AND INFRASTRUCTURE FOCUS
For the financial year 2025–26, a budgetary allocation of Rs.18,249.71 crore has been made for Urban 
Development programmes. Of this, Rs.12,183.58 crore has been expended up to the end of December 2025, 
reflecting steady progress in implementation.
Urban infrastructure encompasses critical services such as drinking water supply, sanitation, sewerage 
systems, electricity and gas distribution, urban transport, primary health services, and environmental 
regulation. These services are essential for sustaining economic growth, managing population expansion, 
and enhancing the quality of urban life.
Karnataka is among the water-stressed states in India. Approximately 38 per cent of its population resides 
in urban areas, compared to the national average of 28 per cent. In this context, effective water resource 
management and sustainable sanitation systems are indispensable to prevent water scarcity from becoming 
a constraint on economic development.
5.3 KARNATAKA URBAN WATER SUPPLY AND DRAINAGE BOARD (KUWS&DB)
The Karnataka Urban Water Supply and Drainage Board (KUWS&DB) is a statutory authority and a designated 
implementing agency responsible for planning and executing drinking water supply schemes and underground 
drainage (UGD) systems in 316 Urban Local Bodies, excluding areas under the jurisdiction of the Greater 
Bangalore Authority (Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike).
The Board’s mandate is to ensure adequate and safe drinking water from assured sources, along with effective 
sanitation and sewerage services across urban areas of the State. To date, assured and safe surface water–
based drinking water projects have been implemented in 259 Urban Local Bodies. Underground sewerage 
facilities have been provided in 82 Urban Local Bodies.

5.3.3 Information on Innovation and Best Practices
Board has implemented prestigious challenged Projects in the recent years and received award from the 
Government of India. Such projects are:-  
“Drink from Tap” Continuous Water Supply (24x7) in Alnavar Town, Karnataka - A Scalable Model for Small-
Town Water Reform:
Alnavar, a town in Dharwad District in Karnataka, successfully transitioned from a severely intermittent and 
inefficient water supply system to a fully metered, 24x7 Drink from Tap (DfT) model. 
Alnavar stands as the first small town in Karnataka to deliver universal, continuous, and pressurized Drink 
from Tap (DfT) 24x7 water supply system which can be referred to as ‘A Scalable Model for Small-Town Water 
Reform’. 
The Water Supply Scheme to Alnavar Town with an estimated cost of Rs.71.90 crores, with the Kali River as 
the source was commissioned in July 2022 The Government of India has identified the said project and an 
Appreciation of Special Mention for Local Solutions in Regional Language in the Urban Learnathon 2023 was 
given by National Institute of Urban Affairs, Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, GoI.
5.3.4 Replenishment of Tolanakeri lake using PHYTORID Technology STP for replenishment of 
Tolanakeri lake, Hubballi city under AMRUT
Recognized by National Water Mission, Ministry of Jal Shakti, Department of Water Resources, Government of 
India (https://nwm.gov.in/replenishment-tolanakeri-re-using-treated-used-wate)as a BEST PRACTICE under 
the theme of REUSE OF TREATED WATER during December 2024 and documented on the official National 
Water Mission portal.
5.3.5 Background
Tolanakeri Lake, located in the Akshay Park area of Hubballi city, Dharwad District, Karnataka, usually dried up 
during the summer, to address this, an alternative water source was established through a decentralized Used 
Water Treatment Plant (UWTP) near the lake to treat used water collected from surrounding areas via the 

PDF_PAGE 171
163
Urban Development
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
existing sewer line, in compliance with KSCPB norms. The UWTP was also designed to integrate aesthetically 
with the lake environment and surrounding landscaping.
Accordingly, the Karnataka Urban Water Supply & Drainage Board (KUWS&DB) implemented a 1 MLD Phytorid 
UWTP under the AMRUT scheme on the upstream side of the lake. The plant draws used water from a nearby 
sewer trunk main, treats it to tertiary standards, and discharges the treated water into Tolanakeri Lake to 
replenish and maintain water levels.
5.3.6 Objectives
Replenishment of Tolanakeri lake which has a capacity of about 900 ML with the following objectives:
 Y Maintain water level in the lake at FTL (Full Tank Level) throughout the year.
 Y Provide alternative source of water to the lake in absence of rains.
 Y Improve the ground water table.
 Y Improvements in the bio-diversity of the lake.
 Y Improvement of recreational activities.
5.3.7 Innovation
The construction of a decentralized Used Water Treatment Plant (UWTP) using Phytorid technology in the 
vicinity of a water body, utilizing sewer mains aligned with the natural topography, represents an innovative 
approach to providing a sustainable water source for lakes or other water bodies.
5.3.8 Outcome
Operational Status and Outcomes of Tolanakeri UWT.
The Used Water Treatment Plant (UWTP) was commissioned in May 2020. The implementation of this project 
has resulted in the following improvements:
 Y Continuous discharge of approximately 1 MLD of treated used water prevents the lake from drying up, 
providing an alternative water source in the absence of rainfall.
 Y Increase in the groundwater table in the surrounding area.
 Y Enhanced recreational activities in and around the lake.
 Y Improved aesthetic environment through the cultivation of ornamental and flowering plants.
 Y Enhancement of the lake’s biodiversity.
5.3.9  Phytorid Technology For Used Water Treatment Plant
It is a self-sustaining technology developed by National Environmental Engineering Research Institute 
(NEERI), CSIR that works on the principle of natural wetland. It has been developed and patented by CSIR- 
National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (CSIR - NEERI). This technology has also obtained the 
authorization from Council of Scientific & Industrial Research.
PHYTORID system is based on natural treatment methods and has distinctive advantages over conventional 
treatment plants. In this technology, treatment occurs via natural methods such as filtration, sedimentation, 
nutrient uptake by plants and microbial action in a constructed system which is filled with filter media. 
Specifically identified species of plants which are known to have good nutrient uptake are planted in the filter 
media.

Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
5.4 KARNATAKA URBAN INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT AND FINANCE CORPORATION 
(KUIDFC)
Development of Infrastructure works in ULBs and also to provide technical, financial, consultancy and other 
assistance, KUIDFC has been established during 1993.
5.4.1 Nodal Agency
KUIDFC has been appointed as the Nodal Agency of the State for implementation of various External Aided 
Project and Central & State Government sponsored urban infrastructure development projects in the state. 
KUIDFC acts as nodal agency for utilizing funds from Government of Karnataka, Government of India, World 
Bank, ADB and raise resources from Financial Markets, provides financial and technical assistance to all Urban 
Local Bodies also provides financial assistance in the form of loans and grants for Urban Infrastructure Projects 
taken up by the ULBs.
5.5 KARNATAKA INTEGRATED URBAN WATER MANAGEMENT INVESTMENT PROGRAM 
(KIUWMIP)
The Karnataka Integrated Urban Water Management Investment Program (KIUWMIP): KIUWMIP is 
implementing ADB assisted programme to provide Under Ground Drainage (UGD) facility and continuous 
water supply to selected Eight (08) towns/cities namely, Davanagere, Harihara, Ranebennur, Byadgi, 
Mangalore, Udupi, Puttur & Kundapura and also implementing reforms in selected Urban Local Bodies. 
The cost of the project is of Rs.2607.00 crores (Tranche-1 & 2) and the cumulative expenditure is of Rs.2427.00 
crores. This project covers 377 Sq.km area and benefits 1.3 million population. During the current year, an 
amount of Rs.50.00 crores is allocated in the budget, of which Rs.33.74 crores has been spent up to the end

5.6 BANGALORE WATER SUPPLY AND SEWERAGE BOARD
The Bengaluru Water Supply & Sewerage Board (BWSSB) is a statutory body of the Government of Karnataka 
responsible for providing potable water supply and sewerage services to Bengaluru city and its expanded 
areas, including newly added villages. The Board manages water sourcing (primarily from the Cauvery River), 
treatment, transmission, distribution, sewerage networks, sewage treatment plants (STPs), wastewater 
reuse, billing, and customer services.
5.6.1 Vision and Mission
 Y  T o ensure sustainable, reliable, and equitable water supply and sewerage services for Bengaluru while 
protecting water resources and the environment.
 Y Provide safe and adequate drinking water to all sections of society.
 Y Achieve comprehensive sewerage coverage and effective wastewater treatment.
 Y Promote water conservation, reuse, rainwater harvesting, and smart water management through 
technology and innovation.
5.6.2 Projects Status
 Y  Cauv ery Water Supply Scheme (including Stage V): Augmentation of water supply to meet the needs of 
a growing population and newly added areas.
 Y Sewerage & STPs: Expansion and upgradation of Sewage Treatment Plants with tertiary treatment 
facilities.
 Y Treated Water Reuse: Supply of treated wastewater for industrial use, lake rejuvenation, gardening, 
construction, and groundwater recharge.
 Y Smart Metering & Digital Initiatives: Pilot implementation of smart water meters for real-time consumption 
monitoring, leak detection, reduction of non-revenue water, and improved billing efficiency.

5.9 URBAN TRANSPORT
5.9.1 Directorate of Urban Land Transport 
The Directorate of Urban Land Transport has implemented several initiatives including service level 
benchmarking in Bengaluru, preparation of policies on parking, preparation of comprehensive mobility 
plans for 16 cities; feasibility studies for mass transit systems (Suburban Rail Projects) etc. It is also working 
in tandem with BBMP and other city corporations on Non-Motorized Transport (NMT) initiatives. The Bus 
Rapid Transit (BRT) system between the twin cities of Hubballi and Dharwad, taken up by Directorate of 
Urban Land Transport has been completed and commissioned for public use. DULT is also spearheading the 
implementation of Suburban Rail Projects in Bengaluru through K-RIDE. To improvise Public Transport in the 
State, DULT has closely collaborated with state transport undertakings for the development of infrastructure 
like terminals, workshops, depots etc.

5.9.3 State Urban Transport Fund
The State Urban Transport Fund has been leveraged to promote DULT’s mandate across cities in Karnataka. 
The fund has been used to provide assistance for introduction of Public Transport System in cities of Karnataka, 
assistance for construction of Transit Infrastructure in cities, implementation of Non-Motorised Transport 
systems and development of projects/feasibility study reports etc. 
Over a period of 12 years from 2012 to 2024, 93 projects have been completed. The completed projects 
include projects such as construction of bus terminals, bus depots, tyre re-treading workshops, bus-only 
flyovers, introduction of public transport in the 16 cities for the first time and in 8 cities augmentation of 
city bus services enhancing the existing Public Transport services by the agencies (BMTC, KSRTC, NEKRTC, 
NWKRTC). 
All the completed projects have been commissioned for public use. About Rs.837.31 crores have been provided 
as financial assistance under SUTF over these years.  There are 56 urban transport projects implemented 
through Road Transport Corporations for which Rs.424.67 crores financial assistance under the SUTF is made 
and Rs.246.94 Crores has been released.

5.9.6 Public Bicycle Sharing System in Bengaluru
The public bicycle sharing system in Bengaluru is a dock-less model, where multiple private bicycle sharing 
operators will offer their services in various parts of the city. The cycles can be located and unlocked using a 
mobile phone application provided by the service provider and the user will be charged based on the duration 
of usage. 
M/s YULU Bikes Pvt. Ltd., has been issued permits to operate 100 PBS and 7000 SMMS vehicles for the 
implementation of new Public Bicycle Sharing – Shared Micro Mobility System.
5.9.7 Public Bicycle Sharing System in Mysuru
With an intent to upgrade the existing PBS system and expand to larger area in Mysuru, PBS system in Mysuru 
is being revamped by introducing 1000 new pedal assisted bicycles spread across 100 stations. The system 
provides an alternative. Currently, the system is operationalized with 500 pedal assisted electric bicycles, by 
the successful bidder. The revamped system shall also improve the sustainability of the PBS projects. 
5.9.8 ASPIRE 2.0
“ASPIRE” is DULT’s annual research program under Center for Research and Innovation (CERI) to identify 
priority research areas in urban mobility, encompassing both technological and policy-focused studies. After 
the successful completion of 1st edition of ASPIRE program, which funded six research projects on diverse 
urban mobility topics, 2nd edition of ASPIRE program was launched in 2025. DULT received 50 applications 
for five research statements from academic institutions, consultants and individual researchers across the 
country. After detailed examination of proposals with the assistance of an expert committee, 5 research 
entities were selected and the research study for all the topics are underway.

5.10 BENGALURU METRO RAIL CORPORATION LIMITED (BMRCL) 
The objective of BMRCL is to provide fast, comfortable, safe and affordable mass transportation system. In 
order to augment to the public transportation in Bengaluru and also to reduce the pressure of traffic, Metro 
Rail has come up in Bengaluru. It is a vital component of the transformation of the urban transport scenario. 
With urban population continuously growing, there is a need for green solutions. Mass Rapid Transit Systems 
are fast, safe and comfortable to travel. This alone will encourage people to switch over from personalized 
vehicles to public transport. 
5.10.1 Bangalore Metro Rail Project Phase-2 consists of Extensions to 4 existing lines of Phase-1 and 2 New 
Lines. The total length of Phase-2 is 75.06 Kms with 61 stations (49 Elevated and 12 Underground).  The 
estimated project cost is Rs. 30,695 crores.  Presently, 53.80 Kms is completed and commissioned.  7.50 Kms 
length of elevated section in Reach-6 from Kalena Agrahara to Tavarekere is scheduled to be opened in May-
2026.  13.76 Kms Underground section in Reach-6 is scheduled to be opened in December-2026.  
5.10.2 Bangalore Metro Rail Project Phase-2A and 2B
Phase-2A and 2B from Central Silk Board to Kempegowda International Airport is having a length of 58.19 
Kms with 29 Stations.  GoI has approved the project with an estimated cost of Rs. 14,788.10 Crores. The work 
is under progress. The Project Phase-2A having a length of 19.75 Kms is programmed to be completed by 
December-2026 and Phase-2B having a length of 38.44 km is programmed to complete in two stages, 27.44 
Kms from Hebbal to Airport in June-2027 and 11.00 Kms from Krishnarajapura to Hebbal in December-2027.
5.10.3 Bangalore Metro Rail Project Phase-3
Phase-3 is having a length of 44.65 Kms with 31 Stations, comprises of J.P . Nagar 4th Phase to Kempapura 
(32.15 Kms with 22 Stations) and Hosahalli to Kadabagere (12.50 Kms with 9 Stations).  GoI has approved the 
project with an estimated cost of Rs. 15,611 crores.  
This Phase 3 is having a Double Decker with elevated 4-lane road at level-1 & Metro at level-2. 
The Double Decker project with a total project cost of Rs. 9700 Crores for 37.121 Kms has been approved by 
the State Government.
Presently, preliminary works of Land acquisition, Trees clearances, Utilities Shifting are under progress.
5.10.4 Proposed Project: Bangalore Metro Rail Project Phase-3A
Sarjapura has developed very fast with lot of residential layouts and industries coming around Sarjapura.  
To address the travel needs of this area, 36.59 Kms (22.14 Kms Elevated & 14.45 Kms UG) of Metro is being 
planned from Sarjapura to Hebbal along Agara, Koramangala, Dairy Circle and Mekhri Circle.  
DPR has been approved by GoK and submitted to GoI for approval.
5.11 GREATER BENGALURU AUTHORITY (GBA)
The Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) has been established with the objective of ensuring integrated 
metropolitan governance, coordinated planning, and uniform service delivery across the Bengaluru 
metropolitan area. To effectively address the city’s rapidly growing needs related to infrastructure, mobility, 
environment, and service delivery, GBA provides strategic oversight, policy direction, and coordination among 
the five Corporations and other parastatal agencies.

PDF_PAGE 182
174
Urban Development
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
The five Corporations function as, the primary urban local bodies which is responsible for the implementation 
and operation of civic services within their respective jurisdictions. These services include roads, storm water 
drains, footpaths, solid waste management, public health, and local infrastructure development. GBA acts as 
a unified platform to ensure standardisation, efficiency, and accountability across all Corporations.
5.11.1 Vision and Mission of the GBA
To develop Bengaluru into a sustainable, safe, inclusive, and globally competitive metropolitan city through 
integrated planning, high-quality infrastructure, and governance that is responsive to citizens’ needs and his 
Mission is to improve the quality of infrastructure and public services, and to make city governance more 
efficient, transparent, and citizen-centric.
5.11.2 Ongoing Programmes / Schemes, Current Status
 Y  Cabine t has approved proposed construction of vehicular tunnel corridors in two directions: a North–
South corridor of 16.75 km at an estimated cost of Rs.16,980.00 crores, and East–West corridor of 23.00 
km at an estimated cost of Rs.23,500.00 crores. As the first phase, the Detailed Project Report (DPR) for 
the 16.75 km long North–South vehicular tunnel corridor has been prepared and the project is presently 
under the tender process. For the second phase, preparation of the DPR for the 23.00 km long East–West 
vehicular tunnel corridor is under progress.
 Y Preparation of the Detailed Project Report (DPR) is in progress for construction of 13 elevated corridors 
with a total length of 126.44 km, at an estimated cost of Rs 23,500.00 crores.
 Y To prevent monsoon-related disasters in Bengaluru, works are being taken up with World Bank assistance 
at an estimated cost of Rs 2,000.00 crores for construction of 173 new major storm water drains (Raja 
Kaluves) and upgradation of 80 existing Raja Kaluves, including permanent protective structures. The 
projects are presently at various stages of the tender process.
 Y Under the Special Infrastructure Support Scheme, an amount of Rs 1,241.57 crores has been sanctioned 
for asphalting of arterial and sub-arterial roads within the jurisdiction of the Greater Bengaluru Authority 
(GBA), and the tender process for execution of the works is in progress at various stages.

5.11.4  Innovation, Best Practices and Success Stories
The establishment of GBA and the coordinated functioning of the Corporations represent a significant shift  
towards integrated metropolitan governance. Under GBA, metropolitan-level centralised planning is being 
implemented, along with data-driven monitoring of road works and road safety interventions. The reforms 
and initiatives currently being undertaken with in an aim to improve the quality of infrastructure, safety, 
sustainability, and service delivery. These efforts support Bengaluru’s long-term economic growth and 
enhance the overall liveability of the city.

The Bengaluru Development Authority is a Planning Authority and also under takes major infrastructure 
works for development of Bengaluru City. The following are the activities of BDA:- 
 Y Preparation of Comprehensive Development Plan (CDP) / Master plan for Bangalore city.
 Y Preparation of Development Plan for BDA.
 Y Approval of Development Plan for group housing and layout plan.
 Y Approval of building license plan within the jurisdiction of the Authority.
 Y Implementation of other statutory authority functions under Karnataka Urban and Rural Planning Act.
 Y Construction of PRR- project to alleviate traffic congestion and to facilitate smooth and safe public 
transport in the city.
 Y Rejuvenation of lakes to restore to its original possession and increase ground recharge.
 Y Construction of grade separators to make signal free roads.

activities like: 
 Y Development of layout and formation of residential and commercial sites, Civic Amenity sites & Park /

 Y Construction of commercial complexes for general public.  
 Y Construction of flats/housing for the economically backward / lower income groups / middle income

 Y Providing basic infrastructure facilities to the public.

5.12.6 Bangalore Business Corridor – Part 1 (PRR)
Due to extreme congestion of population  and vehicles in the central areas of the city, the Bangalore 
Development Authority (BDA) had planned the Outer Ring Road (ORR) project with the objective of easing 
traffic movement within the city.
The proposed Peripheral Ring Road (PRR) road will start from Tumakuru Road and connect Ballary Road, Old 
Madras Road, Sarjapur Road, and Hosur Road. It is planned to construct a road of approximately 73.04 km in 
length, providing connectivity to the already constructed NICE Road. To promote commercial activities, it is 
proposed to develop plots for commercial purposes on one side of the road. For this purpose, about 2,565 
acres of land will be acquired.
The Peripheral Ring Road will connect five major National Highways, enabling city residents to travel quickly 
from one direction to another by bypassing city congestion through the outer periphery. It will also facilitate 
smooth and convenient access to the international airport. In this context, even though the project has been 
delayed, it is essential to take it up on a priority basis.

Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
The estimated cost for land acquisition for this project is Rs.21,000 crores, and the construction cost is 
estimated at Rs.6,000 crores, bringing the total project cost to Rs.27,000 crores. To implement the project, 
it has been decided to obtain the required Rs.27,000 crores as a loan from HUDCO, for which the State 
Government will provide a guarantee.

5.14 MUNICIPAL FINANCE AND ULBS IN KARNATAKA 
5.14.1 Directorate of Municipal Administration (DMA) 
The Directorate of Municipal Administration act as a nodal agency to control and monitor administrative, 
developmental and financial activities of the urban local bodies and act as an interface in compilation and 
dissemination of information from local bodies to Government. 
In accordance with the powers conferred upon by the Karnataka municipalities Act, 1964, the Directorate 
of Municipal Administration oversees the administration of 13 City Corporations, 64 City Municipal Councils 
(CMCs), 120 Town Municipal Councils (TMCs), 120 Town Panchayats (TPs) and 04 Notified Area Committees. 
The DMA monitors these urban local bodies through a network of District Urban Development cells (DUDCs) 
headed by a Project Director which reports to the Deputy Commissioner of the said district. The Directorate is 
responsible for ensuring that the urban local bodies deliver the obligatory functions such as lighting of street, 
providing water and cleaning of public places and also discretionary and special functions.
5.14.2 Role & Responsibilities 
 Y Nodal Agency for regulating day to day governance of 317 ULBs including Corporations in the State 
(except BBMP).
 Y Supervising administration in Corporations & ULBs as mandated in Corporations Act, Municipal Acts and 
its interpretation.
 Y Facilitating implementation and monitoring of schemes of State and Central Government.
 Y Formulating recruitment and service rules for corporations, municipal employees and officers.
 Y Regulating service delivery in Corporations & ULBs.
 Y The Directorate of Municipal Administration is the Nodal Agency to monitor the Administrative, 
Developmental and Financial Activities of the Corporations & ULBs coming under its jurisdiction.
5.14.3 Chief Minister Amrutha Nagarothana (Municipality) Phase-4
The Chief Minister’s Amrutha Nagarothana (Municipality) Phase-4 scheme is being implemented in 302 Urban 
Local Bodies with a total allocation of Rs.3,885.00 crores. Under this scheme, priority has been given to basic 
infrastructure works such as road improvement, roadside drains, footpaths and traffic management, drinking 
water supply, storm water drains, construction and improvement of office buildings, community and public 
toilets, and development of modern bus stands and market complexes. Budgetary amount of Rs. 500.00 
crores allocated for the year 2025-26. An expenditure of Rs.590.40 crores has been incurred including opening 
balance Rs.208.27 crores against the released amount of Rs.500.00 crores up to the end of December 2025.

5.17 URBAN HOUSING
Housing is a basic and very important need for every citizen. Housing not only provides social security to 
human beings but it also provides status in the society.  Housing is one of the important and most basic 
needs of the people. Housing has evolved as a prime component over the period of time not only in providing 
shelter but also for providing employment opportunities and in development of localities. To meet the 
growing demand for housing, the State Government has been pro-active in its housing policies.   Housing for 
the poor and down-trodden assumes greater importance both in Rural and Urban areas in the State.  Every 
successive Government has given greater attention to the problem of housing scarcity and increased the 
budgetary allocation year after year. 
Karnataka Housing Board (KHB) caters to housing needs of low income, middle income and high-income 
groups. The Karnataka Slum Development Board (KSDB) is responsible for improvement of slums and 
resettlement of slum dwellers. 
5.17.1 Rajiv Gandhi Housing Corporation Limited
With an objective to implement all the State and Central Government sponsored housing schemes for 
economically and socially weaker sections of the Society both in rural and urban areas. Rajiv Gandhi Housing 
Corporation Limited has been established. The main objectives are:
 Y To provide houses to the Socially and Economically Weaker sections of the society. 
 Y Speedy implementation of schemes.
 Y Transparency in implementation.
 Y Smooth flow of funds to ensure that the funds reach the ultimate beneficiaries in time.
 Y To encourage cost effective technology in construction through District Nirmithi Kendras. 
 Y Strengthening of Nirmithi Kendras.
Karnataka Government is implementing many schemes like “Vajpayee Urban Housing Scheme”, Dr.B.R. 
Ambedkar Nivasa Yojane, Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana- Housing for All (PMAY –U), Devraj Urs Housing Scheme 
etc,.  to caters to need of urban poor and distribution of sites to site less persons through Vajpayee Urban Site 
Scheme in urban areas for EWS site-less families in the state. These schemes are implemented through Rajiv 
Gandhi Housing Corporation Limited.
Totally 52,45,881 houses have been constructed under various housing schemes and 2,52,528 sites have 
been distributed from 2000-01 to 2025-26 up to end of December-2025. 
5.17.2 Dr.B.R. Ambedkar Nivasa Yojane
The main objective of this scheme is to provide housing facility to the houseless families of Schedule Caste 
and Schedule Tribes. The scheme is being implemented in both Rural and Urban areas. Under this scheme 
Rs.2.00 lakh subsidy is being provided in rural and urban areas. The income limit of the beneficiary is Rs. 
1,20,000/- in Rural and Rs.2,00,000/-in urban areas. 
During last 3 years 94,652 houses have been completed as against the target of 1,20,000 houses in Rural area 
and 10,199 houses have been completed as against the target of 15,000 houses in Urban area.  For the year 
2025-26 as against the target of 16,500, 9,705 houses in Rural & 730 houses in Urban have been completed 
at the end of December-2025 and remaining houses are under progress. District-wise details of the houses 
constructed are provided in the Appendix 5.1.

5.17.4 Vajpayee Urban Housing Scheme
Vajpayee Urban Housing Scheme is implemented to provide housing facilities to the economically and socially 
backward homeless people in urban areas. The annual income limit of the beneficiaries under this scheme is 
fixed at Rs. 2,00,000/-. The selection of beneficiaries will be done through the Urban Local Bodies from the 
list of Houseless List. The Government is providing subsidy amount of Rs. 1.20 lakhs per house.  
During the last three financial years, total of 20,090 houses have been constructed as against the total target 
of 25,000 houses. A target of 2,500 houses has been given for the year 2025-26, against which 1,315 houses 
have been constructed till the end of December 2025. The details of the houses constructed district-wise are 
given in the Annexure 5.2.
5.17.5 DEVARAJ URS HOUSING SCHEME
This scheme is introduced with an objective to provide houses to special category i.e. People living on 
footpath/living in public places, physically handicapped, leprosy cured, HIV affected, Transgender, Sex 
workers, Devadasis, Widows, Freed bonded labourers, Scavengers, Exploited- including “women/girls who 
have been subjected to acid attacks”, People affected in communal riots & during strikes, Nomadic Tribes, 
Special occupation groups. The selection of beneficiaries is done by the District Committee headed by the 
Deputy Commissioner. Under this scheme the unit cost per house is Rs.1.20lakhs for General category and 
Rs.1.50 lakhs for SC/ST beneficiaries.
During the last three years, 24,495 houses have been constructed in rural areas against the target of 25,520 
houses and 1,387 houses in urban areas against the target of 3,480 houses. For the year 2025-26, a target of 
4,000 houses has been given in rural areas, against which 1,995 houses have been constructed and 38 houses

5.17.7 House Site
The Government is implementing the Rural House Site Scheme in rural areas and Vajpayee Urban Site Scheme 
in urban areas for EWS site-less families in the state. In rural areas 30 X 40 and in urban areas 20X 30 sites 
are provided at free of cost.  In rural areas beneficiaries are selected through gram sabha and in urban areas 
through Ashraya committee. 
From 2004-05 to 2024-25, a total 2,48,373 sites have been distributed (1,37,179 sites in rural areas, 1,11,194 
sites in urban areas). For the year 2025-26, it is targeted to distribute 10,000 sites, 3,570 sites in rural areas 
and 585 sites in urban areas totaling 4155 sites have been distributed up to the end of December-2025. 
5.17.8 “1 Lakh Multi Storey Bengaluru Housing Programme”
The “1 Lakh Multi Storey Bengaluru Housing Programme” has been formulated based on a Self-Sustaining 
model for construction of “1 Lakh multi-Storey Houses” in and around Bengaluru for the EWS and other 
eligible poor on the Government land provided by Revenue Department by mobilizing the funds under  
State Schemes viz., Dr. Ambedkar Nivas Yojana and Vajpayee Urban Housing etc., in convergence with the 
“Pradhan Manthri Awas Yojana (Urban) -Housing for all (HFA)” scheme of the Government of India along with 
beneficiary contribution and cross-subsidy by leveraging suitable Government lands wherever possible under 
PPP model. 
5.17.9 Highlights of Housing Schemes
The Government sponsored Economically Weaker Section (EWS) housing schemes helps the society directly 
and also indirectly.
 Y EWS housing improves the quality of living standards of poor beneficiary.
 Y Under various Government Sponsored EWS housing Schemes Rs.2273 lakhs direct and Rs.1136 lakhs 
indirect employments have been generated so far.
 Y This reduces the housing stock in the country in massive scale.
 Y Indirectly it is one of the basis for country’s economic development.
5.17.10 Challenges
 Y The Govt. of Karnataka has fixed Unit cost of Rs.2.00 Lakhs in Rural & Urban areas for SC/ST beneficiaries. 
While compare to General/Minority beneficiaries unit cost of Rs.1.20 Lakhs is been fixed. There is a 
requirement of enhancement of unit cost of all beneficiaries.
 Y In case of distribution of site to site less families, due to drastic increase in the land cost and non-
availability of Government lands in both rural and urban areas, a lot needs to done as compared to the 
total demand.  
 Y There is no proportionate increase in subsidy as compared to increase in construction cost.

5.18 THE KARNATAKA SLUM DEVELOPMENT BOARD
The Karnataka Slum Development Board was constituted in July 1975 as per Karnataka Slum Areas 
(Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1973 for the welfare and development of slums. This was re-designated 
as Karnataka Slum Development Board during 2010. The main objective of the Board is to provide basic 
amenities to the slum dwellers and to provide shelter to the needy beneficiaries in the slums. 
As per the survey conducted by Board, there are 3025 slum areas in state as at the end December 2025, 
of which 435 slum areas are in Bengaluru City only. Totally 2866 slums are notified in the State under the 
Karnataka Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act 1973 and 159 are non-notified slums. 
5.18.1 Slum Improvement Scheme
Action Plans for basic infrastructure works such as roads, drains, sewerage, drinking water, street lights, 
community toilets, and community halls are prepared and executed by getting approval from the Competent 
Authority under Slum Improvement Scheme.
5.18.2 Housing Scheme 
The Karnataka Slum Development Board has received approval for the construction of 1,80,253 Affordable 
Housing in Partnership (AHP) houses across various urban/town limits of the state. This is being implemented

INTRODUCTION 
The vital role of agriculture and allied sectors in Karnataka’s development is effectively articulated through 
three integrated pillars. First, primary production systems, such as agriculture, horticulture, animal husbandry, 
and fisheries, sustain rural livelihoods, generate employment, and strengthen food and nutritional security. 
Second, natural resources and sustainability systems, including watershed development and climate-resilient 
practices, safeguard soil, water, and long-term productivity. Third, value chains and food management 
systemscovering processing, marketing, and price support enhance farmers’ incomes and improve food 
access.
Building on this integrated framework, Karnataka state’s progressive path in strengthening these 
interconnected sectors. It brings together production trends, climate resilience, technological advancement, 
institutional support, and market reforms as part of a coordinated development approach. Through sustained 
public investment and farmer-centric initiatives, the state continues to reinforce resilience, expand livelihood 
opportunities, and promote sustainable and inclusive growth across rural Karnataka
6.1 AGRICULTURE 
Agriculture remains central to Karnataka’s economy and rural livelihoods, sustaining a large proportion 
of the population through farming and allied activities. Beyond its contribution to income generation and 
employment, the sector underpins food security and social stability. The State’s diverse agro-climatic zones 
enable the cultivation of a wide range of crops, supporting both subsistence agriculture and commercial 
farming systems.
Karnataka has a geographical area of 190.50 lakh hectares, of which 118.05 lakh hectares are cultivated 
by 86.81 lakh farm families under rainfed and irrigated conditions. The Department of Agriculture, as one 
of the State’s major development departments, plays a pivotal role in strengthening farm productivity by 
disseminating research findings, modern technologies, and improved practices to farmers.
To enhance agricultural output and resilience, the Department implements several Central and State 
schemes, including the National Food Security Mission (NFSM), Crop Insurance Scheme, PM-Kisan, Rashtriya 
Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY), Soil Health Mission, CM Raitha Vidya Nidhi, Farm Mechanization, Agro-Processing, 
Custom Hiring Centres, Crop Harvest Experiments, Micro-Irrigation, Organic Farming, and Quality Control 
initiatives. Timely supply of essential inputs—such as quality seeds, micro-nutrients, bio-fertilisers, and plant 
protection chemicals—remains a key component of service delivery.
VISION AND STRATEGIC DIRECTION
The State’s vision for agriculture focuses on enhancing productivity while reducing cultivation costs to ensure 
sustainable growth, higher farm incomes, and long-term food security. The mission is to achieve a sustained 
annual growth rate of 4.5 per cent in the agriculture sector through climate-resilient practices, drought-
proofing measures, and conservation of natural resources.
The strategy emphasizes farmer-friendly research and technology transfer, institutional strengthening of 
Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs) and federations to promote aggregation and Public-Private Partnerships, 
6
Agriculture and  
Food Management
CHAPTER

PDF_PAGE 198
190
Agriculture and Food Management
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
and encouragement of rural youth participation in agribusiness enterprises. Accelerated mechanization, post-
harvest technology development, value chain integration, policy convergence, and efficient delivery of quality 
inputs are integral to this approach.
BUDGETARY SUPPORT AND PROGRAMME FOCUS (2025–26)
For 2025–26, Rs.4,028.30 crore has been earmarked for agriculture schemes, of which Rs.2,513.69 crore has 
been expended up to December 2025. Emphasis has been placed on flagship programmes such as supply 
of quality seeds, farm mechanization, crop surveys, Krishi Bhagya, crop insurance, Soil Health Mission, and 
micro-irrigation. Special focus has also been accorded to millet production and processing, reflecting both 
nutritional priorities and climate suitability.
KEY INITIATIVES IN 2025–26
The State is establishing a Digital Agricultural Service Centre to assist farmers and policymakers in making 
informed crop decisions. By leveraging digital platforms, artificial intelligence, and geospatial technologies, 
the Centre aims to address productivity challenges and climate-related risks with data-driven solutions.
Joida taluka in Uttara Kannada district is being developed as Karnataka’s first “organic taluka,” promoting 
sustainable organic farming. Farmers will be supported with organic certification facilities to access better 
markets and price realisation.
In response to recurring natural calamities, an Expert Committee will be constituted to review and re-delineate 
existing agro-climatic zones to improve planning and risk management. Simultaneously, departmental 
laboratories are being strengthened with advanced scientific instruments to enhance soil testing and quality 
assessment of seeds, fertilisers, and pesticides.
To improve sustainability in rainfed regions, a comprehensive Rainfed Agriculture Policy will be implemented. 
Integrated soil and water management, efficient water utilisation, waste management, and nutrient 
management practices will be undertaken in collaboration with sugar factories across 3,000 hectares in 
Belagavi, Bagalkot, Vijayapura, Kalaburagi, and Mandya districts.
Further, bio-agricultural inputs developed by agri start-ups will be marketed through Raitha Samparka Kendras 
at appropriate prices, promoting innovation and ensuring farmer access to quality alternatives.
Collectively, these initiatives reflect Karnataka’s commitment to building a resilient, technology-driven, and 
farmer-centric agricultural system that enhances productivity, safeguards natural resources, and strengthens 
rural livelihoods.
6.1.1 Monsoon in 2025
Pre-monsoon Rainfall
During Pre-Monsoon season of 2025, the state as a whole recorded an actual amount of 286 mm of rainfall 
as against the Normal rainfall of 115 mm with percentage departure from Normal being (+)149%. Thus, the 
State as whole is classified under Large Excess Category. During Early Kharif 2025 a total of 3.06 lakh hectares 
(107%) has been sown against a set target of 2.86 lakh hectares.

PDF_PAGE 199
191

Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
Southwest Monsoon
The Southwest Monsoon has set in over Kerala on the 24th May, 2025, against the normal date of 1st June. It 
advanced into the Karnataka State on the same day and covered the entire State on 28th May 2025. Overall, 
during South-West season of 2025, the State as a whole recorded an actual amount of 882 mm of rainfall as 
against the Normal rainfall of 852 mm with percentage departure from Normal being (+)4%. Thus, the State 
as whole is classified under Normal Category. Out of 236 taluks, 124 taluks received normal rainfall and 39 
taluks received less than normal rainfall.
Northeast Monsoon
The Northeast Monsoon rainfall activity has commenced over Tamil Nadu, Puducherry &Karaikal, Coastal 
Andhra Pradesh, Rayalaseema, South Interior Karnataka and Kerala, on 16th October. Cumulative rainfall 
during the northeast monsoon period from 1st October to 31st December was 149 mm as against a normal 
of 182 mm with percentage departure from Normal being (-)18%. Thus, the State as whole is classified under 
Normal Category. Totally (January-1st to December-30th) normal average rainfall was 1153 mm against actual 
rainfall 1319 mm (14%). Thus, the State as whole is classified under Normal Category.
Crop Loss
During the year 2025 due to excess rainfall/Flood in the southwest monsoon many agriculture crops were 
damaged.According to the district joint survey report, a total of 13.83 lakh hectares of agricultural crops have 
been damaged due to heavy rains. Major districts that were affected are Kalaburagi (3.24 lakh ha.), Vijayapura 
(3.15 lakh ha.), Bidar (1.65 lakh ha.), Yadgiri (1.43 lakh ha.) and Gadag (1.22 lakh ha.). Major crops that were 
affected are Tur, Greengram, Cotton, Maize and Soyabean. The input Subsidy amount for the damaged crops 
is distributed to the farmers by the revenue department.
6.1.2. Agricultural Production- Performance and Prospects
The First advance estimates of production for 2025-26 have been arrived based on area coverage under various 
crops during Kharif and loss of crops due to excess rains/floods in some parts. It indicates likely production 
of 96.81 lakh tonnes of Cereals and 12.43 lakh tonnes of Pulses against the target of 96.14 lakh tonnes and 
15.27 lakh tonnes respectively. Oilseeds production is estimated to be 7.37 lakh tonnes against the target of 
8.68 lakh tonnes. Production of cotton is likely to be 25.55 lakh bales against the target of 24.03 lakh bales.
The Final advance estimates of production for 2024-25 was arrived based on area coverage under various 
crops during Kharif and Rabi seasons and coverage during Summer and crop loss due to excess rains/floods 
in some parts. It indicates likely production of 132.22 lakh tonnes of Cereals and 19.24 lakh tonnes of Pulses 
against the target of 126.12 lakh tonnes and 22.28 lakh tonnes respectively. Oilseeds production is estimated 
to be 10.06 lakh tonnes against the target of 13.89 lakh tonnes. Production of cotton is likely to be 22.71 lakh 
bales against the target of 24.48 lakh bales.

Land Utilization and Operational Holdings
Land Utilization
As per the report of 2022-23 (2021-22 data), out of the total 190.50 lakh hectares geographical area of the 
State, the net cropped area was 111.66 lakh hectares accounting to 59% of the total geographical area. Gross 
cropped area was 147.48 lakh hectares including 35.82 lakh hectares area sown more than once and this works 
out to 132% cropping intensity. Around 16% of the area was covered under forests, 8% area was under non-
agricultural uses, 4% of the land was barren and uncultivable land and 2% of the land was cultivable waste. 
Permanent pastures, grazing land and miscellaneous tree crops constituted 5% of the total geographical area. 
About 1% of the total area falls under current fallow and other fallow lands. 
Year wise classification of geographical area is given in Appendix 6.5.
Agriculture Land Holdings
As per Agriculture Census 2015-16, there are 86.81 lakh farm holdings operating an area of 118.05 lakh 
hectares. The average size of holding is 1.36 hectare. Small and marginal holdings account for 80% of total 
holdings and operate 44% of the total operated area.The average land holding size has gradually decreased 
over the years it has reduced from 1.95 hectares during 1995-96 to 1.36 hectares during 2015-16.
Cropping Pattern
The major districts of Karnataka State falls is in Zone X (Southern Plateau and Hilly region) and districts like 
Udupi, Uttar Kannada and Dakshina Kannada come under Zone XII (West Coast Plains and Ghats region). The 
State is divided into 10 Agro-climatic zones on the bases of distribution and percentage of Rainfall, soil quality, 
height from the sea and based on major crops. 
On account of this varied agro-climatic features, almost all cereals, pulses, oilseeds and commercial crops 
are cultivated in different parts of the State. Farmers in Karnataka are very innovative and take lead in 
diversification as per the market trends. The average area (2020-21 to 2024-25) of agriculture crops grown 
in three seasons’ viz. Kharif (82.25 lakh ha.), Rabi (23.64 lakh ha.) & summer (6.09 lakh ha.) is 111.99 lakh 
hectares. Cereals, Pulses, Oilseeds, Cotton, Sugarcane and Tobacco account for 45%, 28%, 10%, 7%, 9% and 
1% respectively of the total agricultural cropped area. Maize, Tur, Green gram, Soyabean and Sugarcane are 
witnessing a higher trend in recent years, whereas crops like Paddy, Jowar, Bajra, Groundnut, Sunflower and 
Cotton are witnessing a declining trend. 
The details of cropping pattern are given in Appendix 6.6.
6.1.3 Key Performance Indicators (KPI) under Karnataka State Action Plan on Climate Change 
Version 2.0) (KSAPCC V-2.0)
Climate change plays prime role in altering the distribution and functioning of natural resources, significantly 
reducing health, lifestyle, and development benefits. In response to this, the State of Karnataka formulated 
the State Action Plan on Climate Change (SAPCC) in 2015 and revised it in 2021. Further, in accordance with the 
“Common Guidelines for Revision of State Action Plans on Climate Change” of the Ministry of Environment, 
Forest and Climate Change, Government of India, the Karnataka State Action Plan on Climate Change Version 
2.0 (KSAPCC V-2.0) has been prepared by the Institute of Environmental Management and Policy Research. 
The National Steering Committee on Climate Change (NSCCC) of the Government of India held on 16.02.2024 
has approved KSAPCC V-2.

“In the era of agricultural innovation, traditional farming practices have undergone significant changes and 
agricultural geospatial database is being developed to predict crop productivity based on advanced technologies

 During 2025-26 Kharif Bidar and Kalaburagi districts were selected for soyabean crop and Mandya and

6.1.5 Redefining of Agro-climatic Zones in Karnataka (New Scheme 2025-26)
In light of the changing climatic conditions and since the classification of 10 agro climatic zones were done 
many years ago,a new scheme has been announced in the budget speech during the current year for 
redefining agro-climatic zones and an amount of 50.00 lakh was allocated for the same. In this regard, a 
committee has been formulated with a government order under the Chairmanship of Dr.B.V. Patil, Ex-Vice 
Chancellor, University of Agricultural Sciences, Raichur for redefining the Agro-Climatic zones of Karnataka. 
The Karnataka State Remote Sensing Applications Centre (KSRSAC), Bengaluru has been entrusted with the 
task of redefining the Agro-Climatic Zones, with necessary technical assistance and data support from other 
institutions. The task of redefining the Agro climatic zones is in progress.

d) Agricultural implements
Farm Mechanization
Farm mechanization is adopting usage of machinery and technology in agriculture to replace manual labor and 
animal power, boosting productivity. Mechanization of Farm Operations helps to reduce the drudgery of farm 
operations, saves time, and improves efficiency and farm productivity. The objective of farm mechanization is 
achieved through implementation of various schemes.  
Farm Mechanization Programme is being implemented to provide a subsidy of 50% to general farmers and 
90% subsidy to Schedule caste/Schedule Tribe farmers.
Sub Mission on Agricultural Mechanization (SMAM): The scheme is being implemented to promote the 
usage of farm mechanization and increase the ratio of farm power to a cultivable unit area up to 2.5 kW/ha. 
Agro-Processing: To protect the agriculture, produce/ food grains from rain, wind and other unnatural 
weather conditions and to maintain quality, 8mx6m. size tarpaulin is distributed to the farmers at 50% subsidy 
for General Category and 90% to Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribes farmers limited to Rs. 1.00 Lakh and 
Small Automated Oil Machines are distributed at 75% subsidy for general category and 90% subsidy limited 
to Rs. 1.00 Lakh is provided for farmers belongs Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe farmers.
Hi-tech Harvester Hub: The main objective of the scheme is to facilitate provision of Farm Machineries like 
combined harvester on rental basis to farmers by strengthening the existing Custom Hiring Service Centers 
through establishment of Hi-tech Harvester hubs in a phased manner. Under the scheme, establishment of 
Hi-tech Harvester Hub through existing Custom Hiring Centers, Agencies/ Organization (including FPOs) and 
Individual Beneficiaries by providing subsidy @ 40% to 70% limited Rs. 100.00 Lakhs is facilitated.

2.  Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY)
RKVY is a central sector scheme empowering Indian states to develop agriculture and allied sectors via 
flexible, district-level planning. Now it has been revamped as RKVY-RAFTAAR, it focuses on making farming a 
remunerative economic activity by promoting agribusiness, entrepreneurship, and innovation, with funding 
shared 60:40 between the Centre and States. It incentivizes the States to increase public investment in 
Agriculture and allied sectors and aims at achieving the goal of reducing the yield gaps in important crops and 
thus maximizes returns to the farmers.
Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Government of India has restructured the scheme in 2022-
23 where in Annual Action Plan (AAP) based scheme have also been brought under RKVY umbrella. The two 
streams under RKVY are:
1.  De tailed Project Report (DPR) based component.
2.  Annual Action Plan (AAP ) component.

3. Micro Irrigation 
Micro irrigation (MI) programme is  being promoted both by Central and State Sector schemes, by providing 
different kinds of financial, institutional and technical support. These technologies are promoted primarily 
as: (1) a means to save water in irrigated agriculture, (2) as a strategy to increase income and reduce poverty, 
and (3) to enhance the food and nutritional security of rural households. The real thrust on promoting MI 
adoption largely started with the recommendations of the Task Force on Micro Irrigation Programme in 2004. 
The report sought to increase the emphasis on MI technology and recommended the Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme (CSS) in 2005-06. 
The Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY) with the very important component of Per Drop 
More Crop (PDMC) – Micro Irrigation, is being implemented since 2015-16. the PDMC component focuses 
on improving water use efficiency at the farm level through promotion and support of Precision or Micro 
Irrigation (MI) which includes Drip and Sprinkler Irrigation units distribution at subsidized rates.
As per the Government order, during 2025-26, the Micro Irrigation programme is implemented under 
Pradhana Manthri Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (PMRKVY) Per Drop More Crop (PDMC).
During 2025-26, an amount of Rs.44092.86 lakhs has been allocated and Rs.27059.81 lakhs has been spent 
up to end of December  2025 as against the releases of Rs. 38304.59 lakhs. The Area covered under Micro 
irrigation is 100956 hectares.
4. Support to State Extension Programmes for Extension Reforms (ATMA Scheme)
The extension system is an important pillar in agricultural development, to empower farmers with relevant 
information, technology, skills and support, all of which are necessary to enhance sustainability, farmers’ 
income and agriculture as an enterprise.
The ATMA (Agricultural Technology Management Agency) scheme in Karnataka is a central-sponsored 
initiative to modernize agricultural extension, making it farmer-driven by creating district-level bodies (ATMA) 
to link research, extension, and farmers for technology transfer, capacity building (like Farmer Field Schools), 
and promoting innovation, ensuring farmers adopt better practices and increase productivity through 
participatory approaches. 
Use of interactive and innovative methods of information dissemination will be used and to ensure convergence 
under different programmes and scheme at village level through the institution of ATMA (Agriculture 
Technology Management Agency) and Block Technology Teams (BTTs) laid out as per the guidelines. 
During the current year of 2025-26, an amount of Rs.6235.00 lakhs have been allocated in the budget, an 
amount of Rs.3175.00 lakhs have been released and Rs.2529.62 lakhs expenditure has been incurred up to 
end of December 2025.

5. Crop Insurance Scheme: Karnataka Raitha Suraksha Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana
Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) was launched from Kharif 2016 with an aim to support production 
in agriculture by providing an affordable crop insurance product to ensure comprehensive risk cover for crops 
of farmers against all non-preventable natural risks from pre-sowing to post-harvest stage 
The main objective of the scheme is to provide insurance coverage and financial support to the farmers in 
the event of failure of any of the notified crop due to adverse climatic conditions like Hailstorm, Inundation, 
landslide, Cloud burst and natural fire due to lightning covering Prevented Sowing, Mid-Season Adversity, 
Localized Calamities and Post-Harvest Losses and to stabilize farm income in disaster years
I. The Scheme is being implemented in the State as per GOI guidelines since 2016-17. The scheme operates 
on the principle of “Area Approach” in the selected defined areas called Insurance Units. From the year 
2023-24, the scheme is implemented as per the Operational Guidelines Kharif 2023. 
II. F or Kharif 2025, 36 crops are notified in all 31 districts under KRS-PMFBY .  For 2025-26 Rabi season, 21 
crops are notified in 28 districts (excluding Bangalore (Rural), Bangalore (Urban) and Kodagu districts) 
and for 2025-26 Summer season 06 crops are notified in 26 districts (excluding Udupi, Bidar, Bengaluru 
Urban, Bengaluru Rural and Kodagu) covering food and oil seeds crops as well as annual commercial & 
annual crops under KRS-PMFBY . Taluka-wise major crops are notified at Grama Panchayath level and 
other crops are notified at Hobli level.
III. F armers’ may enroll under the scheme by paying through Financial Institutions/Bank/Grama-One 
Centers/Common Service Centers. After deducting farmer’s share of premium from the gross premium, 
the remaining share of premium amount is equally shared between the State and Central Government in 
the ratio of 50:50.
IV. Sin ce Kharif 2023, FRUITS ID has been made compulsory for enrolment under KRS-PMFBY .
V. The total number of farmers enrolled up to the end of December 2025 is 25,76,388 and premium paid by 
farmers is Rs.22324.79 lakhs covering 22.64 lakh hectares. 
VI. The Insurance Companies implementing PMFBY during 2025-26 Kharif, Rabi and summer season are-
Agriculture Insurance Company of India Ltd., Oriental General Insurance Company, IFFCO Tokio General 
Insurance Company, Universal Sompo GIC and TATA-AIG GIC.
Details of claim settlement in Karnataka Raitha Suraksha Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojane from 2016 to till 
date is provided in Appendix: 6.8
Karnataka State has secured first rank in the overall performance ranking of the States implementing 
PMFBY and certificate of commendation is awarded to Haveri and Koppal districts for good implementing 
of PMFBY by the Government of India.
