1) Krishi Bhagya Scheme – 2025-26 
Krishi Bhagya scheme (Phase I) was implemented from 2014-15 to 2020-21 with the objective of transforming 
64% of rainfed agriculture into sustainable agriculture in turn improving the standard of living of farmers, as 
per Rainfed Agriculture Policy, 2014. During this period about 2,89,827 farm ponds have been constructed, 
which have the capacity to store about 1472.32 lakh cum. of water.
Krishi Bhagya scheme was re-launched in 2023-24 and is being implemented in a package model. During 
2023-24 the scheme was implemented in 106 taluks of 24 rain-fed districts of 5 Agro-climatic dry zones of 

PDF_PAGE 208
200
Agriculture and Food Management
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
the State, as per Rainfed Agriculture Policy-2014 and from 2024-25 the scheme has been extended across the 
State (including command areas). 
The main objective of the scheme is to transform the rainfed agriculture to sustainable agriculture in the 
state,to increase crop productivity and enhance farm income by efficient conservation and improved rain 
water use efficiency and to conserve rain water in the farm ponds dug at selected sites and to provide 
protective irrigation to crops at critical crop stages .
For 2025-26 Rs.100.00 crores grant is allocated for Krishi Bhagya scheme and it is targeted to Implement 
about 5063 Krishi Bhagya packages all over the State. In addition to this, under Krishi Bhagya (SDMF) scheme 
a grant of Rs. 100.00 crores has been provided and it is targeted to implement about 5482 Krishi Bhagya 
Package units in 223 taluks of the State.
During 2023-24, A sum of Rs.50.00 crores grants has been released and Rs.49.90 crores expenditure has 
been incurred by constructing 6601 farm ponds. In the year 2024-25, Rs.200.00 crore has been released and 
rs.185.72 crores has been spent and 15525 farm ponds have been constructed.
During the current year 2025-26, Rs.175.00 crores grant has been released and Rs.58.07 crores has been 
spent by constructing 4529 farm ponds up to end of December-2025.
Expected Outcome
 Y  The runoff rainwater from the agricultural land can be stored in the farm ponds constructed in selected 
places and the excess water can be absorbed in the land to raise the ground water level.
 Y  W ater storage Capacity of farm ponds:
 ) Red Soil: Farm pond of size 10*10*3 mt. to 21*21*3 mt. shall have the capacity to store 1.56 lakh- 
9.81 lakh liters of water.
 ) Black Soil: Farm pond of size 12*12*3 mt. to 21*21*3 mt. shall have the capacity to store 1.89 lakh- 
8.37 lakh liters of water.
 ) Laterite Soil: Farm pond of size 10*10*3 mt. to 21*21*3 mt. shall have the capacity to store 2.19 
lakh- 11.43 lakh liters of water.
 Y A farm pond of size 12*12*3 mt. has the capacity to store about 2.50 lakh lt. water annually. The stored 
water can be used to provide protective irrigation during critical stages of the crop.
 Y  In case of failure of rains, with 2.50 lakh lt. of water is stored in the farm pond, one protective irrigation 
can be given to the crop grown in 2-hectare area through Sprinkler Irrigation and to 4-hectare area 
through Drip Irrigation.
 Y  Cons truction of trench cum bund helps to infiltration of rainwater and thereby for ground water recharge 
and prevention of soil erosion.
 Y  F acilitates beneficiary farmers to sustain their crops in the years of deficit rainfall and also to get an 
average of 20-30% additional yield and income.

of its 80th Anniversary and presented during the Fourth Edition of the Rome Water Dialogue held from

3) Conservation and Promotion of landraces
The programme is being implemented after the announcement in the budget of 2024, with the aim of 
identifying, conserving and promoting land races that are disappearing and suitable for the respective local 
area. This programme has announced in the 2024 budget speech.
The major components such as support/incentives for farmers cultivating and conserving land races, 
production and certification incentives, organization of workshops at the state and district levels to conduct 
basic surveys, pilot trials of land races, capacity building, establishment of seed banks of indigenous varieties, 
awareness about the nutritional value of land races, market support, promotion and awareness programs 
about land races are included in the programme.
Currently, 20 crops have been selected under the program, i.e., Rice, sorghum, millet, buckwheat, groundnut, 
chickpea, safflower, sesame, millets, and chilies.

4) Organic Carbon Mission
The scheme is being implemented since 2021-22 to address low soil organic carbon (SOC) levels by boosting 
soil health, fertility, and promoting sustainable agriculture. Key initiatives include distributing green manure 
seeds at a 75% subsidy, organizing demonstrations (Rs.2,500/hectare), and encouraging organic inputs 
like vermi compost and bio-fertilizers. Apart from enhancing organic carbon of soil the scheme also aims 
in chemical free quality food production and control the drought situation in rainfed areas. The progress 
achieved up to December 2025 is Rs.255.12 lakhs against  target and releases of Rs.300.00 lakhs.
5) Soil Health laboratories Programme 
The scheme aims at promoting soil test based and balanced use of fertilizers to enable farmers to realize 
higher yields at lower cost. Soil health card provides information to farmers on nutrient status of their soil 
along with recommendation on appropriate dosage of nutrients to be applied for improving soil health and 
its fertility.
In Karnataka, 86.81 lakh farm holdings exist. At present, 30 Soil testing laboratories (29 static & 1 mobile 
soil testing lab) of the Agriculture Department are catering to the needs of farmers in respect of soil testing. 
In addition to this, 291 village-level soil testing labs have been established by providing subsidy to selected 
beneficiaries under NMSA Soil Health Management Programme.
The Objectives of the programme are:
1. T o issue soil health cards to all farmers of the State in a span of every two years, so as to provide a basis 
to include nutrient deficiencies in fertilization practices.
2. T o diagnose soil fertility related constraints with standardized procedures for sampling and analysis and 
design taluka/block level fertilizer recommendations in targeted districts.
3. T o develop crops specific nutrient management in the districts for enhancing nutrient use efficiency.
4. T o promote soil test based balancing of nutrients to manage fertility related risks for higher production.
5. T o conduct demonstrations with diversified crops to quantify benefits of improved nutrient management 
practices in terms of increased crop yields and economic viability of farmers. 
During 2025-26, an amount of Rs.553.00 lakhs is allocated as the budget and Rs.396.65 lakhs is releases and 
Rs.348373 lakhs expenditure has been incurred up to end of December 2025.

6.1.10 State Directorate of Secondary Agriculture
Overview
Karnataka state pioneered in establishment of the Directorate of Secondary Agriculture with the mission of 
doubling the farmer’s income. Secondary Agriculture is defined to be an activity/operation that utilizes the 
primary produce of agriculture and adds value to it by any process using local manpower and skills thereby 
providing more returns to the farmer through Agriculture, Horticulture, dairy, processing of animal products, 
cottage & rural industries. 
Mission
 Y  The State Directorate of Secondary Agriculture is planning to implement the project in the state of 
Karnataka as the first model in the country.
 Y  Activitie s / functions that provide more income to farmers are defined as secondary farming by using the 
primary products of agriculture, using local human resources and skills.
 Y  In Agriculture, so far, more emphasis has been given to increase “yields”, but now through secondary 
Agriculture, more emphasis has been given to enhance the income by employment creation through 
production of by-products. 
 Y  T o create more market opportunities for agricultural primary products by adding value to them and 
increasing farmer’s income.
Objectives
 Y With the view of increasing farmer’s income, to utilize the primary product and by-products of agriculture 
and other biological resources as raw materials for processing value addition, packing, branding and 
providing market facilities is the main objective of Secondary Agriculture.
 Y  Sec ondary Agriculture acts as a bridge for employment and income generation through agriculture and 
allied activities.
 Y  T o work towards creation of various sources of income to farm household thereby overcoming the 
problems of Agriculture.
 Y  T o promote agriculture/rural & cottage industries and usage of low capital and technology.
Activities
Mainly 3 types of activities which can be taken under secondary agriculture are Value addition to primary 
agriculture production.(Type A), Alternative enterprises (E.g.: Mushroom cultivation, Bee keeping, etc. (Type 
B) and Enterprises that use crop residues and wastes of primary agriculture i.e.waste to wealth creating 
enterprises (Type C)
Activities such as providing more income to farmers by using local human resources and skills for value 
addition can be undertaken under this scheme. (E.g.: Pickles, ketchup, manufacture of bio pesticides, agro 
tourism, beekeeping, mushroom cultivation, fiber board manufacture, etc.)
In the year 2025-26, a grant of Rs. 100.00 lakhs have been earmarked and also a grant of Rs. 79.2 lakhs have 
been earmarked under the RKVY Scheme. An amount of Rs.75.00 lakhs has been released and Rs.64.21 lakhs 
expenditure has been incurred and the program is being implemented in five districts (Vijayapura, Kalaburagi, 
Mandya, Davangere and Chikkamagaluru). Under this  scheme, 50% subsidy will be provided to all categories 
of farmers for setting up  of units related to secondary agricultural industry., reflecting an average Utilization 
of 85.623%.

6.2 WATERSHED DEVELOPMENT DEPARTMENT
Karnataka has the highest proportion (79%) of drought prone area among all major States in the country 
and in absolute terms it has the second largest area of dry land in the country after Rajasthan. These lands 
are subject to periodic droughts, severe soil erosion, erratic rainfall, and depleting groundwater, eroding the 
natural resource base and significantly hindering agricultural productivity. Average yieldof the most common 
ten crops in these regionis estimated 2-5 times less than optimal. More efficient and sustainable use of natural 
resources, especially of soil, water and vegetation is therefore a basic need for the economic and agricultural 
development of these areas. Hence Watershed development is being given importance in the State. 
The Vision of the Department is: 
1. T o achieve sustainable development of land resources in the rainfed / degraded areas of rural Karnataka 
and to enhance their productivity. 
2.  To achieve the goal of sustainable development through participatory approach of stakeholders in 
watershed development programme and enhance livelihood opportunities for the people living in the 
rainfed / degraded areas. 
The mission is to develop, promote and implement a decentralized, cost effective, productive, transparent 
and sustainable watershed development treatment package through participatory approach for the following.
1. T o meet rural livelihood needs.
2.  T o enhance employment and income opportunities for the poor.
3.  T o improve the productive potential of natural resource base. 
4.  T o reduce the poverty and degradation of natural resources like soil, water, plant and livestock resource.

The geographical area of the State is 190.50 lakh ha., of which 129.70 lakh ha. is available for watershed 
interventions.  Up to the end of March 2025, an area of 74.94 lakh ha has been developed with watershed 
interventions (treated) and 54.76 lakh ha. (out of which 3.02 is under treatment) is yet to be treated. 
Water harvesting structures are being constructed under various watershed development schemes, mainly 
with the objective of improving ground water recharge through harvest of rain water.   In the current year, 
1177 different water harvesting structures (check dam, vented dam, nala bund, gokatte, percolation tank,farm 
pond) are constructed and estimated to cover 1765 ha area under protective irrigation.
For the year 2025-26, Rs. 353.01 crore is provided in the budget, of whichRs.245.29crore has been released 
and Rs.199.76 crore expenditure has been incurred till December 2025.
6.2.1 Watershed Development component of Pradhana Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojane 2.0  
(WDC-PMKSY 2.0)
The scheme envisages to accelerate the economic growth rate of rainfed area agriculture. At watershed 
level, the development plan shall be guided by the need to achieve higher incomes for farmers, expanded 
livelihood options for landless, equity in distribution of benefits, community ownership and management, 
and ecologically sustainable action plan. 
Watershed development activities are being implemented in 78 watershed projects in 78 taluks of the State 
with an area of 3.294 lakh ha with average project size of 4800-5000 hectares area, under the scheme, in 
saturation approach and also in convergence with MGNREGA, PMKSY-PDMC and other Central and State 
Government programmes for a period of 5 years.  The Central and State Governments approved the total 
project cost of Rs.769.66 Crores with the sharing pattern 60:40. The unit cost for the plain areas is Rs.22,000/- 
per hectare and hilly/difficulty areas is Rs. 28,000/- per hectare.
2025-26 is the Final year for implementation of Scheme and remainig Programme is  Rs. 145.49 Crore. During 
the 2025-26, Rs.37.30 crore has been released of which Rs.32.31 crore is utilised till December 2025.  Under 
this programme, along with construction of 228 different water harvesting structures, 13855 ha of rainfed 
area is treated with different watershed activities and 4962 farmers are benefited.
6.2.2 Rainfed Area Development (RAD) - RKVY RAFTAAR 
The scheme has been formulated for enhancing agricultural productivity especially in rainfed areas focusing 
on integrated farming, water use efficiency, soil health management and synergizing resource conservation.
The scheme is being implemented in the State with the sharing pattern of 60:40 between Central and State 
Government and it is brought under RKVY in 2022-23.
Rainfed Area Development (RAD) programme aims at promoting Integrated Farming System (IFS) with 
emphasis on Crops (Millets Crops / Oilseed/Pulses/Vegetables/fodder) + Trees (Horticulture/ Agro Forestry) 
+Livestock {Milch cows/ Buffaloes/small ruminants (10 animals (Sheep or Goat or Pigs) / 50 birds (Duck/ 
Poultry) and value addition activities such as Fishery (Fingerlings) Units, Apiculture (Bee Keeping), Silage 
making Vermi compost Units to be converged with the  other schemes.
An amount of Rs.53.27 crore has been allocated for the year 2025-26 and is targeted to implement  
IFS activities in an area of 17757 ha.  Out of the releases of Rs.18.16 crore, an expenditure of Rs. 3.27 crore 
has been incurred till December 2025 and IFS activities are being implemented in an area of 1091 ha, covering 
1108 beneficiaries.

6.2.3 World Bank Assisted REWARD Project (Rejuvenating Watersheds for Agricultural Resilience 
through Innovative Development)
The Scheme is being implemented and in the lines of Sujala-III. The program aims to introduce modern 
watershed practices Karnataka and focused on modernizing watershed management using scientific data (like 
Land Resource Inventory-LRI ) to boost agricultural resilience, improve soil/water conservation, and enhance 
rural livelihoods by creating decision-support systems for better resource planning. The Budget approval 
for implementation of the program is Rs.600.00 crores (State Share: 30% and World Bank loan: 70%) in 25 
districts.  It is a multi-State watershed development program wherein Karnataka will be the Light house State 
and provide technical guidance to other participating States.
The Objective of the Programme is to strengthen capacities of national and state institutions to adopt 
improved watershed management for increasing farmers’ resilience and support value chains in selected 
watersheds of participating states.
Major activities:  Land resource inventory (LRI) in 25 lakh hectares rain-fed area of 25 project districts; 
Watershed treatment on saturation mode in 1.0 lakh ha (20 sub-watersheds) based on LRI recommendations; 
15 FPOs and Value chain development; providing improved Agro-met advisories to farmers; establishment of 
Centre of Excellence on science-based watershed management at UAS Bengaluru to provide 1044 trainings to 
State and other States officials and technical staff.
Program technical partners: National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning (ICAR-NBSSLUP), Indian 
Institute of Science (IISc), State Agricultural and Horticultural Universities, Karnataka State Remote Sensing 
and Applications Centre (KSRSAC), Karnataka State Natural Disaster Monitoring Cell (KSNDMC) and VTU are 
the technical partners in the implementation of the program.
During 2025-26 action has been taken to complete the LRI studies for 11 lakh hectare area under the World 
Bank assisted REWARD Program with the help of technical Partners. As per this, till now LRI studies are 
completed in 10 lakh Ha. Accordingly, improved LRI and Hydrology based agro advisories are provided to the 
farmers through this program.
During the current year, an amount of Rs.150.00 Crore has been allocated for the project. So far, Rs.75.00 
Crore released and Rs.97.83 Cr. have been incurred till December 2025 including opening balance.
6.2.4 Farmer Producer Organizations (FPO)
FPO is a collective of farmers—mainly small and marginal—who come together to improve their economic 
strength through cooperation and scale. Registered as a legal entity (like a Producer Company or cooperative), 
an FPO helps farmers access quality inputs, credit, technology, and markets at better prices, while also 
enabling value addition, storage, processing, and collective marketing of produce. By reducing dependence 
on middlemen and increasing bargaining power, FPOs aim to enhance farmers’ incomes, reduce risks, and 
promote sustainable and inclusive agricultural development. These organizations are created depending upon 
the needs of the producers considering the demand potential to adopt a value chain approach to enhance 
producer’s economic and social benefits.  
Formation and promotion of farmer producer organizations is implemented under 2 schemes: 
a) Central Sector Scheme- Formation and promotion of 10000 FPOs
Under centrally sponsored scheme, 100 Farmer Producer Organizations are formed in the State and are 
promoted. During 2025-26 an amount of Rs.2.00 Cr. has been released and incurred an expenditure of            
Rs.1.81 Cr.

6.3 AGRICULTURAL MARKETING
Agriculture Marketing forms the cornerstone of economic development by creating efficient pathways 
between producers and consumers. It is the backbone of economic development that connects rural 
prosperity with GDP growth. Agricultural marketing serves as the crucial bridge between farm production and 
economic transformation, driving resource optimization, market expansion, and technological advancement 
while creating employment and boosting incomes across entire communities.
The state has 170 Agricultural Produce Market Committees (APMC’s) to facilitate and regulate agricultural 
markets, protect farmers from exploitation by middlemen, ensure fair prices and timely payments through 
regulated auctions, and develop market infrastructure like yards and storage, though recent reforms aim 
to offer farmers more selling options beyond APMC mandis. They provide transparency, enforce rules, and 
manage the sale and transport of notified produce, but their monopoly is being challenged by new laws for 
more flexible markets.  Since the Department has provided infrastructure facilities for better marketing of the 
commodities; the arrival of agricultural commodities to the market yard is increasing year by year. 
The Department of Agricultural Marketing was established to function under the Karnataka Agricultural 
Produce Marketing (Regulation and Development) Act, 1966 and Rules 1968. The Department of Agricultural 
Marketing supervises and guides the working of APMCs to implement the provisions of the Act and Rules. The 
APMCs are managed by an elected Managing Committee. The Secretary and supporting staff are Government 
servants working in the APMCs. 
Vision: To promote and encourage participatory and equitable socio economic development of farmers in 
particular and stakeholders of the market in general of Karnataka state through vibrant and self-reliant and 
competitive Agricultural Marketing System.
The main objective of the department is to develop and encourage a dynamic and self-sustaining agricultural 
marketing system in the state through adequate infrastructure and user-friendly electronic system and 
specially to achieve partnership and equitable social and economic development of farmers and all marketing 
stakeholders by developing a transparent, scientific agricultural produce marketing system.
The challenges of the Department are to provide the additional required infrastructure for trade in the 
markets, to ensure transparency in the markets, to modernize the markets, and to ensure competitive price 
to the farmers produce. In this regard, action has been taken to implement an online trading system in all the 
APMCs of the state in a phased manner. 167 APMCs have been linked to Unified Market Platform of Rashtriya 
e-Market Services and the Kalaburagi & Chincholi APMCs have been linked to the e-NAM platform of the GoI. 
In addition to this, action has also been taken to link 3 more APMCs to the e-NAM platform.

6.3.1 The budgetary allocation for the department 
An amount of Rs.137.49 crores has been allocated in the budget during the current year 2025-26 and 
Rs.37.50 crores has been released under Minimum Support Price scheme and the same has been transferred 
to revolving fund.
Under Development of Rural Markets, an amount of Rs.82.87 crores has been allocated in the budget and 
Rs.62.02 crore has been released for completion of the works taken under NABARD.
a) Rashtriya e-Market Services Limited (ReMSL)
To ameliorate the agricultural marketing system in the State, Karnataka’s 2013 Agriculture Marketing Reforms 
Committee (AMRC) was formed to modernize agricultural marketing, leading to the Karnataka Agricultural 
Marketing Policy 2013 on September 4th and amendments to the KAPM Act, introducing features like a 
single trader license, warehouse-based sales, private markets, e-trading (Unified Market Platform via ReMS), 
and farmer-friendly measures like market fee waivers for perishables, aiming for better farmer prices and 
transparency. An SPV (Special Purpose Vehicle) Rashtriya e-Market Services (ReMS), has been established 
on 20th January 2014 for the implementation of reforms measures and to create a hassle-free, competitive 
market environment, reducing transaction costs and ensure farmers remunerative prices for their produce. 
On line trading system is being implemented to sell the agricultural produce of the farmers in the markets 
through the electronic trading system to ensure transparency, simplify the marketing procedures, ensure a 
competitive price for farmers’ produce by introduction of technology in all market activities including auction 
system, price discovery and payment of sale proceeds to farmers on line. The different markets in the State 
are linked by the technology adoption facilitating the traders to participate in buying the commodities online 
from any of the markets of the state where the farmers have offered for sale. 
As on December 2025, 167 markets are brought under Unified Market Platform. The Unified Market Platform 
has transacted 12.67 Crore MTs of agricultural commodities worth Rs.4,39,852.54 Crore.  
b) Minimum Floor Price scheme
The Minimum Floor Price Scheme in Karnataka is a state-level policy designed to protect farmers in situations 
where market prices fall sharply below their cost of production. Minimum Floor Price Scheme is a state-
led tool to augment support price protection when farmers otherwise would be forced to sell below cost. 
The scheme applies to all the notified Agricultural & Horticultural commodities as per Karnataka Agricultural 
Produce Marketing (Regulation & Development) Act 1966. In addition to this Scheme, the Price Support 
Scheme of Government of India is also being implemented to stabilize the agricultural prices in the markets 
and ensure a better price for farmers produce by avoiding the distress sale of commodities.
A corpus of Revolving Fund was created  for the successful implementation of the said scheme and is being 
operated by Karnataka State Agricultural Marketing Board as per the decision taken by the Cabinet Sub-
Committee for Price Stabilization of Agriculture/ Horticulture Commodities.
During 2025-26, under support price scheme, approximately 88,252 lakh quintals of Green gram, Urad 
dal, Sunflower, Soyabean, Ground nut, Maize and Cotton commodities have been procured from 1,55,793 
registered farmers, at an estimated cost of Rs. 1,239 crore. Procurement operation is under progress.

6.4 HORTICULTURE
Horticulture sector has emerged as an important component of the economy of our State has contributed 
more than one third share to the economy of agriculture and allied sectors. Horticultural crops have evolved 
as an alternative crop to agricultural crops in many dry regions of the State. Horticultural crops covers an area 
of 25.84 lakh hectares and the annual production is 200.79 lakh Metric Tons during 2024-25. The average 
productivity of horticultural crops in the State is 7.77 Metric Tons per hectare. The share of Horticultural 
produce in total GSDP of the state was 3.05%.

The department has under taken several schemes as mentioned below.
(i) National Mission on Edible Oil - Oil Palm
India imports around 150-165 lakh tones of edible oil costing around 1,60,000 crore.  Therefore, in order 
to achieve self-sufficiency in edible oil production, both Central and State Govt. are encouraging oil palm 
cultivation. As per the reassessment by Indian Institute for Oil Palm Research in 2020, Karnataka has the 
potential to grow Oil palm in an area of about 72642 ha.  Since, Oil Palm is a water loving crop, its cultivation 
is mainly taken up in 19 districts which comes under Command areas of Cauvery, Bhadra, Thungabhadra, 
Malaprabha, Ghataprabha and Krishna and in 5 districts in non-command areas through PPP module. 
Currently in the State, around 9254 farmers are cultivating oil palm in an area of 13223 ha. out of which 
4442 ha. is yielding  area. The annual production of oil palm Fresh Fruit Brnaches (FFBs) is about 16745 
M.T, from which 2883.49 M.T of Crude Palm Oil (CPO) is being extracted. During 2025-26 (upto the end 
of December-2025) 1,80,000 seedlings were distributed to the farmers for area expansion under oil palm. 
Government of India has announced Rs.15,488/MT as Viability Price, for the oil  year from 1st Nov, 2025 to 
31st Oct, 2026. The industry payment price for FFB’s  procured from the farmers  during December-2025 has 
been fixed at Rs.16010.00/MT.  
(ii) Pradhan Mantri Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (Per Drop More Crop)
Under the Centrally Sponsored Pradhan Mantri Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana – Per Drop More Crop (PM-RKVY-
PDMC), the Department of Horticulture provides financial assistance for installation of drip and sprinkler 
irrigation system. From 2024–25 onwards, subsidy is extended to all categories of farmers at 90% up to 2.00 
hectares and 45% for area above 2.00 hectares up to 5.00 hectares.
For the year 2025-26, an amount of Rs. 545.66 crores has been allocated and an area of 30653.66 hectares 
has been brought under Micro Irrigation by providing subsidy of Rs. 24666.50 lakh to 35021 farmers who have 
installed Drip/ Sprinkler for Horticulture up to the end of December 2025.

(iii) National Horticulture Mission (NHM)
For overall development of Horticulture, the Government of India started implementation of the National 
Horticulture Mission (NHM) Scheme. At present, NHM  is a sub scheme of Mission for Integrated Development 
of Horticulture (MIDH). It covers Area expansion, Adoption of protected cultivation method, rejuvenation 
of the unproductive orchards, rain water harvesting, organic farming, induction of Integrated Nutrition 
Management (INM) and Integrated Pest Management (IPM), providing post harvest support, improving 
marketing, enhancing the technical knowledge and skills of farmers, extension officials and entrepreneurs 
through an array of training programmes. 
During the year 2025-26, an amount of Rs. 129.73 crores was allocated upto the end of December-2025.  
Rs.62.80 crore has been spent. The annual physical target for area expansion of major categories of  
Horticultural crops (like fruits, plantation crops, spices, flowers) and aromatic crops are 6350.50 ha. and 
financial target is Rs.18.79 Crore. Financial assistance of Rs. 14.75 Crore has been provided for area expansion 
of 4872.68 ha. upto the end of December 2025. More emphasis is given for providing water storage structures, 
mechanization, protected cultivation and Post-Harvest Management. 
(iv) Bio Centre
Activities such as tissue culture-based plant propagation, mushroom development, production of organic 
fertilizers, biocontrol agents and analysis of nutrients in soil, leaves and water are being carried out at the bio 
centers. Propagation of horticulture crops including medicinal and aromatic plants and production of fruit 
grafts/seedlings, is also an important activity of this centre. 
During 2025-26, under the KSHDA and departmental of developmental lab schemes, a budget of Rs. 98.78 
lakh has been used to produce 10.67 lakh of tissue culture banana plants, Rs. 225.36 lakh to produce 290 tons 
of organic fertilizers/biocontrol agents/ manure and 71670 litres of liquid organic fertilizers. Additionally, with 
a grant of Rs. 95.50 lakh, 52764 soil, water and leaf analysis has been carried out. Furthermore with a budget 
of Rs. 16.47 lakh, 82370 numbers of mushroom spawn (250 grams per packet) has been produced by the end 
of December 2025.
(v) Paramparagath Krishi Vikas Yojana (PKVY)
The Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (PKVY) is a sub-component of the Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY). 
One of the primary objectives of the scheme is to promote the production of high-quality, safe food by 
reviving the vision of sustainable agriculture from the past. This is achieved by integrating the vast wealth 
of authentic, skill-based agricultural knowledge—gained through generations of labour, self-discovery, and 
experimentation—with modern scientific, logical perspectives and recommendations. At the same time, the 
scheme prioritizes ensuring that the quantity and quality of natural agricultural resources do not deteriorate. 
Furthermore, another major objective is to develop organic plots through a cluster-based model, certify 
organic production using a simplified and farmer-friendly Participatory Guarantee System (PGS), and provide 
value addition and market linkages wherever necessary.
The scheme aims to promote natural resource based integrated and climate resilient sustainable farming 
systems that ensure maintenance and increase of soil fertility, natural resource conservation, on-farm nutrient 
and minimize dependence of farmers on external inputs. The main objective will be to validate, value add and 
create a marketing system. During the current year an amount of Rs. 237.00 lakhs has been spent as against 
the available grant of Rs. 2666.67 lakhs at the end of December 2025.

Third phase of PKVY is being implemented in the state. A total of 32000 ha. has been identified for conversion 
for three years in PKVY Phase III which aims to convert agriculture/horticulture area to organic and provide

(vi) Comprehensive Horticulture Development Plan
Under the Comprehensive Horticulture Development Program, 40% subsidy will be provided to all categories 
of farmers as per the guidelines of the Comprehensive Horticulture Development (AEP) Sub-scheme as per 
the unit cost fixed under the MIDH scheme. For the year 2025-26, Rs. 7850.00 lakh has been allocated, of 
which Rs. 5464.49 lakh has been released, and by the end of December 2025, Rs. 4118.36 lakh has been spent 
covering 6603 beneficiaries. 
(vii)  Apiculture Development Programme
Apiculture is emerging as a profitable industry providing export opportunity. It plays a major role in providing 
financial independence to the bee keepers. As Honey bees help cross-pollination in Horticulture and 
Agriculture crops, high and good quality yield can be obtained. Having many medicinal properties, Honey is 
the gift of nature to the human kind and Bee keeping can be practiced without much investment by landless 
small and marginal farmers, women and handicapped. Under this scheme 859 beneficiaries have received 
scientific beekeeping training and a total of 7245 honey boxes have been distributed. Also 17 Madhuvana 
have been established and assistance has been given for purchase of 48 honey extractors. 
A total grant of Rs.200.00 lakhs under the State sector and Rs.369.31 lakhs under the District sector scheme 
has been allotted for the implementation of the Bee keeping development scheme in the year 2025-26. 
Rs.200.00 lakhs and Rs. 275.93 lakhs  has been released of which  Rs. 106.46 lakhs and  Rs. 225.69 lakhs has 
been achieved  upto the end of  December -2025 under state sector and district sector schemes respectively.
(viii) Horticulture Training Programme  
11 training centers are functioning In the department. Every year 400-450 Farmers children are being trained.

a constraint which in turn leads to increased demand for farm machineries. Hence, to promote mechanization

The main objectives of this programme are:

2. T o provide impetus to low-cost mechanization that could provide effective solution for increasing

b) Crop Diversification Programme for replacing tobacco farming with alternate Horticulture 
crops/cropping systems
The objective of this programme is to encourage the cultivation of suitable alternative horticultural crops 
instead of this crop to prevent the adverse effects of tobacco cultivation on human health. Continuous 
cultivation of tobacco crop not only reduces soil fertility but also increases soil erosion. In this context, the 
several benefits can be obtained by growing horticultural crops as an alternative to tobacco. During the year 
2025-26, an amount of Rs. 100.00 lakhs has been  approved and released fully by the end of December 2025.
c) Assistance to Power Tiller program purchased by Schedule Castes and Scheduled Tribes under

(xii) PM-Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojane (PM-RKVY)
Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY) is a centrally sponsored scheme which is focused to reorient the 
development strategies for rejuvenation of agriculture and allied sectors and to meet the needs/demands 
of farmers.  The scheme is designed to incentivize the state and to draw up plans for horticulture more 
comprehensively and to set up investment in horticulture. 
The main objectives of this programme are:
1. T o improve the quality production, optimize the cost of production in Horticulture crops through providing 
components like Micro nutrients and bio-pesticides, solar pump sets and automated weather stations at 
subsidised rate. 
2. T o promote Post Harvest handling and Value addition of Horticultural crops which will reduce fruits & 
Vegetables wastage and helps in handling excess produce during glut season.
3. T o introduce water harvesting techniques to community for handling the water scarcity and to save the 
crop during summer. 
1. Incentives for Post-Harvest Management Activities in Horticulture
Horticultural crops such as flowers, fruits and vegetables have low shelf life resulting in rapid spoilage and crop 
loss. Therefore, The main objectives of this programme are, to give greater impetus to Post Harvest handling, 

PDF_PAGE 226
218

Processing and Value addition of Horticultural crops, to encourage farmers groups and entrepreneurs to 
establish horticultural crop based processing and value addition units suiting to the requirements of the 
region and the needs of the consumer. 
Under this programme financial assistance is extended to farmers to construct Primary processing units, farm 
gate/Horticulture produce grading & storage units, Post harvest handling materials like Punnet, corrugated 
box & plastic crates and low cost onion & coconut storage structures to increase the quality of horticulture

2. Water Harvesting Structures for cultivation of Horticulture Crops
The main objective of the programme is to make water available for irrigation in the cultivation of Crops to 
save the crop during summer by giving life saving irrigations. Under this programme financial assistance up 
to 75% of the unit cost is extended to farmers for construction of different dimensions of Water Harvesting 
Structures for Cultivation of Horticultural Crops. During the year 2025-26, out of approved amount of  
Rs. 1260.00 lakhs, Rs.283.55 lakhs was released and Rs.262.02 lakhs was spent at the end of December-2025. 
3. Special Interventions for Quality Production in Horticulture Crops
Under this program, the department intends to encourage farmers by distributing subsidies to the tune of  
25-50% of the unit cost to enable them to adopt the technologies already adopted by some farmers to a 
greater extent. Under this scheme financial assistance is extended to farmers for use of micro nutrient and 
bio-pesticides, for installation of solar pump sets and automated weather stations which helps in better 
quality production as well as minimising the input cost to generate better income. During the year 2025-26, 
out of approved amount of Rs. 716.00 lakhs, Rs.388.20 lakhs was released and Rs.316.25 lakhs was spent at 
the end of December-2025.

Dharwad

materials of promising varieties to farmers which enables them to export flowers without any hurdle. During

6.5 ANIMAL HUSBANDRY AND VETERINARY SERVICES
As per the 20th Livestock Census, Karnataka has 3.03 crores of livestock and 5.95 crores of poultry population 
and its share in all India was 5.41% and 6.98% respectively. The share of Animal Husbandry in total Gross 
State Domestic Product (GSDP) of the state was 3.64%. Karnataka state stands 8th rank in the Country. The 
production of milk in the state was 13.89 million metric tones during the year 2024-25.
6.5.1  Animal Health and Veterinary Services
The Department of Animal Husbandry and Veterinary provide services through its institutional network. 
During 2025-26, the livestock and poultry are rendered health services through a network of 4342 Veterinary 
Institutions, comprising of 01 Super Specialty hospital, 04 Speciality Hospitals, 27 District Polyclinics, 663 
Taluk/Hobli level Veterinary Hospitals, 2266 Hobli/Village Veterinary Dispensaries, 1205 Primary Veterinary 
Centers and 176 Mobile Veterinary Clinics. Further other Veterinary Institutions are also rendering services.
In Karnataka, the number of in-milk animals has reduced in recent years. However, overall milk production 
in the State has been continuously increasing. This is mainly due to the rise in crossbred cattle population 
with higher milk-yield potential. Improved availability of quality fodder and better feeding practices has also 
contributed. Milk incentive are given to the farmers from government of Karnataka.

c. Accelerated Breed improvement Programme using Sex Sorted Semen (ABIP-SS)
Objectives of the scheme 
 Y To promote use of Sexed semen for production of female calves with 90% accuracy
 Y To enhance milk production and farmers income through production of female calves.

 Y To make sexed semen technology affordable to farmers thereby increasing acceptability of artificial

 Y To create visible demand of sexed semen in the country thereby attracting private entrepreneurs in

The project period is of 5 years from 2021-22 to 2025-26 and the target is to obtain 45.7 lakh assured

which 56,000 doses have been utilized. 8145 animals were pregnant and 5551 calves have been born of 
which, 5160 are female calves (92.95%).
(ii) National Livestock Mission
a. Disaster Management Livestock Insurance Scheme
On the eventuality of loss of the animals due to accidental death or other causes, the cattle are covered 
under the Livestock Insurance Scheme. Maximum of 10 cattle (Cows/buffaloes/bulls etc) or 50 sheep/goat/
pig/rabbits per beneficiary can be insured according to the National Livestock Mission guidelines. Premium 
subsidy of 50% to APL families and 70% to BPL and SC, ST beneficiaries is made available under this scheme. 
During 2024-25 Rs 208.33 lakh has been released to insure the animals and total of 7432 animals have been 
insured under this scheme.
b. Assistance for fodder seed production
It is a centraly sponserd scheme under NLM with 100% GoI share. The objectives of this scheme are mentioned 
below.
1. T o encourage fodder production
2. T o make availability of fodder during lean period
3. T o Provide Nutritive and qualitative fodder to enhance milk & meat production.
Fodder Seeds will be distrubuted in the form of mini kits to the farmers.  During 2025-26 up to the end 
December-2025, the Government of India has released Rs.15.61 crores and a total of 3,96,907 certified 
fodder seed mini kits were distributed to farmers.

A. Foot and Mouth Disease Vaccination Programme
Foot and Mouth disease is a rapidly spreading disease in animals and has a major impact on the farmers 
economy. Therefore, for the control of the said diseases, a mass vaccination programme is being conducted 
every six months. In each round, before vaccination (day 0) and on the 28th day after vaccination, serum 
samples are collected from the animals and sent to the laboratory to measure the immunity produced by the 
vaccine. In the state, 8 rounds of vaccination programme have already been completed.
A grant of Rs. 8544.52 lakh has been requested for the FMD, Brucellosis, PPR & CSF vaccination program and 
equipments with 100% Central Government grant in the year 2025-26. The state Government has received 
administrative approval for Rs. 6413.61 lakh, and an amount of Rs. 1332.08 lakhs has been released of the 
approved action plan for the implementation of the National Animal Disease Control Programme (NADCP) 
Foot and Mouth diseases (FMD) & Brucellosis Control Programme (BCP) and  Critical Animal Disease 
Control Programme (CADCP)- Peste des Petits Ruminands (PPR) and Classical Swine Fever(CSF) vaccination 
programmes. 
Under this program, it is mandatory to identify each livestock (cattle, buffalo, sheep, goat and Pig) by 
inserting a 12-digit unique ear tag and enter the details of the vaccination in the Bharath Pashudhan Portal. In  
2025-26, under 7th and 8th round of FMD vaccination, 91.91 lakh doses and  90.80 lakh doses of foot-and-
mouth disease vaccine have been administered to cattle and buffaloes respectively. In the vaccinated cattle, 
details of 88.70 lakh in the 7th round and 90.80 lakh in the 8th round have been entered in the Bharath 
Pashudhan portal and the information record of the remaining cattle and buffaloes is in progress.
B. National Animal Disease Control Proramme (NADCP) - National Programme for Control of 
Brucellosis
Brucellosis infection causes abortion in pregnant cows. This infection can also be transmitted to people in 
contact with pregnant cattle. This disease can be prevented by giving lifelong preventive vaccination to female 
calves aged 4 to 8 months. In the year 2025-26 under Brucella Phase IV Round 1 vaccination programme 
2.92 lakh (Cattle & Buffalo) female calves were vaccinated and under Brucella Phase IV Round 2 vaccination 
programme 1.63 lakh (Cattle & Buffalo) female calves have been vaccinated.
C. National Animal Disease Control Programme: PPR Disease Control Programme 
A mass Peste des Petits Ruminants (PPR) vaccination programme for sheep and goats in the state has been 
implemented since 2011-12 as a preventive measure. From the year 2022-23, the Department of Animal

6.5.2 Karnataka Co-Operative Milk Producers’ Federation (KMF)
The Karnataka Co-operative Milk Producers’ Federation Limited  was established in 1974, with the assistance 
of the World Bank, under the “Operation Flood–I” project as the “Karnataka Dairy Development Corporation” 
(KDDC). Subsequently, through the implementation of “Operation Flood–II and Flood–III” projects, dairy 
development activities were expanded across the State. Over the years, this organisation evolved into the 
present Karnataka Milk Federation (KMF), which has today emerged as a key pillar of the co-operative dairy 
movement in Karnataka.
 Y Objectives of the Organisation
The primary objective of the organisation is to provide a continuous and assured market to rural milk producers 
at remunerative prices, while ensuring the supply of quality milk and milk products to consumers.
 Y Organisational Structure
The Karnataka Milk Federation has been structured on co-operative principles and functions under a three-
tier system.
Level Unit Details
State Level Karnataka Co-operative Milk Producers’ Federation Apex Federation
District Level 16 District Milk Unions Covering 24,325 villages
Village Level 16,142 Primary Milk Producers’ Co-operative 
Societies
Including 4,813 Women Milk Co-operative 
Societies
 Y Membership and Milk Procurement
At present, within the KMF network, there are a total of 27.19 lakh milk producer members, of whom 9.06 
lakh are active members. During the current year, the organisation procures an average of 1.00 crore litres 
of milk per day and makes daily payments of approximately Rs. 35.36 crore to milk producers through direct 
bank transfer (Direct Benefit Transfer – DBT). The Federation has achieved second position at the national 
level and first position among the Southern States in the co-operative dairy sector.
 Y Milk Processing and Infrastructure
Milk procurement activities within the jurisdiction of KMF Milk Unions are carried out through 12,985 AMCU 
units at the society level. The infrastructure also includes 2,324 Bulk Milk Coolers (BMCs), 30 Chilling Centres, 
and 45 Milk Processing Plants, with a combined milk processing capacity of 1.37 crore litres per day.
 Y Central Quality Assurance
The Central Quality Assurance Laboratory is the second laboratory in the co-operative sector in the country 
to be accredited by NABL. In accordance with the accreditation standards, the laboratory carries out quality 

PDF_PAGE 238
230
Agriculture and Food Management
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
testing of various parameters of milk and milk products, as well as animal feed and packaging materials. 
Testing of private milk samples is also undertaken and test reports are being issued as per requests received 
by the Department.
 Y Market
During the financial year 2025–26, KMF expanded its extensive market network for Nandini products across 
the state and in other states. On an average per day, sales included 46.56 lakh litres of sachet milk, 9.97 lakh 
kgs of curd, and 6.91 lakh litres of UHT or Flexi Pack milk. In addition, Nandini ice cream recorded a peak 
(highest) sale of 39,430 litres, reflecting strong market demand and effective distribution strategies.
 Y Veterinary Services Provided to Milk Producers by KMF
Comprehensive veterinary and livestock support services are being continuously provided to milk producers 
through the Karnataka Milk Federation (KMF) and its District Milk Unions. These include 24×7 emergency 
veterinary services, mobile veterinary units, emergency call facilities, animal health camps, vaccination 
programmes, deworming drives, calf-rearing guidance, artificial insemination services, sex-sorted semen 
programme, and advanced reproductive technologies such as IVF embryo transfer.
In addition, several welfare and support schemes are being effectively implemented, such as financial 
assistance for construction of own buildings for Dairy Cooperative Societies, group insurance schemes for 
cattle, supply of cattle feed, distribution of fodder seeds, educational hostel support for daughters of milk 
producers, and health insurance facilities, thereby ensuring overall animal health, productivity, and socio-
economic welfare of milk producers.
 Y Nandini Semen Station and Artificial Insemination
During the current year, the Nandini Semen Station processed 40 lakhs frozen semen doses annually, and 
through 2,855 Artificial Insemination (AI) centres, about 40 lakhs artificial inseminations were carried out. As 
a result, the birth of approximately 10 lakhs calves has been reported.
 Y Sex-Sorted Semen Programme
Under the Sex-Sorted Semen Programme, concerted efforts are being made to significantly increase the birth 
of female calves through the use of sex-sorted semen. Consequently, an average success rate of about 86% 
female calf births has been achieved. The cost of each sex-sorted semen dose is Rs.265, of which Rs.90 per 
dose is subsidised by KMF and Rs.75 per dose by the District Milk Unions. With this support, sex-sorted semen 
doses are made available to milk producers at a highly subsidised rate of only Rs.100 per dose.
 Y Cattle Feed
Within the jurisdiction of the Karnataka Milk Federation (KMF), a total of 9 cattle feed plants are in operation. 
About 75,000 metric tonnes of cattle feed and 550 metric tonnes of mineral mixture are produced an a 
monthly basis, using the least-cost formulation method and are supplied to milk producers through Dairy 
Cooperative Societies as per demand.
With an objective of safeguarding the interests of Maize growing farmers in the state, the Karnataka Milk 
Federation (KMF) has decided to procure maize directly from farmers at the Minimum Support Price (MSP) 
during the harvest season as per orders of the Government. This maize is required for the production of 
approximately 9.0 lakh metric tonnes of cattle feed annually for milk production by dairy animals of farmers 
associated with the 16 district milk unions under the jurisdiction of KMF.

PDF_PAGE 239
231
Agriculture and Food Management
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
 Y Automatic Milk Collection System (AMCS) Software – Digital Transparency
With the support of the National Dairy Development Board (NDDB), the AMCS software has been implemented 
to establish a data-driven and transparent governance system at the Dairy Cooperative Society level. Through 
this system, all information related to milk quantity, quality, collection schedules, payments to farmers, and 
outstanding receipts is captured and maintained in a real-time digital record system. Through the AMCS 
Farmer App, details such as milk weight, quality parameters, and payment information are made instantly 
available to farmers, enabling fair, quality- and quantity-based, and timely payments. At present, the AMCS 
software has been implemented in more than 13,000 societies under the KMF network, and over 70% of 
total milk procurement has been digitised. In the future, it is also envisaged to directly disburse government 
incentive payments to farmers based on the data available in the AMCS system.
 Y Ksheera Sanjeevini Scheme – Women Empowerment
In collaboration with the Karnataka Milk Federation (KMF) and the Karnataka State Rural Livelihoods Promotion 
Society (KSRLPS), the Ksheera Sanjeevini Phase-IV and Phase-V schemes are being implemented across the 
jurisdictions of all 16 District Milk Unions. Each phase covers 250 Women Milk Producers’ Cooperative Societies, 
ensuring that 10,000 women milk producers per phase benefit from socio-economic empowerment and skill 
development programmes. The approved project cost is Rs. 2,061.38 lakh for Phase-IV and Rs. 2,177.06 lakh 
for Phase-V. So far, an amount of Rs.857.00 lakh has been released for effective implementation and has 
achieved about 90% progress under Phase -IV, while Phase-V is currently under implementation.

6.6 FISHERIES
Karnataka state has vast marine, backwater and inland water resources, including a 320 km long coast line, 
27,000 sq. km continental shelf area and 5.83 lakh hectares of inland water resources. The state also has 
about 8,000 hectares of brackish water areas, offering extensive opportunities for shrimp and brackish water 
fish culture. There are about 9.84 lakh fishermen engaged in various fisheries activities across the state, out of 
which 3.31 lakh are in marine sector and 6.53 lakh are in inland sector. Fish being one of the nutritious foods 
and plays an important role in combating malnutrition. The fisheries sector not only provides high-quality 
animal protein but also generates significant employment opportunities. The total fish production during 
2024-25, is 9.63 lakh metric tonnes. The share of fisheries sector to GSDP of the state is 0.48%.
Fisheries have emerged as an important industry in the state for food production and foreign exchange earning 
activities. So far, 62 FFPOs (Fish Farmer Producer Organisation) have been registered by fishermen, there by 
promoting entrepreneurship in the fisheries sector. Also, 12,122 Kisan Credit Cards have been distributed to 
fishermen by the end of December 2025.
6.6.1 Fish Production
Regarding coastal fisheries, a total of 25246 fishing boats are engaged in marine fishing in the state, out 
of which 4828 Mechanized boats, 11443 Motorized boats, 8953 traditional boats and 22 Deep Sea Fishing 
Vessels are operating.
With respect to Inland fisheries, the state has 16 fish seed production centers. Fish seed production during 
the year 2024-25 was 7843.20 lakhs (Size: Fry fish seeds). During the year 2025-26, 6311.50 lakh fish seeds 
(size: Fry fish seeds) is produced as against the target of 10,000 lakhs up to end of December 2025.
The annual fish production in Karnataka has shown a considerable increase from 5.81 lakh metric tonnes in 
2015-16 to 9.63 lakh metric tonnes in 2024-25 with an annual average growth rate of 8.31%. During the year 
2025-26, upto the end of December 2025, 6.59 lakh MTs fish was produced.
During the year 2025-26, an amount of Rs.43,529.51 lakhs has been allocated in the budget, out of which            
Rs.26,345.87 lakh has been released and Rs.15,596.20 lakhs has been spent  up to the end of December 2025.
The schemes implemented by the department are as mentioned below: 
A) Centrally Sponsored Schemes and works
1) Pradhan Manthri Matsya Sampada yojana-Integrated Development and Management of 
Fisheries
Central Government has implemented a flagship programme called Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana 
during the period 2020-21 to 2024-25 to bring about a significant growth in the fisheries sector and has 
been extended to 2025-26. Under the said scheme, beneficiaries belonging to Scheduled Caste/Scheduled 
Tribe/Women and General Categories will be provided financial assistance of 60% and 40% of the allocated 
unit cost respectively. All aspects of the fisheries sector are included in the scheme and the beneficiaries 
can take up components in culture, capture, value addition, marketing and infrastructure development. The 
assistance is shared by the central and state government on a 60:40 basis. During the year 2025-26, a total of  

PDF_PAGE 242
234

Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
Rs. 19.37 Crores expenditure was incurred and a total of 245 beneficiaries have received the assistance under 
this scheme up to the end of December 2025.
2) Savings-cum-relief scheme for marine fishermen
Under this Scheme, a total amount of Rs.1500 will be collected from each fisherman during fishing period and 
a matching contribution of Rs. 1500 from Central Government and Rs. 3000 from state government is given. 
Thus, a total amount of Rs. 6000/- will be paid as relief to the fishermen during the fishing ban period (June 
and July). During 2025-26, an amount of Rs. 513.42 lakh expenditure has been incurred against the release of 
Rs. 515.58 lakh up to the end of December 2025.
3) Construction of fishing harbours
Under this scheme, the preference will be given for construction of new fishing harbours and jetties. Apart 
from this, emphasis is laid on the expansion of major fishing harbours and jetties and the development of 
basic infrastructure facilities in these harbours and jetties, which will facilitate the movement of mechanised 
fishing boats.  
4) Group Accident Insurance Scheme
Under this centrally sponsored scheme, fishermen, fish farmers, and those directly engaged in fisheries-
related activities are eligible to receive death and accident insurance. For the year 2025–26, a premium of 
Rs. 25.62 lakh (state share) has been paid to the National Fisheries Development Board (NFDB) to cover the 
insurance of 80,099 registered fishermen.
B) State Sector Schemes
a) Marine Fisheries Sector
1) Subsidy on the electricity used by ice plants
Under this scheme provision was made to provide subsidy @Rs.1.75 per unit of the electricity consumed 
by the Ice plants subjected to a maximum of Rs.3.50 lakh per ice plant. During 2025-26 an allocation of 
Rs.400.00 lakhs has been released, and an expenditure of Rs.400.00 lakhs has been incurred and subsidy was 
distributed to 180 Ice plants up to end of December 2025.
2) Reimbursement of sales tax on diesel used by fishing boats
For the year 2025-26, a total of 2,00,000 kiloliters of state sales tax exempted diesel has been earmarked 
under this scheme. Out of this, by the end of December 2025, a total of 1,60,000 kiloliters of diesel has been 
distributed to mechanized fishing boats through diesel bunks designated by the department.
3) Supply of Kerosene to traditional boats
There are 8,030 mechanized fishing boats in Karnataka state. The Central Government is providing a quota of 
300 liters of kerosene per month per boat at subsidized rates. In addition, the State Government is supplying 
industrial kerosene at a concessional rate of Rs.35 per liter. As a result, a large number of traditional fishing 
boats along the coast have been fitted with outboard engines, enabling fishermen to travel far from the shore 
within a short time and carry out fishing activities more efficiently. During 2025-26, an amount of Rs. 5000.00 
lakhs has been allocated and Rs. 3787.50 lakh expenditure has been incurred up to the end of December 
2025.

b) Inland Fisheries Sector
During the year 2025-26, 2804.69 lakh finger lings in 2697 departmental tanks, 801.93 lakh fingerlings in 3233 
gram panchayat tanks and 409.88 lakh fingerlings in 3342.68 hectares of private pond shave been stocked 
and developed upto December 2025. It is estimated that around 2.10 lakh Metric Tonnes of fish have been 
produced from the inland resources of the state up to December 2025.
Comprehensive Fisheries Development Plan (Inland Fisheries Development)
The following programmes are being implemented under this scheme.
1) Dis tribution of fisheries requisite kits.
2) Fish  seed stocking in reservoirs.
3) Dis tribution of subsidy for purchase of fish seeds.
4) Dis tribution of subsidy for construction of fish ponds on the edge of tanks/reservoirs.
5) Enc ouragement for shrim pand brackish water fish farming.
6) St ocking of fish seeds in brackish water area.
During the year 2025-26, Rs.935.00 lakh budget has been released and incurred an expenditure of  Rs. 755.98 
lakh up to the end of December 2025 for the implementation of the above programmes.
c) Reimbursement of differential interest to commercial banks
Provision has been made to the fisher women to avail loan up to Rs.3,00,000/-at 0% interest from Commercial 
Banks and Regional Rural Banks. And fishermen are eligible to avail loan up to Rs. 50,000/- at 2% interest from 
Commercial Banks and Regional Rural Banks. Under this scheme the difference of interest will be reimbursed 
to the banks which extend the loans to fishers. Fishers of both marine and inland sector are eligible to avail 
this facility under this scheme. An allocation of Rs. 50.00 lakh has been released during 2025-26 and  the 
same has been fully utilized  up to the end of December 2025.
d)  Fishermen’s Distress Relief Fund
In case of death/disability while engaged in fishing, medical reimbursement and for loss of fishing boats/
nets financial relief is provided to their dependents/fishermen from the Fishermen’s Distress Relief Fund. 
For death cases of fishermen Rs. 10,00,000/-, for disability cases a maximum of Rs. 4,00,000/, for medical 
reimbursement cases up to a maximum of Rs.3,00,000/- and for boat/net loss cases compensation will be 
provided up to 50 percent of the purchase value or up to a maximum of Rs.10,00,000/-will be provided as 
relief. In the current year, Rs.7.05 crores relief is given for 135 cases from the Fishermen’s Distress Relief Fund 
up to the end of December 2025.
C) District Sector
1. Assistance for development of inland fisheries
Expenditure incurred towards the operation cost for production and rearing of fish seeds in production 
centers and rearing centers are covered under this scheme. During the year 2025-26,  Rs. 940.26 lakh has 
been allocated  and an expenditure of Rs. 387.97 lakh has been incurred up to December 2025.

2. Assistance to construction of fish markets and fish marketing
In order to help fisher folk, to sell and transport the harvested fish in fresh and hygienic condition, financial 
assistance is being provided under this scheme for the purchase of different vehicles at a subsidy of 25%. 
For purchase of Bicycle, two-wheeler, Three-wheeler (goods vehicle) and Four-wheeler (goods vehicle) with 
insulated boxes, a subsidy of maximum upto Rs.4000/-, Rs.30,000/-, Rs. 1,20,000/- and Rs. 2,40,000/- is given 
respectively. Owners of the Non-motorized boats (Paathidoni and Rampani) can avail a subsidy of 50% or 
maximum up to Rs.5000/- for purchase of fishing nets/other fishing material. During 2025-26, Rs.231.60 lakh 
has been allocated and an expenditure of Rs. 71.45 lakh is incurred up to the end of December 2025.

 Y In the year 2025-26, Rs. 7.05 crores relief is given to 135 cases from fisher men Distress Relief Fund 
scheme.
 Y Under the Savings and Relief Scheme, a relief of Rs. 5.13 crores  have been provided to 17114 fishermen.

 Y During 2025-26 an Rs. 4.00 crores subsidy is distributed to 180 Ice plants up to the end of December

Challenges and Way Forward
 Y Diversification of aqua culture practices.
 Y Non-availability of alternative fast growing candidate species to diversify the aquaculture practices.
 Y Support and incentives/subsidies to be given for culture of new candidate species like Pungasius, 
Genetically Improved Farmed Tilapia and local varieties of carps.
 Y Introduction of high yielding and eco friendly culture systems.
 Y Due to the non-availability of fish feed locally, the cost of fish feed is high, which has adversely affected 
feed based aquaculture activities.
 Y To reduce the cost of production, subsidy on use of electricity for incorporation of innovative aqua culture 
techniques like RAS/Bio-floc may be given.
 Y Encouraging the establishment of fish feed mills by giving financial assistance.
 Y Inadequate availability of inputs for fish culture including fish seed.
 Y Since the breeding period of fishes is short, there is a need to improve both the quality and quantity of 
brood stock to ensure the continuous functioning of fish hatcheries.
 Y Establishing more number of new hatcheries in the production centers.
 Y To promote open sea cage culture as an alternative to capture fishery.
 Y Paradigm shift towards new opportunities in the sector to achieve the intended objectives of “BLUE 
REVOLUTION”.
 Y Strengthening of Marine and Inland fish marketing infrastructure and cold chain.
 Y Lack of field functionaries to take up effective extension activities.
 Y Up-gradation of existing fisheries training centers and need based trainings/ IEC programmes to be 
conducted to the fish farmers/fish processers.

6.7 FOOD SECURITY
6.7.1 Pr ovision of Food to the Poor through Public Distribution System in Karnataka
Food, Civil Supplies and Consumer Affair Department is one of the major Government Departments involved 
in providing food security to the poor through Public Distribution System (PDS).  Fixed quantity of food grains 
are being distributed in every month to eligible households under Public Distribution System free of cost. 
The intention of implementing this system is to provide food security to eligible households and achieve 
hunger free state.  Under this Act the Central Government has specified percentage population coverage 
under priority household as 76.04 % in rural area and in 49.36% in urban area. Under National Food Security 
Act (NFSA) Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) and Priority Household (PHH) are covered for food grain allocation.  
35 kg food grain per AAY household and 5 kg food grain per PHH beneficiary is allotted every month.  
Ration Card category Rice/Ragi/Jowar
Distribution Qty (in Kg) Price per kg (in Rs.)
Anthyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) 35 kg Free
Priority Household (PHH) 5 kg per member Free
Computerisation of PDS has been adopted by the State under which Aadhaar details of every PDS beneficiary 
is linked to the ration card and data base of PDS beneficiary has been created.  Also online allotment and 
stock management has also been implemented successfully. Out of totally allotted quantity 1879620.473 MT, 
1344432.253 MT Rice, 345900.290 MT Ragi and 189287.930 MT Jowar was distributed during 2025-26 by the  
end of December 2025. 
During 2025-26 an amount of Rs.1718.75 crore has been allocated in the budget, of which Rs.1162.19 crore 
is released and Rs.483.84 crore has been spent up to the end of December 2025 for the implementation of 
various programms of the department.             
6.7.2. Distribution of foodgrains to ration cards beneficiaries under the Anna Bhagya Scheme
1.   Anthyodaya Anna Yojane (AAY)
The Central Government has implemented Anthyodaya Anna Yojane (AAY) which is in force w.e.f. August-2002 
in the State. It considers the poorest of the poor and the concept has been evolved for those who are not 
able to afford two square meals per day. They are the poorest segment of the population such as landless 
agricultural labourers, households headed by widows, terminally ill,  persons affected by HIV, households 
headed by old age person with meagre income or no-income etc. Such beneficiaries are identified in the 
Grama Sabha by the concerned Grama Panchayath. As stated above, 35 kgs foodgrain is being distributed to 
each AAY household.  Accordingly, during 2025 December, 10,47,370 AAY cardholders have been allotted 35 
kgs foodgrains (per card) free of cost under NFSA. 
2. Priority Household Ration Cards (PHH) 
Priority Household Ration Card is being distributed to each beneficiary under the Central Govt. Sponsored 
Pradhan Manthri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana, 5 kg of rice per month and  the State under the Anna Bhagya 
Guarantee Scheme additional 5 k.g of rice Per month is being distributed free of cost to each beneficiary. 
Under the State-sponsored Anna Bhagya Direct Cash Transfer (Guarantee) Scheme, an amount of Rs. 170/- 
per beneficiary family per month, calculated at the rate of Rs. 34/- per kg in lieu of 5 kg of rice. During the 
current year, 1,14,63,046 PHH card holders have been allotted foodgrains up to the  end of December 2025. 

PDF_PAGE 246
238
Agriculture and Food Management
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
3. National Food Security Act 2013
 Y Under the National Food Security Act, with effect from January 2023, foodgrains under NFSA are being 
allocated free of cost by the Government of India to the State 2,17,403 metric tonnes per month under 
the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana.
 Y The additional rice required for distribution to State NFSA beneficiaries was being purchased under 
Open Market Sale Scheme (OMSS) from Food Corporation of India.  This scheme has been discontinued 
from July 2023.  Hence, the required rice quantity is being purchased from agencies like Kendriya 
Bhandar, National Co-operative Consumer Federation of India Limited (NCCF) and National Agricultural 
Cooperative Marketing Federation of India Ltd. (NAFED). Since OMSS scheme was reintroduced by GOI 
from October 2024, State is purchasing Rice required for allotment to State NFSA beneficiaries and GOK 
Welfare Institutions inmates from November 2024.
 Y Karnataka undertakes purchase of Paddy, Ragi and Jowar under minimum support price as per 
Government of India guidelines.  As and when the procured quantity of Custom Milled Rice (CMR), Ragi 
and Jowar becomes available, the same is distributed under Public Distribution System as part of NFSA 
allocation. During 2025-26, MSP Ragi and Jowar procured during  2024-25 has been distributed to State 
NFSA beneficiaries as well.
 GOI has approved distribution of Fortified NFSA Rice under Public Distribution System.  GOI has identified 
14 districts in the State of Karnataka as High Burden and Aspirational Districts for implementation of the 
same. Fortified NFSA Rice has been distributed in these 14 Districts from May 2022. From April 2023 
onwards, allocation of fortified rice under NFSA by GOI has been extended to all the districts of the State.
4.  ANNA BHAGYA YOJANE  (Guarantee)
Karnataka Government introduced Anna Bhagya DBT Scheme for AAY and PHH card holders from July, 2023. 
An amount equvalent to rice i.e Rs.34/- per k.g. of rice multiplied to 5 k.g’s i.e Rs. 170/- per member is 
credited to head of the family. Instead of transferring cash equivalent for  rice every month through DBT to 
the Bank Account of the Head of the Family mentioned in the Ration Card for beneficiaries under AAY and 
PHH Categories, it has been ordered to distribute 5 Kg of Rice to eligible beneficiaries from the month of 
February 2025. Accordingly for the period from February 2025 to December 2025 a total of 23,11,012.000 
MTs rice required has been procured from the FCI under the OMSS scheme and allocated for distribution.

9. Minimum Support Price Scheme (MSP)
As per the GOI order every year the State is purchasing Paddy, Ragi and Jowar from farmers under Minimum 
Support Price at the quantity and rate fixed by the GOI and the same is distributed under PDS. The Central 
Government has set a target  for procurement of  7460 MT Paddy, 6.00 LMT Ragi and  3.00 LMT  Jowar, 0.29 
LMT of Minor Millets during  2025-26.
10. “DASOHA” Scheme
The foodgrain allocation received from Central Government under welfare institutions and Hostel scheme 
is being distributed free of cost to State run/aided welfare institutes such as Nariniketans, Old Age Homes, 
Orphanages, Hostels, Homeless/Beggar rehabilitation Centres, Swadhar homes, Hostels for blind children, 
Remand homes, Hostels providing free accommodation and food run by religious institutions etc. Accordingly, 
15 Kg rice is distributed to each beneficiary of the Welfare Institution of Government of Karnataka Welfare 
Institutions and  to each beneficiary of  Government of India Welfare Institutions 10 Kg Rice and 5 kg wheat 
per beneficiary is being distributed to the welfare institutes in the State.   As of the end of December 2025, 
under the Dasoha Scheme, a total of 104.590 metric tonnes of rice and 52.295 metric tonnes of wheat have 
been allocated to 10,459 inmates of 168 welfare institutions of the Central Government, and 462.240 metric 
tonnes of rice have been allocated to 30,816 inmates of 255 welfare institutions of the State Government.

Karnataka’s approach to natural resource governance reflects a progressive and structured commitment to 
ecological security, sustainable utilisation, economic development, livelihood sustainability, and environmental 
resilience. Forests, water resources, biodiversity, minerals and coastal ecosystems together constitute the 
State’s natural capital, requiring careful conservation and scientific management. Trends in forest area and 
cover, district-wise distribution, biodiversity status and inter-state comparisons reflect measurable progress, 
while also highlighting emerging environmental pressures such as climate variability, human–wildlife conflict, 
habitat fragmentation and resource degradation.
The Government has adopted a structured and progressive approach encompassing expansion of the protected 
area network, wildlife conservation, mitigation of human–animal conflict, watershed and afforestation 
programmes, eco-restoration, and promotion of responsible eco-tourism. Supported by State initiatives and 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes such as Project Tiger, Project Elephant, and the Green India Mission, alongside 
institutional strengthening and resource mobilisation, Karnataka advances a balanced strategy that integrates 
conservation, tourism development, community participation and sustainable resource use to ensure long-
term ecological resilience and inclusive growth.
NATURAL RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND ENVIRONMENTAL GOVERNANCE 
Natural resource management and environmental governance form a cornerstone of Karnataka’s sustainable 
development strategy. The State has consistently sought to reconcile economic expansion with ecological 
stewardship, recognising that long-term growth depends on the preservation of natural capital. With 
substantial forest and tree cover, globally significant biodiversity zones and scientifically designed watershed 
systems, Karnataka’s environmental assets play a critical role in sustaining livelihoods, regulating climate and 
maintaining ecosystem balance.
However, rapid urbanisation, climate variability, rising waste generation, and competing land-use pressures 
have intensified environmental stress. In response, the State has strengthened institutional frameworks 
for climate governance, disaster monitoring, biodiversity management and technology-driven resource 
administration. These efforts reflect a commitment to resilient, inclusive and environmentally sustainable 
growth that safeguards both ecological integrity and economic opportunity.
7.1 FORESTS
Forests constitute a vital component of Karnataka’s natural capital, supporting biodiversity, economic activity, 
and ecological stability. The State encompasses nearly 60 per cent of the Western Ghats, one of the world’s 
recognised biodiversity hotspots. This region forms part of one of the 35 global biodiversity hotspots and one 
of the four in India, underscoring its ecological significance.
To strengthen local biodiversity governance, 6,554 Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) have been 
constituted at the Gram Panchayat level. Conservation of unique genetic resources is further promoted 
through notification of Biodiversity Heritage Sites, such as the 400-year-old tamarind groves at Nallur in 
Devanahalli taluk of Bengaluru Rural district. These initiatives reflect an effort to embed conservation within 
local governance structures.
Despite measurable progress in forest protection, ecological pressures persist, particularly in the Western 
Ghats. While the rate of deforestation has declined and forest cover has improved quantitatively, concerns 
7

remain regarding forest quality and ecological integrity. Degradation affects ecosystem services such as water 
regulation, soil conservation, carbon sequestration and habitat stability, thereby posing risks to environmental 
sustainability and the livelihoods of forest-dependent communities.
Forest resources contribute significantly to the State’s economy through timber, medicinal plants, non-timber 
forest products (NTFPs), grazing, eco-tourism, watershed services, and carbon storage. At the same time, 
population growth, infrastructure expansion, mining, encroachment, habitat fragmentation, illegal timber 
extraction, poaching, excessive fuelwood collection and unregulated grazing exert sustained pressure on 
forest ecosystems. Balancing developmental imperatives with ecological conservation remains a continuing 
policy challenge.
The Karnataka Forest Department has taken steps to arrest quantitative forest loss through afforestation 
programmes, strengthened protection measures and participatory forest management. Community 
involvement in the regeneration of degraded forests, along with the promotion of eco-tourism and biodiversity 
conservation, has become central to forest governance. Yet, ensuring long-term sustainability requires 
sustained efforts to improve forest quality, restore degraded landscapes and enhance ecosystem resilience.
7.1.1 Area under Forests
Karnataka is the seventh largest State in India, covering 1,91,791 sq. km and accounting for 5.83 per cent 
of the country’s total land area. Its varied climate, topography, and soil conditions have produced diverse 
ecological zones that support rich biological diversity.
The total forest area in Karnataka stands at 40,678.23 sq. km. This includes Reserved Forests, Protected 
Forests, Village Forests, Private Forests, Section 4–notified forests, Unclassed Forests and other forests 
notified under statutory provisions.
According to the Champion and Seth (1968) classification, the State’s forests are grouped into eight major 
forest groups, further subdivided into 21 distinct forest types. The evergreen forests of the Western Ghats 
dominate the landscape, while scrub and thorn forests are found in drier regions. Major tree species include 
teak (Tectona grandis), sandalwood (Santalum album), rosewood (Dalbergia latifolia) and species of Terminalia 
and Pterocarpus, alongside dryland species such as Balanitesroxburghii, Cordiamyxa, Capparis, Acacia and 
Prosopis.
Through biodiversity conservation, participatory forest management and sustainable utilisation of forest 
resources, Karnataka continues to integrate environmental protection with livelihood security and long-term 
ecological resilience.
