7.6.2 Sewage Management in Karnataka
Introduction
Sewage management is a critical component of urban planning, environmental protection, and public health. 
In Karnataka, as in many other states, rapid urbanisation, population growth, industrial expansion, and 
infrastructure development have resulted in increased generation of sewage, placing considerable stress on 
existing collection, conveyance, treatment, and disposal systems. Proper treatment and environmentally safe 
disposal of sewage are essential to prevent contamination of surface and groundwater sources, safeguard 
public health, and protect aquatic ecosystems.

PDF_PAGE 321
313
Natural Resource Management and Environment 
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
Karnataka has several major urban centres, including Bengaluru, Mysuru, Hubli–Dharwad, and Mangaluru, 
where sewage management poses a significant challenge due to high population density and accelerated 
urban growth. Many cities are witnessing expansion beyond planned limits, resulting in gaps between sewage 
generation and treatment capacity, incomplete sewerage networks, and dependence on on-site sanitation 
systems. These challenges necessitate continuous augmentation of sewage infrastructure and strengthening 
of operational efficiency to ensure compliance with prescribed environmental standards.
Sewage management in Karnataka is undertaken through a multi-agency institutional framework. The 
Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board (BWSSB) is responsible for the collection, treatment, and disposal 
of domestic sewage within Bengaluru city limits. In other Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), sewage management 
is overseen by the Directorate of Municipal Administration (DMA). The development and augmentation of 
sewage treatment infrastructure, including Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) and sewerage networks, are 
supported by agencies such as the Karnataka Urban Water Supply & Drainage Board (KUWS&DB) and the 
Karnataka Urban Infrastructure Development and Finance Corporation (KUIDFC). These agencies play a 
crucial role in planning, financing, and implementing sewage management projects to address current gaps 
and meet future demand.
Current Status of Sewage Management in Karnataka
Karnataka has a total of 316 Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), including the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA), of 
which 27 are covered under the Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT) and 288 
fall under the non-AMRUT category. Across the State, sewage treatment facilities have been established in 
132 ULBs to treat domestic sewage and sullage. 
With respect to wastewater management in Bengaluru city, the urban population is approximately 1.5 
crore, and the total sewage generation is estimated at about 1,480 MLD. The city is presently served by 34 
Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) with an aggregate installed treatment capacity of 1,348.5 MLD, against which 
approximately 1,212.71 MLD of sewage is currently being treated. The details of the existing wastewater 
treatment facilities in Bengaluru, along with the utilisation of treated effluent, are presented in Table given

WAY FORWARD
To improve sewage management in Karnataka, a comprehensive and multi-pronged approach is required: 
Priority must be given to expanding sewerage networks in rural, peri-urban, and newly developed urban areas 
to ensure universal access to safe sanitation and sewer connections. At the same time, upgrading, modernising, 
and augmenting sewage treatment capacity—particularly in major urban centres such as Bengaluru—along 
with establishing new Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) in underserved and rapidly urbanising regions, is 
essential to address increasing sewage generation. Strengthening community participation through sustained 
public awareness and capacity-building programmes will promote responsible sanitation practices and 
prevent misuse of sewerage systems. Substantial financial investment from State and Central Governments, 
supplemented by multilateral and international funding, will be required to bridge infrastructure gaps and 
ensure long-term sustainability. Further, adoption of circular economy principles—by promoting reuse of 
treated wastewater for non-potable applications such as industrial processes, landscaping, construction, and 
groundwater recharge, along with recovery of resources such as energy and nutrients from sewage—will 
enhance water-use efficiency, reduce pollution loads on water bodies, and address growing water scarcity 
across the State, supported by strengthened policy and regulatory enforcement.
7.6.3 Polluted River Stretches in Karnataka
Introduction
Urbanization adversely affects physical, chemical, biological aspects and life support system of river 
ecosystem beside landscape changes. Chemical and Physical properties of the urban rivers get altered due 
to municipal and industrial discharges. Direct dumping of sewage and MSW into the river and addition of 
harmful chemicals from agricultural runoff contributes to river pollution and eutrophication. Urban rivers 
are commonly characterized by presence of organic pollutants, high Total Suspended Solid (TSS), Nitrate and 
Eutorphication, high Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD), Chemical Oxygen Demand(COD).
Current Status of Polluted River Stretches in Karnataka
Based on the Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD) value at the water quality monitoring locations along the river 
stretches, CPCB has identified 311 Polluted River Stretches (PRS) throughout India wherein BOC exceeds 03 
mg/l.

PDF_PAGE 324
316
Natural Resource Management and Environment 
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
In the financial year 2016-17, based on water quality, the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) has 
identified the 17 polluted river stretches namely, Arakavati, Lakshmanteertha, Malaprabha, Tungabhadra, 
Bhadra, Kaveri, Kabini, Kagin, Kali, Krishna, Asangi-Krishna, Shimsha, Bhima, Netravati, Kumaradhara, Tunga 
and Yagachi.
For the rejuvenation and restoration of river pollution, an action plan has been prepared. This action plan 
included the installation of sewage treatment plants (STPs) and wastewater treatment units. To rejuvenate 
the polluted rivers, a time-bound action plan has been formulated and with the approval of the CPCB the plan 
has been implemented since 2019-2020.
In the year 2022, the Central Pollution Control Board, due to improvements in the water quality of 5 rivers, 
the river basins of Yagachi, Asangi-Krishna, Kumaradhara, Kali and Malaprabha have been removed from the 
list of 17 polluted river stretches and Karnataka has only 12 polluted river stretches. 
Further, the Central Pollution Control Board in 2022-23, has included the following additional 4 nos of rivers 
from Karnataka to the list of polluted rivers namely, Gangavali, Aghanashini, Sharavathi and Dakshina Pinakini 
(Thenpennai).
The River Thenpennai is not in Karnataka and hence requested the CPCB to exclude from the list of Karnataka 
PRS and 3 PRS namely Gangavali, Aghanashini, Sharavathi where the BOD is observed to be <3mlg/l since year 
2020 and hence, the CPCB has been requested to delete the same on 14.10.2022.
Presently, 12 PRS namely, Arkavathi, Laksmanteertha, Tungabhadra, Bhadra, Tunga, Kaveri, Kabini, Kagina, 
Krishna, Shimsha, Bhima and   Netravati are in Karnataka under the catchment of 30 ULBs.
Among the 12 polluted river stretches (PRS) in Karnataka, 1 PRS namely Arkavati river is identified as ‘P1’ 
(BOD in the range of >30mg/l), there are no rivers in ‘P2’ (BOD in the range of 20 - 30mg/l) & ‘P3’ (BOD in the 
range of 10 - 20mg/l) and 3 rivers, Tungabhadra, Bhadra and Shimsha are identified as ‘P4’ (BOD in the range 
of 6.1 - 10.0mg/l), while the remaining 8 rivers, Lakshmantirtha, Tunga, Cauvery, Kabini, Kagina, Krishna, 
Bhima and Netravati are identified as ‘P5’ (BOD in the range of 3.1 - 6.0mg/l).
A basic inventory to identify the pollution source reveals that the 40 ULBs cummilatively generate 817.31 
MLD sewage. A total of 14 sewage treatment plants (STP) in these ULBs of capacity 614.1 MLD capacity 
utilization of existing 14 STPs of the generated sewage is 527.56, while 203.21 MLD sewage is untreated which 
eventually enters the rivers making them highly polluted.
Karnataka has taken special interest in rejuvenation of 12 PRS and facilitating the preparation of River 
Rejuvenation Action Plan for regular basis by analysing with complying time lines. The Water quality is 
monitoried on regular basis by analysing the parameters such as pH, DO, BOD, Faecal coliform and TC. Under 
the River Rejuvenation programmed, 42 STPs with capacity 413.69 MLD have been proposed and 22 STPs of 
capacity 298.91 MLD is under construction.

support system of sacred rivers is continuously available for future.

7.6.4 Industries Effluent Management 
Introduction
The industrial activities are associated with increased levels of pollution. Increased level of Environmental 
pollution reduces the quality of environmental attributes like air, water, soil fertility etc and diminishes the 
carrying capacity of natural ecosystem. The healthy ecosystem services are basic needs for a safe living on 
this earth. Increased level of industrial activity causes increased level of pollution thereby making the people 
to agitate against industrial ecosystem in their neighbourhood. Any amount of economic benefit cannot 
compensate the threatened ecological comforts of the people.
Industrial Effluent management in Karnataka
In Karnataka, there are 52,458 industries categorised as green, orange and red category Out of these, 5147 
industries are water intensive industries thereby generating trade effluent. All these industries have provided 
the ETPs to treat the trade effluent and few small and medium size industries have tie-up with Common 
Effluent Treatment plants (CETPs) that are spread out across various district of Karnataka by following the due 
procedure.
The concept of CETP was introduced in the early 1990s to help Small and Medium size industries. Currently 
there are 14 Numbers of CETPs established in Karnataka State, out of 14 numbers only 09 are operating. 
After treating the trade effluent the treated water are being used for on land gardening and for secondary 
applications viz., boiler feed, cooling and washing.

7.6.5 Electronic Waste (E-Waste) Management
E-Waste Overview  
E-waste refers to discarded electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) no longer in use, including computers, 
mobiles, appliances, medical devices, batteries, TVs, gaming consoles, solar panels, UPS, and more.
E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022  
Notified by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change on November 2, 2022 (GSR 801(E)), these 
rules took effect April 1, 2023, superseding the 2016 rules. They promote environmentally sound management 
(ESM) and a circular economy via Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) [Rule 4(1)].
EPR Entities and Registration 
Provides for the following four types of entities namely:
a. Manuf acturer
b. Pr oducer
c. R efurbisher
d. R ecycler
All must register on the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)’s online portal [Rule 3(1)(s)] at https://
eprewastecpcb.in. Unregistered operations are prohibited, and registered entities cannot deal with 
unregistered ones.
Manufacturer Responsibilities
1) R egister on the portal.
2) Col lect and recycle/dispose e-waste from manufacturing.
3) File  annual/quarterly returns by the end of the succeeding month/year.

PDF_PAGE 327
319
Natural Resource Management and Environment 
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
Producer Responsibilities  
1) R egister on the portal.
2) Implemen t EPR targets per Schedules III and IV.  
3) Pr oviso: Producers under 2016 rules migrate per CPCB/Steering Committee procedure.
4) Raise a wareness via media, ads, posters, etc.
5) File  annual/quarterly returns by the end of the succeeding month/year.
The CPCB has launched an EPR portal under the E-waste (Management) Rules, 2022, for registering producers, 
manufacturers, recyclers, and refurbishers.
Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR)  
EPR holds producers accountable for their products’ environmental impacts across the lifecycle. Forms 
include:
1) Manda tory targets with penalties for non-compliance.
2) R equired collection and recycling via certificates.
EPR targets for each product are set based on producer-submitted data, the product’s CPCB-defined lifespan, 
and Schedules III & IV of the Rules.
EPR Fulfilment Process
 Y Producers must buy EPR certificates online only from registered recyclers and submit them via quarterly 
returns.
 Y Portal cross-checks data from producers and recyclers; the lower figure prevails for EPR compliance.
 Y Certificates undergo environmental audits by CPCB or authorized agencies.
EPR Certificate Role  
Manufacturers/producers manage product waste by establishing collection centers, ensuring segregation/
recycling, and meeting compliances. EPR certificates drive e-waste recycling/reuse, lowering raw material 
costs and ensuring environmentally sound management.
E-Waste Management in Karnataka: Embracing Circular Economy Principles
Karnataka, especially Bengaluru as its technology hub, faces substantial e-waste generation. The state 
proactively adopts circular economy principles to tackle this, emphasizing resource efficiency, waste reduction, 
and environmental sustainability.
Circular Economy Initiatives
Karnataka promotes a circular economy by designing products for extended use, encouraging reuse and 
refurbishment, and ensuring material recycling at end-of-life. Manufacturers must register under Extended 
Producer Responsibility (EPR), mandating management of electronic product disposal. This reduces e-waste’s 
environmental impact and fosters sustainable production and consumption.

PDF_PAGE 328
320
Natural Resource Management and Environment 
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
Challenges and Opportunities
Challenges remain, as the informal sector handles 90-95% of e-waste recycling without proper infrastructure 
or knowledge, posing environmental and health risks. Limited data on Electrical and Electronic Equipment 
(EEE) market introduction also hinders accurate e-waste generation assessments.
E-Waste Management in Karnataka
Karnataka, with Bengaluru as a major centre for information technology and electronics manufacturing 
and services, is a significant generator of electronic waste. In accordance with the E-Waste (Management) 
Rules, 2022, the State has undertaken measures to promote environmentally sound management of e-waste 
through adoption of circular economy principles, including resource efficiency, waste minimisation, reuse, 
refurbishment, and recycling of electrical and electronic equipment. Extended Producer Responsibility 
(EPR) provisions have been implemented to ensure producer accountability for end-of-life management 
of e-waste. However, a substantial proportion of e-waste handling continues to take place in the informal 
sector, estimated at approximately 90–95%, which operates largely outside the formal regulatory framework 
and often without adequate pollution control measures or occupational safety practices. Further, limitations 
in the availability and reliability of data on electrical and electronic equipment placed on the market pose 
challenges in accurate assessment of e-waste generation, monitoring of EPR compliance, and planning of 
infrastructure for e-waste management.

WAY FORWARD
To strengthen e-waste management, Karnataka proposes to focus on formalisation of the recycling sector by 
integrating informal recyclers into the authorised system through capacity building, training, and certification, 
thereby ensuring environmentally sound and safe processing of e-waste. Enhanced public awareness 
initiatives will be undertaken to sensitise consumers on proper e-waste disposal and participation in take-back 
and recycling mechanisms. Further, the State intends to strengthen policy and enforcement frameworks by 
drawing upon international best practices, including elements of the European Union’s e-waste management 
regime. In alignment with the Government of India’s Critical Minerals Mission, Karnataka has also initiated 
measures to promote recovery of critical and strategic minerals from e-waste through authorised recycling 
and material recovery processes. Through continued adoption of circular economy principles and targeted

interventions to address existing gaps, the State aims to enhance resource security, regulatory compliance, 
and environmental protection, while contributing to national and global sustainability objectives.
7.6.6 Plastic Waste Management in Karnataka: Circular Economy Approach
Plastic goods are essential to everyday life and commerce, manufactured on a vast global scale. Yet, handling 
plastic refuse poses escalating challenges due to its ecological and social effects. Karnataka, like other areas, 
is tackling this through creative tactics that prioritize cutting, reusing, and transforming plastic, advancing a 
viable circular economy.
Current State of Plastic Waste Handling in Karnataka
In 2024-25, Karnataka produced 4,08,537 tonnes of plastic waste. The State boasts 135 licensed recycling 
facilities with a total approved capacity of 2,31,834 tonnes, indicating notable advances in recycling systems.
To combat unlawful plastic usage, the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board (KSPCB), partnering with 
municipal authorities, executed 18,111 checks/raids in 2024-25. These actions resulted in confiscating 223.09 
metric tonnes of plastic and levying fines totalling Rs.63.787 lakh, demonstrating the State’s dedication to 
regulatory compliance.
Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) System
Under the EPR framework, producers of plastic products are held accountable for the entire life cycle of 
their products, including waste management. This incentivizes the design of recyclable products and fosters 
investments in recycling infrastructure.
In Karnataka, the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board has registered 1,336 PIBOs (Producers, Importers, 
and Brand Owners) & 135 plastic waste processors (PWPs) are registered on the CPCB centralized EPR portal 
for the period from 2022 to till date.

Circular Economy in Plastic Waste Handling
A circular economy stresses prolonging material lifespans via reuse, recycling, and repurposing, curbing 
reliance on fresh plastic and slashing refuse. It supplants the conventional “extract-produce-discard” pattern 
with a “closed-loop” strategy, emphasizing recyclable designs and green production methods.
Core elements of the circular economy encompass
 Y Recycling and Reuse: Transforming plastic refuse into new items like plastic timber, packaging, and fabrics.
 Y Advancement: Creating sustainable substitutes for conventional plastics, including biodegradable or bio-
based options.
 Y Policies and Rules: Implementing Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) and backing recycled/upcycled 
goods.
Opportunities in Secondary Plastic Products
The manufacture of value-added products from recycled plastics offers significant environmental and 
economic advantages. Key application areas include construction materials such as plastic lumber, paver 
blocks, insulation and composite panels; consumer products including packaging, textiles, and durable 
reusable alternatives; and industrial applications such as automotive components, furniture, and lifestyle 
accessories. By promoting innovation, quality standards, and sustainable manufacturing, Karnataka can 
reduce plastic waste leakage while creating new green enterprises and employment opportunities.
WAY FORWARD
Karnataka proposes to strengthen plastic waste management by promoting the use of secondary plastic 
products through supportive policy and procurement measures, while reinforcing restrictions on single-use 
plastics. Efforts will be directed towards expanding recycling and material recovery infrastructure, including 
through public–private partnerships for advanced recycling technologies. The State will focus on strengthening 
implementation of Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) by improving traceability, enforcement, and 
ease of compliance for Producers, Importers and Brand Owners. Integration of the informal sector through 
capacity building and linkage with authorised recyclers, along with sustained public awareness initiatives on 
plastic reduction and source segregation, will be prioritised. Further, research and innovation in up-cycling, 
biodegradable plastics, and diversified applications of recycled plastics will be encouraged, supported by 
improved digital monitoring systems for data-driven planning and compliance.

8.1 INTRODUCTION
Karnataka has emerged as one of India’s foremost industrial States, driven by a strong policy environment, 
skilled technical workforce and stable labour relations. Over the past few decades, the State has recorded 
significant industrial expansion, particularly in high-technology and knowledge-intensive sectors such as 
electrical and electronics, information and communication technology (ICT), biotechnology and more recently, 
nanotechnology.
The State’s industrial structure reflects a balanced and diversified composition. On the one hand, it hosts 
globally competitive high-tech industries and capital goods manufacturing; on the other, it sustains traditional 
consumer goods and small-scale industries that contribute to employment generation and regional economic 
stability. This dual character has enabled Karnataka to combine innovation-led growth with broad-based 
industrial development.
Karnataka’s progress in industrialisation and innovation is reflected in national performance assessments. 
According to the NITI Aayog SDG India Index 2023–24, the State ranks 7th among Indian states under 
Sustainable Development Goal 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure), securing a score of 62 out of 
100. States ranked above Karnataka include Delhi, Haryana, Kerala, Punjab, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal. 
Performance of Karnataka vs India and performer States-Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure (SDG 9) is 
given Table 8.1. 
This performance underscores Karnataka’s sustained commitment to strengthening industrial infrastructure, 
promoting innovation ecosystems and enhancing manufacturing capabilities. As the State advances toward 
higher levels of technological sophistication and global competitiveness, industry continues to serve as a 
critical pillar of economic growth, employment generation and structural transformation.

8.4 MICRO, SMALL & MEDIUM ENTERPRISES
Karnataka continues to be a premier destination for industrial Investment in India, driven by its dynamic 
economy, progressive governance and innovation-centric industrial ecosystem. The state’s industrial landscape 
has evolved to encompass not only traditional manufacturing and MSMEs, but also high-tech sectors such 
as aerospace, biotechnology, renewable energy and advanced manufacturing. Karnataka’s strategic position 
is strengthened by robust policies, supportive infrastructure and initiatives fostering an investor-friendly 
environment.
The Karnataka Industrial Policy 2025-30
The Industrial Policy 2025–30 has been announced to make Karnataka a strong, competitive  and sustainable 
industrial State by attracting investments of about INR 7.5 lakh crore and creating around 20 lakh jobs by 
2030. 
Vision: To position Karnataka as a global leader in manufacturing, innovation and sustainable industrial 
growth while ensuring inclusive development across all regions.
Core Objectives
 Y Attract Investments: Target total investments of INR 7.5 lakh crore by 2030. 
 Y Employment Generation: Create 20 lakh new jobs through industrial expansion. 
 Y Manufacturing Growth: Achieve an accelerated manufacturing sector growth rate of 12% annually. 
 Y Sustainability Leadership: Incentivize green and sustainable industrial practices. 
 Y Regional Equity: Strengthen industrial development in backward and under-developed taluks through 
differential incentives. 
 Y Ease of Investment: Enhance digital and single-window systems for faster approvals and investor 
facilitation. 
The policy provides strong support to MSMEs through reservation of industrial land, financial incentives, 
technology upgradation and market support, with special encouragement for SC/ST, women and first-
generation entrepreneurs. 
It also promotes innovation, research and development and Global Capability Centres, while aligning skill 
development and training programmes with industry needs to build a future-ready workforce. Overall, the 

PDF_PAGE 336
328
Industry
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
Karnataka Industrial Policy 2025–30 seeks to promote inclusive, innovation-driven and environmentally 
sustainable industrial growth, while strengthening Karnataka’s position as a preferred destination for domestic 
and global investors.
8.4.1 Role and Growth of the MSME Sector

crucial role next only to agriculture. By fostering entrepreneurship and generating large-scale employment 
with relatively low capital investment, MSMEs significantly contribute to inclusive and balanced economic 
growth.

8.4.4 Karnataka Udyoga Mitra
Karnataka Udyoga Mitra is a key initiative by the Government of Karnataka, established to promote industrial 
development and facilitate ease of doing business in the state. During 2024–25, a total of 444 projects 
were approved by the State Level Single Window Clearance Committee (SLSWCC) with an investment of 
Rs.25,226.25 crore and generating employment for 1,06,801 persons. In addition, 10 projects were approved 
by the State High Level Clearance Committee (SHLCC) with an investment of Rs.11,246.31 crore, generating 
employment for 6,954 persons.
During 2025–26, 6 meetings of the State Level Single Window Clearance Committee (SLSWCC) were held, 
approving 350 projects with an investment of Rs.65,979.54 crore, expected to generate employment for 
98,279 persons. Further, up to the end of January 2026, the State High Level Clearance Committee (SHLCC) 
approved 19 projects with an investment of Rs.43,018.43 crore, generating employment for 15,738 persons.
8.4.5 Invest Karnataka 2025 – Outcomes of Global Investors Meet
“Invest Karnataka 2025 – Global Investors Meet”, held at Bangalore Palace in February 2025, sustained and 
structured follow-up actions have been undertaken to translate the investment intentions expressed during 
the Summit into tangible outcomes. It is noteworthy that several leading industrial enterprises which made 
investment announcements at the Summit have subsequently initiated formal implementation processes 
by submitting their investment proposals through Karnataka Udyog Mitra (KUM) under the Single Window 
Clearance mechanism. This progression clearly indicates that the Invest Karnataka 2025 Summit has moved 
beyond the stage of announcements and entered the phase of actual implementation.
Based on the investment proposals received under the Single Window system, estimated investments 
aggregating to approximately Rs. 4,16,848 crore, with the potential to generate about 1,19,047 employment 
opportunities, have been recorded. These outcomes reflect the Summit’s effectiveness in converting investor 
interest into real investment pipelines. They underscore a clear momentum towards accelerated industrial 
activity and employment generation, with expected long-term positive implications for the State’s economic 
growth and balanced regional development.

8.5.1 Food Karnataka Limited
The Food Karnataka Limited (FKL) is a special purpose vehicle to provide state of art infrastructure to food 
parks. Under the administrative control of Karnataka State Agricultural Produce Processing and Export 
Corporation Limited (KAPPEC). Since it started functioning, FKL has been liaising with the line departments 
such as Agriculture, Horticulture, Animal Husbandry, Fisheries, Food Processing and Commerce & Industries 
Departments, towards attracting investments into agribusiness and food processing sector. Government of 
Karnataka and the Union Governments have been giving special focus and thrust on the agribusiness and food 
processing activities in order to provide an effective market linkage and value addition to the farm produce so 
that farming community at large reap the benefits of getting a reasonable return for their produce.

food processing units. Under this food park, 14 food processing units are operating and Rs. 400 lakh each 
has been released by state and central government.

8.5.3 Sericulture
Sericulture is one of the major employment generating sectors in the State and its growth has immense 
employment generation potential, particularly in rural Karnataka. A total budgetary provision of  
Rs.395.110 crore was made to the department during 2025–26 under State Sector and District Sector schemes. 
In addition, financial assistance of Rs.13.736 crore was provided under the Central Sponsored Scheme – 
Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchai Yojana (PMKSY) and Rs.78.210 crore under the Central Sector Scheme – Silk 
Samagra. Thus, an overall allocation of Rs.487.059 crore was provided for the development of the sericulture 
sector during the year.
During 2024–25, mulberry silk production in Karnataka was 13,276.64 metric tonnes (MTs). As of the end of 
December 2025, the area under mulberry cultivation in the State stood at 1,22,939 hectares, which is higher 
than the area recorded during the corresponding period of 2024–25. Owing to its labour-intensive nature, 
employment generation in the sericulture sector continues to remain significant.
Financial assistance provided to the sericulturists is Rs. 5,740.28 lakh and for  reelers is Rs. 602.05 lakh during 
2025-26 up to December. The State’s raw silk production stands at 10,854.57 MTs till December 2025, while 
India’s raw silk imports till December(Provisional) 2025 stands at 2,003 MTs.
During 2025–26, the Government announced several new initiatives to strengthen the sericulture 
sector
(i) Aut omatic silk reeling units of 120 ends are being encouraged for establishment by middle-class silk 
reelers to meet domestic demand for international-grade bivoltine raw silk.
(ii) The first phase of works relating to the Hi-Tech Silk Markets at Ramanagara and Shidlaghatta has been 
completed and the second phase will be taken up during 2025–26 at an estimated cost of Rs.250 crore.
(iii) A new silk cocoon market will be established at Mysuru with financial assistance from NABARD, benefiting 
silk farmers of Mysuru and surrounding districts.
(iv) T o ensure international quality standards and better price realisation, assayers will be deputed for 
scientific quality testing and grading of silk cocoons in Government silk cocoon markets.
8.5.4 Karnataka Silk Marketing Board Ltd.
The Karnataka Silk Marketing Board Ltd. (KSMB) is primarily entrusted with the responsibility of price 
stabilisation of silk yarn, which is inherently a non-profit-oriented activity.

8.6 STATUS OF PUBLIC ENTERPRISES IN KARNATAKA
8.6.1 Karnataka State Small Industries Development Corporation (KSSIDC)
Karnataka State Small Industries Development Corporation Limited (KSSIDC) promotes the development of 
Small Scale Industry (SSI) sector by developing Industrial Estate. Thereby, the department provides industrial 
plots and sheds to entrepreneurs, for production and for procurement and distribution of raw materials.
To date, KSSIDC has developed 195 industrial estates throughout Karnataka, contributing significantly to the 
state’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP). 6,633 number of sheds and 10,488 industrial plots are established till 
December 2025. 
For the financial year 2024–25, the Corporation achieved a total income of Rs.10,729.96 lakh, incurred a total 
expenditure of Rs.3,647.54 lakh and registered a net profit after tax of Rs.4,741.89 lakh.
During the year 2025–26, land has been identified and acquired / is in the process of acquisition by the 
Corporation for the establishment of new industrial estates in various locations. At Mettikuriki, Chitradurga 
District, an extent of 100 acres has been received through land allotment from KIADB. At Shahapura, Yadgir 
District, 48 acres have been identified, for which sanction has been obtained from the Revenue Department. 
In Kolar, an extent of 60 acres has been proposed and a proposal has been submitted for sanction of KGF 
land. Further, in Yadgir, 100 acres of land is proposed to be acquired and a demand survey is currently being 
conducted for land adjacent to the Yadgir–Raichur National Highway.
 Y Under the 2023–24 Government of Karnataka Budget Announcement, KSSIDC has undertaken the 
establishment of new industrial estates from its own resources across various districts. Works at 
Chittapura, Kalaburagi District, covering 27.35 acres are 98% complete. Development works at Kodkani, 
Uttara Kannada District, Kanagala, Belagavi District, Badanaguppe, Chamarajanagar District and Indi 
Vijayapura District, covering extents ranging from 19.38 to 47.06 acres, are in progress with completion 
levels between 70% and 95%. Work orders are issued to establish Industrial estates at Halisagara–
Shahapura Yadgir District, Metikurke-I and Metikurke-II Chitradurga District. Further, the proposed 
industrial estate at Jagaluru Davanagere District is at the tender evaluation stage.
 Y The Corporation has taken up the construction work of Ekta Mall at the Exhibition Grounds, Mysore 
with a 50-year interest-free loan of Rs. 192.98 crore under the Central Government’s One District One 
Product (ODOP) programme.
 Y The Corporation is implementing the construction of multi-storey complexes under the Public-Private 
Partnership (PPP) model at industrial estates. Under this PPP model, the private partner will construct 
the buildings, the annual rent will be paid to the corporation. The building will be handed over to the 
corporation after 30 years. This project will be implemented at important locations in various industrial 
estates of the Corporation. The projects are proposed at Yadavagiri, Mysuru, Uyambag and Anagol 
Stockyard, Belagavi, Gokul Road, Hubballi, Tumakuru, Bykampady and Yeyyadi, Mangaluru covering built-
up areas ranging from 533.08 Sq. Mtrs to 4,725.00 Sq. Mtrs.
 Y The Corporation is undertaking infrastructure upgradation works in these industrial estates. The works 
at Malur, Kolar District over 6.88 acres are nearing completion, while the projects at Sindagi, Vijayapura 
District covering 21.24 acres and Peenya 4th Phase, Bengaluru Urban District over 283 acres have been

is currently under progress.

8.6.3 Karnataka State Electronics Development Corporation Limited (KEONICS)
The Karnataka State Electronics Development Corporation Limited (KEONICS), established in 1976, with the 
sole objective of promoting electronics industries in Karnataka and digital transformation and IT-enabled 
governance across the State of Karnataka. To nurture the ambition of the State Government and ensure that 
the vision of the State is realised, KEONICS has been striving hard to cater to the needs of the IT Sector in 
Karnataka. The Company has set up IT parks in Bengaluru, Hubballi, Shivamogga and Kalaburagi. It also acts 
as the nodal agency for for setting up IT Parks in Tier- II cities and to provide necessary IT infrastructure and 
support to the IT Industry throughout the State.
Innovation Developments/Achievements
KEO: KEO is the one of its kind innovative development by KEONICS. Karnataka has launched KEO, an 
innovative personal computer designed to be affordable, open-source, Artificial Intelligence (AI) capable, 
energy-efficient, small footprint with adequate performance suitable for a wide spectrum of use cases. KEO AI 
PC is powered by a RISC-V based System-on-Chip (SoC). The 64-bit quad-core processor integrates dedicated 
hardware for graphics, media processing  and AI tasks. With its integrated Neural Processing Unit (NPU), 

PDF_PAGE 347
339
Industry
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
the system can run small, pre-loaded AI models for local inference, enabling fast and private AI operations 
without connecting to cloud LLMs. 
AI PC is preloaded with the open-source Ubuntu operating system and open-source productivity tools and 
programming IDEs. It is preloaded with AI chatbot and Sikshanapedia applications for learning. The open-
source licensing ensures zero licensing costs to the end users. Open-source operating systems and applications 
generally work well on Intel and AMD processors but with substantial efforts by the team, the open-source 
applications have been created and performance optimized for open-source RISC-V architecture.
KEO’s hands-on experience amongst the students and youths, especially in rural Karnataka, is expected 
to significantly up skill the students and youths in the areas of IT, AI/ML, electronics, etc., augmenting the 
much needed skilled workforce required by the IT and Electronics industry in Karnataka. The availability of 
the skilled workforce across Karnataka, including rural Karnataka, will enable Karnataka to establish IT and 
Electronics hubs across Karnataka, beyond Bengaluru. This is ideal for students and Educators, Researchers 
and Innovators and Government & Digital offices.

the users can place orders for ICT goods empaneled by the Company. Additional modules for IT Services, ICT

8.6.4 Department of Factories, Boilers, Industrial Safety and Health
The Department of Factories, Boilers, Industrial Safety and Health is responsible for ensuring the occupational 
safety, health and welfare of workers in registered factories and at construction activities with investments 
above Rs.25 crore through effective enforcement.

8.6.7 Public Enterprises
Government of Karnataka established the Karnataka State Bureau of Public Enterprises in 1981 with the 
objective of providing an institutional mechanism for monitoring and improving the performance of State-
owned Public Sector Undertakings. The Bureau was reorganised in 2002 as the Department of Disinvestment 
and Public Enterprises Reforms and was subsequently accorded independent status in 2005 and renamed as 
the Department of Public Enterprises. In 2022, the Department of Public Enterprises was abolished and its 
entire functions relating to policy formation, monitoring, regulation and reform of State PSUs was transferred 
to the Finance Department, which has since been functioning as the nodal authority for supervision and 
reform of PSUs, ensuring improved inter-departmental coordination and strengthening financial discipline 
across the PSU ecosystem.
Profile of State PSU’s
In terms of statutory definition, a Government Company, as per Section 2(45) of the Companies Act, 2013,  
 is a company in which not less than 51 percent of the paid-up share capital is held by the Government. 
In Karnataka, Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) include both Government Companies and Statutory 
Corporations.
PSUs in the State operate across a wide spectrum of sectors such as power generation and transmission, 
transport services, infrastructure development, textiles, mining, manufacturing, financial services, trading 
activities etc. While many of these companies operate on commercial principles, they also discharge important 
public service and developmental functions. As per data of Comptroller and Auditor General (C&AG), 127 
PSUs are in existence in Karnataka including Statutory Corporations.

PDF_PAGE 350
342
Industry
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
Governance and Policy Framework
The Finance Department has incorporated a result oriented governance framework to improve accountability 
and operational efficiency of PSUs. Periodic performance reviews are undertaken to evaluate financial 
outcomes, compliance status and administrative effectiveness. Emphasis is placed on strengthening Board-
level functioning, improving financial reporting quality and ensuring adherence to statutory and regulatory 
requirements.
As part of the governance framework, PSUs are monitored against a defined set of governance, financial 
and operational parameters, supported by policy directives, circulars and Government Orders issued by the 
Finance Department to ensure uniformity and consistency in governance practices which includes: 
 Y Mandatory conduct of four Board Meetings and four Audit & Accounts Committee meetings annually.
 Y Functioning of Nomination and Remuneration Committees and Investment Committees wherever 
applicable.
 Y Compliance with Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) norms specified under Section 135 of Companies 
Act.
 Y Implementation of prudent financial management practices.
 Y Appointment of Independent Directors with appropriate professional expertise and gender diversity.
 Y Use of digital platforms such as e-Office for file and workflow management.
 Y Maintenance and reconciliation of investment and deposit (FDR) registers.
Rationalisation and Restructuring of PSUs
As per the observations contained in Chapter 5 of the State Finance Audit Report of the Comptroller and 
Auditor General of India for the year ended March 2023, a review of the performance and operational status 
of State Public Sector Undertakings was undertaken. In the course of this review, 16 PSUs were identified as 
defunct and are presently at various stages of liquidation, merger or amalgamation. The inactive PSUs have 
investment of Rs.160.21 crore towards capital and Rs.449.39 crore towards long term loans (as per C&AG 
report no 1 of 2025). Necessary actions are being taken in coordination with the concerned Administrative 
Departments to address pending statutory, financial and legal issues and to ensure an orderly process of 
closure or consolidation.
In line with the review and restructuring objectives, Government approval has been accorded for the merger 
of select PSUs, namely: 
i. K arnataka Cashew Development Corporation with Karnataka Forest Development Corporation.
ii. K arnataka Silk Marketing Board with Karnataka Silk Industries Corporation.
iii. K arnataka State Textile Infrastructure Development Corporation with Karnataka Handloom Development 
Corporation. 
These mergers are expected to reduce administrative costs and improve operational and functional efficiency.

developmental activities and has a direct impact on fiscal sustainability, service delivery and employment

Government Support and Human Resource Reforms
The Government continues to extend financial support to PSUs in the form of equity, grants, loans and 
Government guarantees based on operational necessity and fiscal capacity. Such support is provided 
selectively to ensure continuity of essential services and long-term sustainability.

PDF_PAGE 352
344
Industry
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
Government Order No. FD-CAM/1/2025 dated 21.02.2025 has been issued mandating adoption of the Salary 
Package for all officers/employees in State Government departments. Adoption of the Salary Package enables 
coverage of PSU employees under nationally administered social security insurance schemes, namely PMJJBY , 
PMSBY & PAI, thereby ensuring life and accident insurance protection at nominal cost and enhancing financial 
security for employees and their families. PSU’s are being regularly directed to adopt the Salary Package so 
as to ensure that the benefits of social security coverage are extended to all eligible PSU employees. At the 
national level, estimated enrolment of Government officers/employees under PMJJBY is 232.30 lakh persons 
and 93.25 lakh persons under PMSBY across India.
Financial Resource Optimisation through Inter-PSU Mechanisms
In order to optimise utilisation of surplus funds within the public sector, the Inter Corporate Deposit (ICD) 
mechanism has been operationalised. The ICD framework enables PSUs with surplus liquidity to lend to other 
PSUs at competitive interest rates, thereby reducing borrowing costs and improving overall financial efficiency.
As on date, ICDs aggregating Rs.1,625 crore have been transacted, resulting in an estimated interest cost 
saving of Rs.32.5 crore. The mechanism has contributed to improved cash management and reduced reliance 
on market borrowings.
Capacity Building and Knowledge Sharing
During the year, structured training programmes were conducted for senior management and officials of 
Public Sector Undertakings to strengthen institutional capacity and governance standards. These training 
programmes are organised in collaboration with the Institute of Company Secretaries of India (ICSI) and the 
Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), focusing on emerging areas such as Artificial Intelligence, 
governance practices, financial management and compliance with the Companies Act. 
In addition to formal training programmes, the Finance Department has conducted Best Practices and various 
other training programmes for the PSUs as part of a peer-learning approach. Under this programme, selected 
PSUs were invited to share their successful operational and governance practices and implementation 
experiences for effective and sustainable functioning with other PSUs. 
During 2025-26, Best Practices Training Programmes were conducted for MDs, CFOs, Finance Officers and 
Nominee Directors from PSUs, covering ICAI with 116 participants, KSDL, KSIIDC, KATCOand KAMCO with 
115 participants, HGML and KSIC with 108 participants, KRIDL and BMTC with 120 participants and JLR and 
KEONICS with 112 participants.
Also, efforts are underway to explore new areas of training aimed at further enhancing the operational 
efficiency, professional competence and institutional credibility of PSUs in the coming years.
The ongoing reforms and policy interventions have strengthened governance structures, improved financial 
discipline and enhanced monitoring of State PSUs. Continued emphasis on rationalisation, professional 
management, capacity building and fiscal prudence is expected to further improve the performance and 
sustainability of Public Sector Enterprises in Karnataka.

8.7.2 Major Industrial Initiatives to drive the growth of Industry and Service Sectors 
Karnataka IT Policy 2025-30
Vision: To position Karnataka as a globally competitive and inclusive digital economy driven by innovation, 
talent and technology-led growth.
Mission: To promote the growth of the IT and IT-enabled services sector by enabling a robust policy ecosystem, 
fostering innovation and startups, enhancing digital infrastructure and creating large-scale employment 
across the State.
The Government of Karnataka unveiled the new IT Policy 2025–30 at the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2025, 
reinforcing the state’s leadership in deep-tech and Artificial Intelligence  while accelerating the growth of 
emerging clusters across the Beyond Bengaluru region. Anchored on four strategic pillars—Smart & amp; 
Green Infrastructure, Future-Ready Talent, Business-Ready Support  and Market Acceleration—the policy 
introduces key interventions to strengthen R&D, nurture innovation and enable global competitiveness. By 
fostering inclusive regional growth and building robust innovation ecosystems, the policy aims to position 
Karnataka as a premier destination for next-generation technologies and AI-driven transformation.
Karnataka Biotechnology Policy 2024-2029: The Karnataka Biotechnology Policy 2024-2029 sets a forward-
looking vision to position Karnataka as a global leader in biotechnology, focusing on sustainable and inclusive 
growth. Building upon its existing ecosystem, the policy aims to leverage the state’s rich talent pool, advanced 
infrastructure and favorable government support to accelerate growth in key biotech areas. These initiatives 
reflect the state’s on going commitment to developing a thriving biotech ecosystem. Biotech Policy outlines a 
roadmap for sustainable growth, innovation, and regulation in the sector.
Karnataka Startup Policy 2025-2030 aims to position the state as a global innovation leader by supporting 
the creation of 25,000 new startups, with strong emphasis on DeepTech, rural innovation and decentralized 
growth. Backed by an allocation of Rs.518.27 crore, the policy provides funding, mentorship and infrastructure 

PDF_PAGE 354
346
Industry
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
support to strengthen the startup ecosystem beyond Bengaluru. It promotes incubators, accelerators and 
Technology Business Incubators, while offering reimbursements for quality certifications, patent support 
and access to global markets through mentorship initiatives. The policy also encourages social inclusion and 
regional participation. Eligible startups must be recognized by the Karnataka Startup Cell, registered as a 
Private Limited Company or Partnership, be less than 10 years old and have an annual turnover below Rs.100 
crore. 
Aerospace & Defence Policy 2022-27: Karnataka has announced Aerospace & Defence Policy 2022-27 aims to 
attract more investments and to establish Karnataka as the preferred investment destination for Aerospace & 
Defence manufacturing sector. Promote development of indigenous and advanced technologies, encourage 
manufacturing for space-related applications, develop world class skilled manpower and support MSMEs in 
the supply chain with increased technological access for global competitiveness. The policy offers a range 
of incentives and concessions, including Capital Investment Subsidy, Exemption/ Reimbursement of Stamp 
Duty, Concessional Registration Charges, Reimbursement of Land Conversion Fee, Subsidy for ETP (Effluent 
Treatment Plant), Power Tariff Reimbursement, Exemption from Electricity Duty and also Production Linked 
Incentive etc. This policy is designed to foster innovation, strengthen the ecosystem and position Karnataka 
as a global hub for Aerospace and Defence manufacturing.
Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in Karnataka:  State has 38 operational SEZ’s with an investment of Rs.23,331 
crore and generating employment for 4,25,696 persons during the financial year 2025-26 upto December 
2025. There are 396 SEZ units working in the State.

8.8.1 Tourism Policy 2024-29
For integrated development of Tourism in the State the department of Tourism has introduced new tourism 
policy “2024-29”. Karnataka Tourism Vision Group report envisaged that during the 2024-29 policy period Rs. 
5,000 crore investments will be made which will generate around 10 lakhs employment directly or indirectly. 
More investment expected from the private sector or under PPP .
The Policy proposes strategic interventions in the incentives and requisite regulatory reforms to facilitate 
investment in the tourism sector. Continuously striving towards creating a comfortable and sustainable 
tourism eco system, the policy lays emphasis on providing a safe and high-quality experience for tourists and 
greater prosperity and happiness for the people of Karnataka. 
Vision
 Y The Vision is to provide a holistic enabling package wherein school children, youth, women and senior 
citizens can fulfil their desire for travel, learning and experiencing, in all its manifestations including 
spiritual, leisure & fun and intellectual, to give them break from routine and recharge their energies. 
 Y Moreover, the Vision is to reach out to all segments of society and people from within the state, within 
the country and even foreign tourists by providing suitable tourism environment.
Objectives
 Y To make Karnataka one among the top States of India in terms of domestic and international tourist visits.
 Y To harness tourism’s potential for its effects on employment generation, economic development and 
entrepreneurial opportunities.
 Y To increase the visibility and accessibility of lesser-known destinations to promote balanced regional 
development. 
 Y To initiate and support skill development programs to meet the needs of Karnataka’s tourism sector. 
 Y To sustainably develop Coastal Karnataka into a multi-product tourism destination.
 Y To position Karnataka as a preferred destination for tourism investments.
 Y To empower Karnataka Tourism with suitable institutional frameworks and administrative structures for 
the development and promotion of tourism.
The budget allotment for the year 2025-26 is Rs. 191.70 crore, of which Rs. 103.95 crore is incurred as 
expenditure up to December 2025 for the implementation of various schemes.

9.1 SKILL DEVELOPMENT , ENTREPRENEURSHIP AND LIVELIHOOD
Introduction
Karnataka’s strategy for skill development, entrepreneurship, livelihood promotion and labour market 
reforms reflects a comprehensive and future-oriented approach to harnessing its demographic dividend. The 
State has adopted a progressive and forward-looking framework to strengthen institutional capacity, expand 
skilling opportunities and promote sustainable livelihoods across sectors.
Through structured interventions under the Department of Skill Development, Entrepreneurship and 
Livelihood, the Government aligns skill training, enterprise promotion and labour market reforms with 
emerging economic opportunities. Institutional frameworks have been strengthened through initiatives 
such as the Kaushalya Missions, CMKKY 2.0, Yuvanidhi, modernisation of ITIs, apprenticeship expansion and 
international workforce mobility facilitation. Complementary efforts through CEDOK, Sanjeevini–KSRLPS and 
DAY–NULM further promote entrepreneurship and rural–urban livelihoods, alongside financial inclusion, 
support for farm and non-farm enterprises, women-led initiatives, progressive labour legislation and expanded 
social security, collectively fostering productive employment and inclusive growth.
9.1.1 Harnessing the Demographic Dividend through Skill Development and Livelihood Promotion
Karnataka’s demographic profile presents a significant opportunity for the next 25 years. With a large and 
youthful population, the State possesses the potential to strengthen its position as a global economic leader, 
provided this demographic dividend is effectively channelled through skill development, employability 
enhancement and entrepreneurship promotion. Recognising this, the Government of Karnataka established 
the Department of Skill Development, Entrepreneurship and Livelihood (SDEL) in 2016 to equip youth with 
market-relevant skills, promote sustainable livelihoods, and bridge the gap between labour demand and 
supply.
Skills and knowledge are critical drivers of economic growth and social progress. Karnataka has long been 
recognised as a hub of innovation, attracting national and multinational corporations across sectors. However, 
the rapid expansion of industry has highlighted a persistent gap between the demand for skilled manpower 
and its availability. Addressing this mismatch has become central to the State’s human capital strategy.
By 2030, nearly 1.88 crore young individuals are projected to require vocational education. This group 
includes informal workers in agriculture and non-agriculture sectors, school dropouts, secondary and higher 
secondary graduates and young homemakers, while excluding those already engaged in higher education or 
formal vocational training. This scale of demand underscores the need for a structured, inclusive and future-
oriented skilling ecosystem.
Alignment of Karnataka’s Skill Development Strategy with the Sustainable Development Goals 
(SDGs)
Karnataka’s skilling initiatives are closely aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), reinforcing 
both economic and social objectives.

SDG 1: No Poverty: Through the Yuvanidhi scheme, Karnataka provides financial assistance to unemployed 
graduates and diploma holders, offering temporary income support during their transition from education 
to employment. This social protection measure reduces vulnerability and helps prevent poverty arising from 
short-term unemployment.
SDG 4: Quality Education: The State strengthens access to affordable technical and vocational education 
through ITIs, GTTCs, KGTTIs, and short-term programmes such as KalikeJotheKaushalya. These initiatives 
enhance employability by equipping youth with industry-relevant skills aligned to evolving labour market 
needs.
SDG 5: Gender Equality: Focused skilling and livelihood programmes for women promote economic 
independence and social empowerment, ensuring greater participation of women in the workforce and 
advancing inclusive growth.
SDG 8: Decent Work and Economic Growth: By systematically enhancing workforce skills, Karnataka improves 
employment outcomes, raises productivity and supports sustained economic expansion across sectors.
SDG 9: Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure:Investments in modern training infrastructure and industry-
aligned skill development create a competent workforce that drives innovation and strengthens resilient 
industrial ecosystems.
Through this integrated alignment with the SDGs, Karnataka’s skill development strategy addresses youth 
employment challenges while advancing inclusive and sustainable development.
By aligning with these Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), Karnataka is not only addressing domestic 
challenges related to youth employment and industrial demand but also contributing to broader sustainable 
development objectives.
9.1.2 Koushalya Mission
The State, District and Taluka-level Kaushalya Missions have been established under the Department of Skill 
Development, Entrepreneurship and Livelihood to drive skill development initiatives in a mission-oriented 
manner. To ensure effective implementation and measurable outcomes, a Skill Mission Unit has been set 
up at the State level, along with District Skill Development Offices at the district level, focusing on executing 
programs related to Skill Development, Entrepreneurship and Livelihood.
Registration of job seekers under kaushalkar.com
Candidates were registering on www.kaushalkar.com for various job roles in sectors with potential employment 
opportunities will receive skill training aligned with their aspirations. Details of the registered aspirants, 
categorized by district and category, are provided in Appendix 9.1.
Selection of Beneficiary
Any aspiring trainee is considered self-selected upon registering on the website www.kaushalkar.com. If 
the number of registered trainees exceeds the available training slots, priority will be determined based on 
reservation categories, educational qualifications and age. The target segments and priority social groups are 
outlined in Table 9.1.

Skill Development, Entrepreneurship and Livelihood department has following long term targets:
 Y Ensuring all children Complete 10 years of schooling by 2025 compared to the present ratio of only

Department of industrial training and employment
Yuvanidhi Scheme
Yuvanidhi is one of the five guarantee schemes implemented by the Government of Karnataka to support 
youth through the provision of an unemployment allowance. Under this scheme, candidates who have 
completed Graduation or Post Graduation in 2023, 2024 and 2025 and remain unemployed for 180 days 
from the date of result declaration, are eligible to receive a monthly allowance of Rs.3000.00. Diploma 
holders from the same years, under the same conditions, are eligible for a monthly allowance of Rs.1500.00. 
The allowance is provided for a maximum period of two years or until the beneficiary secures employment, 
whichever is earlier.
The scheme was launched on 26.12.2023, with Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) commencing on 12.01.2024. 
As on 31.01.2026, 3,93,358 candidates have registered on the Sevasindhu portal, out of which 3,08,267 
lakh candidates have received benefits. The category-wise and gender-wise distribution of beneficiaries is 
provided in Appendix 9.2a and 9.2b.
Impact of the Scheme:  The unemployment allowance received under this scheme is used by the eligible 
beneficiaries for filling up the application forms for various Job notifications, attend interviews, purchase 
books for compitative exams and attend coaching and skill training classes. This scheme not only provides 
financial assistance but also supports the candidates for a successful career through skilling by Skill Connect 
Portal under Yuvanidhi Plus scheme implemented by Karnataka Skill Development Corporation. 
TATA Udyoga Project
In the year 2021-22, 150 Government Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) across the state were upgraded in 
collaboration with Tata Technologies Limited and 20 of its consortium companies. These upgraded ITIs now 
offer 6 long-term and 23 short-term training courses focused on Industry 4.0 technologies. Together, they 
have the capacity to provide training to 1.20 lakh candidates annually through these short-term and long-
term programs.
Since 2021, these institutions have been delivering training in 6 new Industry 4.0 courses through one and 
two year programs. So far, 22,237 candidates are trained and 3,488 candidates are placed.

GIA industrial training institutions since 2012 as per the DGT, New Delhi and norms. Candidates can apply for 
51 Technical & non-technical courses. Out of the 51 Courses, Qualification for 05 Courses are SSLC failed/8th 
passed for remaining courses SSLC passed are eligible to apply. The Govt and GIA candidates selected as such

Apprenticeship Training
As per the Apprenticeship Act 1961, Apprenticeship training has been imparted in 750 Establishments and 
61,753 apprentices are undergoing training by the end of December 2025.  The Central Government has 
amended the Act, which is establishment friendly. The establishments may engage 2.5% to 15% of total 
manpower as apprentice. Apprenticeship Registration shall be done in DGT website: www.ncvt.gov.in/
apprenticeship.portal  and shall provide training as per Apprenticeship act.
In order to attract more apprentices, the respective enterprises should pay at least Rs.6,000/- to Rs.7,000/- 
as apprentice wages. In this the Central Government will reimburse the enterprises at the rate of 25% or a 
maximum of Rs.1500/- per student per month under NAPS scheme implemented from 19-08-2016.
Apprenticeship training includes 262 Designated and 476 Optional trades. The implementing agencies of 
Apprenticeship Training are Department of Industrial Training and employment, Board of Apprenticeship 
Training, Regional Directorate of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship and National Skill Development 
Corporation. The progress of Apprenticeship training is given in Table 9.4.

New Initiatives
Karnataka Quality Upgradation for Employment and Skill Transformation (K-QUEST): K-QUEST is an Externally 
Aided Project with the total project cost of Rs.1,386.00 crore (Rs.970.00 cr. from Asian Development Bank 
(ADB) and Rs.416.00 cr. from State). The project aims to enhance the employability and productivity of the 
workforce and to support economic growth and competitiveness. The project will be implemented in the 
next financial year. The project includes repairs and renovations, construction of 20 skill labs, 20 library halls, 
additional workshops, additional classrooms, IT labs, toilets, landscaping and campus aesthetics, painting 
of ITI buildings and lounge for female staff and students of Government ITIs, Junior Technical Schools and 
Karnataka German Technical Training Institutes.
Pradhan Mantri Skilling and Employability Transformation through Upgraded ITIs (PM-SETU): A Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme for ITI upgradation and setting up of 5 National Centre of Excellence for skilling. In the 
State, 120 ITIs have been selected for the implementation of this scheme. The following are the expected 
outcomes in ITI ecosystem through this scheme. 
1. Incr eased enrolment and employment opportunities through industry-aligned training and stronger 
placement linkages.
2. Impr oved learning outcomes driven by modern pedagogy, digital platforms and advanced infrastructure.
3. Dir ect linkage of graduates from upgraded ITIs with ELI manufacturing. 
4. Higher quality of pass ou ts with job-ready skillsets and enhanced industry relevance.
5. ITI Skill tr aining can be converged .

courses.

Karnataka Skill Development Corporation (KSDC)
On the recommendations of the National Skill Mission/ State Skill Mission in accordance with the Skill 
Development Policy, the Skill Development, Entrepreneurship and Livelihood Department was reconstituted. 
and renamed as Karnataka Skill Development Corporation. 
Chief Minister’s Kaushalya Karnataka Yojane (CMKKY)
The CMKKY is a skill-development initiative launched by the Government of Karnataka to empower the state’s 
youth by providing industry-relevant training, employment opportunities and entrepreneurship support. 
Objective of this scheme is market driven skilling, re-skilling and up-skilling of youth in the age group of 18-
35 years, recognizing their prior learning and provide them higher skills and make them capable of getting 
decent employment. Impart quality training by building capacity of the training institutions and trainers and 
providing effective incentives. Issue certificates by evaluating on par with international standards. Imparting 
training to eligible beneficiaries in the trade of their choice at least once by avoiding duplication in the 
selection of beneficiaries. 
Providing training by enforcing uniform curriculum, standards and certification etc., by aligning with National 
Skill Qualification Framework and consolidating training programmes of all the departments. To provide career 
counselling and placement services to all. To ensure every trainee has a gainful wage or self-employment with 
decent work. Institutionalize effective monitoring.

Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL): Under the RPL a test is conducted and they are awarded with a certificate.

Kalike Jothe Kaushalya: In July Budget Speech 2023-24, Hon’ble Chief Minister announced that “in skill 
training which was earlier imparted through the private institutions will now be imparted through our ITI, 
GITC, Polytechnic Institutions. Skill training would be institutionalized and systematized by coordinating with 
industry and academy”. Accordingly, in collaboration with Higher Education department, 28 various industrial 
demand oriented short-term training has been imparted for 66,290 students to those who are studying in 5th 
& 6th semester in BA/B.com/BBA/BSc/ Degree in 7 universities viz., Tumkur, Davanagere, Raichur, Kalburgi, 
Vijayapura VSK University, Vijayanagar and Bengaluru North University. It is intended to provide employment 
opportunities directly through the issuance of certificates by industries/enterprises. Also, it is intended to 
extend to impart training from 50 hours to 100 hours duration to the students studying in 102 Government 
Polytechnic Colleges using the facilities available in 150 Upgraded Government ITIs, 32 GTTCs and 8 KGTTIs.

Karnataka Career Planning: In Collaboration with Samagra Shikshana Karnataka, the Department of School 
Education and Literacy and the Department of Pre-University Education, Government of Karnataka, the 
Karnataka Skill Development Corporation (KSDC) is set to launch the “Karnataka Career Planning Program:

Class 8 to Class 12 with personalized counselling sessions, mentor-led sector orientations and an extensive 
online portal encompassing information on over 25 sectors and 500 job roles, academic institutions mapping, 
scholarships and apprenticeship opportunities. The target is fixed to impart training to 2.30 lakh candidates 
in 500 Government schools. So far, 35,000 students are benefitted from 150 schools. 
International Migration Centre - Karnataka (IMC-K): The International Migration Centre has been instituted 
under the Department to build safe, orderly, and humane overseas employment pathways for people from 
Karnataka. Under this program, Karnataka Vocational Training Skill Development Corporation has been 
identified as a Recruitment Agency and registered with the Ministry of External Affairs, Government of India. 
Karnataka Skill Development Corporation identifies candidates for suitable employment opportunities abroad 
and thus so far, provided overseas employment opportunities to 939 candidates in Slovakia, Hungary, UAE, 
Kuwait, as Heavy Trailer, Truck Driver, Assembly Line Operator, CNC Programmer and Domestic Housemaid. 
IMCK provides Pre-Departure Orientation Training (PDOT) to candidates and provided training to more than 
1000 candidates.
Migrant Resource Centres and Migrant Information Centres have been set up in 8 Districts Ballari, Kalaburagi,

approved to establish Pre-Departure Orientation Training Centres in Kalburgi, Hubli, Mangalore and Mysuru

steps have been taken to provide skill training to 3,180 candidates in 17 job roles in 5 sectors (Green Jobs SSC, 
IT–ITeS SSC, BFSI SSC, Automotive and Instrumentation) across 15 districts, for which a grant of Rs. 5.89 crores

Training to Jail inmates: Targeted to train 200 candidates in the current year and for training is underway for

New Initiatives
Skill Policy: The Salient Features of the Policy are as follows:
 Y Vision to position Karnataka as a premier hub for skilled workforce and a 1 trillion USD economy by 2032.
 Y Focus on lifelong learning, reskilling and upskilling to keep pace with changing technologies and industry 
needs.
 Y Integration of vocational education within schools, higher education and universities through credit-
based programmes.
 Y Strong emphasis on industry collaboration, including apprenticeships, industry-led training and ITI 
adoption.
 Y Special attention to equity and inclusivity, with targeted interventions for women, persons with 
disabilities, marginalized communities, urban poor and the informal workforce.
 Y Strengthening of infrastructure through modernization of ITIs, expansion of GTTCs and setting up rural 
and urban skilling hubs.
 Y Leveraging digital technologies and AI-driven tools for training, assessment and career guidance through 
a unified digital portal.
 Y Focus on international workforce mobility with global certifications, migration support and specialized 
training.
 Y Establishing a robust monitoring and evaluation framework, with 5% of scheme budgets earmarked for 
M&E.
 Y CMKKY 2.0 positioned as an umbrella scheme, bringing all state skilling programmes (e.g., Kalike Jothege 
Kaushalya, Nanna Vrutti Nanna Ayke, ILC, IMC-K, RPL, special projects) under one life-cycle approach to 
skilling.

Centre for Entrepreneurship Development of Karnataka (CEDOK) 
Centre for Entrepreneurship Development of Karnataka (CEDOK), Dharwad, is a Government of Karnataka 
promoted organisation created by Department of Industries and Commerce. The centre was registered under 
Karnataka Society Act 1960 No. 2/92-93 on 15th May, 1992.  Now it is transferred to Department of Skill 
Development, Entrepreneurship and Livelihood, Government of Karnataka.  
CEDOK is widely recognised that education can be a very effective instrument to bring-out latent resources 
and capabilities of people. Based on this belief, the main objective of CEDOK is,
 Y To augment the supply of entrepreneurs through education and training.
 Y To produce multiplier effect on opportunities for self-employment.
 Y To improve the managerial capabilities of stake holders.
 Y To contribute to the dispersal of entrepreneurship and thus expand the social base of the entrepreneurial 
class in urban and rural areas.
Target Group
 Y Entrepreneurship Development Programmes covering target groups of unemployed youths, women, 
SHG members and beneficiaries of various Governments sponsored schemes. 
 Y Trainers Training Programmes covering target group of trainers & motivators in the field of entrepreneurship 
development.
 Y Target group for Management Development Programmes are different stake-holders of the programmes.
Area of operation: CEDOK is imparting training programmes in entire Karnataka State.
Details of Components
1. Entrepreneurship Awareness Camps/Programmes
Main objective of these programmes is to create awareness on entrepreneurship among the students, SHG 
members, unemployed youths, women, etc. The durations of Awareness Programmes are from one day to 
three days based on the requirement.
2. Entrepreneurship Development Programmes
Entrepreneurship Development Programmes aim to motivate individuals, develop entrepreneurial skills, 
help to identify suitable self-employment opportunities, create awareness of government self-employment 
schemes, and build knowledge in project planning, management, accounting, banking and legal aspects of 
self-employment. These programmes are conducted over a period of six to ten days.

PDF_PAGE 375
367
Skill, Entrepreneurship and Labour & Employment
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
3. Sector Specific Entrepreneurship Development Programmes
Sector Specific Entrepreneurship Development Programmes (SEDPs) focus on motivating participants, 
developing entrepreneurial qualities and imparting sector-specific skills to enable self-employment. They 
help individuals identify suitable self-employment opportunities, understand government schemes, prepare 
project plans and gain knowledge of managerial, accounting, banking and legal aspects. These programmes 
are conducted over a period of thirty to forty-five days.
4. Training of Trainers Programmes
Main objective of these programmes is to equip the trainers to conduct entrepreneurship related programmes 
effectively. The duration of Training of Trainers Programmes are from three days to one week based on the 
requirements of target groups.
5. Management Development Programmes
Management Development Programmes were organized for the officers and Staff of Industries and 
Commerce Department, Department of Industrial Training and Employment GOK and PSEs, GOK, Bengaluru.  
Eminent Faculties were invited to take sessions in these programmes, so as to motivate the officers for better 
performance. The duration of these programmes varies from three to five days.

Model Cluster Level Federations (MCLFs)
As part of the institutional strengthening strategy under DAY–NRLM, a total of 771 Model Cluster Level 
Federations (MCLFs) have been established across the state. These MCLFs function as key support institutions 
for strengthening governance systems, financial management, business planning, and statutory compliance 
of GPLFs and SHGs. Recognizing their critical role in ensuring sustainability and operational self-sufficiency of 
community institutions, focused capacity-building interventions were undertaken during the period April to 
December 2025.
Local Operating System (LokOS): LokOS is a digital application implemented under NRLM to capture, monitor, 
and analyse the institutional, financial, and operational performance of SHGs and their federations. It provides 
a unified platform for real-time data entry, validation and reporting, thereby enabling evidence-based 
decision-making at all levels. Accurate use of LokOS ensures transparency, accountability and consistency 
in institutional data. The application plays a critical role in cut-off preparation by reflecting the true financial 
and operational status of institutions. It also supports profile creation, progress tracking and identification of 
gaps for timely corrective action. Overall, LokOS strengthens governance, improves monitoring efficiency, and 
supports sustainable institutional development.

Nurturing Aspirations and Resilience For Inclusion - Karnataka Inclusive Livelihoods Programme 
(NARI-KILP)
The Karnataka Inclusive Livelihoods Programme is a holistic initiative aimed at creating long-term economic 
and social change for vulnerable households in Karnataka. The programme runs for 36 months and offers 
support in several areas: access to documents and entitlements, livelihoods, NARI-KILP aims to provide 
access to relevant entitlements that support gender-equitable, ecologically sustainable and climate-resilient 
livelihoods for 6,000 extremely poor and vulnerable rural households/individuals in the pilot phase (phase I), 
and for 14,000 households in the second phase, across 10 districts of Karnataka by 2029. The project initiated 
the participatory identification of extremely vulnerable households in 20 selected blocks (Phase I) and will be 
extended to other 20 selected Talukas in (Phase II) across these ten districts.
NARI-KILP Implemented by engaging 436 SHG Surveyors across 206 Gram Panchayats District Level Committees 
(DLCs) have been constituted and oriented in all 10 districts. Out of 22,157 households identified, 19,747 
household surveys have been completed; the remaining 2,410 households could not be surveyed due to 
migration.
Common Work Shed: Constructed to provide SHG members safe and equipped spaces for production and 
enterprise activities; 647 of 753 sheds completed and 106 under construction across 31 districts under 
MGNREGS.
Stree Shakthi Federations to undertake their activities. 5279 worksheds will be constructed additionally in 
the year 2023-24 with an estimated cost of Rs.17.50 lakhs per unit. So far, 365 works are completed and 308

Farm livelihood  
Agriculture is a key livelihood activity for rural households and Sanjeevini-KSRLPS supports Mahila Kisans 
through SHGs by promoting agro-ecological practices, integrated farming systems and improved livestock 
management, in convergence with line departments and MGNREGS. Emphasis is placed on sustainable 
resource use and creation of durable livelihood assets, generating opportunities in poultry, dairy, goat, sheep 
and other livestock activities.
Under Agro-Ecological Practices, 7.41 lakh Mahila Kisans have been covered against a target of 6.00 lakh 
during 2025–26, achieving 113 percent progress, while Agri-Nutri/Kitchen Gardens have been promoted to 
improve household nutrition, covering 3.67 lakh Mahila Kisans against a target of 4.50 lakh, achieving 83 
percent of the annual target.
Mahila Kisan Shashakthikarna Pariyojana-MKSP- Integrated Farming Cluster (IFC)
Sanjeevini-KSRLPS has promoted Integrated Farming Clusters (IFCs), encouraging Mahila Kisans to adopt 
multiple farm and allied activities to enhance incomes. A total of 682 IFCs have been taken up across 227 
blocks in 30 districts, covering 2.38 lakh Mahila Kisans, with baseline surveys completed for all beneficiaries 
through Krishi Sakhis and Pashu Sakhis, supported by a release of Rs. 64.80 lakh in August 2025. 
So far, 577 DPRs approved by Taluk and District Level Coordination Committees have been received at the 
state level. During 2024–25, a first tranche of Rs.1,600 lakh was released to 318 IFCs at Rs.5.00 lakh per cluster, 
while in 2025–26, Rs.1,900 lakh was released to 118 clusters for establishing Livelihood Service Centers, with 
an additional Rs.1,900 lakh received for the second tranche. 
About 118 Livelihood Service Centres are planned to be operational by February 2026, supported by 
business plan training at KVKs, DATCs, and RSETIs. Capacity building is ensured through trained Community 
Resource Persons and exposure visits to Krishi Melas enabled 65,941 Mahila Kisans and staff to gain practical 
knowledge. Convergence with MGNREGA has further strengthened livelihoods through creation of individual 
and community assets such as farm ponds, sheds, compost pits, agri-nutri gardens, storage facilities and 
common infrastructure.
Livestock Interventions
The interventions focus on reducing mortality and morbidity in livestock and poultry through improved feed 
and breed management, preventive healthcare, ethno-veterinary practices, better housing and scientific 
management. So far, 17.62 lakh Mahila Kisans have been covered under livestock interventions.
