10.3.11 NABARD Infrastructure Development Assistance (NIDA)
NIDA, a new credit support initiative by NABARD  has allocated Rs. 2671.12 crore to support Jaladhare projects 
in four districts: Raichur, Dharwad, Vijayapura, and Mandya. This funding aims to benefit 3636 habitations, 
serving a population of approximately 71.87 lakh, by ensuring safe and sustainable drinking water at the 
household level. As of December 26, 2025, Rs. 2619.19 crore has been released to the Government of 
Karnataka for project execution.
10.3.12  Other Developmental Initiatives
 Y Farmers Producers Organization (FPOs): Since 2014-15, NABARD Karnataka Regional Office has 
established 388 FPOs(387 registered) across 31 districts, supported by over 60 NGOs. 230,256 farmers 
participated in these FPOs, which have received Rs.76.23 crore in grants and mobilized Rs.23.95 crore 
in share capital. The FPOs focus on agri-horticultural production and marketing with some branching 
into high-value crops like chia seeds, coffee, tender coconuts, mango, turmeric, pepper etc. Additionally, 
NABARD collaborates with ONDC to enhance market linkages and promote e-commerce in agriculture.
 Y Tribal Resilience Initiative for Building Environmentally Sustainable livelihoods (TRIBES) : NABARD 
has been implementing integrated tribal development projects using the wadi model (small orchards 
up to one acre)in tribal areas since establishing the Tribal Development Fund in 2003-04. In Karnataka, 
40 projects have been sanctioned with financial assistance of Rs.132.67 crore, benefiting 22,664 tribal 
families across 14 districts and covering 22,464 acres.
 Y Watershed Development Fund: To combat drought in Karnataka, NABARD has sanctioned 356 Watershed 
Development(350 regular, 3 Springshed, 3 non-watershed standalone projects) &  3 JIVA projects 
Projects with Rs.276.37 crore in funding across 3.33 lakh hectares. This includes 35 ongoing projects 
aimed at improving groundwater levels, agricultural productivity and promoting modern farming 
practices. Additional 2 new projects are set to be sanctioned in January 2026. 2 watershed projects (Full 
Implementation Phase) and 1 springshed project (Project Implementation Phase) were sanctioned in 
December 2025.
 Y Standalone Soil & Water Conservation Projects: Designed to share knowledge on soil and water 
conservation, sustainable farming, and climate change adaptation and risk mitigation in vulnerable 
districts, this initiative aims for the adoption of innovative conservation technologies and climate-
resilient practices. Additionally, three projects under non-watershed activities have been sanctioned 
with a financial assistance of Rs.59.39 lakh.
 Y Farm sector Promotion Fund : Under the Farm Sector Promotion Fund (FSPF), NABARD implemented 
initiatives in the Kalyana Karnataka region from 2024-2025 to promote farmer-led value addition and 
market integration. This included establishing Farmers’ Training and Common Facility Centres (FT-CFCs) in 
all seven districts, with support from MPLADS. The efforts were focussed on district-specific processing, 
focusing on chilli in Ballari, pulses in Raichur, millets in Kalaburagi, groundnut in Yadgir, fruits and ginger 
in Koppal, peanut-based products and tamarind in Vijayanagara and soyabean-based products in Bidar.
 Y Climate Change initiatives: NABARD serves as the National Implementing Entity for the Green Climate 
Fund, the National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change and the Adaptation Fund under UNFCCC. In 
partnership with EMPRI(Environment Management and Policy Research Institute)  it approved a loan of 
Rs.180 crore for three biogas plants using by-products from the alcohol and sugar industries in Bagalkot 
and Belgaum districts. Additionally, NABARD financed Rs.2,50,000 for a conference on climate resilience 
through carbon credits and Rs.5,00,000 for the III Global Summit on Diamond Open Access.

10.3.13 Financial Inclusion Initiatives
Financial Inclusion Fund (FIF) has facilitated the development of financial inclusion infrastructure in 
Karnataka, with all 22 RCBs and 1 RRB now integrated into the CBS platform. This integration supports new 
payment systems like Aadhaar Pay, UPI, Micro ATM, and PoS. NABARD has also helped RCBs link to the Public 
Financial Management System (PFMS) for direct beneficiary payments. In FY 2025-26, Rs.785.74 lakh was 
released under FIF, with allocations including Rs.35 lakh for 613 Financial Literacy programs, Rs.2.08 crore to 
Cooperative Banks for deploying Micro ATMs and POS systems, Rs.3.08 crore to RRB under rural connectivity 
projects, and Rs.2.62 crore for 41 Centres for Financial Literacy in Karnataka.
10.3.14  Rural MSME initiatives under Gramya Vikas Nidhi (GVN)
i.  Marketing Infrastructure : In the last seven years 61 rural marts and 28 rural haats have been set up in 21 
districts with an investment of Rs. 549.39 lakh to improve market linkages for farm and off-farm producer 
organizations and self-help groups (SHGs). 
ii.  Skill Development: Through skill development initiatives, NABARD has invested Rs. 339.06 lakh in this 
sector since last 6 years to upskill over 4300 individuals, primarily youth and women in various areas 
including weaving, solar panel installation, health care, computer-based skills, farm machinery repair 
and maintenance, banking, financial services, insurance, panchakarma therapy, yoga fundamentals. 
Approximately 80% of trainees have secured jobs or started their own businesses.
 iii.  Collectivisation- Off Farm Producer Organisations (OFPOs):  Since 2021, NABARD has provided grant 
support of Rs.394.63 lakh for the establishment of five OFPOs benefiting 1550 artisans in Handloom 
(Fabric Weaving and Natural Dye) and Handicrafts (Kasuti Work, Channapatna Toys, Kolhapuri Leather 
Footwear, and Aari embroidery) across Shimoga, Dharwad, Ramanagara and Belgaum districts. Three of 
these OFPOs focus on GI tagged products including Channapatna toys, Kasuti, and Kolhapuri chappals.
iv.  Infrastructure through the DPR Scheme: Initiated in 2021-22 by NABARD. This scheme aims to support 
location-specific developmental projects in the off-farm sector. NABARD has approved two projects under 
this scheme providing a total financial assistance of Rs. 41.76 lakh for Gulbarga and Uttara Kannada 
districts.
v.  Interventions under Geographical Indication (GI):  Interventions for the Geographical Indication (GI) 
registration of various products including Kari Ishad Mango. Hoysala-style Stone Art, Tiptur Coconut, 
Sanikatta Salt, and Kumbi Mudli Tuber have received Rs.8.36 lakh in approval from NABARD. An additional 
Rs.9.13 lakh has been granted for post-GI actions such as organizing exposure visits for GI-tagged Ilkal 
Saree and Guledagudda Khana craftsmen, registering authorized users and developing a website for GI-
tagged Udupi sarees.
10.3.15  Status of SHG and JLG in Karnataka
Karnataka has been a key participant in the SHG Bank Linkage Programme implementing the National Rural 
Livelihood Mission (NRLM) as the Karnataka State Rural Livelihood Mission (KSRLM). This initiative aims 
to create sustainable livelihoods for the rural poor living below the poverty line within 5 to 7 years. Key 
components of the program include regular savings, book keeping, internal lending and bank credit support.
As on 31 March 2025, a total no of 9,24,321 SHGs were saving linked with Rs.3049.67 crore. During 2024-25, 
6,31,007 SHGs were credit linked in tune of Rs.22143.59 crore.

Micro Entrepreneurs Development Programme (MEDP) for SHG members, Livelihood Enterprises Development 
Programme for SHGs for income generation, grant support to Banks and NGOs for formation and credit linkage

10.3.17  Institutional Development 
(i)  NA BARD holds quarterly High-Level Committee meetings led by the Secretary of the Department of 
Cooperation, Government of Karnataka, to assess the financial health of rural cooperative institutions, 
focusing on key parameters like NPA, Share Capital, weak bank positions, capital Infusion, supervisory 
concerns, fraud incidents and governance issues in RCBs.During 2025-26, two HLC meetings were held 
on 31st July 2025 & on 25th November 2025 and also  District Level Monitoring and Review Committee 
(DLMRC) were held at quarterly intervals. 
(ii)  NA BARD provides various support through the Cooperative Development Fund, including capacity 
building for cooperative staff, training via institutes like BIRD (Bankers’ Institute of Rural Development), 
exposure visits and grants for establishing innovation and product diversification Cells.
 P ACS (Primary Agricultural Credi Societies) as MSC (Multi Service Centre) - In 2025-26, NABARD allocated 
Rs.27.14 lakh to 15 PACS in Haveri District under KCCB Dharwad, supporting a range of activities such as 
pre-survey, DPR preparation, technology adoption, and capacity building as part of enhancing PACS as 
member-oriented institutions offering credit-plus services.
 SO FTCOB (Scheme of Financial Assistance for Training of Cooperative Banks Personnel) - During 2025-26, 
NABARD has sanctioned 112 programs to 3 Cooperative Training Institutes (CTIs) like ACSTI, SAHARDA 
and NIRB to extend training and capacity building of the staff of PACS, DCCBs and Apex Bank. An amount 
of Rs.78.24 lakh has been reimbursed towards conduct of 25 programs and Capital expenditure in these 
institutes during 2025-26.
(iii) Initiatives for PACS/Cooperative Sector: In line with the National Plan formulated by the Ministry of 
Cooperation (MoC), Karnataka showed strong momentum in formation of MPACS. Against the target of 
218 till FY 25-26, 233 MPACS were formed as on 19 Dec 2025. 
(iv) Interventions by NABARD: NABARD assesses district-level potential to identify potential GPs for M-PACS 
formation, liquidation of defunct PACS, encouraging DCCBs to act as Resource Support Agencies (RSAs) 
and appoint Resource persons (RPs) to facilitate formation and effective functioning of MPACS. The newly 
formed MPACS have disbursed Rs.44.16 crore till date (19 December 2025).
(v) `Regional Rural Banks (RRBs):  NABARD has taken several initiatives to ensure the smooth amalgamation 
of RRBs into Karnataka Grameena Bank (KGB) with effect from 01 May 2025 and to strengthen its 
functioning.
10.3.18  NABARD’S initiatives for RRB
NABARD conducted 8 State Level Monitoring Committee meetings to oversee the amalgamation and IT 
integration process, launching a unified logo for all Regional Rural Banks (RRBs). The Jan Sethu Portal was 
introduced as a digital platform for rural credit providing various loan options. As of May 1, 2025, the bank 
reported a CRAR (Capital to Risk Weighted Assets Ratio) of 8.26% and Net Profit earned as on 01 May 2025 
during FY 25-26 (i.e. in the period between 01 April 2025 and 01 May 2025) is Rs.15.78 crore. After adjusting 
the accumulated losses of previous years and the net profit earned during FY 25-26, the Net accumulated 
losses as on 01 May 2025 stands at Rs. 255.57 crore.  RRB performance in terms of ACP , NPAs, and financing 
activities is reviewed in Empowered Committee meetings by the RBI, with the 91st meeting held on June 25, 
2025, and the 92nd on December 2, 2025.

10.3.19 Initiatives for PACS/Cooperative Sector
1.  PACS Computerisation: Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) are integral to the 3-tier Short Term 
Cooperative Credit Structure which comprises District Cooperative Central Banks and State Cooperative 
Banks. A budget of Rs. 175.26 crore has been allocated for the computerization of 5,491 PACS with Rs. 
70.10 crore provided by the State. Currently, 3,535 PACS are operational, 3,425 reaching day end stage 
and an additional 403 PACS are scheduled for computerization in the next phase. This initiative seeks to 
enhance PACS efficiency, reflecting the vision of ‘Sahakar Se Sammridhi’.
2.  ARDB Computeriszation: Under this scheme, 207 units of KSCARDB/PCARDBs will be computerized with 
a total budget of Rs.11.70 crore, funded by the Government of India, State Government, and KSCARDB.
10.3.20  Supervision of RRBs, StCB and DCCBs
The Statutory inspections of Regional Rural Banks, State Cooperative Banks, and Central Cooperative Banks 
are conducted by NABARD under Section 35(6) of the Banking Regulation Act of 1949. The inspections aim to 
protect depositor interests, ensure proper business conduct and adherence to regulations. The assessment 
of banks financial, operational and managerial soundness is done using the CAMELSC(Capital Adequacy, 
Asset Quality, Management, Earnings, Liquidity, Systems and Compliance) approach. Annual inspections are 
conducted for Banks with a business volume of Rs. 3000 crore or more as of the previous year’s March 31. 
CCBs rated “C” or “D” are also inspected annually, while those rated “A”, “B+”, or “B” are inspected biennially.
10.3.21 Process of Supervision of StCBs, DCCBs, RRBs 
The supervision of StCBs, DCCBs, and RRBs involves on-site inspections and off-site surveillance by NABARD, 
focusing on financial compliance and risk identification. They utilize tools like the Vulnerability Index for Cyber 
Security and the Fraud Vulnerability Index. In Karnataka, all cooperative banks met the 9% CRAR requirement 
except Bidar DCCB, which stands at 2.32%. NABARD intends to inspect 20 DCCBs in 2025-26. Additionally, 
two RRBs namely Karnataka Vikas Grameena Bank (KVGB) and Karnataka Grameena Bank (KGB) have been 
merged to create a single entity named Karnataka Grameena Bank (KGB) with Headquarters in Ballari and 
with assets of Rs.68703.09 crore and accumulated losses of Rs.255.57 crore while the CRAR is 8.26% as of 
May 1, 2025.
10.3.22 Urban Infrastructure Development Fund (UIDF) 
This scheme was announced in Union Budget 2023-24 with an initial Rs.10,000 crore corpus supports public 
agencies in creating infrastructure in Tier-2 (population 50,000 to < 1 lakh) and Tier-3 (1 lakh to < 10 lakh) . 
Managed by the National Housing Bank (NHB), key Aspects of the UIDF Scheme includes supplementing state 
govt. in developing mid-sized cities in areas focusing on water supply, sanitation, sewerage, and solid waste 
management. Projects are implemented by State/Public Agencies, Municipal Corporations, and Urban Local 
Bodies. The present rate of interest is 1.5% less than the bank rate i.e 4.5%. The Department of Muncipal 
Administration(DMA),  KUWSDB (Karnataka Under Water Supply and Drainage Board)  are the implementing 
departments under this scheme.
In 2023-24, under Tranche-I, works worth Rs.898.57 Cr were sanctioned against a Normative Allocation of 
Rs.640.11 Cr with Rs.193.47 Cr reimbursed. In 2024-25, under Tranche-II, 265 works totaling Rs.678.48 Cr 
have been submitted so far against the Normative allocation with no disbursements so far. Under Tranche-III 
against a Normative Allocation of Rs.640.11 Cr, projects worth Rs.870.09 Cr are anticipated to be submitted 
by DMA to NHB.

10.3.24 Karnataka State Industrial Infrastructure & Development Corporation (KSIIDC)
KSIIDC, established in 1964, has been greatly instrumental in the industrialization of the State, especially in 
the large and medium sector.  KSIIDC has stopped financial lending activity since October 2002 onwards. At 
present, recovery of the past lending/advances and loans and disinvestment of Equity are the main activity. 
However, certain Investments as per the directions of Government of Karnataka are being made from time 
to time.  
KSIIDC continued its proactive role in the promotion of infrastructure projects on Public Private Partnership 
model and its role as nodal agency for Bangalore International Airport Project.  Duly noting the initiatives 
taken up by KSIIDC in the infrastructure sector, the name was changed to “Karnataka State Industrial and 
Infrastructure Development Corporation Limited” with effect from November 22, 2010.
Vision & Mission of KSIIDC: “To implement industrial infrastructure & civil aviation infrastructure in the State 
of Karnataka”.
Way forward
As the nodal agency of the State Government, KSIIDC has initiated activities for the development of the 
following projects which will be pursued for completion during next coming years.
a) Development of Major Infrastructure Projects as Nodal Agency for GoK
The Government of Karnataka has appointed KSIIDC as the Nodal Agency for various infrastructure projects 
undertaken by the state. In this capacity, KSIIDC has implemented and is currently implementing the following 
projects on behalf of the Government of Karnataka. KSIIDC as the Nodal Agency for various infrastructure 
projects undertaken by the state and is currently implementing the following projects on behalf of the 
Government of Karnataka
 Y Kempegowda International Airport (KIA)
 Y Aviation Development including development of Airports & Heliports
 Y Assisting Government regarding PPP Projects
 Y Tadadi Eco Tourism Project
 Y Development of Dash Board (Project Monitoring Software)
 Y Bengaluru Signature Business Project (BSBP)

10.3.25 Co-operative Credit
The Cooperative Credit System in Karnataka is crucial for credit delivery in rural and urban regions. It includes 
Urban Cooperative Banks and Primary Agricultural Cooperative Societies/Banks, which significantly contribute 
to rural credit. Karnataka uniquely features two types of Cooperative Credit Institutions, one for short-term 
and medium-term credit, and other for long-term credit.
a.  Short Term and MediumTerm Credit Co-operative Structure (STCCS): The Karnataka State Cooperative 
Apex Bank, alongside its 21 District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs-with 879 branches) and 6,302 
Primary Agricultural Cooperative Societies (PACS) offers short-term credit to farmers and has initiated a 
Business Development Plan (BDP) under NABARD guidelines. An MoU signed in June 1995 with NABARD 
and the State Government has been extended periodically. As of March 31, 2024, the DCCBs’ working 
capital was Rs.42,870.17 crore it increased  to Rs.45,889.50 crore (7.04% growth) by March 31, 2025. 
With 19 of the 21 DCCBs reporting profits in 2024–25 from diverse credit services to PACS, other societies 
and individual borrowers as shown in Table 10.41.

e.  Sub sidised Agriculture Loans to farmers @ 0 and 1 per cent : Agricultural loans were given to the farmers 
at 6 % from 01.04.2004 through Agricultural Cooperative Credit Institutions in the state. During 2013-14 
Govt. reduced the interest rate to 0% up to 2.00 lakhs and 1% for upto 3 lakhs of short term agricultural 
loans. The medium term and long-term agricultural loans up to Rs.10.00 lakhs are being disbursed to 
farmers at 3%. 
During the year 2021-22, 24,81,359 farmers were given Rs.1022.90 crore and in 2022-23 Rs. 1078.02 crore 
was released to 25,67,520 farmers. During the year 2023-24 Rs 1178.22 crore was released to 30.38 lakh 
farmers.
In 2024-25, Rs. 1416.91 crores of budget provision was made and till now, an amount of Rs.1041.16 crores 
have been released to 33.08 lakhs farmers.
In 2025–26, a budgetary provision of Rs.1,591.74 crore was made of which Rs.946.29 crore has so far been 
released to cooperative societies on behalf of 19.02 lakh farmers.
f.  In terest waiver scheme on Medium and long term Agricultural loans:  Under this scheme, interest will 
be borne by the Government for farmers repaying overdue principal on agricultural loans due by March 
2024. As of now, 36,146 farmers repaid Rs.287.98 crore, leading to an interest waiver of Rs.239.26 crore. 
In 2024–25, KASCARD Bank provided Rs.10.13 crore under this scheme. With a subsidy of Rs.229.13 
crore in 2025–26, loan recovery  improved which supported cooperative financial stability.
g.  In terest subsidy to Self Help Groups : The scheme of advancing loans to Self Help Groups in Karnataka at 
4 % is being implemented from 01-04-2007. 
During 2017–18 to 2020–21, Women Self Help Groups (SHGs) received loans at a net interest rate of 0%, 
whereas Men SHGs at4% as part of NRLM/NULM schemes. In 2021–22, the Kayaka scheme merged with the 
SHG scheme, allowing loans up to Rs.5 lakh for women at 0% interest and for men at 4%. Loans between Rs.5 
lakh and Rs.10 lakh for self-employment continued at a 4% interest rate, extending into 2024–25.
In the financial years 2022-23 and 2023-24, a total of 50,013 and 24,875 groups received loans of Rs.2,206.96 
crore and Rs.1,010.05 crore respectively, with outstanding amounts of Rs.2,650.54 crore and Rs.2,146.47 
crore. In 2022-23, Rs.96.61 crore in interest subsidies was released to 85,025 groups, while a budget of 
Rs.99.00 crore for 2023-24 was fully utilized. For the financial year  2024-25, by March, loans of Rs.936.91 
crore were disbursed to 20,067 self-help groups (SHGs), with outstanding loans reaching Rs.1,825.33 crore 
from 91,531 SHGs. A budget of Rs.124.80 crore was allocated for recoveries. 
In the 2025-26 period, as of December Rs.512.61 crore was disbursed to 11,640 SHGs, with outstanding loans 
of Rs.1,881.76 crore with 90,214 SHGs and a budget provision of Rs.108.26 crore for recoveries was made.
h.  The Central Government has initiated measures to strengthen Primary Agricultural Cooperative 
Societies (PACS) to improve service delivery in rural areas

46,986 cooperative societies aiming to enhance the cooperative sector’s development.

11.1   HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE
Karnataka has made significant progress in improving the health status of its people in the last few decades. 
The state has made remarkable progress in improving its health infrastructure at different levels in both 
rural and urban areas. The State has a wide institutional network providing health services both in urban 
and rural areas. The primary health infrastructure in rural areas has fulfilled the norms required under the 
“Minimum Needs Programme” at the aggregate level. 12 district hospitals, 68 Mother & Child Hospitals/wings 
45 Autonomous teaching hospitals, 147 Taluka / General hospitals, 205 Rural Community Health Centers 
and 9 Urban Community Health Centers, 2161 Rural Primary Health Centers and 365 Urban Primary Health 
Centers, 155 Rural Health Extension Centers, 9160 Sub Centers and 746 Namma Clinics are providing health 
care facilities. 
Further, 31920 private medical establishments are registered under Karnataka Private Medical Establishment 
Act for providing quality care according to medical ethics by prescribing service quality of which 9214 (29%) 
are in Bengaluru district alone followed by Dakshina Kannada 2341 (7%) and Dharwad 1229 (4%) during the 
year 2025-26. 
Finance 
During 2024-25 an amount of Rs.11545.28 crores was allocated in the budget under various schemes to 
provide health facilities, of which an amount of Rs.10909.48 crores (Including OB) was released and the 
expenditure incurred was Rs.10237.68 crores. During 2025-26 as against the allocation of Rs.11991.17 crores, 
an amount of Rs. 8239.32 crores (Including OB) released.  The expenditure incurred is Rs.7294.88 crores up 
to December-2025.
Under National Health Mission during 2024-25 the allocation was Rs. 1819.53 crores and expenditure incurred 
was Rs. 1812.76 crores. During 2025-26 out of total allocation of Rs. 1096.87 crores, an amount of Rs. 1049.93 
crores is incurred as expenditure (up to Dec 2025).

11.1.1 Maternal Health
Janani Suraksha Yojane (JSY)
Janani Suraksha Yojane (JSY) is a centrally sponsored scheme under National Health Mission implemented in 
Karnataka since 2006. It is an important initiative of the Government to reduce maternal mortality and early 
neonatal mortality. Incentives (Urban deliveries - Rs 600/- and Rural Deliveries Rs.700/-) is to be paid within 
48hrs of delivery at the facility where delivery occurs through Seva Sindhu portal on to the Aadhar linked bank 
account of the pregnant women of any age and belonging to BPL/SC/ST.
The Government of Karnataka has made Treasury interface mandatory so, a separate portal (Seva Sindhu 
Portal) for Direct Benefit Transfer Scheme (DBTS), has been developed to enable the disbursal of JSY incentives.

Following the launch of mission-mode interventions through Mission Zero Preventable Maternal Death 
Initiative, maternal deaths have shown a notable downward trend, declining from 430 during April–December 
2024 to 340 during April–December 2025. This represents an approximate 21% reduction within a period of 
nine-months, reflecting the early and encouraging impact of targeted interventions, strengthened service 
delivery and improved health system responsiveness.

 Y Effective implementation of maternal health programs at the grassroots level.
11.1.2 Child Health
The Child Health Programme comprehensively integrates interventions that improve child survival and 
addresses factors contributing to Infant and Under 5 Mortality. As per latest Sample Registration System (SRS) 
2023 Report; the Under 5 Mortality Rate (U5MR) in Karnataka is 17 per 1000 live births, Infant Mortality Rate 
(IMR) is 14 per 1000 live births and Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR) is 11 per 1000 live births. Neonatal care 
and child health services are considered as ambitious services of the state to reduce the mortality rate of 
newborn babies and the mortality rate of under five years children to reach at least single digit. The mortality

Many initiatives have been taken up to provide preventive, promotive, curative & rehabilitative health care 
services through evidence-based interventions like facility based Newborn Care services, Pediatric care 
services. Community based services, Community awareness programme, Capacity building and financial 
assistance to schemes.
a) Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakrama (JSSK)
Introduced in early 2012 to reduce the out of pocket expenditure of the parents towards the treatment of 
sick newborn. An amount of Rs. 200/- for Drugs and Consumables, Rs. 100/- for diagnostics and Rs.300/- for 
Referral Transport was allocated per sick newborn. From 2013-14 the facility was extended for any sick child 
below one year of age. During 2025-26 (up to Dec 2025) 1,59,633 beneficiaries are covered.

Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
b) Iron and Folic Acid Prophylaxis
Under Anaemia Muktha Poushtika Karnataka programme 43,79,441 children aged 6 months to 5 years are 
estimated to provide biweekly prophylactic Iron and Folic acid syrup to prevent anaemia. As per HMIS April to 
December 2025 there is an approximate coverage of 65% of under 5 years children.
c) Neonatal Ambulance
The ambulances are specially equipped for neonatal transport with specific equipment such as transport 
incubator, transport ventilator, oxygen source, air way suction device, syringe pump, multi-channel monitor, 
pulse oximeter, glucometer with special life-saving medications. All the neonatal transports are carried out by 
trained staff nurses stationed at SNCUs of 4 districts – Mysuru, Bengaluru, Raichur and Shivamogga.
11.1.3 Family Welfare
The State offers an excellent family welfare Programmes operating through the existing health infrastructure. 
The main objective of the Programme is to provide better health services in general and family planning 
services in particular to check the rapid growth of population. Though sterilization continues to be the main 
method of family planning the spacing between the births of two children is also equally emphasized. 
During 2025-26 (up to December 2025) 1.40 lakhs sterilization conducted as against the target of 2.52 lakhs. 
The achievement of IUD & PPIUCD is 1.55 lakhs as against the target of 5.28 lakhs. The Couple Protection rate 
was 51.8 as per NFHS-4 (2015-16) and it is gradually increased to 68.7 in NFHS 5 (2019-20) by implementing 
various family planning methods like Sterilization (Vasectomy, Tubectomy & IUD insertion etc.) 
In October 2023, Karnataka State rollout of Subdermal Single Rod Contraceptive Implants in Bengaluru 
and Bidar districts in the first phase. After the success of this pilot phase, the program was extended to 
eleven additional districts including Hassan, Tumakuru, Bengaluru South (Ramanagar), Mandya, Kalaburagi, 
Chikamagaluru, Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA), Belgaum, Davangere, Vijayapura and Bagalkot during 
2025.
The rollout of Subcutaneous MPA (Subcutaneous-MPA) under the Antara program was also started in Mysore 
and Yadgir districts in October 2023. The service has been extended to ten more districts:  Kolar, Haveri, 
Chikkaballapura, Chikkamagaluru, Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA), Tumakuru, Chitradurga, Dakshina 
Kannada, Raichur and Bengaluru urban.
A total of 7501 implants insertions and 9324 doses of Subcutaneous-MPA have been given from October 2023 
till December 2025. 
11.1.4   Major Health Sector related initiatives
a) National Health Mission
The NHM seeks to provide Accessible Affordable and Quality Health Care to the rural population especially 
the vulnerable sections. 11 programs are RMNCH+A including immunization, National Vector Borne Disease 
Control Programme (NVBDCP), Revised National Tuberculosis Control Programme (RNTCP), National Leprosy 
Eradication Programme (NLEP), National Programme for Control of Blindness (NPCB), Integrated Disease 
Surveillance Project (IDSP), Additional Services under National Health Mission, Programme of Pulse Polio, 
Mission Indradhanush, Health Education Training, Preventive of Deafness and other Programs, Strengthening 
of public health facilities by providing new constructions, additional alteration and renovation are implemented 
under National Health Mission.

c) National Tuberculosis  Elimination Programme (NTEP)
National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme has been implemented under the National Health Mission 
(NHM) with the aim to declare a TB-free India by 2025. (The World Health Organization target of 2030). 
1464 out of 5690 Panchayats in Karnataka are declared as TB Free Gram Panchayats. 74616 TB patients were 
notified from January 2025 to December 2025 against the target of 80000, which is 93% of the target. TB 
patient cohort recorded a mortality rate of 6% and a treatment success rate of 88% of 2024.
d) National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP)
The State Prevalence of Leprosy rate which was 40 per 10,000 population in 1986 has been decreased to 
0.40/10000 in 2015-16 and further dropped to 0.30/10000 in December 2024. Currently, leprosy is prevailing 
in 6 districts namely Ballari, Gadag, Koppal, Uttara Kannada, Yadgiri & Vijayanagara. The prevalence rate in 
these districts is 0.50 to 1 per 10000 population as on December 2025. Currently 2158 Leprosy cases are 
under treatment in the State. The Leprosy prevalence rate from 2015-16 to 2024-25 (upto December 2025) 
is depicted in the Figure 11.2.

e) National Programme for Control of Blindness
National Program for Control of Blindness was launched in 1976 with the goal to reduce the prevalence of 
blindness from 1.4% (1974) to 0.3% by the year 2020 by developing eye care infrastructure human resources, 
improving accessibility quality of eye care services. As per the survey of 2007, level of prevalence of blindness 
has come down to 1.0%. The present prevalence rate of blindness is 0.36 % as per National Survey 2015-19. 
The present prevalence rate of blindness is 1.61 in Karnataka as per National Rapid Assessment of Blindness 
Survey (2015-2019) carried out by NPCB & VI, GOI. The current strategy is to reduce prevalence of Blindness 
to 0.25% by 2025.
48 Eye Banks registered under the Human Organs Transplantation Act are functioning in Karnataka including 
8 Government eye hospitals (Minto Eye Hospital, SIMS Shivamogga, MIMS Mandya, VIMS Ballari, KR Hospital 
Mysuru, BIMS Belagavi, HIMS Hassan, KIMS Hubballi Dharwad). As per the policy of Govt. of India under 
NPCB, eye bank infrastructure is also improved to increase cornea collection and Keratoplasty. Incentives are 
also given to all the eye banks registered under HOTA for collecting eye balls in order to increase the cornea 
collection.
25 Districts (Tumakuru, Belagavi, Kolar, Bengaluru Rural, Hassan, Udupi, Bengaluru Urban, Bidar, Ballary, 
Uttarkannada, Dakshina Kannada, Chamarajanagar, Chikkamagaluru, Haveri, Koppal, Kalaburgi, Dharwad, 
Davanagere, Mysuru, Gadag, Bagalkot, Mandya, Shivamogga, Vijayapura, Yadgiri) are strengthened with 
mobile ophthalmic units including van to reach the underserved and unreached. 
Vision Centers are established in Govt. Sector at PHC level to improve eye care infrastructure so as to provide 
quality eye care services to rural patients. 501 Vision Centres have been opened till now. 
Ashakirana: In its third phase, the Ashakirana Program has undergone a major implementation redesign 
to ensure sustainable and permanent eye care access. Total 393 Vision Centers have been established 
across all District Hospitals (DHs), Medical College Hospitals, Taluk Hospitals (THs) and Community Health 
Centers (CHCs), allowing walk-in access for free eye check-ups & spectacles distribution (for eligible) by para 
medical ophthalmic officer.  Field workers including ASHAs and Community Health Officers (CHOs) continue 
preliminary screening during routine house-to-house visits and refer individuals with suspected eye issues to 
nearest Ashakirana Drusti Kendras.
As per the district physical reports Eye-examination is being conducted in vision centres and free spectacles 
have been distributed to 2,91,400 beneficiaries and 375958 cataract surgeries have been conducted                         
(till December 2025) (in Govt facilities-52,620 and Private Hospitals-323338).

11.1.7 National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme (NIDDCP)
National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme (NIDDCP) is implemented in the State to create 
awareness about usage of Iodized salt in daily diet to prevent Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDD) like Cretinism, 
Deaf autism, Dumbness, Physical and Mental Retardation, Goiter, etc. During 2025-26 an amount of Rs.59.75 
lakhs has been released of which Rs.10.49 lakhs expenditure incurred (upto December 2025) under this 
programme.
11.1.8. National Urban Health Mission
National Urban Health Mission aims to improve the health status of the urban poor particularly the slum 
dwellers and other staged sections by facilitating equitable access to quality health care through a revamped 
public health system partnership and with the active involvement of the urban local bodies.
 Y The Urban Health and Wellness Centres (Namma Clinics)
With the objective of delivering comprehensive primary health care services to the urban poor and vulnerable 
population, 365 Urban Primary Health Centres (UPHCs) are functioning under the National Urban Health 
Mission (NUHM) at the norm of one centre per 50,000 urban populations. Further, with financial support 
from the 15th Finance Commission and the PM-ABHIM scheme, a total of 817 Urban Health and Wellness 
Centres (UHWCs), known as Namma Clinics, have been approved across urban areas of the State at the 
norm of one centre per 15,000–20,000 population. Of these, 232 centres are located within the Greater 
Bengaluru Authority jurisdiction and 514 in the remaining districts, with a total of 746 Urban Health and 
Wellness Centres (Namma Clinics) currently operational. Remaining 71 Namma Clinics are planned to be 
operationalized by March 2026. During 2025-26 an amount of Rs. 10050.29 lakhs expenditure has been 
incurred (Upto December 2025) as against total budget of Rs.34462.98 lakhs allocated.

484
Human Development
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
 Y Ayushman Arogya Kendra
As a part of the National Health Policy 2017, Ministry of Health & Family Welfare has envisaged provision 
of Comprehensive Primary Health Care services, by integrating components of preventive, promotive and 
rehabilitative healthcare along with basic curative services. This is in line with the needs as per the changing 
disease burden across the country. The paradigm shift from selective primary health care to comprehensive 
approach is the backbone of AAKs.
The goal of Universal Health Coverage is to ensure that all people obtain the health services they need: 
preventive, promotive, curative, rehabilitative and palliative without the risk of financial hardship. Department 
of Health and Family Welfare is committed to the vision of accomplishing UHC, also outlined in National 
Health Mission framework as- “Enabling Universal Healthcare Access to Equitable, Affordable and Quality 
health care services, Accountable and Responsive to people’s needs. As on December 2025, 9058 health & 
wellness centres are upgraded of which 6532 are Rural Sub Centres, 2161 are rural PHCs and 365 are Urban 
Primary Health Centres.
11.1.9.  HMIS & RCH in Karnataka
a) HMIS (Health Management Information System)
HMIS is to collect the information uniformly and timely from all the states the Government of India has 
prescribed HMIS formats throughout the country. At present around 15,050 health facilities are reporting in 
HMIS portal in Karnataka. District Level Action Plans / PIP formulation and monitoring the progress through 
Star rating of facilities by using Human Resources, Infrastructure data, equipment availability and service 
utilization are being done based on HMIS data. State Health Index (Ranking of States) by NITI Aayog and 
District hospitals ranking Indicators data is taken from HMIS portal.
b) RCH Portal (Reproductive and Child Health)
This software is a web based centralized software which is used to monitor all the services provided to the 
eligible couple, pregnant woman and child.  Application facilitates to ensure timely delivery of full component 
of antenatal postnatal & delivery services and tracking of children for complete immunization services. During 
the year 2025-26 (up to December 2025) 783901 of pregnant women and 694536 of children registered. 
Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA) number is a 14digit number to identify a person and update their 
health records across multiple health service providers. 805825 RCH ID linked with ABHA ID in Karnataka, 
which stands second among the state in India.
ANMOL : ANMOL is TAB based version of RCH portal. This application will act as a job aid tool to the Jr.HAF 
by providing them with readily available information such as due list dashboard and guidance based on 
data entered etc. Videos/audios on subjects like high-risk pregnancy immunization, family planning etc. are 
also available in the application for counselling to beneficiary. ANMOL application works offline as well and 
can also be synchronize with RCH web portal automatically when connected with internet and also on user 
request. This will ensure more prompt entry and updating of data as well as improve the data quality since 
the data will be entered “at source” (by providers of health services themselves).
c) Kilkari
Kilkari is a national mobile-based audio messaging service of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare 
(MoHFW) designed to deliver stage-based information on reproductive, maternal, newborn, child health, 
immunization, and family planning directly to beneficiaries based on the entries on RCH portal. Upon feedback 
from MoHFW, the earlier 72-message version of Kilkari has been rationalized to a concise 18-message format 

PDF_PAGE 493

to improve effectiveness, recall, and engagement. Kilkari messages begin from the 4th month of pregnancy 
and continue until the child completes one year of age. Kilkari 2.0 was initiated from November 2025 and is

d) Nutrition Rehabilitation Centres (NRCs) in Karnataka
Nutrition Rehabilitation Centers refers to a unit for ‘inpatient, center based’ care of children with severe 
malnutrition (SAM) are usually treated either in facility/hospital based care units without medical 
complications. Currently, there are 119 Nutrition Rehabilitation Centres are functioning in the State.  
Karnataka has a high burden of under nutrition, with 35.4 percent (NFHS-5) of children are stunted, 19.5 
percent are wasted and 32.9 percent are underweight. Similarly, 47.8 percent of women and 65.5 percent 
of children (6 months to 59 months) are suffering from Anaemia in the state. The incidence is high in North 
Karnataka and in the Kalyana Karnataka Region. Targeting adolescent girls and women with anemia and child 
with malnutrition will help to reach to the root cause and providing treatment in Nutrition Rehabilitation 
Centres.

11.1.13 Causes of Death
The major causes of infant deaths are due to prematurity or low birth weight, in addition to this Pneumonia, 
heart disease and birth asphyxia. During 2025-26 (up to December 2025) out of 4709 infant deaths, number 
of the deaths occurred due to various diseases are Pneumonia 204, Diarrhea 12, Neonatal infections (Sepsis) 
(0-1 month) 872 Birth asphyxia 724 Prematurity 814, Fever related 18, Measles 1 and the remaining 2064 
deaths were due to other causes. 
Hypertensive disorders in pregnancy (Includes eclampsia, pre-eclampsia, hypertension) and Hemorrhage are 
the leading causes of death among females in the age group of 15-49 years. The total maternal deaths occurred 
in 2025-26 (up to December 2025) were 430 of which death due to Hypertensive disorders in pregnancy 
143, Post-Partum Hemorrhage 123, Abortion 3, Sepsis 42, Cardiac related 19, Infections 17, Amniotic fluid 
embolism 17, Pulmonary embolism 16, Endotoxins related 18, Multi Organ dysfunction Syndrome 6, and 
other causes including high fever are 26.
11.1.14 NCD- Non Communicable Disease
a) ST-Elevation Myocardial Infraction (STEMI)
The ST-Elevated Myocardial Infraction (STEMI) program has been implemented in 31 districts through Hub & 
Spoke model to manage cardiac emergencies caused by Non-communicable diseases. Under this program, 
from March 2023 to 31st December 2025, a total of 10,75,535 ECGs were done, 16,161 acute heart attack 
patients were identified and 9,202 patients were provided with successful treatment.
Under the Dr. Puneeth Rajkumar Hrudaya Jyothi Scheme, the highly effective injection Tenecteplase is being 
administered at Spoke hospitals. So far, this life-saving injection has been given to 1,340 patients suffering 
from myocardial infraction.
b) Day Care Chemotherapy Care Center
The Day Care Chemotherapy Care Center programme has been implemented in 16 district hospitals since 
May 2025. From June 2025 to December 2025, a total of 373 cancer patients received 1,606 advanced 
chemotherapy sessions under this initiative.
c) Gruha Arogya Yojane 
Under the scheme, screening for a total of 14 non-communicable diseases, including hypertension and 
diabetes, is being carried out at Ayushman Health Centers. Free drugs are being provided to diagnosed cases 
based on the recommendations of doctors.

11.1.17 National Quality Assurance Programme (NQAP)
Quality Assurance division under National Health Mission is enable for maintenance of quality related aspects 
of all the public health care facilities in the state. Quality Assurance Programs under NHM, Government of 
Karnataka implementation started in 2015-16. Quality Assurance Programs are,1)National Quality Assurance 
Standards (NQAS), Kayakalpa, Mera Aspataal (MA), Patient Safety , Infection Prevention & Control (IPC) and    
MusQan.
National Quality Assurance Standards (NQAS) envisage to instill the culture of quality and Safety in our health 
systems. It includes development of standards and tools which are pro public health, flexible, evidence based, 
current as per professional knowledge, explicit, user friendly and have a uniform measurement system.
5111 Public Health Facilities is the target set by QI NHSRC  to Karnataka for National Certification for  
2025-26. Until December 2025, NQAS State certified is 2743 and 706 are NQAS National Certified, total 3449 
PHFs NQAS Certified.
Kayakalp program in public health facilities as a major mechanism of social protection to meet the health 
care needs of large segments of the population. Cleanliness and hygiene in hospitals are critical to preventing 
infections and also provide patients and visitors with a positive experience and encourages moulding behavior 
related to clean environment. “Kayakalp”-an initiative for awards to public health facilities.  
“Mera Aspataal” is a simple, intuitive, and multi-lingual application that captures patient feedback in a very 
short time on the services received from the health facilities.  It works through multiple communication 
channels, including Short Message Service (SMS), Outbound Dialing (OBD), a mobile application, and a web 
portal. 
The application allows feedback to be consolidated, analyses and disseminated on a frequently updated 
dashboard. Analyses data is used to improve quality of services in healthcare facilities. Thus, the Mera 
Aspataal allows patients to connect with the healthcare providers and policymakers and to have their opinion 
heard and acted upon.
Presently Total 526 (57 District Hospital, 149 Taluk Hospital 16 Community Health Centre, 225 Primary 
Healh centre  and 79 Urban Primary Health centre ) Health Care Facilities are integrated with Mera Aspataal 
Application. 
MusQan aims to ensure provision of quality child-friendly services in public health facilities to reduce 
preventable newborn and child morbidity and mortality. A total of 25 DHs are MusQan National Certified and 
additional 21 Facilities are State certified in the State.

testing for HIV at designated sentinel sites typology wise and ANC HSS was conducted biennial (once in two 
years). HIV prevalence among ANC attendees indicates decline in adult HIV prevalence in the state from 1.5% 
in 2004 to 0.57% in 2022-23.

11.1.19 Drugs Control & Food Safety
By exercising strict control and vigilance on the drugs marketed in the State, the Department eradicates the 
menace of Spurious and substandard drugs, ensures safety of drugs and their availability at the controlled 
prices to the public. The Department is providing 26 services under the Karnataka Sakala Services Act 2011 
and (Amendment) Act, 2014. Among these 26 services, 16 services are providing under Seva Sindhu 2.0.  
With migration of online services to the ONDLS Portal, licenses to blood banks are issued entirely online. The 
department has also developed its online portal to issue RMI Certificates for the use of essential narcotic 
drugs in Recognized Medical Institutions. Following issuance of a revised Government Order, RMI Certificates 
have increased from 30 earlier to 320 hospitals currently providing palliative care. For the financial year 2025-
26, an amount of Rs.7282.31 lakhs has been released of which expenditure incurred up to December 2025 is 
Rs. 4457.95 lakhs.
Food Safety
The Food Safety Wing and Drug Administration Department is functioning to ensure that the citizens of the State 
receive good quality and healthy food. Further, it is mandatory for food business operators in the State (such 
as hotels, restaurants, manufacturing units, storage units, cold storage units, street food vendors, meat shops, 
distribution units, etc.) to obtain food registration/license. The Food Safety Wing is making continuous efforts 
to bring all such establishments under the food registration/licensing system to prevent food adulteration 
in the State, during the financial year, the Food Safety Wing and Drug Administration Department collected 
9,876 statutory food samples and subjected them to analysis. Out of these, 147 samples were reported as 
unsafe and 187 as substandard, and appropriate action has been taken against the concerned parties under 
the provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act.
11.1.20 Karnataka State Medical Supplies Corporation Limited
The main objective of Karnataka State Medical Supplies Corporation limited is to cater to the needs of 
Health Institutions of the State by Procuring Drugs, Equipment, Consumables and management of supply 
chain.  Essential need based drugs are provided to 2889 Health Institutions in the State. During 2025-26 the 
Expenditure incurred for Drugs & equipments is Rs.41750.56 lakhs (upto January 2026).

11.1.22  Blood Safety
Blood Transfusion Service (BTS) is an essential part of modern health care system. Appropriate Standardized 
measures to ensure adequate and safe blood play a major role in preventing the transmission of HIV, Hepatitis 
B, C and other emerging blood borne pathogens which are consistent threat in health care settings. The blood 
and its Components should not only be safe but also be of consistent quality to be clinically effective.
State Blood Council was established in Karnataka during 1996-97 to provide adequate and safe blood and 
blood products at reasonable rates. At present there are 266 registered blood centre in Karnataka of which 
66 are supported by DGHS. Out of 266 blood centre, 45 are in Governments Sectors (State Govt. - 41, Central 
Govt.- 4), IRCS blood centres are - 11, and 210 are in private sector.
11.1.23 National Tobacco Control Program (NTCP)
National Tobacco Control Program is being implemented in all the districts of the state. The Cigarettes and 
Other Tobacco Products Act -2003(COTPA) amendment at the state level, increase in fines for public for 
tobacco use from Rs.200 to up to Rs.1000 raising the legal age for purchasing tobacco products from 18 to 
21 years. Ban on hookah bars, tobacco sales within 100 meters of any educational institutions. A state-level 
notification has been issued banning the sale of all types of hookahs and the operation of hookah bars in 
public places. 185 villages have been declared as “tobacco-free” by the Gram Sabhas.
11.1.24 National Programme for Prevention and Control of Fluorosis (NPPCF)
Fluorosis, a public health problem is caused by excess intake of fluoride through drinking water/food products/
industrial emission over a long period. It results in major health disorders like dental fluorosis, skeletal 
fluorosis and non-skeletal fluorosis. The NPPCF programme has been implemented in 20 districts of Karnataka 
(Bagalkot, Bengaluru Rural, Bengaluru Urban, Ballari, Vijayanagar, Chikkaballapur, Chitradurga, Davanagere, 
Gadag, Hassan, Kalaburagi, Kolar, Koppal, Mandya, Mysuru, Raichur, Bengaluru South, Shivamogga, Tumakuru, 
and Vijayapura). Fluorosis district laboratories have been established and are functioning in all 20 districts.
11.1.25 National Oral Health Programme 
The National Oral Health Program was launched by the Government of India to improve oral health disparities 
across states. During 2025-26 (Upto December 2025) an amount of Rs. 259.43 lakhs expenditure has been 
incurred as against total budget of Rs.299.70 lakhs allocated. Under Danta Bhagya Yojana 41218 Dentures 
have been distributed .
11.1.26 Community Monitoring
Under National Health Mission untied funds are provided to take up necessary civil works and patient friendly 
amenities. Each District Hospital, Taluk Hospital, Community Health Centre and Primary Health Centre is 
allotted an untied fund of Rs.10.00 lakhs, Rs.5.00 lakhs and Rs.1.75 lakhs respectively every year. Grants to 
health institutions are released in accordance with the health centre’s performance based on number of In-
Patients, and Out-Patients, laboratory tests and Surgical interventions done.

11.1.27 Asha Programme
The ASHA is an Accredited Social Health Activist and selected by the community, who is trained and supported 
to function in her village/area to improve the health status of the community through securing people’s 
access to health care services and improved health care practices and behaviors. In Rural areas there is one 
ASHA per 1000 population and in urban area there is one ASHA per 2500 population. 
11.2 EDUCATION  
In recent years there is an unimaginable advancement in the field of knowledge and social and national 
aspirations of the people all over the world.  This changes in the field of education have become indispensable 
for the better. It is the responsibility of education to nurture the all-round development of an individual’s 
personality, thus help him/her become an active member of a knowledge society and a productive citizen of 
this country. There are significant developments in all fields of education. Education is having both intrinsic 
and instrumental value and provides useful services for the development of nation and enrichment of an 
individual’s life.
The positive externalities of education make it a public good, and therefore it needs to be supplied by the 
State as markets cannot provide it to the socially optimal levels. The human development paradigm recognizes 
the role of education in the expansion of choices for wellbeing, security and comfort. Therefore, the right to 
education is recognized as one of the fundamental human rights and, the drive towards universal elementary 
education aims at ensuring its delivery. Karnataka State is a fast growing economy and this growth is largely 
based on the knowledge base of the society. The State has embarked on significant reforms in the education 
sector with increased public investment to ensure access, equity and quality in education, with community 
involvement.
11.2.1 Literacy in Karnataka 
A review of growth of literacy during the 2001–2011 decade shows that Karnataka has achieved significant 
progress. The literacy rate in the State during 2001 was 66.64 per cent, which increased to 75.36 per cent in 
2011 (Table 11.8).

increase in literacy rate in the State during this decade is 9 %.

11.2.3 Elementary Education 
Article 21 A of the Constitution of India talk about Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Elementary 
Education. Right to Education Act, 2009 became operative in April 2010. The State Rules under the RTE Act 
were notified in 2011. These developments have thrown open fresh opportunities for quality schooling for 
children. 
a) Access: There has been significant progress in improving access to schools in the State. The State has 
the policy to start a new primary school within one kilometer in habitations where the population is 
more than 100 and child population is more than 10. HPS is provided within 3 Kilometer radius and 
High Schools in 5 Kilometer radius. Feeder schools or transportation facilities are provided in small and 
sparsely populated habitations. All habitations with a population of 100 and above now have access to a 
primary school within a distance of one kilometer. HPS are being upgraded to include class 8, wherever 
there are no High Schools within 3 Kilometers. A total of 519 HPS has been upgraded so far.
b) Number of Schools:  As of 2025-26, there are a total of 51383 primary schools in the state. Out of which, 
21864 are lower primary schools, 29519 are upper primary schools and 19009 are high schools. There 
are a total of 70392 schools in the state.

(d) Out of School Children – Mainstreaming Strategy
As per the Right to Education Act, 2009, no child should be left out of school. It is mandatory for the appropriate 
government to provide at least 08 years of formal education. To implement this objective Government of  
Karnataka has adopted the policy that if any child is absent from school for seven consecutive days without 
proper reasons and  prior permission from the school, such children are considered as potential “Out of 
School Children”. Therefore, teachers should pay attention to this and ensure that the children do not remain 
absent. According to preventive protocols of RTE act 6 A, B, C and D Poverty alone is not the reason for 
children to be out of school. Other social deprivation factors are also included in this, migrant children, SC/ST 
children orphan and other deprived children. The objectives are:
 Y To provide minimum 8 years of schooling as it is compulsory for all the children of age from 6 to 14 years. 
 Y To enable children to receive education equally, irrespective of the caste, creed and sex. 
 Y To ensure that no child is remaining out of school. 
 Y To conduct comprehensive survey of household and school survey every year to identify children who 
are out of school. 
 Y To conduct updation survey every year to verify the current year and previous year admissions from the 
school records to identify the dropout.

494
Human Development
Karnataka Economic Survey 2025-26
(e) Steps taken to ensure continuation of mainstreamed children in regular schools
 Y School dropout period for out of school children is considered to be 7 days instead of 60 days.
 Y To prevent absenteeism of children and to attend schools regularly Education Coordinators (ECOs) is 
appointed as Attendance Authority.  In case absenteeism is more than 7 days, ECO is supposed to visit 
the students’ family to persuade the parents to bring their children to schools and this method is being

a) Infrastructure 
Provision of infrastructure facilities and adequate classrooms is the basic strategy for quality schooling. In 
addition, every school is given School Grant and Maintenance Grant. They are directly transferred from the 
district educational office to individual schools and jointly operated by the President of the School Development 
and Monitoring Committee (SDMC) and the Head Teacher. The School Grant is used for procurement of charts, 
maps, specimens, newspapers, consumable chemicals, chalk and other sundry items. Maintenance Grant is 
used for paying electricity, water bills, white-washing, hygienic maintenance of school and similar heads. 
Major repairs grants are given on the basis of evidence-based demands.

Dharwad (Gantikeri), Dakshina Kannada (Belthangady), Mysore (Nazarabad) and Shimoga (Agumbe). Later in 
the year 2023-24 another Residential School at Banglore south-2 (Sulthan Pet) was sanctioned. The intake 
capacity of each school is 100 children (boys and girls) from classes 6th to 8th.

d) Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya (KGBV TYPE-1, 3 and 4)
The establishment of Kasturba Gandhi BalikaVidyalaya (KGBV) by the Central Government in 2004 was a 
special program implemented by Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan to encourage girls’ education.  The criteria for starting 
KGBV schools, based on the 2001 census, is establishment in educationally backward blocks with lower than 
the national rural female literacy rate (46.13%) and higher than the national gender disparity rate (21.59). 
The objective of the program is to reduce the gender disparity gap and promote gender equality in relation to 
girls’ primary school education. The details of KGBV Residential Schools and hostels are given in Table 11.11.

growth.

National Skills Qualifications Framework (NSQF)
The National Skills Qualifications Framework (NSQF) is an ambitious initiative launched by the Ministry of 
Human Resource Development (MHRD), Government of India.
1. The primary objective of this scheme is to integrate vocational education with general education and 
provide students with employment-oriented skill training. It is a progressive reform that aims to bridge 
the gap between the education system and the employment market, paving the way towards the goal of 
“Education to Employment.”
2.  The students of 9th and 10th std who have opted vocational subject under NSQF are exempted in studying 
3rd Language and the students of 11th and 12th std opted vocational subject under NSQF are exempted 
from in studying either one of the languages.
3.  “Sh ikshana Kirana”, the Students Achievement Tracking System that tracks every child enrolled in school, 
by unique identity and name, regularity, academic performance, promotions, transfers, identify drop 
outs etc., has captured student specific data of about 1 crore students studying in all schools of the 
state. The system is designed for online monitoring of the performance of students, teachers and school 
managements. This system could already digitize the records of more than 1 crore students, 4,28,147 
teachers and 70,392 schools in the whole state including private aided and unaided schools. Aadhaar, 
income certificate and caste certificate information of the child is linked with the student detail in SATS. 
Opportunity in given to the school HM’s to verify the nominal roll, admission ticket through their school 
login ID. It is made mandatory to take the indent for the text books only through SATS.

With the objective of providing theoretical and practical activities to high school and pre-university students

11.2.6 Department of State Educational Research and Training (DSERT)
The Department of State Educational Research and Training, (DSERT) is the academic wing of the Department 
of School education and Literacy. It aims at providing academic leadership in school education as well as 
improving the quality of education in primary and secondary schools in the state. It also aims to achieve 100% 
literacy through mass education programme.
Objectives 
 Y Improving the quality of education in primary and secondary schools in the state.
 Y Monitoring Pre-service and In-service teacher Education (Elementary and Secondary).
 Y Management of Government Colleges of teacher education: District Institutes of Education and           
Training and other Government teacher training institutions.
 Y Promoting Science Education in the State. 
 Y Designing and implementing in service teacher training courses in content, pedagogy, innovative methods 
like theatre in education, use of low cost and no cost teaching learning  materials in schools, etc. 
 Y Organizing Satellite based training programmes. 
 Y Enhancing the teaching skills of Primary and Secondary School teachers, as per identified needs.
 Y Improving the educational quality of Teacher Training Institutes. 
 Y Providing vocational skills through organizing music, Drawing, Dance, Drama, and other activities under 
art research center of DSERT.
 Y Promoting use of technology in education.

Since teachers play a major role in improving the quality of education, teacher training is considered as highly

1.  In- service teacher trainings:  In the year 2025–26, a 10-day residential training program has been organis 
at IISc., Bengaluru to in service teachers. 
2.  Ganit a ganaka:  In the year 2025–26, the Ganita Ganaka Program has been extended to enable students 
of Grades 3 to 5 in all government schools of the state to learn basic mathematical operations through 
the telephone after school hours.  Phone tutoring is also being implemented in 69 taluks of 17 districts, 
and in all the remaining districts, teachers are being provided training for the Ganita Ganaka Program.
3.  Marusinch ana:  In the year 2025–26, based on the SSLC results of the state, a Marusinchana Program 
is being implemented for kannada medium students of Grades 6 to 10 in all government schools of 27 
educational districts, excluding Dakshina Kannada, Uttara Kannada, Sirsi, Udupi, Shivamogga, Hassan, 
Chikkamagaluru, and Kodagu.  MRP trainings at the state and district levels have been completed, and 
Marusinchana training is currently being provided to teachers at the district level.
4.  Odu Karnataka: Under the Odu Karnataka scheme, a program has been designed to develop foundational 
literacy and numeracy skills among students of Grades 4 and 5. Training has been provided to MRPs at 
the state and district levels. Teacher training at the district level is in progress.  This is a 60-days program, 
during which trained teachers conduct daily Mathematics and Language activities for 120 minutes (1 
hour for Language and 1 hour for Mathematics). 
5.  Ganit a Kalika Andolana:  The Ganitha Kalika Andolana (GKA) program is a mathematics support initiative 
developed by Akshara Foundation to strengthen mathematics learning in primary classes. The goal of this 
program is to enhance the mathematical skills of students from Grades 1 to 5, and now also Grades 6, 7, 
and 8, as well as to improve teacher’s ability to use.
6.  T eaching–Learning Materials (TLMs) effectively : For the year 2025–26, it has been decided to provide 
a 2-day MRP training in the 3 divisions of the state Kalaburagi, Belagavi, and Mysuru through Akshara 
Foundation. This training is meant for quality-support officials regarding the purpose, importance and 
implementation of the GKA (Ganitha Kalika Andolana) 2.0 Kit related to Classes 6, 7, and 8.
7.  Bridg e Course programme 2025-26: The basic objective of Bridge Course programme is to identify the 
learning level and abilities of children according to their age and class, and prepare them for further 
learning; to create a connection between the concepts learned and those being learned. In this regard, 
in the year 2024-25, Bridge Course literature for classes 1 to 10, including the desired learning outcomes 
of the previous class and the respective class, has been prepared and uploaded on the DSERT Website, 
a circular regarding implementation has been issued and guidance and follow-up is being done through 
DIETs.
8.  Sambhr ama Shanivara 2025-26:  ‘Sambhrama Shanivara’ is a program to celebrate Bag-less Day on the 
third Saturday of every month with the aim of reducing the burden of bags and instilling civic consciousness 
in children through co-curricular activities and developing professional skills. In this regard, 10 modules 
and a teacher’s guide manual have been prepared to celebrate 10 days of Bag-less Day in a year. These 
have been uploaded on the DSERT Website and a Circular has been issued regarding implementation. 
This is being followed through the DIET and is reviewed in the progress review meetings of the nodal 
officers and principals.

11.2.7 Karnataka School Examination and Assessment Board
Karnataka Secondary Education Examination Board came into existence in the year 1966 and got renamed as 
KARNATAKA SCHOOL EXAMINATION AND ASSESSMENT BOARD in the year 2022.It conducts examinations for 
class 10th and 12th of affiliated Schools and Junior Colleges. Examinations related to Karnataka Open School, 
Diploma in Education, Music, Commerce, etc are also conducted by the Board.   Every year, approximately 
8.5 lakh students appear for the 10th-grade (SSLC) examinations conducted by the Board during March/April. 
For students who fail and wish to reattempt, a marks improvement system has been introduced, under which 
three examinations are conducted. Similar examination procedures are followed for the 12th-grade as well.  
Various steps have been initiated from the year 2017-18 to digitalize the whole examination process. 
Registration for the examination has become online and the same method is followed for downloading of 
admission tickets and the results. The Board has done away with the usage of OMRs for the purpose of 
communication of marks from evaluation centres and is instead, using online portal for the purpose. This 
has not only saved the time but also avoided possible wrong scanning in case of faulty shadings in OMRs.  
Results are conveyed to the students through SMS and web portal. Online services like issuing of Migration 
Certificate, Marks card Verification and Second/Third/ Fourth copy of marks card/Failed marks card of previous 
years, Photocopy, Retotalling & Revaluation of answer scripts are made available under Pragathi-10 program.  
Students can also download the marks card using digi-Locker app.
During 2024-25 an amount of Rs. 95.33 crores was incurred as expenditure for the SSLC and other examinatios. 
For the year 2025-26 of an amount of Rs. 104.42 crores has been provided in budget estimate for 2025-26, 
of which as at the end of 16.1.2025 an amount of Rs. 81.09 crores is incurred as expenditure for the same.
SSLC results 2025: In 4 Educational Districts namely, Udupi, Dakshina Kannada, Hassan and Uttara Kannada 
out of total students appeared 90% of them passed the SSLC examination (regular), whereas in 5 educational 
districts namely, Madhugiri, Chitradurga, Yadgiri, Kalburgi and Bidar pass percentage was less than 75%. 
Districtwise details of SSLC results during 2024 and 2025 is furnished in Appendix 11.5.

11.2.9  Public Libr aries
Public Library is an institution established by the Government in order to inculcate interest in education, 
communication and reading among the General Public.  It is an open public service system.  Under the act, 
a network of about 1,301 libraries have been functioning all over the State. “Public Libraries are people’s 
university” It is a democratic institution working on democratic principles.

District level and City Central Libraries at all places having a population of more than one lakh together with

11.2.10 Department of Printing, Stationery and Publications   
The Department of Printing, Stationery and Publications is basically established to cater to the Printing and 
Stationery requirements of the State Government offices namely Governor’s Office, Legislature, Government 
Secretariat, High Court, Other Govt. Departments. The print requirements and Stationery requirements of 
Government owned bodies are also taken care by the Department on chargeable basis. It is also engaged in 
selling of the Government Publications to General Public through a network of Book Depots. In addition to 
this, the Department has extended its technical assistance to the various other departments whose printing 
works, are being executed by the private printers. This Department also undertakes the Printing works and 
supply of Stationery to Government of India Departments namely Chief Electoral Office, Directorate of Census 
Operations, on chargeable basis. 
The Director is also Compiler of Karnataka Gazette which is being published regularly on every day and the 
Extraordinary Gazettes are being published through e-gazette in the web site www.gazette.kar.nic.in . This has 
resulted in saving of Paper and also printing and supply expenses to the Government offices.

11.2.11 Medical Education
In 2025-26, there are 72 Medical Colleges (MBBS degree) in the State which have a summated intake  
capacity of 13945 students, of which 24 colleges are run by the Government.  There are 46 dental colleges 
in the State which have summated intake capacity of 3405 students, of which 3 dental colleges are run by 
the Government.  682 Nursing colleges recognized by Indian Nursing Council turn out 44,420 Nurses (B.Sc. 
graduates) in 2025-26.
1) Post Graduate Institutions & Enrolments in the State
Medical Colleges are permitted to provide post Graduate Courses in the State. They offer Degree and 
Diploma Courses in various specialties. There are several Super-specialties of which training is imparted in 
subjects like Cardiology, Cardiothoracic Surgery, Cardiac Anesthesia, Neurology, Nephrology, Urology, Surgical 
Gastroenterology, Plastic Surgery, Medical Oncology and Surgical Oncology. There has been a great demand 
for specialists, due to which many Medical Graduate of the State who do not get Post Graduation seats enroll 
with the National Board of Examinations and qualify as Diplomat of the National Board (DNB).
 Enrollment Capacity across Medical Course for the Post Graduate Degree for the year 2025-26 is 7211 and PG 
Diploma is 10.  The details of total post graduate seats for 2025-26 in Government and Deemed Universities 
given in Appendix 11.7. 
For the year 2025–26, a total grant of Rs.4986.50 crore has been allocated to the Department of Medical 
Education. In this, Revenue Head Rs.4106.88 crore and Capital Head Rs.879.62 crores have been allocated 
respectively. By the end of December 2025, expenditures of Rs.2550.15 crore and Rs.473.17 crore has been 
done respectively.

11.2.12 Department of Technical Education
Technical Education all over the world is gaining importance day by day because of rapid advancement in 
science, technology and innovations.  The Department of Technical Education is playing a vital role to compete 
and to keep Karnataka ahead in industrial growth and in the field of Information Technology. There were only 
57 technical institutes under Department of Technical Education initially but now during 2025-26, there are 
a staggering 544 institutes across the state ranging from Diploma to Degree and Junior Technical Schools. 
For the year 2025-26, an amount of Rs. 1332.95 crores is provided of which Rs. 896.67 crores is incurred as 
expenditure up to December 2025. 62 Teaching staff have been deputed for M.E/M.Tech Higher education 
during 2025-26 as against 44 deputed in 2024-25. 865 staff of the Technical Education have been deputed to 
the 48 short term training programmes held at NITTR, Chennai during 2025-26.
1. Center for Continuing Technical Education, Karnataka (CCTEK):  The Centre For Continuing Technical 
Education was established as an autonomous centre in 2000. There are 66 sub-centres working in different 
Government Polytechnics and 16 sub-centres in Government Engineering colleges in the State. In these sub-
centres, the following programs are being held.
a) Pr oviding IT related courses to non-IT students.
b) T raining the teacher’s time-to time as per the requirement of the new curriculum.
c) Con ducting technical-know-how training to unskilled labourers in industries.
d) T raining programs to the teaching staff.
e) In ternal Revenue Generation by organizing various training programs and utilizing the same to strengthen 
the polytechnics.
During the year 79 programmes are organised in Centre for continuing Technical Education sub units and 
7609 beneficiaries are trained. 
2. Accreditation through National Board of Accreditation (NBA): The Department of Collegiate and Technical 
Education (DCTE) has Initiated the accreditation of technical institution by National Board of Accreditation 
New Delhi to improve the quality of teaching-learning process, self-evaluation, accountability, and fulfils the 
expectations of its stakeholder viz., academicians, industries, statutory regulators, students and parents. In 
this context, for the first phase, 40 Government Polytechnics and 04 Government Engineering Colleges have 
been identified for NBA accreditation. Government Polytechnic Ballary, CPC Government Polytechnic Mysore 
and Government Polytechnic Kalburgi have submitted the Self Assessment Report (SAR) to National Board of 
Accreditation new Delhi and awaiting the visit of NBA peer team to the above colleges in this academic year.

with a grant of Rs. 1.00 crore each.
 Y Facilities to Physically Challenged Students:Under the Centrally sponsored scheme 25 seats over and 
above the intake are being filled-up in three Govt. Polytechnics viz., GPT-Belagavi, Smt. L.V.GPT-Hassan 
and GWPT-Mangaluru. Apart from this, 3% of the total intake in all the Govt. and Pvt. Aided Polytechnics 
are reserved for the physically challenged students. Further, one Pvt. Aided Polytechnic named JSS 
Polytechnic for differently-abled in Mysuru has been setup exclusively for these students with all the 
required amenities.
 Y SDP/CGP and EAP programs: The Training programs are conducted for the students of Govt./Aided 
engineering colleges & polytechnics, to train them in life-leading, inspectional & developmental skills.

11.2.13 Collegiate Education
Department of Collegiate Education was established in the year 1960 and it oversees the administration of 
411 Government First Grade Colleges, 12 Government Residential First Grade Colleges, 02 Government Fine 
Arts colleges, 03 Government Sanskrit Colleges and 320 Private Aided Degree colleges, 53 Private Aided B.Ed 
colleges, 27 Private Aided Law colleges, 23 Private Aided Fine Arts colleges through  6 Regional Joint Directors’ 
Offices located at Bangalore, Mysore, Mangalore, Shimoga, Dharwad and Kalaburagi. 
1. Vision of the Department
 Y To achieve excellence in Higher Education.
 Y To create opportunities for people of all categories to pursue Higher Education at an affordable cost , 
while providing social justice.
 Y To empower women through Higher Education.
 Y  To enhance the employability of students by imparting skill training.
 Y To achieve holistic development of students and present good citizens to society.

The student enrolment to Science stream is lower in comparison with the total enrolment in Higher Education. 
Students who have studied Arts and Commerce in Pre-university classes naturally get admitted to Degree 
Courses. But students who have studied Science in Pre-university classes seek admission to Professional 
courses on priority and then to Degree Courses, as a result of which total enrolment in the Science stream is 
low.  
The total budget for Collegiate Education increased from Rs. 56415.59 Lakhs in 2013-14 to Rs. 327729.58 
Lakhs in 2025-26. The major share of the increase in the amount of budget allocation was towards creating 
additional infrastructure and facilities required for colleges.

3) Achievements-2025-26 (up to November 2025)
a)  P ermission to start New Courses: Recent Advances in Science and Technology have been at the 
root of the emergence of several new subjects, courses and branches of study in each discipline and 
pertinent requests were being made for several years by students and public alike to commence these in 
Government First Grade Colleges. This significant matter which remained undecided for the past 4 years 
was taken up seriously by the student-friendly State Government and granted permission to start 77 
new courses in 47 Government First Garde Colleges from the academic year 2023-24. Accordingly, these 
courses are being offered in these colleges from the present academic year.
b)  R ecruitment: The Karnataka Examinations Authority has conducted entrance examinations to fill 310 
principal posts out of the total 410 vacant principal posts in Government first grade colleges in the State. 
The recruitment process is in progress.
c)  NAA C Accreditation: To improve the quality of higher education, the Government has strengthened the 
Internal Quality Assurance Cells (IQACs) in 421 Government First Grade Colleges across the State with 
the objective of enhancing educational standards. Financial assistance is being provided to colleges for 
the purchase of essential equipment such as printers. In addition, special workshops and seminars are 
being organized to enable faculty members to function in accordance with NAAC accreditation standards. 
Further, to promote quality teaching, permission has been granted to invite expert resource persons and 
provide appropriate training to faculty members under Faculty Development Programs (FDPs).
d)  Car eer Advancement: A total of 73 Assistant Professors/Librarians/Directors of Physical Education of 
Government First Grade Colleges have been promoted from academic levels 10 to 11, 11 to 12, 12 to 13A.

13A to 14 to the post of Professor. A total of 245 Assistant Professors/Librarians/Directors of Physical 
Education of Private Aided Colleges have been promoted from academic levels 10 to 11, 11 to 12, 12 to 
12A.

Directors have been transferred since May 2023.
